xs: **Love** and **Rayleigh** waves are **surface waves** — option **(1)**.
They **move along the surface** and arrive **last**.
xa: ⚠ **Love** = side to side; **Rayleigh** = rolling, like ocean waves.
Surface (L) waves **cause most damage**.
**P** (1st) and **S** (2nd) waves travel through the Earth's interior.

10.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the movement and damaging potential of surface waves?
o: They move through the outer core and cause limited damage.
They arrive last and generally cause the greatest damage.
They arrive first and produce compressional motion only.
They travel only through liquids and have no particle motion.
10.x: Surface waves arrive after the body waves and usually cause the greatest damage. Love waves show side-to-side motion, while Rayleigh waves have a rolling motion.
10.tq: Compare arrival time, motion and damage rather than memorising one feature alone.
xs: Surface waves **arrive last** and **cause most damage** — option **(2)**.
They move **along the surface**, not through the core.
**P-waves** arrive **first** with compressional motion — option (3).
xa: Surface waves include **Love** (side to side) and **Rayleigh** (rolling).
**S-waves** arrive **2nd** and pass through **solids only**.
Shaking is **strongest at the epicentre**.

10.s: Which one of the following statements about P-waves (primary waves) is correct?
o: They are transverse waves that travel only through solids.
They arrive first and travel through solids, liquids and gases with push-pull motion.
They travel only along the Earth's surface and cause the most damage.
They are the slowest seismic waves and are stopped by the outer core.
10.x: P-waves are the fastest and arrive first; they are longitudinal (compressional, push-pull) and pass through solids, liquids and gases. Transverse waves confined to solids are S-waves; surface (L) waves travel along the surface, arrive last and cause most damage; it is S-waves that the liquid outer core stops.
10.tq: P = primary = push-pull = passes everything; S = shear = solids only.
xs: **P-waves** arrive **first** and travel through **solid, liquid, gas** with **push-pull** motion — option **(2)**.
They are **longitudinal/compressional**: back and forth along the direction of travel.
**S-waves** are transverse, solids only; **surface waves** cause most damage.
xa: S-waves are **stopped** by the liquid **outer core** — not P-waves.
**S-wave shadow**: no S-waves beyond about **105°**.
Surface waves are the **slowest** and arrive **last**.

10.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes the magnitude of an earthquake from its intensity?
o: Magnitude denotes observed damage at a place, whereas intensity denotes energy released at the focus
Magnitude varies from place to place, whereas intensity has one value for the entire earthquake
Magnitude denotes energy released at the focus, whereas intensity denotes the observed effects at a particular place
Both magnitude and intensity denote the energy released at the focus
10.x: Magnitude is the quantitative measure of energy released at the focus and has one value for an earthquake. Intensity is the qualitative measure of observed effects at a particular place and varies with distance from the epicentre.
10.tq: Split the options by matching each term with its defining measure.
xs: **Magnitude** = **energy released at the focus**; **intensity** = **observed effects at a place** — option **(3)**.
Magnitude has **one value per quake**; intensity **varies from place to place**.
Options (1) and (2) swap the two.
xa: Magnitude: **Richter scale**, now **Moment Magnitude (Mw)**.
Intensity: **Modified Mercalli (MMI)** and **MSK**, both **I to XII**.
APPSC **2025**: magnitude = energy at focus; intensity = effect at a place.

10.s:
With reference to earthquake measurement, consider the following statements:
1. The Richter scale was developed by Charles F. Richter in 1935.
2. The Richter scale is used to measure earthquake intensity.
3. Moment magnitude is based on the rupture area of the fault and the size of seismic waves.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
10.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. The Richter scale measures magnitude, not intensity; intensity is measured using scales such as Modified Mercalli and MSK.
10.tq: Use the magnitude–intensity distinction to reject the swapped measurement statement.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(3)**.
Statement 1 correct: **Charles F. Richter** devised the scale in **1935**.
Statement 2 wrong: the Richter scale measures **magnitude**, not intensity.
Statement 3 correct: **Mw** is based on **rupture area** of the fault + size of seismic waves.
xa: Mw has largely **replaced Richter** for strong quakes.
Intensity is measured on **MMI** and **MSK** scales.
⚠ APPSC **2022**: "Richter scale measures intensity" is wrong.

10.s: An earthquake increases from magnitude 5 to magnitude 6 on the Richter scale. Which one of the following best describes the change?
o: Its wave amplitude becomes 6 times and energy becomes 36 times
Its wave amplitude becomes 31 times and energy released becomes 10 times
Its wave amplitude becomes 10 times and energy released becomes approximately 31 times
Both its wave amplitude and energy released become 10 times
10.x: An increase of one magnitude unit on the Richter scale represents a tenfold increase in wave amplitude and an approximately 31-fold increase in energy released.
10.tq: Separate the amplitude factor from the energy factor instead of treating both as identical.
xs: One step up gives **10x amplitude** and about **31x energy** — option **(3)**.
The **Richter scale** is **logarithmic** and measures wave amplitude.
Option (2) swaps the two numbers; option (4) ignores the bigger energy jump.
xa: **Mw** (Moment Magnitude) is based on **rupture area** and has largely replaced Richter.
Richter devised the scale in **1935**.
Magnitude has **one value per quake**.

10.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the scales used for earthquake measurement is correct?
o: Modified Mercalli and MSK scales measure magnitude from I to XII
Moment magnitude is a qualitative scale based only on building damage
The Richter scale measures intensity from I to XII
Modified Mercalli and MSK scales measure intensity from I to XII
10.x: Modified Mercalli and MSK are qualitative intensity scales, each ranging from I to XII. Richter and moment magnitude are magnitude scales.
10.tq: Discriminate between quantitative magnitude scales and qualitative intensity scales.
xs: **Modified Mercalli** and **MSK** measure **intensity** from **I to XII** — option **(4)**.
MMI runs from **I (not felt)** to **XII (total destruction)**.
**Richter** and **Mw** measure **magnitude**, not intensity — options (1), (2), (3) wrong.
xa: Intensity is **qualitative** and **varies from place to place**.
Mw uses the **rupture area** of the fault.
Each Richter step = **10x amplitude**, ~**31x energy**.

10.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below.

List-I (Instrument)
a. Seismograph
b. Seismometer
c. Seismoscope
d. Tiltmeter

List-II (Function)
i. Sensor used in a seismograph
ii. Shows that a tremor occurred and records its time
iii. Records and measures earthquakes
iv. Measures ground tilt at faults and volcanoes
10.x: A seismograph records and measures earthquakes; a seismometer is its sensor; a seismoscope only indicates that a tremor occurred and its time; and a tiltmeter measures ground tilt.
10.tq: Start from the sure instrument–function pair and eliminate codes containing mismatches.
xs: **a-iii, b-i, c-ii, d-iv** — option **(1)**.
**Seismograph** records and measures earthquakes (APPSC **2025**); **seismometer** is its **sensor**.
**Seismoscope** only shows a tremor occurred and its **time**; **tiltmeter** measures **ground tilt**.
xa: **Creepmeter**: slow slip (**creep**) along a fault.
India's national network uses **broadband seismometers**.
⚠ Earthquakes **still cannot be predicted accurately** (APPSC **2022**).

10.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the function of a creepmeter?
o: It shows only the time at which a tremor occurred
It measures the tilt of volcanic ground
It measures the slow slip or creep along a fault
It records the energy released at the earthquake focus
10.x: A creepmeter is used to measure slow slip, or creep, along a fault. Ground tilt is measured by a tiltmeter, while a seismoscope only indicates occurrence and time of a tremor.
10.tq: Use confusable-instrument discrimination by matching each device with its specific function.
xs: A **creepmeter** measures **slow slip (creep) along a fault** — option **(3)**.
**Tiltmeter** = ground tilt (option 2); **seismoscope** = time of a tremor (option 1).
Energy at the focus is **magnitude**, read from a **seismograph**.
xa: **Seismometer** is the sensor of a seismograph.
**Seismograph** records and measures quakes (APPSC **2025**).
Mw is based on the fault's **rupture area**.

10.s: Which one of the following statements about earthquake prediction is correct?
o: Earthquakes are accurately predicted through the Richter scale
Earthquakes still cannot be predicted accurately
Earthquakes can be predicted accurately only in stable continental regions
Earthquakes can currently be predicted accurately for a precise time and place
10.x: Despite monitoring and seismological research, earthquakes cannot yet be predicted accurately in terms of their precise time, location and magnitude.
10.tq: Reject the extreme claim that a measurement scale can provide precise prediction.
xs: Earthquakes **still cannot be predicted accurately** — option **(2)** (APPSC **2022**).
The **Richter scale** only measures **magnitude** — it does not predict quakes.
xa: ⚠ "Richter scale measures intensity" is wrong — it measures **magnitude**.
Monitoring: **NCS** runs the **National Seismological Network** of **160 observatories**.
Public alerts: **IndiaQuake** app; MoES app **RISEQ**, now "**Bhookamp**".

10.s: Which one of the following belts is associated with the greatest concentration of earthquakes in the world?
10.x: The Circum-Pacific belt, also called the Ring of Fire, contains the world's greatest concentration of earthquakes and is associated largely with subduction around the Pacific basin.
10.tq: Use the ranking of earthquake belts to select the most active belt.
xs: The **Circum-Pacific belt (Ring of Fire)** has the most earthquakes — option **(3)**.
The **Mid-Continental (Alpine-Himalayan)** belt comes next.
**Mid-oceanic ridges** give **shallow, milder** quakes.
xa: The Ring of Fire is driven by **subduction** around the Pacific basin.
Examples: **Japan, Philippines, Indonesia, Chile, Andes, Alaska**.
**2026** Ring of Fire quakes: **Flores M 7.7**, **Colombia M 7.4**, **Kyushu M 7.1**.

10.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Belt)
a. Pacific Ring of Fire
b. Mid-Atlantic belt
c. Mediterranean-Himalayan belt
 d. Hotspot belt

List-II (Plate setting or process)
i. Mantle plume beneath a moving plate
 ii. Divergent ridge
 iii. Subduction around a basin
 iv. Continental collision

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
10.x: The Pacific Ring of Fire is linked to subduction, the Mid-Atlantic belt to a divergent ridge, the Mediterranean-Himalayan belt to continental collision, and hotspots to mantle plumes.
10.tq: Start with the sure plate-setting pair and eliminate codes containing a wrong association.
xs: **a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i** — option **(1)**.
**Ring of Fire** = **subduction**; **Mid-Atlantic** = **divergent** ridge.
**Mediterranean-Himalayan** = **continental collision**; **hotspots** = **mantle plume** under a moving plate.
xa: Hotspot examples: **Hawaii, Galapagos**, Reunion.
Mid-Atlantic example: **Iceland**.
Mediterranean-Himalayan: **Italy, Türkiye, Himalayas / India**.

10.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
10.x: Chile lies along the Pacific Ring of Fire, not the Mid-Atlantic belt. Iceland is associated with the Mid-Atlantic belt, the Himalayas with the Alpine-Himalayan belt, and Hawaii with a hotspot.
10.tq: Find the location that belongs to a different seismic belt.
xs: **Chile — Mid-Atlantic belt** is wrongly matched — option **(4)**.
**Chile** lies on the **Pacific Ring of Fire**.
**Hawaii** (hotspot), **Iceland** (Mid-Atlantic), **Himalayas** (Mediterranean-Himalayan) are correct.
xa: Ring of Fire also has **Japan, Philippines, Indonesia, Andes, Alaska**.
Mid-Atlantic belt is a **divergent** ridge.
Mid-oceanic ridges give **shallow, milder** quakes.

10.s: The earthquakes associated with mid-oceanic ridges are generally:
10.x: Mid-oceanic ridge earthquakes are generally shallow and milder, reflecting activity at divergent plate boundaries.
10.tq: Use the depth-and-severity comparison among the major earthquake belts.
xs: Mid-oceanic ridge quakes are **shallow, milder** — option **(4)**.
The ridges are **divergent** settings, not collision zones.
xa: Ranking: **Circum-Pacific** (most) → **Alpine-Himalayan** → **mid-oceanic ridges**.
**Mid-Atlantic belt** example: **Iceland**.
Tsunamis need a focus shallower than **~70 km** and **vertical seafloor uplift**.

10.s: The 1993 Latur earthquake was significant because it occurred in an intraplate region that had earlier been rated as which risk zone?
10.x: The Latur earthquake occurred in an intraplate region that was then classified as low-risk Zone I.
10.tq: Use the numerical-zone clue to distinguish a low-risk intraplate event.
xs: **Latur 1993** struck a zone then rated **Zone I** (low-risk) — option **(3)**.
It was an **intraplate** quake, **M 6.2**, **~10,000 dead**.
xa: After Latur, **IS 1893: 2002** merged **Zone I into Zone II** → four zones.
⚠ **Bhuj 2001** → **DM Act 2005**; **Latur 1993** → Zone I merged into Zone II.
Latur showed quakes strike **stable areas along hidden faults** (APPSC **2025**).

10.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
10.x: Bhuj (Kutch) struck on 26 January 2001 with M 7.7. The other pairs are wrong: Gorkha was 2015 (M 7.8), Tohoku was 2011 (M 9.0), and Uttarkashi was 1991 (M ~6.8).
10.tq: Start from the sure year–magnitude pair and eliminate swapped entries.
xs: **Bhuj — 26 Jan 2001 — M 7.7** is correct — option **(1)**.
**Gorkha** was **2015, M 7.8**; **Tohoku** was **2011, M 9.0** — options (2) and (3) swap them.
**Uttarkashi** was **1991, M ~6.8** — option (4) wrong.
xa: Bhuj (Kutch) killed **20,000+** and led to the **DM Act 2005** and **NDMA**.
**Myanmar (Mandalay)**: **2025**, **M 7.7**.

10.s: The Bhuj earthquake of 2001 led directly to which of the following institutional and legislative developments?
o: The enactment of the Disaster Management Act, 2005 and the establishment of the NDMA
The creation of the Tsunami Early Warning System and GSI
The establishment of the National Centre for Seismology and the RISEQ app
The introduction of Zone VI under IS 1893: 2016
10.x: The 2001 Bhuj earthquake contributed to the Disaster Management Act, 2005 and the establishment of the National Disaster Management Authority.
10.tq: Link a major disaster to the institutional response that followed it.
xs: **Bhuj 2001** led to the **Disaster Management Act, 2005** and the **NDMA** — option **(1)**.
The **Tsunami Early Warning System** came after the **2004 Sumatra quake** — option (2) wrong.
**Zone VI** was in the **2025** code, not 2016 — option (4) wrong.
xa: Bhuj: **26 Jan 2001**, **M 7.7**, **20,000+** dead, intraplate Kutch.
NDMA's **six pillars** begin with building to **IS 1893, IS 4326 and IS 13920**.
⚠ **Latur 1993** → Zone I merged into Zone II.

10.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Gorkha earthquake:
1. It occurred in Nepal in 2015.
2. It had a magnitude of 7.8.
3. It occurred along the Main Himalayan Thrust.
4. It caused liquefaction in Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
10.x: All four statements are correct. The 2015 Gorkha earthquake in Nepal had a magnitude of 7.8, occurred along the Main Himalayan Thrust and caused liquefaction in parts of the Gangetic plain.
10.tq: Verify the event through its year, magnitude, tectonic setting and secondary effect.
xs: All four — **1, 2, 3 and 4** — are correct — option **(4)**.
On the **Main Himalayan Thrust**; caused **liquefaction** in **Bihar, UP, WB**.
xa: Liquefaction hits the **soft soils of the Indo-Gangetic plain**.
**Uttarkashi** (**1991**, M ~**6.8**) also lay in the **Himalayan thrust zone**.
Indian plate pushes north at about **5 cm/year**.

10.s:
Match List-I (Earthquake) with List-II (Tectonic setting):
List-I
a. Tohoku, Japan (2011)
b. Turkey-Syria (Feb 2023)
c. Myanmar, Mandalay (2025)
List-II
i. East Anatolian Fault (Anatolian-Arabian plates)
ii. Sagaing Fault - strike-slip, Indian vs Eurasian plate
iii. Pacific plate subduction
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
10.x: Tohoku 2011 (M 9.0) was a Pacific plate subduction quake (tsunami, Fukushima) = iii. Turkey-Syria 2023 (M 7.8) was on the East Anatolian Fault = i. Myanmar 2025 (M 7.7) was on the strike-slip Sagaing Fault between the Indian and Eurasian plates = ii. Option B swaps Tohoku and Turkey-Syria, option C swaps Turkey-Syria and Myanmar, option D mismatches all.
10.tq: Japan = subduction; Turkey = East Anatolian; Myanmar = Sagaing strike-slip.
xs: **a-iii, b-i, c-ii** — option **(1)**.
**Tohoku (2011)** = **Pacific plate subduction** (tsunami, **Fukushima**).
**Turkey-Syria (Feb 2023)** = **East Anatolian Fault**; **Myanmar (2025)** = **Sagaing Fault**, strike-slip.
xa: Tohoku: **M 9.0**; Turkey-Syria: **M 7.8**; Myanmar: **M 7.7**, **2,000+** dead.
**Seismic seiches** were reported during the **Myanmar** earthquake.
The **Sagaing Fault** is the **Indian-Eurasian** boundary.

10.s: Seismic seiches are
o: standing waves in rivers, reservoirs and ponds
waves generated only by volcanic ash
10.x: Seismic seiches are standing waves that may develop in enclosed or partly enclosed water bodies such as rivers, reservoirs and ponds. They were reported during the Myanmar earthquake.
10.tq: Distinguish a water-body phenomenon from earthquake source types and fault movements.
xs: **Seismic seiches** are **standing waves** in rivers, lakes, reservoirs, ponds — option **(3)**.
They were reported during the **Myanmar earthquake**.
Slow slip along a fault is **creep** — option (1) wrong.
xa: **Landslides**: fragile **Himalaya** and **North-East**.
**Liquefaction**: soft soils of the **Indo-Gangetic plain**.
**Fires**: from **broken gas and power lines**.

10.s: Which combination of conditions is most conducive to the generation of a tsunami?
o: Magnitude below 5.0, deep focus and horizontal movement only
Magnitude above 6.5, shallow focus and vertical uplift of the sea floor
Volcanic ash fall without any displacement of water
Deep continental earthquake and subsidence of an inland basin
10.x: A tsunami generally requires an earthquake of magnitude greater than 6.5, a focus shallower than approximately 70 km and vertical uplift of the sea floor.
10.tq: Apply the necessary-condition test instead of relying on magnitude alone.
xs: A tsunami needs **M > 6.5**, a **shallow focus** and **vertical seafloor uplift** — option **(2)**.
The focus must be shallower than **~70 km**.
Horizontal movement or a deep focus will not do — option (1) wrong.
xa: Over **80%** of tsunamis come from **megathrust subduction** quakes.
**Kamchatka (Aug 2025)**: **M 8.8** megathrust quake caused only a **limited tsunami**.
The **Tsunami Early Warning System** was built after the **2004 Sumatra** quake.

10.s: Approximately what proportion of tsunamis originate from megathrust earthquakes at subduction zones?
10.x: More than 80 percent of tsunamis originate from megathrust earthquakes occurring at subduction zones.
10.tq: Select the quantitative threshold associated with the dominant tsunami source.
xs: **More than 80 percent** of tsunamis come from **megathrust subduction** quakes — option **(1)**.
Conditions: **M > 6.5**, focus shallower than **~70 km**, **vertical seafloor uplift**.
xa: **Kamchatka (Aug 2025)**: **M 8.8** megathrust quake, only a **limited tsunami**.
**Tohoku (2011)**: Pacific plate subduction, tsunami, **Fukushima**.
NCS detects global quakes of **M 6.0+**, including tsunami-capable ones.

10.s:
Match the earthquake effect with the region or cause most closely associated with it:

List-I (Effect)
a. Landslides
b. Liquefaction
c. Seismic seiches
 d. Fires

List-II (Associated setting or cause)
i. Broken gas and power lines
 ii. Lakes and reservoirs
 iii. Fragile Himalaya and North-East
 iv. Soft soils of the Indo-Gangetic Plain

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
10.x: Earthquakes trigger landslides in the fragile Himalaya and North-East, liquefaction in soft Indo-Gangetic soils, seiches in lakes and reservoirs, and fires through broken gas and power lines.
10.tq: Match each hazard with its distinctive physical setting or immediate cause.
xs: **a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i** — option **(1)**.
**Landslides** = fragile **Himalaya and North-East**; **liquefaction** = soft soils of the **Indo-Gangetic plain**.
**Seiches** = rivers, **lakes, reservoirs**; **fires** = **broken gas and power lines**.
xa: Seiches were reported during the **Myanmar earthquake**.
**Gorkha (2015)** caused liquefaction in **Bihar, UP, WB**.
**95%** of quake deaths occur in poorly built **1-3 storey houses**.

10.s: India forms part of which major seismic belt?
10.x: India lies in the Alpine-Himalayan seismic belt, which extends eastward through the North-East into Myanmar.
10.tq: Recall the major global seismic belt associated with India.
xs: India lies in the **Alpine-Himalayan belt** — option **(1)**.
The **Indian plate** pushes north at about **5 cm/year** into the **Eurasian plate**.
The belt continues east through the **North-East** into **Myanmar**.
xa: **Sagaing Fault** = Indian-Eurasian boundary in Myanmar.
**Zone V** runs along the Himalayan front, where **magnitude-8** quakes have struck.
The **Circum-Pacific** belt has the most quakes; Alpine-Himalayan is **next**.

10.s: The Indian Plate is moving approximately how far northward each year into the Eurasian Plate?
10.x: The Indian Plate moves northward into the Eurasian Plate at approximately 5 centimetres per year.
10.tq: Identify the central value in a set of plausible plate-motion rates.
xs: The **Indian plate** moves north at about **5 cm per year** — option **(3)**.
It pushes into the **Eurasian plate**, placing India in the **Alpine-Himalayan belt**.
xa: In Myanmar the **Sagaing Fault** marks the Indian-Eurasian boundary.
**Gorkha (2015)**: **Main Himalayan Thrust**, **M 7.8**.
Prone Himalayan areas: **J&K, Ladakh, HP, Uttarakhand, Sikkim, Arunachal**.

10.s: Which fault marks the Indian–Eurasian plate boundary in Myanmar?
10.x: In Myanmar, the Sagaing Fault marks the continuation of the Indian–Eurasian boundary through the eastern part of the seismic belt.
10.tq: Locate the named fault along the eastward continuation of the Himalayan seismic belt.
xs: The **Sagaing Fault** is the **Indian-Eurasian** boundary in Myanmar — option **(4)**.
It is a **strike-slip** fault.
**Main Himalayan Thrust** = Gorkha; **East Anatolian Fault** = Turkey-Syria.
xa: **Myanmar (Mandalay) 2025**: **M 7.7**, **2,000+** dead, on the Sagaing Fault.
Seismic **seiches** were reported in that quake.
The Alpine-Himalayan belt continues east through the **North-East** into **Myanmar**.

10.s: Which of the following regions is NOT identified as a prone area for significant earthquake activity in India?
10.x: Kutch, the North-East and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands are earthquake-prone areas. Visakhapatnam is cited as an example of a low-risk stable-shield area.
10.tq: Find the location that does not belong to the group of earthquake-prone regions.
xs: The **stable shield around Visakhapatnam** is not a prone area — option **(2)**.
**Visakhapatnam** lies in **Zone II** (low risk).
**Kutch**, the **North-East** and **Andaman & Nicobar** are prone areas, all in **Zone V**.
xa: ⚠ **Visakhapatnam** = Zone II; **Vijayawada** = Zone III.
AP is mostly in **Zones II and III**.
**Koraput-Jeypore quake (6 Apr 2026)**: **M 4.4**, shook **Araku** and **Paderu**.

10.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Liquefaction is a particular concern in the Indo-Gangetic plain.
2. Peninsular faults associated with Latur and Koyna can produce earthquakes.
3. The Himalaya, North-East and Andaman and Nicobar Islands are among the earthquake-prone regions of India.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
10.x: All three statements are correct. Earthquake vulnerability in India is associated with Himalayan and North-Eastern regions, liquefaction-prone alluvial plains, peninsular faults and the Andaman and Nicobar region.
10.tq: Combine regional distribution with the associated hazard or geological setting.
xs: All three — **1, 2 and 3** — are correct — option **(4)**.
Statement 1 correct: the **Indo-Gangetic plain** (Bihar, UP, WB) is highly prone to **soil liquefaction**.
Statement 2 correct: peninsular faults (**Latur, Koyna**) can give severe **intraplate** quakes.
Statement 3 correct: the **Himalaya**, **North-East** and **Andaman & Nicobar** are prone areas.
xa: **Kutch** is another prone area (**Zone V**).
**Jabalpur** is also an intraplate example.
Indian plate pushes north at about **5 cm/year**.

10.s: Under IS 1893:2016, which sequence correctly represents the seismic zones from lower to higher risk?
o: Zone II, Zone III, Zone IV, Zone V
Zone V, Zone IV, Zone III, Zone II
Zone III, Zone II, Zone V, Zone IV
Zone II, Zone IV, Zone III, Zone V
10.x: Under the four-zone map in force, Zone II represents low risk, Zone III moderate risk, Zone IV high risk and Zone V very high risk.
10.tq: Arrange the zones by increasing risk rather than by geographical location.
xs: Low to high risk: **Zone II, Zone III, Zone IV, Zone V** — option **(1)**.
The map in force (**IS 1893: 2016**) has **four zones**; **Zone II is the calmest**.
xa: **Zone V** runs along the Himalayan front where **magnitude-8** quakes have struck.
**Zone VI** came in the **2025** code, **withdrawn on 3 Mar 2026**.
**Zone I** was merged into Zone II after **Latur 1993**.

10.s: Which of the following areas is included in Zone V under the seismic zoning map in force?
10.x: Kutch is included in Zone V, the very-high-risk zone. Visakhapatnam and Hyderabad are examples of Zone II, while Vijayawada is cited under Zone III.
10.tq: Distinguish locations by their assigned seismic-risk zones.
xs: **Kutch** (Gujarat) is in **Zone V** — option **(3)**.
**Visakhapatnam** and **Hyderabad** are **Zone II**; **Vijayawada** is **Zone III**.
xa: Zone V also covers the **entire North-East**, **J&K, Ladakh, HP, Uttarakhand**, north **Bihar**, **Andaman & Nicobar**.
The withdrawn **2025** code placed parts of **Kutch** in **Zone VI**.

10.s:
Consider the following statements about seismic zones under IS 1893: 2016:
1. Delhi lies in Zone IV.
2. Vijayawada lies in Zone III.
3. Visakhapatnam lies in Zone III.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
10.x: Statement 1 is correct: Delhi, the rest of the Himalayan foothills and the Indo-Gangetic belt are Zone IV (high). Statement 2 is correct: Vijayawada is cited under Zone III (moderate). Statement 3 is wrong: Visakhapatnam is on the stable shield in Zone II (low). Hence 1 and 2 only.
10.tq: AP cities: Visakhapatnam = Zone II, Vijayawada = Zone III; AP has no Zone V.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: **Delhi** is in **Zone IV** (high).
Statement 2 correct: **Vijayawada** is in **Zone III** (moderate).
Statement 3 wrong: **Visakhapatnam** is in **Zone II** (low), on the stable shield.
xa: ⚠ **Visakhapatnam** = Zone II; **Vijayawada** = Zone III.
Zone III also includes **Chennai**, the **Latur-Koyna** belt and the **Amaravati** region.
AP has **no area in Zone V**.

10.s: Which of the following States or Union Territories has no area in Zone V?
10.x: Andhra Pradesh has no area in Zone V. Assam, Bihar and Jammu and Kashmir are identified as having areas in Zone V.
10.tq: Use the exception-based regional comparison to identify the outlier.
xs: **Andhra Pradesh** has **no area in Zone V** — option **(3)** (APPSC **2024**).
**Assam, Bihar and J&K** do have Zone V areas.
AP lies mostly in **Zones II and III** (low to moderate risk).
xa: **Visakhapatnam** = Zone II; **Vijayawada** = Zone III.
Reservoir-triggered tremors possible near **Nagarjuna Sagar, Srisailam and Polavaram**.
Old **Eastern Ghats** faults can also trigger tremors.

10.s: Zone I was merged into which zone after the 1993 Latur earthquake?
10.x: After the 1993 Latur earthquake, Zone I was merged into Zone II, resulting in the four-zone classification under IS 1893:2002.
10.tq: Link a classification change to the event that prompted it.
xs: After **Latur 1993**, **Zone I** was merged into **Zone II** — option **(3)**.
This came in **IS 1893: 2002**, giving **four zones**.
xa: **IS 1893 (Part 1): 2025** (BIS, **6 Nov 2025**) added **Zone VI** using a **probabilistic (PSHA)** model.
BIS **withdrew** it on **3 Mar 2026**; the **2016** four-zone map is back in force.
The 2025 map put **over 60%** of India's land in moderate-to-high zones.

10.s:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
A. Withdrawal of IS 1893 (Part 1): 2025
B. Notification of IS 1893 (Part 1): 2025
C. 1993 Latur earthquake
D. Bhuj earthquake
10.x: The correct order is the 1993 Latur earthquake, the 2001 Bhuj earthquake, notification of the 2025 revision on 6 November 2025, and its withdrawal on 3 March 2026.
10.tq: Use the first and last events, then place the two intermediate dates.
xs: Order: **Latur (1993) → Bhuj (2001) → notification of 2025 code → its withdrawal** (**C, D, B, A**) — option **(1)**.
**Latur 1993** came first; **Bhuj** struck on **26 Jan 2001**.
BIS notified **IS 1893 (Part 1): 2025** on **6 Nov 2025** and **withdrew it on 3 Mar 2026**.
xa: After Latur, **IS 1893: 2002** merged **Zone I into Zone II**.
⚠ **Bhuj 2001** → **DM Act 2005**; **Latur 1993** → Zone I merged into Zone II.
After the withdrawal, **IS 1893 (Part 1): 2016** was restored.

10.s: Which feature was introduced by the IS 1893 (Part 1): 2025 revision?
o: The abolition of all seismic zones in India
The exclusion of the North-East from the highest-risk category
The restoration of Zone I as the lowest zone
A new top Zone VI covering parts of Kashmir, the North-East and Kutch
10.x: The 2025 revision introduced a new top Zone VI for parts of Kashmir, the North-East and Kutch, and placed more than 60% of India’s landmass in moderate-to-high zones.
10.tq: Identify the distinctive institutional change rather than a reversed zoning claim.
xs: The **2025** revision added a new top **Zone VI** for parts of **Kashmir, the North-East and Kutch** — option **(4)**.
It used a **probabilistic (PSHA)** model.
It put **over 60%** of India's landmass in moderate-to-high zones.
xa: The map was built by **IIT-Madras** for **NDMA**; **PGA 0.15-0.75 g** from Zone II to Zone VI.
Basis: **69,519 events** and **36 seismogenic zones**.
BIS **withdrew** it on **3 Mar 2026**.

10.s: The 2025 revision of IS 1893 was withdrawn on 3 March 2026 primarily after objections relating to which issue?
o: The inability to identify earthquakes of magnitude 3.0 and above
The absence of earthquake data from the North-East
The replacement of the National Seismological Network
The cost implications raised by MoHUA, Metro Rail corporations and the NDSA
10.x: The 2025 revision was withdrawn after MoHUA, Metro Rail corporations and the NDSA objected to the cost implications. The 2016 code was restored.
10.tq: Match the policy rollback with the specific administrative objection.
xs: The 2025 code was withdrawn after **cost objections** from **MoHUA, Metro Rail corporations and the NDSA** — option **(4)**.
BIS **withdrew it on 3 Mar 2026**; the **2016** code was restored.
xa: A **review panel** is to report to the **Cabinet Secretariat**.
Debate: safer **PSHA-based codes** vs **construction cost**.
Experts call the restored 2016 values **too low for the Himalaya**; NDMA called the new ones "**too high**".

10.s: Which code is currently restored after the withdrawal of the 2025 seismic zoning revision?
10.x: The withdrawal of the 2025 revision restored IS 1893 (Part 1): 2016 as the code in force.
10.tq: Distinguish the currently restored standard from the withdrawn revision.
xs: **IS 1893 (Part 1): 2016** is restored — option **(3)**.
It keeps the **four-zone map**, with **Zone II** the calmest and **Zone V** the highest.
The **2025** code was **withdrawn on 3 Mar 2026**.
xa: **IS 1893: 2002** came after **Latur 1993**, merging **Zone I into Zone II**.
The 2025 code had a new top **Zone VI**.
Experts say the 2016 values are **too low for the Himalaya**.

10.s: The National Seismological Network of India consists of how many observatories?
10.x: The National Seismological Network operated by the National Centre for Seismology consists of 160 observatories.
10.tq: Distinguish the network size from the separate GNSS-station figure and event count.
xs: The **National Seismological Network** has **160 observatories** — option **(3)**.
It is run by the **National Centre for Seismology (NCS)**, New Delhi.
xa: NCS is an attached office of **MoES**.
It detects every Indian quake of **M 3.0+** and global quakes of **M 6.0+**.
First observatory: **Alipore, Calcutta (1898)**.

10.s: The National Centre for Seismology detects which combination of earthquakes through its monitoring network?
o: Only earthquakes capable of producing tsunamis
Indian earthquakes of magnitude 3.0 and above and global earthquakes of magnitude 6.0 and above
Indian earthquakes of magnitude 1.0 and global earthquakes of magnitude 3.0 and above
Only earthquakes occurring in the Himalayan region
10.x: The network detects every Indian earthquake of magnitude 3.0 or above and global earthquakes of magnitude 6.0 or above, including tsunami-capable events.
10.tq: Separate the two magnitude thresholds instead of treating them as identical.
xs: NCS detects every **Indian** quake of **M 3.0+** and **global** quakes of **M 6.0+** — option **(2)**.
Global coverage includes **tsunami-capable** quakes.
xa: NCS runs the **National Seismological Network** of **160 observatories**.
Public alerts: **IndiaQuake** app.
**Tsunami Early Warning System** was built after the **2004 Sumatra** quake.

10.s: The first seismological observatory in India was established at which place in 1898?
10.x: India’s first seismological observatory was established at Alipore in Calcutta in 1898.
10.tq: Recall the earliest observatory by combining its place and year.
xs: India's **first observatory** was at **Alipore, Calcutta (1898)** — option **(2)**.
**New Delhi** is the seat of the **National Centre for Seismology**, not the first observatory.
xa: NCS is attached to **MoES**.
The National Seismological Network has **160 observatories**.
MoES app **RISEQ** is now "**Bhookamp**".

10.s: RISEQ, the earthquake-related app of the Ministry of Earth Sciences, is now known by which name?
10.x: The MoES app RISEQ is now called “Bhookamp.” IndiaQuake is the public-alert app of the National Centre for Seismology.
10.tq: Discriminate between two similarly themed earthquake applications.
xs: The MoES app **RISEQ** is now "**Bhookamp**" — option **(1)**.
**IndiaQuake** is the separate **public alerts** app.
xa: NCS (New Delhi) is an attached office of **MoES**.
First observatory: **Alipore, Calcutta (1898)**.
NCS detects Indian quakes of **M 3.0+**.

10.s: Which application provides public earthquake alerts through the National Centre for Seismology?
o: RISEQ only under its former name
10.x: The NCS’s IndiaQuake app provides public earthquake alerts. RISEQ, now called Bhookamp, is the MoES app referred to in the monitoring system.
10.tq: Use the app-function distinction rather than relying only on similar names.
xs: **IndiaQuake** provides **public alerts** — option **(2)**.
**Bhookamp** is the new name of the MoES app **RISEQ** — options (1) and (4) are the trap.
xa: The **National Seismological Network** (**160 observatories**) is run by NCS.
NCS detects global quakes of **M 6.0+**.
**Tsunami Early Warning System**: built after the **2004 Sumatra** quake.

10.s: India developed its Tsunami Early Warning System after which event?
10.x: India built its Tsunami Early Warning System after the 2004 Sumatra earthquake and tsunami.
10.tq: Match the warning-system initiative with the triggering disaster.
xs: India's **Tsunami Early Warning System** was built after the **2004 Sumatra quake** — option **(3)**.
**Bhuj 2001** led to the **DM Act 2005** and **NDMA** instead.
xa: Tsunamis need **M > 6.5**, focus shallower than **~70 km**, **vertical seafloor uplift**.
Over **80%** come from **megathrust subduction** quakes.
**Tohoku (2011)**: tsunami and **Fukushima**.

10.s: Which of the following is NOT a volcanic product?
10.x: Pyroclastic debris, volcanic bombs and lava are volcanic products. Atmospheric air is not listed as a volcanic product.
10.tq: Classify the physical materials emitted or produced by volcanoes and identify the outsider.
xs: **Oxygen-rich atmospheric air** is not a volcanic product — option **(1)**.
Volcanic products: **pyroclastic debris**, **ash**, **volcanic bombs**, **lava**.
xa: Volcanic gases: mostly **water vapour**, then **CO2, SO2, H2S**.
**Strombolian** eruptions: frequent, mild bursts of **bombs and ash**.
**Composite** volcanoes make up **~60%** of Earth's volcanoes.

10.s: Which gas is present in the greatest proportion among the principal gases released by volcanoes?
10.x: Volcanic gases consist mostly of water vapour, followed by carbon dioxide, sulphur dioxide and hydrogen sulphide.
10.tq: Recall the stated order of abundance rather than confusing gases with solid volcanic products.
xs: **Water vapour** is the most abundant volcanic gas — option **(3)**.
It is followed by **CO2**, **SO2** and **H2S**.
xa: Products: **pyroclastic debris, ash, volcanic bombs, lava**.
**Vulcanian** eruptions are **more explosive** than Strombolian.
**Shield** volcanoes have **fluid basaltic lava**.

10.s: Shield volcanoes are generally characterised by:
o: Several vents and overlapping lava domes in every case
Fluid basaltic lava and gentle slopes
A large depression formed only by erosion
Thick viscous lava, steep cones and explosive eruptions
10.x: Shield volcanoes have fluid basaltic lava and gentle slopes. Thick viscous lava and explosive steep cones are characteristic of composite volcanoes.
10.tq: Use the contrast between lava viscosity and slope to distinguish shield and composite volcanoes.
xs: **Shield** volcanoes have **fluid basaltic lava** and **gentle slopes** — option **(2)**.
**Thick, viscous lava, steep cones, explosive** describe **composite** volcanoes — option (4).
**Several vents, overlapping cones, lava domes** describe **complex** volcanoes — option (1).
xa: Shield example: **Mauna Loa**, Hawaii (active).
**Caldera**: large depression from **collapse** after an explosive eruption.
Composite examples: **Etna, Mayon, Fuego**.

10.s:
Consider the following statements about composite or stratovolcanoes:
1. They generally have thick and viscous lava.
2. They commonly form steep cones.
3. They are associated with explosive eruptions.
4. They constitute approximately 60% of the Earth's volcanoes.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
10.x: All four statements are correct. Composite or stratovolcanoes have viscous lava, steep cones, explosive activity and constitute approximately 60% of Earth's volcanoes.
10.tq: Test a group of defining characteristics together, including the quantitative share.
xs: All four — **1, 2, 3 and 4** — are correct — option **(4)**.
**Composite/stratovolcanoes** have **thick, viscous lava**, **steep cones** and **explosive** eruptions.
They form **~60%** of Earth's volcanoes.
xa: Examples: **Etna, Mayon, Fuego**.
**Mayon** (Philippines) is a **symmetrical composite cone**.
**Fuego** gives **Strombolian** eruptions every **15-20 min**.

10.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Mauna Loa — caldera formed by explosive collapse
Mount Aso — one of the world's largest calderas
Etna — complex volcano with several overlapping vents only
Dukono — shield volcano with gentle basaltic slopes
10.x: Mount Aso is one of the world's largest calderas. Mauna Loa is a shield volcano, while Dukono is listed as a complex volcano.
10.tq: Start with the distinctive example of a landform and then eliminate type-example reversals.
xs: **Mount Aso — one of the world's largest calderas** is correct — option **(2)**.
**Mauna Loa** is an active **shield** volcano — option (1) wrong.
**Etna** is a **stratovolcano**; **Dukono** a **complex** volcano — options (3) and (4) wrong.
xa: A **caldera** is a large depression from **collapse** after an explosive eruption.
**Taal** is listed both as a caldera and a **complex** volcano.
**Dukono** is on **Halmahera, Indonesia**.

10.s: Which of the following is correctly matched with a complex or compound volcano?
10.x: Taal in the Philippines is a complex or compound volcano. Dukono is in Indonesia, while Mount Aso is a caldera in Japan.
10.tq: Use the sure example-location pair and reject nearby country substitutions.
xs: **Taal — Philippines** is the complex (compound) volcano match — option **(3)**.
Complex volcanoes have **several vents, overlapping cones, lava domes**.
**Dukono** is in **Halmahera, Indonesia**, not Guatemala; **Mount Aso** is a **caldera**.
xa: The other complex example is **Dukono**.
**Mayon** (Philippines): **symmetrical composite cone**.
**Volcan de Fuego** is the Guatemala volcano.

10.s: Which statement correctly distinguishes Strombolian and Vulcanian eruptions?
o: Vulcanian eruptions consist only of gentle lava flows.
Strombolian eruptions are frequent and mild, whereas Vulcanian eruptions are more explosive.
Strombolian eruptions are always more explosive than Vulcanian eruptions.
Both terms refer exclusively to dormant volcanoes.
10.x: Strombolian eruptions involve frequent, mild bursts of bombs and ash, whereas Vulcanian eruptions are more explosive.
10.tq: Compare the intensity and nature of the two similarly named eruption styles.
xs: **Strombolian** = frequent, **mild** bursts; **Vulcanian** = **more explosive** — option **(2)**.
Strombolian bursts throw **bombs and ash**.
Option (3) reverses the two.
xa: **Stromboli** (Italy) gives its name to **Strombolian** eruptions.
**Volcan de Fuego** has Strombolian eruptions every **15-20 min**.
Stromboli is the "**Lighthouse of the Mediterranean**".

10.s: A large, often dome-shaped mass of granite occurring at great depth and exposed after denudation is called:
10.x: A batholith is a huge mass of granite emplaced at depth. It may become exposed after denudation removes the overlying rocks.
10.tq: Identify the intrusive landform from its scale and depth.
xs: A huge dome-shaped **granite** mass cooled deep in the crust is a **batholith** — option **(3)**.
It forms **mountain cores** and is **exposed after denudation**.
**Sill** = horizontal sheet; **lopolith** = saucer; **phacolith** = wavy, lens-shaped mass.
xa: Intrusive bodies form from magma that **cools inside the crust**.
The **Ladakh Magmatic Arc** went through a **batholith phase**.
**Laccolith**: dome with a **flat base**, fed by a pipe.

10.s: Which intrusive landform is dome-shaped, has a flat base and is fed by a pipe from below?
10.x: A laccolith is a dome-shaped intrusive body with a flat base, generally supplied by a pipe from below.
10.tq: Match the characteristic shape and feeder arrangement to the landform.
xs: A **dome-shaped** body with a **flat base**, fed by a **pipe**, is a **laccolith** — option **(1)**.
Example: **Karnataka granite domes**.
**Lopolith** = saucer; **dyke** = vertical; **sill** = horizontal.
xa: ⚠ **Sill** = horizontal; **dyke** = vertical; **laccolith** = dome; **lopolith** = saucer.
⚠ APPSC G1 **2024**: "phacoliths are large domed mounds" is wrong — domes are **laccoliths**.
**Batholith**: huge **granite** mass, deep in the crust.

10.s:
Consider the following statements about intrusive volcanic forms:
1. A laccolith is a dome-shaped body with a flat base.
2. A lopolith is a saucer-shaped body, concave upward.
3. A sill is a vertical wall cutting across the rock beds.
4. Dykes fed the Deccan Traps.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
10.x: Statement 1 is correct: a laccolith is dome-shaped with a flat base, fed by a pipe. Statement 2 is correct: a lopolith is saucer-shaped (concave upward). Statement 3 is wrong: a sill is a horizontal sheet parallel to the beds; the vertical wall cutting across beds is a dyke. Statement 4 is correct: dykes fed the Deccan Traps. Hence 1, 2 and 4 only.
10.tq: Sill = horizontal/parallel; dyke = vertical/across.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 4** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: a **laccolith** is **dome-shaped** with a flat base.
Statement 2 correct: a **lopolith** is **saucer-shaped** (concave upward).
Statement 3 wrong: a **sill** is **horizontal**; the vertical wall is a **dyke**.
Statement 4 correct: **dykes** fed the **Deccan Traps** (western Maharashtra).
xa: **Phacolith**: wavy mass at the base of a **syncline** or top of an **anticline**.
Thin sills are called **sheets**.
⚠ APPSC G1 **2024**: domes are **laccoliths**, not phacoliths.

10.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Lopolith — wavy mass in a folded structure
Phacolith — wavy mass at the base of a syncline or top of an anticline
Laccolith — vertical wall cutting across rock beds
10.x: A phacolith is a wavy intrusive mass occurring at the base of a syncline or the top of an anticline. A lopolith is saucer-shaped, a laccolith is dome-shaped with a flat base, and a dyke is a vertical wall.
10.tq: Match each intrusive form with its distinctive shape or structural position.
xs: **Phacolith — wavy mass at the base of a syncline or top of an anticline** is correct — option **(3)**.
**Batholith** is a huge granite mass, not saucer-shaped; the **lopolith** is the saucer — options (1), (2) wrong.
A **laccolith** is a **dome**; the vertical wall is a **dyke** — option (4) wrong.
xa: ⚠ APPSC G1 **2024**: "phacoliths are large domed mounds" is the wrong statement.
**Sill / sheet**: **horizontal**, parallel to the beds.
**Dykes** fed the **Deccan Traps**.

10.s: The Ladakh Magmatic Arc lies between which two suture zones?
o: Main Boundary and Main Central suture zones
10.x: The Ladakh Magmatic Arc is located in the Trans-Himalaya between the Indus and Shyok suture zones.
10.tq: Use the paired geographical boundaries to identify the magmatic arc.
xs: The **Ladakh Magmatic Arc** lies between the **Indus and Shyok suture zones** — option **(2)**.
It is in the **Trans-Himalaya**.
xa: It went through a **batholith phase**.
It formed as the **Neo-Tethys** plate subducted under **Eurasia**, **~160 Ma** to **<45 Ma**.
**Batholiths** are huge **granite** masses that form mountain cores.

10.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the geological development of the Ladakh Magmatic Arc?
o: It formed when the Neo-Tethys plate subducted under Eurasia and underwent a batholith phase from about 160 Ma to less than 45 Ma.
It formed from the Reunion hotspot during the end of the Cretaceous and consists only of flood basalts.
It formed at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge through present-day divergent movement.
It developed when the Indian plate subducted beneath the Pacific plate during the Quaternary period.
10.x: The Ladakh Magmatic Arc formed through subduction of the Neo-Tethys plate beneath Eurasia and experienced a batholith phase from approximately 160 Ma to less than 45 Ma.
10.tq: Combine the tectonic process with the geological time interval and reject unrelated settings.
xs: The arc formed as the **Neo-Tethys plate subducted under Eurasia**, with a **batholith phase** from **~160 Ma** to **<45 Ma** — option **(1)**.
Flood basalts belong to the **Deccan**, not Ladakh — option (2) wrong.
xa: It lies in the **Trans-Himalaya** between the **Indus and Shyok** suture zones.
**Batholith**: dome-shaped granite mass exposed after **denudation**.
Extrusive landforms include **lava plateaus (Deccan)**.

10.s: Which one of the following is an extrusive volcanic landform?
10.x: Lava plateaus, cinder and composite cones, craters, calderas and lava flows are extrusive volcanic landforms. Batholiths, lopoliths and phacoliths are intrusive forms.
10.tq: Separate surface-formed extrusive features from underground intrusive bodies.
xs: A **lava plateau** is an **extrusive** landform — option **(2)**.
Other extrusive forms: **cinder and composite cones, craters, calderas, lava flows**.
**Lopolith**, **phacolith** and **batholith** are **intrusive** — magma cooled inside the crust.
xa: Example lava plateau: the **Deccan**.
**Dykes** fed the Deccan Traps.
⚠ **Sill** = horizontal; **dyke** = vertical.

10.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Stromboli — Lighthouse of the Mediterranean
2. Hekla — Iceland
3. Mauna Loa — Hawaii, USA
4. Tungurahua — Ecuador
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
10.x: All four pairs are correctly matched. Stromboli is known as the Lighthouse of the Mediterranean, Hekla is in Iceland, Mauna Loa is in Hawaii, and Tungurahua is in Ecuador.
10.tq: Check each country or regional location before selecting the coded combination.
xs: All four pairs — **1, 2, 3 and 4** — are correct — option **(4)**.
**Stromboli** (Italy) = "**Lighthouse of the Mediterranean**"; **Hekla** = **Iceland** (Mid-Atlantic Ridge).
**Mauna Loa** = **Hawaii, USA** (shield); **Tungurahua** = **Ecuador** (active).
xa: Stromboli gives its name to **Strombolian** eruptions.
⚠ **Kilimanjaro** and **Fuji** = dormant; **Etna, Stromboli, Vesuvius** = active (all Italy).
**Ojos del Salado** (Chile) is the **world's highest active volcano** (**6,893 m**).

10.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: Mount St. Helens — Volcano of Iceland
Krakatoa — Volcano between Sicily and mainland Italy
Mauna Loa — Stratovolcano of the Andes
10.x: Stromboli gives its name to Strombolian eruptions and exhibits near-continuous activity. Mauna Loa is a shield volcano in Hawaii, Mount St. Helens is in the USA, and Krakatoa lies between Java and Sumatra.
10.tq: Use the distinctive namesake relationship and reject geographically displaced volcanoes.
xs: **Stromboli — Strombolian eruptions** is correct — option **(2)**.
**Mount St. Helens** is in the **USA (Cascades)**, not Iceland.
**Krakatoa** lies between **Java and Sumatra**; **Mauna Loa** is a **shield** in Hawaii.
xa: Stromboli has **near-continuous activity** — the "**Lighthouse of the Mediterranean**".
Mount St. Helens: active stratovolcano, **1980** eruption.
Krakatoa's **1883** eruption brought collapse and catastrophic **tsunamis**.

10.s: Krakatoa is located between:
o: New Zealand's North and South Islands
10.x: Krakatoa is in Indonesia, between Java and Sumatra. Its 1883 eruption caused collapse and catastrophic tsunamis.
10.tq: Test the precise location rather than the broader country alone.
xs: **Krakatoa** (Indonesia) lies between **Java and Sumatra** — option **(2)**.
Its **1883** eruption caused **collapse** and catastrophic **tsunamis**.
xa: **Mount Dukono** is on **Halmahera, Indonesia**.
**White Island (Whakaari)** is in **New Zealand** (erupted **December 2019**).
**Etna** is in **Sicily**, Italy.

10.s: Which one of the following statements regarding Mount Etna is correct?
o: It is Europe's largest and most active volcano, rises to about 3,300 m and became a UNESCO site in 2013.
It is Africa's highest peak and has been dormant since 1707.
It is the world's highest active volcano at 6,893 m.
It is an extinct volcano that buried Pompeii in AD 79.
10.x: Etna is Europe's largest and most active volcano, is approximately 3,300 m high and has been a UNESCO site since 2013.
10.tq: Distinguish closely related volcano facts by checking the continent, height, status and historical association.
xs: **Etna** is **Europe's largest and most active** volcano, **~3,300 m**, a UNESCO site since **2013** — option **(1)**.
**Africa's highest peak** is **Kilimanjaro**; dormant since **1707** is **Fuji** — option (2) wrong.
The **world's highest active volcano** (**6,893 m**) is **Ojos del Salado** — option (3) wrong.
**Pompeii (AD 79)** was buried by **Vesuvius** — option (4) wrong.
xa: Etna is in **Sicily**, an active **stratovolcano**.
APPSC G1 **2018** cited Etna as a classic **volcanic mountain**.
Etna, **Stromboli** and **Vesuvius** are all active and all in **Italy**.

10.s: The volcano associated with the burial of Pompeii in AD 79 is:
10.x: Mount Vesuvius is an active volcano in Italy and buried Pompeii in AD 79.
10.tq: Apply the famous-event association to identify the correct volcano.
xs: **Vesuvius** buried **Pompeii (AD 79)** — option **(3)**.
Vesuvius is an **active** volcano in **Italy**.
**Etna** is in Sicily; **Stromboli** in the Aeolian Is.; **Tungurahua** in **Ecuador**.
xa: ⚠ **Etna, Stromboli, Vesuvius** = active (all Italy).
**Etna**: Europe's largest and most active, UNESCO since **2013**.
**Italy** lies in the **Mediterranean-Himalayan** belt (continental collision).

10.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
10.x: Ojos del Salado is in Chile and is the world's highest active volcano, at 6,893 m; it is not dormant.
10.tq: Find the mismatched status by separating country facts from active-dormant classifications.
xs: **Ojos del Salado — Chile — Dormant** is wrongly matched — option **(1)**.
Ojos del Salado is the **world's highest active volcano** (**6,893 m**).
**Tungurahua** (Ecuador) is active; **Fujiyama** and **Kilimanjaro** are **dormant** — all correct.
xa: **Kilimanjaro** is **Africa's highest peak** (**5,895 m**).
**Fuji**'s last eruption was in **1707**; Japan has **100+** active volcanoes.
⚠ **Kilimanjaro** and **Fuji** = dormant.

10.s: The last recorded eruption of Fujiyama mentioned in the geographical record was in:
10.x: Fujiyama in Japan is dormant, and its last eruption occurred in 1707.
10.tq: Test the precise historical year rather than relying only on the volcano's country or status.
xs: **Fujiyama**'s last eruption was in **1707** — option **(1)**.
Fuji is a **dormant stratovolcano** and **Japan's highest peak**.
xa: Japan has **100+ active volcanoes**.
⚠ **Kilimanjaro** and **Fuji** = dormant.
**Kyushu, Japan M 7.1** quake struck on **29 Jul 2026**.

10.s: Popocatepetl, which has been active since 1994, is located in:
10.x: Popocatepetl is an active volcano in Mexico and has been active since 1994.
10.tq: Use the country-status-year combination to distinguish neighbouring Latin American volcanoes.
xs: **Popocatepetl** (active since **1994**) is in **Mexico** — option **(1)**.
The first **3D image** of it reaches **18 km** below the crater (**Jan 2026**).
**Tungurahua** is Ecuador's; **Ojos del Salado** Chile's; **Volcan de Fuego** Guatemala's.
xa: **Fuego** gives **Strombolian** eruptions every **15-20 min** and erupted again **Jun 2026**.
**Ojos del Salado**: world's highest active volcano (**6,893 m**).
**Mount Spurr** is in **Alaska** (Aleutian Arc).

10.s: Which of the following recent volcano-related events is correctly matched?
10.x: Mayon is in the Philippines and is noted for its symmetrical composite-cone form. Mount Dukono is in Halmahera, Indonesia, while Mount Spurr is in Alaska's Aleutian Arc.
10.tq: Match each volcano with its location and distinguishing description, rejecting swapped-location traps.
xs: **Mayon — Philippines — symmetrical composite cone** is correct — option **(3)**.
**Mount Spurr** is in **Alaska, Aleutian Arc**; **Mount Dukono** in **Halmahera, Indonesia** — options (1), (2) swap them.
"Active since **1994**" fits **Popocatepetl** (Mexico) — option (4) wrong.
xa: **Taal** is also in the **Philippines** — a complex volcano.
Mount Spurr was in the news in **Apr 2025**; Dukono on **19 May 2026**.
Composite volcanoes are **~60%** of Earth's volcanoes.

10.s: White Island (Whakaari), a volcano that erupted in December 2019, is located in which country?
10.x: White Island (Whakaari) is in New Zealand and erupted in December 2019. Indonesia has Krakatoa and Dukono, Japan has Fujiyama and Mount Aso, and the Philippines has Taal and Mayon.
10.tq: Whakaari = Maori name; New Zealand, Dec 2019 (APPSC PYQ).
xs: **White Island (Whakaari)** is in **New Zealand** — option **(3)**.
It erupted in **December 2019** (APPSC PYQ).
**Indonesia** has **Krakatoa** and **Dukono**; the **Philippines** has **Taal** and **Mayon**.
xa: **Krakatoa**'s **1883** eruption caused catastrophic tsunamis.
**Fujiyama** (Japan) last erupted in **1707**.
**Mount St. Helens** (USA, Cascades) erupted in **1980**.

10.s: Which of the following recent earthquake-event pairs is correctly matched?
o: M 7.7 — off Flores Island, Indonesia — August 2026
10.x: An M 7.7 quake struck off Flores Island, Indonesia, on 18 August 2026. The others are mismatched: the Koraput-Jeypore quake (April 2026) was M 4.4, the M 8.8 megathrust quake was off Kamchatka (August 2025), and Caracas, Venezuela was hit by a seismic doublet in June 2026.
10.tq: Check magnitude, location and date together to defeat swapped-event distractors.
xs: **M 7.7 — off Flores Island, Indonesia — August 2026** is correct — option **(2)**.
**Koraput-Jeypore** (**6 Apr 2026**) was only **M 4.4**.
The **M 8.8** megathrust quake was off **Kamchatka** (**Aug 2025**); **Caracas** had a **seismic doublet** (**26 Jun 2026**).
xa: Flores quake date: **18 Aug 2026**.
**Colombia M 7.4** (**12 Aug 2026**) killed over **100**.
**Kyushu, Japan M 7.1** (**29 Jul 2026**).

10.s: The M 8.8 megathrust earthquake off Kamchatka in August 2025 was notable because it:
o: Produced a tsunami that completely inundated the Pacific coast
Occurred on the Caracas strike-slip boundary
10.x: Despite its M 8.8 megathrust magnitude, the Kamchatka earthquake caused only a limited tsunami.
10.tq: Focus on the unusual consequence of the event rather than inferring impact solely from magnitude.
xs: The **M 8.8** Kamchatka megathrust quake (**Aug 2025**) caused only a **limited tsunami** — option **(1)**.
**M 4.4** was the **Koraput-Jeypore** quake; **Caracas** lies on a **strike-slip** boundary — options (3), (4) wrong.
xa: Tsunamis need **M > 6.5**, focus shallower than **~70 km**, **vertical seafloor uplift**.
Over **80%** come from **megathrust subduction** quakes.
The **Tsunami Early Warning System** followed the **2004 Sumatra** quake.

10.s:
Consider the following statements about seismicity in Andhra Pradesh:
1. Most of Andhra Pradesh lies in Seismic Zones II and III.
2. Reservoir-triggered tremors cannot be ruled out near Nagarjuna Sagar, Srisailam and Polavaram.
3. Old faults in the Eastern Ghats are relevant to the possibility of tremors.
4. Visakhapatnam lies in Zone V.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
10.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Visakhapatnam is in Zone II, not Zone V.
10.tq: Find the location-based false statement by checking the specific seismic zone assigned to Visakhapatnam.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: most of AP is in **Zone II-III**.
Statements 2 and 3 correct: reservoir-triggered tremors are possible near **Nagarjuna Sagar, Srisailam, Polavaram** and along old **Eastern Ghats** faults.
Statement 4 wrong: **Visakhapatnam** is in **Zone II** (May 2026).
xa: AP has **no area in Zone V** (APPSC **2024**).
**Koraput-Jeypore quake (6 Apr 2026)**: **M 4.4**, **5 km** deep, shook **Araku** and **Paderu** in ASR district.
⚠ **Visakhapatnam** = Zone II; **Vijayawada** = Zone III.

10.s: Experts criticised the restored 2016 earthquake-hazard values mainly because they considered them:
o: Applicable only to coastal Andhra Pradesh
10.x: Experts argued that the restored 2016 hazard values were too low for the Himalaya. NDMA, in contrast, described the new values as too high.
10.tq: Separate the contrasting positions of experts and NDMA instead of treating both criticisms as identical.
xs: Experts say the restored **2016** values are **too low for the Himalaya** — option **(1)**.
**NDMA**, by contrast, called the new (2025) values "**too high**" — option (3) is the trap.
xa: The withdrawn map was based on **69,519 events** and **36 seismogenic zones**.
Trade-off: safer **PSHA-based codes** vs **construction cost**.
**Zone V** covers the Himalayan front where **magnitude-8** quakes have struck.

10.s: Which of the following statements about earthquake safety and construction is correct?
o: Construction cost is irrelevant to the debate over PSHA-based codes.
Approximately 95% of earthquake deaths occur in poorly built one- to three-storey houses.
Retrofitting is unnecessary when a building follows no seismic code.
Earthquake deaths occur almost exclusively in high-rise steel buildings.
10.x: About 95% of earthquake deaths occur in poorly built one- to three-storey houses. The debate also involves balancing safer PSHA-based codes against construction costs.
10.tq: Apply the risk statistic to a built-environment scenario and reject exaggerated building claims.
xs: About **95%** of quake deaths occur in poorly built **1-3 storey houses** — option **(2)**.
Construction cost **is** part of the debate: safer **PSHA-based codes** vs **construction cost** — option (1) wrong.
xa: NDMA's **six pillars** begin with building to **IS 1893, IS 4326 and IS 13920**.
**Retrofitting** priority buildings is part of the first pillar.
The 2025 code was withdrawn over **cost objections**.

10.s: Which of the following is the FIRST step among NDMA's six pillars of seismic safety?
o: Replacing all reservoirs with underground water tanks
Building according to IS 1893, IS 4326 and IS 13920, along with prioritising important buildings for retrofitting
Banning all construction in Seismic Zone II
10.x: The first pillar begins with construction according to IS 1893, IS 4326 and IS 13920, together with retrofitting priority buildings.
10.tq: Identify the institutional safety measure that directly addresses structural vulnerability.
xs: NDMA's first pillar: build to **IS 1893, IS 4326 and IS 13920** and **retrofit priority buildings** — option **(3)**.
NDMA has **six pillars** of seismic safety.
xa: About **95%** of quake deaths occur in poorly built **1-3 storey houses**.
**IS 1893 (Part 1): 2016** is the code in force.
**Bhuj 2001** led to the **DM Act 2005** and **NDMA**.

11.s: The breaking of rock into smaller particles without a change in its chemical composition is known as
11.x: Physical or mechanical weathering breaks rocks into smaller pieces without changing their chemical composition.
11.tq: Distinguish mechanical breakdown from chemical alteration.
xs: Breaking rock into smaller pieces **without chemical change** is **physical (mechanical) weathering** — option **(2)** is correct.
Examples: **frost wedging**, heating and cooling (**exfoliation**), and **salt crystal growth**.
**Hydrolysis** and **carbonation** are chemical processes: water reacts with silicates (feldspar → clay), and **carbonic acid** dissolves limestone.
xa: Denudation sequence: **weathering → mass wasting/erosion → transportation → deposition**.
Weathering is **fastest in hot, wet climates**; **freeze-thaw** breaks rocks in the **high Himalaya**.
⚠ **Hydration** = swelling (**anhydrite → gypsum**); **hydrolysis** = reaction (**feldspar → clay**, muscovite → **vermiculite**).
Weathering landforms: **exfoliation domes** (onion-like peeling of granite), **tors** (granite block piles), **block disintegration** along joints.

11.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Carbonation — Dissolution of limestone by carbonic acid
Oxidation — Formation of clay from feldspar
11.x: Formation of clay from feldspar is associated with hydrolysis. Oxidation involves the rusting of iron-bearing minerals and may produce red or yellow soils.
11.tq: Find the process whose example belongs to a different weathering category.
xs: **Oxidation — Formation of clay from feldspar** is the wrong pair — option **(4)** is correct.
Clay from **feldspar** is **hydrolysis** (water reacting with silicate minerals); **oxidation** is the **rusting of iron minerals**, giving **red and yellow soils**.
**Carbonation** — carbonic acid dissolving limestone: correct.
**Frost wedging** and **salt crystal growth** are both **physical weathering**: correct.
xa: **Hydration** = minerals absorb water and swell, e.g. **anhydrite → gypsum**.
**Solution** = soluble minerals like **rock salt** and **gypsum** dissolve.
Hydrolysis also turns **muscovite** into **vermiculite** when its potassium is replaced by **hydronium** (**APPSC 2024**).
**Biological weathering**: roots, burrowing animals, **lichens** and micro-organisms.

11.s: Rainwater containing carbon dioxide forms carbonic acid. This process, which dissolves limestone and stores carbon as bicarbonate, is called
11.x: Carbonation occurs when carbon dioxide in rainwater forms carbonic acid, which dissolves limestone and converts carbon into bicarbonate.
11.tq: Link the chemical agent and the affected rock to identify the process.
xs: CO2 in rain forms **carbonic acid** that dissolves **limestone**, storing carbon as **bicarbonate** — this is **carbonation**, option **(3)**.
**Solution** is plain dissolving of soluble minerals (**rock salt**, **gypsum**), with no acid formed.
**Oxidation** is rusting of **iron minerals**; **hydration** is minerals absorbing water and **swelling**.
xa: ⚠ **Hydration** (anhydrite → gypsum) vs **hydrolysis** (feldspar → clay) — a frequent trap pair.
**Hydrolysis**: muscovite → **vermiculite** (**APPSC 2024**).
Chemical weathering is **fastest in hot, wet climates**.
Oxidation gives **red and yellow soils**.

11.s: Which one of the following correctly describes hydration in weathering?
o: Absorption of water by minerals causing them to swell
Dissolution of soluble minerals in water
Reaction of water with silicate minerals to form clay
11.x: Hydration is the absorption of water by minerals, causing them to swell; conversion of anhydrite to gypsum is an example.
11.tq: Separate hydration from hydrolysis by focusing on swelling rather than chemical replacement.
xs: **Hydration** = **absorption of water by minerals causing them to swell** — option **(1)** is correct.
Example: **anhydrite → gypsum**.
Dissolving soluble minerals is **solution**; rusting of iron minerals is **oxidation**; water reacting with silicates to form clay is **hydrolysis**.
xa: ⚠ **Hydration** = swelling; **hydrolysis** = reaction (**feldspar → clay**, muscovite → **vermiculite**).
**Carbonation**: carbonic acid dissolves **limestone**, carbon stored as **bicarbonate**.
**Physical weathering** involves no chemical change: **frost wedging**, **exfoliation**, **salt crystal growth**.

11.s: Muscovite changes into vermiculite when its potassium is replaced by hydronium. This is an example of
11.x: The replacement of potassium in muscovite by hydronium is a hydrolysis reaction.
11.tq: Use the specific mineral transformation as the identifying clue.
xs: Muscovite's potassium replaced by **hydronium** to form **vermiculite** is **hydrolysis** — option **(3)** is correct (**APPSC 2024**).
Hydrolysis is water **reacting** with silicate minerals; the other example is **feldspar → clay**.
**Hydration** is only absorption of water and swelling (**anhydrite → gypsum**); **solution** dissolves rock salt and gypsum.
**Biological weathering** is done by roots, burrowing animals, lichens and micro-organisms.
xa: ⚠ **Hydration** = swelling; **hydrolysis** = reaction — the classic confusable pair.
**Carbonation**: CO2 + rain → **carbonic acid** → dissolves limestone.
**Oxidation**: iron minerals rust → **red, yellow soils**.

11.s:
Consider the following statements about weathering:
1. Weathering is fastest in hot, wet climates.
2. Freeze-thaw action breaks rocks in the high Himalaya.
3. Lichens and micro-organisms do not contribute to the weathering of rocks.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
11.x: Statement 1 is correct: weathering is fastest in hot, wet climates. Statement 2 is correct: freeze-thaw breaks rocks in the high Himalaya. Statement 3 is wrong: biological weathering is done by roots, burrowing animals, lichens and micro-organisms. Hence 1 and 2 only.
11.tq: Biological weathering includes lichens and microbes, not just roots.
xs: **Statements 1 and 2 only** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 — correct: weathering is **fastest in hot, wet climates**.
Statement 2 — correct: **freeze-thaw** breaks rocks in the **high Himalaya**.
Statement 3 — wrong: **lichens and micro-organisms** do weather rock — this is **biological weathering**, along with roots and burrowing animals.
xa: Physical weathering examples: **frost wedging**, heating and cooling (**exfoliation**), **salt crystal growth**.
Rainforest soils are poor because heavy rain **leaches** nutrients and dead matter decays fast.
Denudation: **weathering → mass wasting/erosion → transportation → deposition**.

11.s: Exfoliation domes are commonly formed by
11.x: Exfoliation domes develop through onion-like peeling of granite, commonly associated with weathering and pressure or temperature effects.
11.tq: Identify the weathering landform from its distinctive surface appearance and rock type.
xs: **Exfoliation domes** form by **onion-like peeling of granite** — option **(1)** is correct.
Peeling comes from **heating and cooling** — a form of **physical weathering**.
**Rotational slipping of saturated soil** is a **slump**, a mass-wasting type, not a weathering landform.
xa: **Tors** = granite **block piles**.
**Block disintegration** = breaking along **joints** due to temperature change.
Other physical weathering: **frost wedging**, **salt crystal growth**.
Denudation agents: **water** (most powerful), wind, ice, gravity.

11.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
11.x: Tors are piles or groups of granite blocks. Block disintegration occurs along joints, often due to temperature changes.
11.tq: Match the landform with its material and mode of formation.
xs: **Tors — Granite block piles** is correctly matched — option **(1)**.
Tors are piles of **granite blocks** left by weathering, not limestone solution hollows.
**Exfoliation domes** are onion-like peeling of granite, not river levees; **block disintegration** happens along **joints** from temperature change, not coral reefs.
xa: All three — **exfoliation domes**, **tors**, **block disintegration** — are **weathering landforms**.
Physical weathering = rock breaks **without chemical change**.
Weathering is **fastest in hot, wet climates**.

11.s: Which of the following represents the correct sequence of denudation processes?
o: Weathering → mass wasting or erosion → transportation → deposition
11.x: Denudation proceeds through weathering, mass wasting or erosion, transportation and finally deposition.
11.tq: Arrange the processes from source preparation to final accumulation.
xs: Denudation runs **weathering → mass wasting or erosion → transportation → deposition** — option **(2)** is correct.
Rock must first be **weathered** before it can be moved, and **deposition** always comes last.
xa: Denudation agents: **water** (most powerful), **wind**, **ice**, **gravity**.
**Mass wasting** = downslope movement under **gravity** = landslide (**APPSC 2019**).
Weathering is **fastest in hot, wet climates**.

11.s: Which one of the following is regarded as the most powerful agent of denudation?
11.x: Water is considered the most powerful agent of denudation, although wind, ice and gravity also contribute.
11.tq: Identify the principal agent while retaining the role of the other agents.
xs: **Water** is the **most powerful agent** of denudation — option **(1)** is correct.
**Wind**, **ice** and **gravity** are the other agents, but less powerful.
xa: Water is also the **most powerful agent of soil erosion**: **sheet, rill, gully** (**Chambal ravines**).
**Wind erosion** dominates the **Thar**.
Denudation sequence: **weathering → mass wasting/erosion → transportation → deposition**.

11.s:
Match List-I (Mass-wasting type) with List-II (Nature):
List-I
a. Rockfall
b. Slide
c. Slump
d. Debris flow
List-II
i. Rotational slip along a curved surface in weak, saturated soils
ii. Free fall of rocks from steep cliffs
iii. Fast water-soil-rock mix after heavy rain or snowmelt
iv. Coherent mass slipping along a surface
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
11.x: Rockfall is free fall from cliffs (ii); a slide is a coherent mass slipping along a surface (iv); a slump is a rotational slip on a curved surface in weak saturated soil (i); a debris flow is a fast water-soil-rock mix after heavy rain or snowmelt (iii). Option B swaps slide and slump, option C and D misplace rockfall and debris flow.
11.tq: Slump = rotational/curved; slide = planar coherent mass.
xs: Correct code: **a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii** — option **(1)**.
**Rockfall** = free fall of rocks from steep cliffs (ii); **slide** = coherent mass slips along a surface (iv).
**Slump** = rotational slip along a curved surface in weak, saturated soils (i); **debris flow** = fast water-soil-rock mix after heavy rain or snowmelt (iii).
xa: **Creep** = very slow movement by wetting-drying and heating-cooling.
⚠ **Slump** = rotational, curved surface; **creep** = very slow.
Conditions: slopes above **30 degrees**, weak/fractured rock, **bare slopes**.
Most at risk in India: **Himalaya and North-East**.

11.s: Which one of the following statements about mass wasting is NOT correct?
o: Rockfall involves the free fall of rocks from steep cliffs.
Rainfall is the principal trigger of mass wasting in India.
Creep may result from repeated wetting and drying or heating and cooling.
Creep is an extremely rapid movement of material down a slope.
11.x: Creep is a very slow movement, not an extremely rapid one. Rockfall, wetting–drying effects and rainfall as a major trigger are correctly stated.
11.tq: Look for the reversed speed characteristic in the mass-wasting descriptions.
xs: **Creep is an extremely rapid movement** is NOT correct — option **(4)** — creep is **very slow** movement.
**Rockfall** = free fall of rocks from steep cliffs: correct.
**Rainfall** (SW monsoon) is the main trigger in India: correct.
Creep is caused by **wetting-drying** and **heating-cooling**: correct.
xa: ⚠ **Slump** = rotational slip on a curved surface; **creep** = very slow.
**Debris flow / mudflow** is the fast type — water-soil-rock mix after heavy rain or snowmelt.
After rainfall, **earthquakes** are the next trigger.
Most at risk: **Himalaya and North-East**.

11.s: Which combination of conditions is most favourable for mass wasting?
o: Slopes above 30 degrees, weak or fractured rock and bare slopes
Gentle slopes, strong unfractured rock and dense vegetation
Stable rock, low relief and absence of rainfall
Flat terrain, dry soil and thick alluvium only
11.x: Mass wasting is especially common on slopes steeper than 30 degrees, where rocks are weak or fractured and slopes are bare.
11.tq: Combine slope, material strength and surface-cover conditions in the scenario.
xs: Mass wasting is favoured by **slopes above 30 degrees**, **weak or fractured rock** and **bare slopes** — option **(1)** is correct.
Gentle slopes, strong rock, dense vegetation, low relief and flat terrain all resist downslope movement under **gravity**.
xa: Main trigger in India: **rainfall (SW monsoon)**, then **earthquakes**.
Most at risk: **Himalaya and North-East**.
**Clay and silt** get saturated and are **landslide-prone**; sand drains well.
Mass wasting = downslope movement under gravity = **landslide** (**APPSC 2019**).

11.s: In India, the principal trigger of mass wasting is rainfall, followed next by earthquakes. The regions most at risk are the
o: Eastern coastal plain and Malwa plateau
11.x: The southwest monsoon makes rainfall the main trigger of mass wasting in India, while earthquakes are the next major trigger. The Himalaya and North-East are particularly vulnerable.
11.tq: Link the trigger sequence with the high-risk physiographic regions.
xs: The regions most at risk of mass wasting are the **Himalaya and North-East** — option **(3)** is correct.
The main trigger is **rainfall** from the **SW monsoon**, followed by **earthquakes**.
xa: Conditions: slopes above **30 degrees**, weak/fractured rock, bare slopes.
Types: **rockfall**, **slide**, **slump**, **debris flow/mudflow**, **creep**.
**Freeze-thaw** also breaks rocks in the **high Himalaya**.
Saturated **clay and silt** make slopes landslide-prone.

11.s: The downslope movement of earth material under the direct influence of gravity, commonly called a landslide, is known as
11.x: Mass wasting is the downslope movement of earth material under gravity, i.e. landslides (APPSC 2019). Deflation is removal of loose material by wind, weathering is in-situ breakdown of rock without significant movement, and abrasion is scraping by transported particles.
11.tq: Gravity + downslope = mass wasting = landslide (APPSC 2019).
xs: Downslope movement of earth material under **gravity** = landslide = **mass wasting** — option **(1)** (**APPSC 2019**).
**Weathering** breaks rock where it lies; mass wasting comes **after** it in the denudation sequence.
xa: Denudation: **weathering → mass wasting/erosion → transportation → deposition**.
Types: rockfall, slide, **slump** (rotational), debris flow, **creep** (very slow).
Conditions: slopes above **30 degrees**, weak rock, bare slopes; most at risk: **Himalaya and North-East**.

11.s: Which is the correct order of stages in Davis’s cycle of erosion?
11.x: Davis proposed the sequence of youth, maturity and old age, culminating in a low, almost flat peneplain.
11.tq: Arrange the stages in the standard developmental sequence.
xs: Davis's cycle runs **youth → maturity → old age** — option **(2)** is correct.
**W.M. Davis (1899)**: landscape = **structure + process + stage**.
The cycle ends in a low, almost flat **peneplain** with resistant residual hills called **monadnocks**.
xa: **W. Penck**: landform depends on the **ratio of uplift to erosion**, not time-stages; slopes **retreat parallel**.
⚠ **Davis** = time-stages; **Penck** = uplift vs erosion.
India's **Peninsular plateau** = old peneplain, **rejuvenated in places**.

11.s: Residual hills standing above a peneplain because of their resistance to erosion are known as
11.x: Monadnocks are resistant residual hills that remain above the nearly level surface of a peneplain in Davis’s model.
11.tq: Associate the residual hill term specifically with the peneplain concept.
xs: Resistant residual hills on a peneplain are **monadnocks** — option **(1)** is correct.
They mark the end of the **Davis (1899)** cycle, standing above the near-flat **peneplain**.
**Tors** are granite block piles from weathering; **inselbergs** are residual island-hills of **arid/semi-arid** regions formed by desert erosion.
xa: Davis stages: **youth → maturity → old age**.
⚠ Monadnock (peneplain, Davis cycle) vs **inselberg** (desert erosion by **wind + sheet-wash**).
**Peninsular plateau** = old peneplain, rejuvenated in places.

11.s: Which one of the following is associated with W. Penck’s geomorphic theory?
o: Monadnocks are formed only by glacial deposition
All landscapes pass through identical fixed time stages
A peneplain is always formed before uplift begins
