xa: The **D layer** fades at night.
Within the thermosphere it lies at about **80-400 km**.
Topside ionosphere mapped over India up to **1,000 km** for **NavIC/GPS** accuracy.

14.s: Solar flares and geomagnetic storms may disrupt
o: the composition of the homosphere permanently
the formation of all atmospheric dust
14.x: Solar flares and geomagnetic storms can disturb ionospheric conditions and disrupt GNSS signals.
14.tq: Link the space-weather event with its stated communication and navigation effect.
xs: **Solar flares** and **geomagnetic storms** disrupt **GNSS signals** — option **(3)**.
They disturb the **ionosphere**, through which these signals pass.
xa: Indian researchers mapped the **topside ionosphere** up to **1,000 km** for **NavIC/GPS** accuracy.
The ionosphere **reflects radio waves**.
⚠ **E** = Kennelly-Heaviside; **F** = Appleton.

14.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Ionospheric sub-layer)
A. D layer
B. E layer
C. F layer

List-II (Characteristic)
1. Main reflector of short-wave radio
2. Absorbs medium and long waves
3. Reflects medium-frequency radio waves

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
14.x: The D layer absorbs medium and long waves, the E layer reflects medium-frequency radio waves, and the F layer is the main reflector of short-wave radio.
14.tq: Start from the sure D-layer function and complete the one-to-one matching.
xs: **D layer** (**~60-90 km**) absorbs **medium/long** waves.
**E layer** (**~90-150 km**) reflects **medium-frequency** waves; **F layer** is the **main reflector of short-wave** radio.
xa: ⚠ **E** = **Kennelly-Heaviside**; **F** = **Appleton**.
The **D layer** fades at night.
F splits into **F1, F2** by day.

14.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: E layer — 60–90 km — fades at night
E layer — 150 km upward — main reflector of short waves
F layer — approximately 150 km upward — reflector of short-wave radio
D layer — 90–150 km — reflection of medium-frequency radio waves
14.x: The F layer begins at approximately 150 km upward and is the principal reflector of short-wave radio. The E layer lies around 90–150 km, while the D layer lies around 60–90 km.
14.tq: Check both the height and the communication role to detect swapped sub-layer pairs.
xs: **F layer — ~150 km upward — short-wave reflector** is correct — option **(3)**.
The **E layer** is **~90-150 km** and reflects **medium-frequency** waves — options (1), (2) wrong.
The **D layer** is **~60-90 km** and absorbs medium/long waves — option (4) wrong.
xa: F layer = **Appleton** layer; E = **Kennelly-Heaviside**.
The F layer is key for **long-distance radio**.
D layer **fades at night**.

14.s:
Consider the following statements about the ozone layer:
1. About 90% of atmospheric ozone lies in the stratosphere between about 10 and 50 km.
2. Ozone is densest at about 15-35 km.
3. The ozone layer lies mainly in the mesosphere.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
14.x: Statement 1 is correct: about 90% of ozone lies in the stratosphere, 10-50 km. Statement 2 is correct: it is densest around 15-35 km (normal peak 25-30 km). Statement 3 is wrong: the ozone layer is in the stratosphere, not the mesosphere. Hence 1 and 2 only.
14.tq: Ozone = stratosphere; the mesosphere is where meteors burn.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: about **90%** of ozone lies in the **stratosphere**, **10-50 km**.
Statement 2 correct: it is densest around **15-35 km** (normal peak **25-30 km**).
Statement 3 wrong: the ozone layer is in the **stratosphere**, not the mesosphere.
xa: Ozone is measured in **Dobson Units (DU)**.
An unusually dense pocket was found at **21-23 km** over the North Bay of Bengal.
Ozone layer in the stratosphere: APPSC **2025**.

14.s: The principal protective function of the ozone layer is to absorb:
14.x: Stratospheric ozone absorbs harmful UV-B and UV-C radiation and thereby acts as a shield for life on Earth.
14.tq: Discriminate between ultraviolet radiation and other parts of the electromagnetic spectrum.
xs: The ozone layer absorbs harmful **ultraviolet-B and ultraviolet-C radiation** (**UV-B and UV-C**) — option **(2)**.
It is **Earth's shield** (APPSC **2025**).
xa: **UV-B** causes **skin cancer, cataract, immune suppression, lower crop yield**.
Ozone absorbing UV is why stratospheric temperature **rises**.
⚠ Stratospheric ozone = shield; ground-level ozone = **pollutant**.

14.s:
Excessive exposure to ultraviolet radiation resulting from ozone depletion may cause:
1. Skin cancer
2. Cataract
3. Immune suppression
4. Lower crop yield
Which of the statements given above are correct?
14.x: Increased UV exposure is associated with skin cancer, cataract, immune suppression and reduced crop yield.
14.tq: Test the complete set of consequences rather than selecting only the medical effects.
xs: All four — **1, 2, 3 and 4** — are correct — option **(4)**.
**UV-B** causes **skin cancer, cataract, immune suppression** and **lower crop yield**.
xa: The ozone layer absorbs **UV-B and UV-C**.
Ozone depletion is driven by **halocarbons** (**CFCs, HCFCs**).
The **Montreal Protocol** (**1987**) controls nearly **100** ODS.

14.s: The thickness or total column amount of ozone in the atmosphere is expressed in:
14.x: Ozone concentration in an atmospheric column is measured in Dobson Units (DU).
14.tq: Discriminate among scientific units by their measured quantity.
xs: Ozone is measured in **Dobson Units (DU)** — option **(2)**.
The DU expresses the ozone in the **stratospheric** shield, which absorbs **UV-B and UV-C**.
xa: About **90%** of ozone lies in the stratosphere, **10-50 km**.
Normal ozone peak: **25-30 km**.
Antarctic ozone hole **2025** peaked at just over **21 million sq km**.

14.s: Which sequence correctly represents the ozone–oxygen or Chapman cycle?
o: O2 is split by UV, oxygen atoms combine with O2 to form O3, and O3 absorbs UV and dissociates
O3 combines with nitrogen to form O2, which is then converted into methane
O2 absorbs infrared radiation and directly forms carbon dioxide
Ozone is formed only by the action of pollutants in the troposphere
14.x: Ultraviolet radiation splits O2 into free oxygen atoms; these combine with O2 to form O3, which absorbs UV and can split back into oxygen molecules and atoms.
14.tq: Follow the chemical sequence from initiating radiation to the regenerated products.
xs: **Chapman cycle**: **O2 + UV → O + O**; **O + O2 → O3**; **O3 absorbs UV** and splits back — option **(1)**.
It is a **natural balance** of ozone forming and splitting.
Ground-level ozone from **pollutants** is a different thing — option (4).
xa: The cycle runs in the **stratosphere**, densest at **15-35 km**.
**Halocarbons** release **chlorine and bromine** that destroy ozone faster than it forms.
Unit: **Dobson Unit (DU)**.

14.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes stratospheric ozone from ground-level ozone?
o: Ground-level ozone protects living organisms from UV-B, whereas stratospheric ozone is a pollutant
Stratospheric ozone is formed from NOx and VOCs near the surface, whereas ground-level ozone is formed naturally in the polar vortex
Stratospheric ozone absorbs harmful UV-B, whereas ground-level ozone is a pollutant formed from NOx and VOCs in sunlight
Both forms are produced only by volcanic eruptions
14.x: Stratospheric ozone provides UV-B protection. Ground-level ozone is a pollutant produced through reactions involving nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds in sunlight.
14.tq: Separate two similar terms by location, formation and environmental effect.
xs: **Stratospheric ozone** absorbs **UV-B**; **ground-level ozone** is a **pollutant** from **NOx + VOCs** in sunlight — option **(3)**.
Option (1) swaps the two roles.
Ground-level ozone is part of **photochemical smog**.
xa: ⚠ Stratospheric ozone = shield; ground-level ozone = pollutant.
Heatwaves push ground-level ozone up in **north-west India** and the **Indo-Gangetic Plain**.
Ground-level ozone is a **secondary** pollutant.

14.s: Which of the following is the primary cause of stratospheric ozone depletion?
o: Oxygen combining with hydrogen in the mesosphere
Halocarbons releasing chlorine and bromine atoms
14.x: Halocarbons such as CFCs and HCFCs release chlorine and bromine atoms that destroy ozone faster than it can form.
14.tq: Identify the responsible chemical group and the destructive atoms released.
xs: **Halocarbons** releasing **chlorine and bromine** atoms are the primary cause — option **(4)** (APPSC **2023**).
Examples: **CFCs, HCFCs**; they destroy ozone **faster than it forms**.
xa: **CFCs**: refrigeration, ACs, **aerosols**, foam blowing.
**Methyl bromide**: agricultural fumigant.
**Carbon tetrachloride, methyl chloroform**: solvents.

14.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched with its use?
14.x: CFCs were used in refrigeration, air conditioners, aerosols and foam blowing. Halons were used in fire extinguishers, while methyl bromide was used as an agricultural fumigant.
14.tq: Start from the sure substance–use pair and eliminate the swapped applications.
xs: **CFCs — refrigeration and aerosol** uses is correct — option **(1)**.
CFCs were used in **refrigeration, ACs, aerosols, foam blowing**.
**Methyl bromide** was an **agricultural fumigant**, not a fire extinguisher — option (3) wrong.
**Carbon tetrachloride** is a **solvent** that destroys ozone — option (4) wrong.
xa: **HCFCs**: transitional CFC substitute.
India was the first developing country to fully phase out **HCFC-141b** in rigid foam.
**Kigali Amendment** (**2016**) phases down **HFCs**.

14.s: The ozone hole refers to seasonal thinning of ozone mainly over Antarctica during:
14.x: The Antarctic ozone hole develops mainly from August to November, during the Southern Hemisphere spring, aided by polar stratospheric clouds.
14.tq: Use the seasonal and hemispheric clue to reject the opposite-season options.
xs: The ozone hole forms over **Antarctica** from **August to November** (**Aug-Nov**, southern spring) — option **(4)**.
It is helped by **polar stratospheric clouds**.
xa: It came into focus in **1985** (older notes: **1983**).
**2025** hole peaked at just over **21 million sq km** and closed early.
The **2006 record** was **29 million sq km**.

14.s: The Antarctic ozone hole came into scientific focus in:
14.x: The ozone hole came into focus in 1985; some older accounts cite 1983, but 1985 is the stated reference year here.
14.tq: Distinguish the standard reference year from an older alternative date.
xs: The ozone hole came into focus in **1985** — option **(3)**.
⚠ Older notes give **1983** — option (2) is the trap.
xa: **Vienna Convention** was also **1985** (framework: research, monitoring).
**Montreal Protocol**: **1987**.

14.s: Which one of the following correctly compares CFCs and HFCs?
o: CFCs spare ozone, whereas HFCs destroy ozone and have no warming effect.
CFCs destroy stratospheric ozone and are potent greenhouse gases; HFCs spare ozone but have high global-warming potential.
Both CFCs and HFCs destroy stratospheric ozone to the same extent.
Neither CFCs nor HFCs has any significant effect on the atmosphere.
14.x: CFCs deplete stratospheric ozone and act as potent greenhouse gases. HFCs do not harm ozone but have high global-warming potential.
14.tq: Use the contrasting ozone and warming effects to separate the two confusable groups.
xs: **CFCs** destroy **stratospheric ozone** and are potent GHGs; **HFCs** spare ozone but have **high GWP** — option **(2)**.
CFCs have a **GWP 1,000-23,000** and make up **15%** of the enhanced effect.
xa: HFCs **replaced CFCs**.
**Kigali Amendment** (**2016**, in force **2019**) cuts HFCs by **80-85%**.
It could avoid up to **0.5°C** of warming by **2100**.

14.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the Montreal Protocol is correct?
o: It was adopted in 1991 to provide only financial aid to developing countries
It was adopted in 2016 to phase down HFCs
It was adopted in 1987 and phases out nearly 100 ozone-depleting substances
It was adopted in 1985 to establish only a research framework
14.x: The Montreal Protocol was adopted in 1987 and controls or phases out nearly 100 ozone-depleting substances. The Vienna Convention, Multilateral Fund and Kigali Amendment have the other functions and dates.
14.tq: Use the treaty’s year and principal action together to avoid confusing neighbouring instruments.
xs: The **Montreal Protocol** was adopted in **1987** and phases out / controls nearly **100 ozone-depleting substances** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It is universally ratified and is called the **most successful environmental treaty**.
**1985** is the **Vienna Convention** (only a framework for research and monitoring); **2016** is the **Kigali Amendment** (phase-down of **HFCs**).
xa: ⚠ Trap: **1985** = Vienna (framework); **1987** = Montreal (ODS); **2016** = Kigali (HFCs).
Montreal Protocol parties: all **197** UN member countries; some notes say **198** (197 states plus the **EU**).
Main ODS and uses: **CFCs** (refrigeration, ACs, aerosols), **HCFCs** (transitional substitute), **methyl bromide** (agricultural fumigant), **carbon tetrachloride** (solvent).
**India Cooling Action Plan** came in **Mar 2019** with a horizon of **2037-38**.

14.s: The Kigali Amendment, adopted in 2016, primarily seeks to:
o: Create the first ozone research framework
14.x: The Kigali Amendment, adopted in Kigali, Rwanda, in 2016, provides for the phase-down of HFCs, which are ozone-safe but have high global-warming potential.
14.tq: Distinguish HFC phase-down from the Montreal Protocol’s broader ODS phase-out.
xs: The **Kigali Amendment** (**2016**, Kigali, **Rwanda**) seeks to **phase down HFCs** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**HFCs** replaced CFCs: they do **not harm ozone** but have a **high global-warming potential**, so they are cut for climate reasons.
The research framework was the **Vienna Convention (1985)**; the ozone measurement unit is the **Dobson Unit (DU)**, not a treaty.
xa: Kigali came into force in **2019**; it cuts HFCs by **80-85%** — by **2036** (developed) vs **late 2040s** (developing).
It could avoid up to **0.5°C** of warming by **2100**.
⚠ **1987** Montreal Protocol = ozone-depleting substances; **2016** Kigali = HFCs (ozone-safe).
**CFCs** have a GWP of **1,000-23,000** and make up **15%** of the enhanced greenhouse effect.

14.s:
Consider the following statements about the Kigali Amendment:
1. It aims to cut HFCs by 80-85%, by 2036 for developed countries and by the late 2040s for developing countries.
2. It could avoid up to 0.5 deg C of warming by 2100.
3. It entered into force in 2016.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
14.x: Statement 1 is correct: HFC cuts of 80-85% by 2036 (developed) and late 2040s (developing). Statement 2 is correct: it could avoid up to 0.5 deg C by 2100. Statement 3 is wrong: it was adopted in 2016 and entered into force in 2019. Hence 1 and 2 only.
14.tq: Kigali: adopted 2016, in force 2019 - don't mix the two.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: Kigali cuts **HFCs by 80-85%** — by **2036** for developed and the **late 2040s** for developing countries.
Statement 2 correct: it could avoid up to **0.5°C** of warming by **2100**.
Statement 3 wrong: it was **adopted in 2016** (Kigali, Rwanda) but **entered into force in 2019**.
xa: **HFCs** replaced CFCs; ozone-safe but **high GWP**, hence a climate-driven phase-down.
Parent treaty: **Montreal Protocol (1987)**, controlling nearly **100** ODS; framework: **Vienna Convention (1985)**.
India's **India Cooling Action Plan** (**Mar 2019**) runs to **2037-38**.

14.s: India's phase-out of HCFC-141b in rigid foam had which of the following outcomes?
o: It was the first such phase-out among developing countries, with a 44% cut against a 35% target by January 2020.
It concerned HFC-134a in refrigeration and achieved no measurable reduction.
It was the first phase-out among developed countries, with a 35% cut against a 44% target by January 2020.
It achieved a 15% cut against a 10% target by January 2015.
14.x: India was the first developing country to phase out HCFC-141b in rigid foam and achieved a 44% reduction against a 35% target by January 2020.
14.tq: Check the country status, chemical use, target and achieved percentage together.
xs: India was the **first developing country** to fully phase out **HCFC-141b** in **rigid foam**, cutting HCFCs **44%** against a **35%** target by **January 2020** — option **(1)**.
The phase-out concerned **HCFC-141b** (a transitional CFC substitute), not HFCs, and India was a **developing**, not developed, country.
xa: **HCFCs** were the **transitional substitute** for CFCs under the **Montreal Protocol (1987)**.
**India Cooling Action Plan**: **Mar 2019**, horizon **2037-38**.
**HFCs** (ozone-safe, high GWP) are being phased down under the **Kigali Amendment (2016)**.
The **Montreal Protocol** controls nearly **100** ODS and is universally ratified.

14.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes the Vienna Convention from the Montreal Protocol?
o: The Vienna Convention provides a framework for research, monitoring and cooperation, whereas the Montreal Protocol is legally binding for phasing out ODS.
The Vienna Convention legally bans all greenhouse gases, whereas the Montreal Protocol concerns biodiversity conservation.
The Vienna Convention provides financial assistance only, whereas the Montreal Protocol conducts ozone monitoring.
Both instruments have identical objectives and identical legal mechanisms.
14.x: The Vienna Convention, adopted in 1985, established a framework for research, monitoring and cooperation. The Montreal Protocol, adopted in 1987, created legally binding ODS phase-out measures.
14.tq: Compare the nature and legal function of two closely connected international instruments.
xs: The **Vienna Convention** is a **framework for research, monitoring and cooperation**, while the **Montreal Protocol** is the legally binding instrument to **phase out ODS** — option **(1)**.
Vienna came in **1985**; Montreal in **1987**, controlling nearly **100** ozone-depleting substances.
Neither treaty deals with all greenhouse gases or biodiversity; their objectives are different, not identical.
xa: ⚠ **1985** = Vienna (framework); **1987** = Montreal (ODS); **2016** = Kigali (HFCs).
Montreal is **universally ratified** — the **most successful environmental treaty**; **197** UN member parties.
The **ozone hole** came into focus in **1985** (older notes give **1983**), the same year as Vienna.
Primary cause of depletion: **halocarbons** (CFCs, HCFCs) releasing **chlorine and bromine** atoms.

14.s: Meteorites generally burn up on entering the atmosphere in the:
14.x: Most meteors burn up in the mesosphere because of friction with atmospheric particles.
14.tq: Use the direct phenomenon–layer association and avoid confusing it with the ionosphere.
xs: Meteorites burn up in the **mesosphere** — option **(2)** (APPSC-G2 **2025**).
The mesosphere runs from about **50** to **80 km**; temperature falls to about **-100°C** at 80 km, making it the **coldest layer**.
**Troposphere** = weather and clouds; **stratosphere** = ozone layer; **exosphere** = outermost, extremely rarefied layer merging into space.
xa: ⚠ Not the thermosphere/ionosphere — exam angle explicitly says **mesosphere**.
Top of the mesosphere = **mesopause** (~**80 km**).
Temperature trend: falls (troposphere) → rises (stratosphere) → **falls (mesosphere)** → rises (thermosphere).
**Auroras and airglow** occur in the **thermosphere** (ionosphere).

14.s: Auroras and airglow are phenomena primarily associated with the:
14.x: Auroras and airglow occur mainly in the thermosphere, particularly in the ionospheric region.
14.tq: Distinguish upper-atmosphere light phenomena from lower-atmosphere weather phenomena.
xs: **Auroras and airglow** occur in the **thermosphere** (its **ionosphere**) — option **(3)**.
Solar **UV and X-rays** strip electrons from atoms; the resulting **charged particles** produce auroras and airglow.
**Stratosphere** holds the ozone layer, **troposphere** all weather, and **mesosphere** is where meteors burn up.
xa: The thermosphere begins above ~**80 km** and extends to ~**600 km**; temperature **rises rapidly** with height.
The **ISS** orbits at ~**400 km**, in the thermosphere.
Ionospheric layers: **D** (~60-90 km), **E / Kennelly-Heaviside** (~90-150 km), **F / Appleton** (~150-400 km).
The ionosphere **reflects radio waves** — key for long-distance communication.

14.s: Jet aircraft generally cruise near the lower stratosphere because that region is:
o: The region where meteors burn up
Free of clouds and comparatively stable
The coldest part of the atmosphere
14.x: Jet aircraft commonly cruise near the base of the stratosphere because the air is relatively calm and free from most clouds and turbulence.
14.tq: Apply the layer’s stability and cloud conditions to an aviation situation.
xs: Jet aircraft cruise in the **lower stratosphere** because it is **free of clouds and turbulence** — calm, stable air — option **(3)**.
The stratosphere has a temperature **inversion** (ozone absorbs UV), so air is stable and lacks vertical mixing.
Meteors burn up in the **mesosphere**, which is also the **coldest layer**; clouds and turbulence belong to the **troposphere**.
xa: The stratosphere runs from the **tropopause** to ~**50 km** and holds the **ozone layer**.
The calm stratosphere also suits **high-altitude balloons**.
⚠ Some notes put commercial aircraft in the **troposphere**; the standard exam answer is the **lower stratosphere**.
The **tropopause** is ~**8 km** at the poles and ~**18 km** at the equator.

14.s:
With reference to Mission SANA, consider the following statements:
1. It is India's first indigenous stratospheric super-pressure balloon.
2. It was launched from Vijayawada.
3. Its objective includes climate tracking.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
14.x: Mission SANA is India's first indigenous stratospheric super-pressure balloon, launched from Vijayawada for climate tracking.
14.tq: Use the coded statement method and verify each statement independently before selecting the combination.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4)** (**1, 2 and 3**).
**Mission SANA** by **Red Balloon Aerospace** is India's first indigenous stratospheric **super-pressure balloon**.
It was launched from **Vijayawada** into the stratosphere for **climate tracking** (**May 2026**).
xa: AP angle: **World Ozone Day** (**16 Sep**) and Mission SANA from **Vijayawada**.
The **stratosphere** (tropopause to ~**50 km**) has calm, stable air — ideal for **high-altitude balloons**.
On World Ozone Day **2026**, Deputy CM **K. Pawan Kalyan** called for collective action to protect the ozone layer.

14.s: Indian researchers developed an integrated method to map which atmospheric region over India up to a height of 1,000 km, with implications for NavIC and GPS accuracy?
14.x: The method maps the topside ionosphere over India up to 1,000 km and is intended to improve NavIC and GPS accuracy.
14.tq: Identify the exact atmospheric region and match it with the stated technological application.
xs: Indian researchers built the first integrated method to map the **topside ionosphere** over India up to **1,000 km** — option **(2)**.
The mapping is meant to improve **NavIC/GPS accuracy** (PIB, **9 Jul 2026**).
xa: The ionosphere extends from about **60 km to over 1,000 km**; within the thermosphere, about **80-400 km**.
It forms when solar **UV and X-rays** strip electrons from atoms; it **expands by day and shrinks at night**.
**Solar flares and geomagnetic storms** disrupt **GNSS** signals.
⚠ **E** layer = **Kennelly-Heaviside**; **F** layer = **Appleton** (main short-wave reflector).

14.s:
Consider the following statements regarding ground-level ozone in India:
1. Heatwaves can increase ground-level ozone concentrations.
2. North-west India and the Indo-Gangetic Plain are among the regions affected by this phenomenon.
3. Ground-level ozone is necessarily beneficial because all ozone protects the stratosphere from ultraviolet radiation.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
14.x: Heatwaves can raise ground-level ozone in north-west India and the Indo-Gangetic Plain. Statement 3 is false because the beneficial protective role is associated with stratospheric ozone, not necessarily ground-level ozone.
14.tq: Separate the beneficial role of stratospheric ozone from the harmful effects of ground-level ozone.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statements 1 and 2: **heatwaves** push up ground-level ozone in **north-west India** and the **Indo-Gangetic Plain**.
Statement 3 wrong: **ground-level (tropospheric) ozone** is a **"bad" secondary pollutant**; the protective shield is **stratospheric** ozone.
xa: Ground-level ozone forms from **NOx + VOCs in sunlight** and is part of **photochemical smog**.
⚠ Stratospheric ozone = **shield**; ground-level ozone = **pollutant**.
Stratospheric ozone absorbs harmful **UV-B and UV-C**; it lies at **10-50 km** (about **90%** of ozone).
Ozone is measured in **Dobson Units (DU)**.

14.s:
Consider the following statements about the Antarctic ozone hole in 2025:
1. It peaked at just over 21 million square kilometres.
2. It closed earlier than usual.
3. Its extent exceeded the 2006 record of 29 million square kilometres.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
14.x: The Antarctic ozone hole in 2025 peaked at just over 21 million square kilometres and closed early. Statement 3 is false because this was below the 2006 record of 29 million square kilometres.
14.tq: Compare the reported figure with the historical record and identify the reversed comparison.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
The **2025 Antarctic ozone hole** peaked at just over **21 million sq km** and **closed early**.
Statement 3 wrong: it stayed **below the 2006 record** of **29 million sq km**.
xa: The ozone hole is a seasonal thinning over **Antarctica**, **Aug-Nov** (southern spring), helped by **polar stratospheric clouds**.
It came into focus in **1985** (older notes give **1983**).
Cause: **halocarbons** (CFCs, HCFCs) releasing **chlorine and bromine** atoms.
An unusually dense **ozone pocket** was found at **21-23 km** over the **North Bay of Bengal** (16 Aug 2026).

14.s: Which one of the following best explains the greenhouse effect in relation to atmospheric radiation?
o: The atmosphere is transparent to incoming solar radiation but opaque to outgoing terrestrial radiation.
The atmosphere is opaque to incoming solar radiation and transparent to outgoing terrestrial radiation.
The atmosphere absorbs both incoming solar radiation and outgoing terrestrial radiation completely.
The atmosphere reflects all incoming solar radiation and absorbs none of the terrestrial radiation.
14.x: The atmosphere is relatively transparent to incoming solar radiation but absorbs outgoing terrestrial radiation, thereby contributing to the greenhouse effect.
14.tq: Apply the radiation-flow concept by distinguishing incoming solar radiation from outgoing terrestrial radiation.
xs: The atmosphere is **transparent to incoming solar radiation** but **opaque to outgoing terrestrial radiation** — that is the **greenhouse effect**, option **(1)**.
**CO2** is transparent to incoming sunlight but **absorbs outgoing terrestrial radiation**; **water vapour** keeps in earth's heat (**blanket effect**).
The atmosphere neither absorbs all radiation nor reflects all incoming sunlight, so options **(2)-(4)** are wrong.
xa: **Water vapour** is the **most abundant greenhouse gas**; up to **4%** in warm, wet tropics.
CO2 rose **3.5 ppm** to **423.9 ppm** in **2024** — **152%** of pre-industrial (WMO Greenhouse Gas Bulletin 2025).
**CFCs** are about **1,000 times** more heat-absorbent than CO2 and make up **15%** of the enhanced effect.

15.s:
Which of the following factors affect the amount of insolation received at a place?
1. Angle of the Sun's rays
2. Length of the day
3. Transparency of the atmosphere
4. Slope and aspect of the land
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
15.x: The angle of the rays, duration of sunshine, atmospheric transparency, and slope and aspect of land all influence insolation.
15.tq: Test the complete list of controlling factors rather than one isolated cause.
xs: All four — **angle of the sun's rays**, **length of day**, **transparency of the atmosphere** and **slope/aspect of land** — affect insolation: option **(4)**.
Vertical rays heat a **smaller area** more intensely; longer days give more hours of sunshine.
Clouds, dust and vapour cut **transparency**; land's **slope and aspect** change how directly the rays strike.
xa: Other factors: **Earth-sun distance** and **land-sea distribution**, altitude.
⚠ **Perihelion** ~**3 Jan** (**147 million km**); **aphelion** ~**4 Jul** (**152 million km**).
Maximum insolation reaches the **subtropical deserts** (least cloud), not the equator.

15.s: Vertical rays of the Sun produce greater heating because they
o: are always blocked by clouds and dust.
travel through a thicker atmosphere and cover a larger area.
heat a smaller surface area with more concentrated energy.
15.x: Vertical rays concentrate solar energy over a smaller area, producing greater heating than oblique rays.
15.tq: Apply the relationship between ray angle, concentration and heating.
xs: **Vertical rays** heat a **smaller surface area**, so the energy is **more concentrated** — option **(3)**.
The **angle of the sun's rays** is the first factor of insolation in the notes.
Vertical rays are not confined to the poles, nor always blocked by clouds; it is oblique rays that spread over a larger area.
xa: Other factors: **length of day**, **transparency of the atmosphere**, **Earth-sun distance**, **land-sea distribution**, slope/aspect.
Hottest latitudes: **sub-tropical deserts (about 20-30° N)** — clear skies + dry air.
Insolation falls towards the **poles** and is **higher over continents** than oceans at the same latitude.

15.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the Earth's aphelion?
15.x: Aphelion occurs around 4 July, when the Earth is approximately 152 million kilometres from the Sun.
15.tq: Use the paired contrast between perihelion and aphelion.
xs: **Aphelion** (Earth farthest from the sun) falls around **4 July** at about **152 million km** — option **(1)**.
Option (2), ~**3 January** at **147 million km**, is **perihelion** (Earth nearest the sun).
xa: ⚠ Perihelion = **Jan**, nearer (**147**); aphelion = **Jul**, farther (**152**) — a common swap trap.
**Earth-sun distance** is one of the factors of insolation, along with **angle of rays** and **length of day**.
The equator receives the **most annual insolation**; the poles the least.

15.s: Which region generally receives the maximum insolation?
o: The equatorial region, because cloud cover is greatest there
The subtropical deserts, because they have relatively little cloud cover
Oceanic regions at all latitudes, because water absorbs all radiation
The polar regions, because summer days are long
15.x: Maximum insolation is generally received in subtropical deserts, where cloud cover is low; it is not necessarily maximum at the Equator.
15.tq: Distinguish maximum received insolation from annual insolation and from day length.
xs: Maximum insolation reaches the **subtropical deserts**, which have **little cloud cover** — option **(2)**.
The **equator** gets the most annual insolation in total, but cloud cuts what reaches its surface, so it is not the maximum.
The **poles** get the least despite **long summer days**; insolation is **higher over continents than oceans**, not the reverse.
xa: Hottest latitudes: **sub-tropical deserts (about 20-30° N)** — **clear skies + dry air**.
**Transparency of the atmosphere** (clouds, dust, vapour) is a key factor of insolation.
⚠ **Aphelion** ~**4 Jul** (152 million km); **perihelion** ~**3 Jan** (147 million km).

15.s: Which one of the following statements about the latitudinal distribution of insolation is correct?
o: Insolation is always higher over oceans than continents at the same latitude.
Insolation generally decreases towards the poles and is higher over continents than oceans at the same latitude.
Insolation increases continuously from the Equator to the poles.
The poles receive the maximum annual insolation because of long summer days.
15.x: Insolation generally declines towards the poles and, at the same latitude, is higher over continents than oceans. Long polar summer days do not give the poles maximum annual insolation.
15.tq: Check both the poleward trend and the land-sea comparison.
xs: Insolation **decreases towards the poles** and is **higher over continents than oceans** at the same latitude — option **(2)**.
So it does not rise from equator to poles, and is not always higher over oceans.
The **poles receive the least** insolation, though they have **long summer days**.
xa: The **equator** receives the **most annual insolation**; maximum at the surface is over **subtropical deserts**.
Land heats and cools faster than water — hence the land-sea contrast.
Surplus heat in the **tropics**, deficit towards the **poles**; winds and currents carry heat **poleward**.

15.s: The highest temperatures on Earth generally occur in the sub-tropical deserts rather than at the Equator because of:
o: The maximum annual rainfall of the deserts
The permanent presence of cold ocean currents
Persistent cloud cover and humid air
15.x: Sub-tropical deserts around 20°–30° N have clear skies and dry air, permitting very high temperatures; the Equator does not record the highest temperatures merely because it receives strong insolation.
15.tq: Apply the cause-effect relationship instead of choosing the latitude with the strongest general insolation.
xs: Sub-tropical deserts (about **20-30° N**) are hottest because of **clear skies and dry air** — option **(4)**.
Little cloud lets maximum insolation reach the surface; the **equator** has more cloud.
Deserts have scant rainfall, and **cloud cover and humid air** describe the equator, not deserts.
xa: World hottest: **Death Valley**, **56.7°C**; world coldest: **Vostok**, **-89.2°C**.
India coldest: **Dras** (Ladakh), **-45°C** (**1908**).
AP hottest: **Rentachintala** (Palnadu), above **47°C**; AP coldest: **Lambasingi** — the "**Kashmir of AP**".

15.s: Which one of the following correctly describes insolation?
o: Vertical transfer of heat by rising air
Horizontal transfer of heat by moving air
Direct heating of the atmosphere by outgoing long-wave radiation
Direct heating by incoming short-wave solar radiation
15.x: Insolation is the direct heating received from incoming short-wave solar radiation.
15.tq: Use the precise mechanism rather than confusing insolation with atmospheric heat transfer.
xs: **Insolation** is **direct heating by incoming short-wave solar radiation** — option **(4)**.
**Vertical** transfer by rising air = **convection**; **horizontal** transfer by moving air = **advection**.
Outgoing long-wave heat is **terrestrial radiation**, the main source that heats the atmosphere.
xa: APPSC-G2 **2023** matched: **Advection - horizontal**, **Convection - vertical**, **Insolation - direct**, **Conduction - lower layers**.
The sun emits **short-wave** radiation; earth re-emits **long-wave infra-red** (**8,000-25,000 nm**).
Planetary **albedo** is about **35%** of insolation.

15.s:
Consider the following statements regarding atmospheric heating:
1. Conduction heats the lower layers of air in contact with the warm ground.
2. Convection involves the vertical transfer of heat by rising warm air.
3. Advection involves the horizontal transfer of heat by wind.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
15.x: All three statements correctly describe conduction, convection and advection respectively.
15.tq: Match each process with its direction of heat transfer before selecting the coded combination.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4)** (**1, 2 and 3**).
**Conduction** heats the **lower layers** of air in contact with the warm ground.
**Convection** = **vertical** transfer by rising warm air; **advection** = **horizontal** transfer by wind.
xa: APPSC-G2 **2023** matched these: Advection - horizontal, Convection - vertical, **Insolation - direct**, Conduction - lower layers.
Convection is **confined to the troposphere**; the **Loo** of north India is an example of **advection**.
**Terrestrial radiation** needs **no medium** and is the main source heating the atmosphere.

15.s: The Loo, a hot wind of northern India, is an example of which of the following processes?
15.x: The Loo transfers heat horizontally through moving air and is therefore an example of advection.
15.tq: Identify the direction of movement in the example before naming the process.
xs: The **Loo** of north India is an example of **advection** — **horizontal** transfer of heat by wind — option **(2)**.
**Convection** is vertical transfer; **conduction** heats air in contact with the ground; **radiation** is via electromagnetic waves.
xa: APPSC-G2 **2023** match: **Advection - horizontal**, **Convection - vertical**, **Insolation - direct**, **Conduction - lower layers**.
Convection: heated air becomes **less dense and rises**, cooler air sinks.
**Terrestrial radiation** (long-wave) is the **main source** heating the atmosphere.

15.s: Which one of the following statements regarding convection is correct?
o: It is the transfer of heat by electromagnetic waves without a medium.
It is particle-to-particle heat transfer that works best in gases.
It is the vertical transfer caused by heated air becoming less dense and rising, and is confined to the troposphere.
It is the horizontal transfer of heat by wind and occurs mainly in the stratosphere.
15.x: Convection is vertical movement of heat: warm, less-dense air rises and cooler air sinks. In the atmosphere it is confined to the troposphere.
15.tq: Separate vertical convection from horizontal advection and wave-based radiation.
xs: **Convection** is **vertical** transfer: heated air becomes **less dense and rises**, cooler air sinks; it is **confined to the troposphere** — option **(3)**.
Transfer by electromagnetic waves without a medium is **radiation**; particle-to-particle contact is **conduction** (best in **solids**, not gases).
Horizontal transfer by wind is **advection** (e.g. the **Loo**).
xa: APPSC-G2 **2023**: **Convection - vertical**, **Advection - horizontal**, Insolation - direct, Conduction - lower layers.
The troposphere's thickness peaks at the **equator**, where strong heating drives convection currents.
Normal lapse rate: **6.5 °C/km**.

15.s: Conduction works most effectively in solids because it involves
15.x: Conduction transfers heat through direct particle-to-particle contact and is most effective in solids.
15.tq: Use the defining physical mechanism to distinguish conduction from convection and radiation.
xs: **Conduction** works by **particle-to-particle contact**, so it is best in **solids** — option **(4)**.
In the atmosphere it heats the **lower layers** of air in contact with the warm ground.
Electromagnetic waves = **radiation**; vertical movement = **convection**; horizontal winds = **advection**.
xa: APPSC-G2 **2023**: **Conduction - lower layers**, **Insolation - direct**, Convection - vertical, Advection - horizontal.
Air is heated **from below** by terrestrial radiation, not directly by the sun.
The **Loo** is an example of **advection**.

15.s: Albedo of a surface refers to the
o: share of incoming radiation reflected by the surface
amount of heat stored below the surface
rate at which terrestrial radiation is emitted
amount of moisture absorbed by the surface
15.x: Albedo is the proportion or share of incoming radiation that a surface reflects.
15.tq: Use the exact definition and distinguish reflection from absorption and emission.
xs: **Albedo** is the **share of incoming radiation a surface reflects** — option **(1)**.
Heat storage, emission of terrestrial radiation and moisture absorption are not albedo.
xa: Ranking: **fresh snow** (highest, APPSC-G1 **2019**) > sand > grass > forest > water.
Fresh snow **80-90%**; water (sun high) **below 10%**.
**Planetary albedo** ≈ **35%** (35 of 100 units).
**Black carbon** on snow cuts albedo; melting ice exposes dark ocean (**ice-albedo feedback**).

15.s: Which one of the following sequences correctly represents the surfaces in descending order of albedo?
o: Fresh snow, sand, grass, forest, water
Fresh snow, grass, sand, water, forest
Water, forest, grass, sand, fresh snow
Sand, fresh snow, forest, grass, water
15.x: The descending albedo sequence is fresh snow, sand, grass, forest and water, with fresh snow reflecting the most and water generally the least.
15.tq: Rank the surfaces from highest reflection to lowest reflection.
xs: Descending albedo: **fresh snow > sand > grass > forest > water** — option **(1)**.
**Fresh snow** reflects most (**80-90%**); **water** with sun high reflects least (**below 10%**).
Dry sand **20-40%** sits above grass **20-25%**, so options placing grass above sand are wrong.
xa: Fresh snow as highest albedo was asked in APPSC-G1 **2019**.
Crop land albedo: **15-25%**.
Clouds: **high, thin** = warming; **low, thick** = cooling.

15.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the effect of clouds on the radiation balance?
o: High, thin clouds tend to trap heat, while low, thick clouds tend to reflect sunlight and produce cooling.
High, thin clouds absorb all incoming short-wave radiation and prevent surface heating.
High, thin clouds generally cool the surface, while low, thick clouds warm it.
Both high, thin and low, thick clouds always produce identical effects.
15.x: High, thin clouds tend to trap outgoing heat and cause warming, whereas low, thick clouds reflect more incoming sunlight and cause cooling.
15.tq: Compare the altitude, thickness and contrasting radiation effects of the two cloud types.
xs: **High, thin clouds trap heat** (warming) while **low, thick clouds reflect sunlight** (cooling) — option **(1)**.
Option (3) reverses the two; the two cloud types do not have identical effects.
xa: ⚠ **High thin = warming; low thick = cooling**.
Of 100 units of insolation, clouds reflect **27**; total reflected **35** (planetary albedo).
**Clear nights** lose more heat; **cloudy nights** stay warmer as clouds send heat back.

15.s: Melting of ice can intensify warming because it
o: converts long-wave radiation into short-wave radiation
increases the albedo of the exposed ocean
exposes a darker ocean surface that absorbs more heat
prevents the ocean from absorbing solar radiation
15.x: Melting ice exposes dark ocean water, which has a lower albedo and absorbs more heat, producing a positive ice-albedo feedback.
15.tq: Trace the cause-effect chain from surface change to albedo, absorption and warming.
xs: Melting ice **exposes a darker ocean surface that absorbs more heat** — option **(3)** — the **ice-albedo feedback**.
Dark water has **lower albedo** (**below 10%**) than ice and snow (**80-90%**), so it does not raise albedo or stop absorption.
xa: The Arctic has warmed at least **2°C** and warms **3-4 times** faster than the global average (Apr **2025**).
**Black carbon** on snow also cuts albedo.
Albedo ranking: **fresh snow** > sand > grass > forest > **water**.

15.s: According to recent assessments (Apr 2025), the Arctic is warming at about what rate compared with the global average?
15.x: The Arctic has warmed by at least 2 deg C and is warming 3-4 times faster than the global average (older estimates said about twice), driven by the ice-albedo feedback in which melting ice exposes dark ocean. It is not slower, equal or ten times faster.
15.tq: Arctic amplification: 3-4x global rate (older: ~2x).
xs: The Arctic is warming about **3-4 times faster** than the global average (Apr **2025**) — option **(1)**.
It has warmed at least **2°C**; older notes said about **twice** as fast.
Driver: the **ice-albedo feedback** — melting ice exposes dark ocean that absorbs more heat.
xa: **Black carbon** on snow cuts albedo, adding to warming.
Global land temperature is up **1.59 °C** since pre-industrial (UNEP Emissions Gap **2025**).
India's annual mean is up **0.7 °C** since **1900**; slower partly because of **Arctic amplification** and aerosol masking.

15.s: In the radiation budget described for the Earth, the planetary albedo is approximately
15.x: Approximately 35 of every 100 units received at the top of the atmosphere are reflected back to space, giving an overall planetary albedo of about 35 percent.
15.tq: Distinguish the total reflected share from the separate contributions of clouds, scattering and snow or ice.
xs: The **planetary albedo** is about **35 percent** — **35 units of 100** — option **(3)**.
The 35 units: **clouds 27**, **scattering 6**, **snow/ice 2**.
**14** units are absorbed by the atmosphere and **51** by the surface; **27** is clouds alone.
xa: The surface returns all **51** units as terrestrial radiation, so earth neither warms nor cools overall.
Of the 51: **17** go straight to space, **34** are absorbed by the atmosphere.
The atmosphere sends **48** (14 + 34) to space.

15.s: Out of 100 units of insolation received at the top of the atmosphere, which of the following distribution is correct?
o: 14 reflected, 35 absorbed by the atmosphere and 51 absorbed by the surface
51 reflected, 35 absorbed by the atmosphere and 14 absorbed by the surface
35 reflected, 51 absorbed by the atmosphere and 14 absorbed by the surface
35 reflected, 14 absorbed by the atmosphere and 51 absorbed by the surface
15.x: Of 100 units, 35 are reflected to space, 14 are absorbed by the atmosphere and 51 are absorbed by the Earth's surface.
15.tq: Reconstruct the three-part heat-budget distribution rather than using one isolated figure.
xs: Of 100 units: **35 reflected**, **14 absorbed by the atmosphere**, **51 absorbed by the surface** — option **(4)**.
Reflected 35 = clouds **27** + scattering **6** + snow/ice **2**.
xa: Earth radiates **51** units: **17** straight to space, **34** absorbed by the atmosphere.
Of the 34: **6** direct, **9** convection/turbulence, **19** latent heat of condensation.
Atmosphere sends **48** (14 + 34) to space: **35 + 17 + 48 = 100** balanced.

15.s:
Consider the following statements about the Earth's heat budget (100 units of insolation):
1. Of the 35 units reflected, 27 are reflected by clouds.
2. Of the 51 units radiated by the earth, 17 go straight to space and 34 are absorbed by the atmosphere.
3. Latent heat of condensation accounts for 9 of the 34 units absorbed by the atmosphere.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
15.x: Statement 1 is correct: 27 by clouds, 6 by scattering, 2 by snow/ice. Statement 2 is correct: 17 to space, 34 absorbed. Statement 3 is wrong: latent heat of condensation is 19 units; convection/turbulence is 9 and direct absorption 6. Hence 1 and 2 only.
15.tq: 35-14-51 in; 17-34 out; 6-9-19 into the air.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: of **35** reflected, clouds **27**, scattering **6**, snow/ice **2**.
Statement 2 correct: of **51** radiated, **17** go to space and **34** are absorbed by the atmosphere.
Statement 3 wrong: **latent heat of condensation** = **19** units; **9** is convection/turbulence and **6** direct absorption.
xa: The atmosphere sends **48** (14 + 34) units to space.
Planetary albedo ≈ **35%**; the surface absorbs **51**, the atmosphere **14**.
Surplus in the **tropics**, deficit towards the **poles**; heat moves **poleward**.

15.s: Which one of the following statements about the distribution of the Earth's heat budget is correct?
o: There is a heat surplus towards the poles and a deficit in the tropics.
The tropics have a heat surplus, while the poles have a heat deficit; winds and ocean currents transport heat poleward.
The tropics and poles receive exactly equal net radiation throughout the year.
Ocean currents transport heat only from the poles towards the tropics.
15.x: The tropics have a surplus of heat and the poles a deficit. Atmospheric winds and ocean currents carry heat poleward.
15.tq: Test the direction of the equator-to-pole heat imbalance and its transport mechanism.
xs: The **tropics have a surplus** and the **poles a deficit**; **winds and ocean currents carry heat poleward** — option **(2)**.
So options claiming a polar surplus, equal net radiation, or currents moving heat only equatorward are wrong.
xa: Overall the surface returns all **51** absorbed units, so earth neither warms nor cools.
Oceans took up a record **+23 zettajoules** of heat in **2025** (vs **+16 ZJ** in 2024) = ~**90%** of excess heat.
India's warming is slower partly because of **poleward heat transfer**.

15.s:
Assertion (A): The atmosphere is heated mainly from below by terrestrial radiation.
Reason (R): The atmosphere is relatively transparent to incoming short-wave solar radiation but absorbs outgoing long-wave terrestrial radiation.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
15.x: Both statements are true, and the selective absorption of outgoing long-wave radiation explains why the atmosphere is heated mainly from below.
15.tq: Check whether the reason directly explains the stated atmospheric heating mechanism.
xs: **Both A and R are true** and **R is the correct explanation** of A — option **(1)**.
A: the atmosphere is heated mainly **from below, by terrestrial radiation**.
R: it is **transparent to short-wave** sunlight but **opaque to long-wave** terrestrial radiation — which is why heating is from below.
xa: ⚠ Trap: "heated more by incoming solar radiation" is **wrong**; greenhouse gases absorb long waves is **right** (UPSC **2024**).
Earth re-emits **long-wave infra-red** (**8,000-25,000 nm**), absorbed by **CO2 and water vapour**.
Without the atmosphere: about **-18 °C** instead of **+15 °C**.

15.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: Methane — paddy fields, wetlands, livestock and landfills
Nitrous oxide — ocean tides and volcanic waves
Carbon dioxide — fossil fuels, deforestation and cement
15.x: Nitrous oxide is associated mainly with fertilisers and the burning of coal or biomass, not ocean tides and volcanic waves.
15.tq: Find the mismatched source while retaining the correctly paired greenhouse gases.
xs: **Nitrous oxide — ocean tides and volcanic waves** is wrongly matched — option **(3)**.
N2O's main sources are **fertilisers** and **burning coal/biomass**; it gives ~**5%** of the greenhouse effect.
The rest are correct: **methane** — paddy, wetlands, livestock, landfills; **CFCs** — refrigeration, aerosols; **CO2** — fossil fuels, deforestation, cement.
xa: Methane is called "**marsh gas**".

15.s: Which one of the following gases is the most abundant greenhouse gas and acts importantly as a feedback in the climate system?
15.x: Water vapour is the most abundant greenhouse gas and functions importantly as a climate feedback.
15.tq: Distinguish abundance from the percentage contribution estimates of the other gases.
xs: **Water vapour** is the **most abundant greenhouse gas** and acts as a **feedback** — option **(1)**.
**CO2** has the largest share (~**60%**) among listed gases; **methane** ~**20%**; **N2O** ~**5%**.
xa: Greenhouse gases: **CO2, CH4, water vapour, N2O** trap heat (APPSC **2025**).
Earth's long-wave radiation is absorbed by **CO2 and water vapour**.
Without the atmosphere: about **-18 °C** instead of **+15 °C**.

15.s: With carbon dioxide assigned a Global Warming Potential of 1 over 100 years, which of the following ranges is correctly matched?
15.x: On the stated 100-year scale, carbon dioxide has a GWP of 1, methane 28–36 and nitrous oxide 265–298.
15.tq: Keep the gases and their ranges in the correct order and avoid reversing methane with nitrous oxide.
xs: With CO2 = **1**, **methane 28-36** and **N2O 265-298** (100-year GWP) — option **(1)**.
Option (4) swaps the two ranges; N2O is far more potent per unit than methane.
xa: ⚠ Older table: methane **21**, N2O **310**.
Shares of the greenhouse effect: **CO2 ~60%**, **methane ~20%**, **CFCs ~15%**, **N2O ~5%**.
N2O sources: **fertilisers**, burning coal/biomass; methane: **paddy, wetlands, livestock, landfills**.

15.s: In the absence of the atmosphere, the average surface temperature of the Earth would be approximately
15.x: Without the atmospheric heat-trapping effect, the average surface temperature would be about −18°C rather than approximately +15°C.
15.tq: Distinguish the observed average from the estimated no-atmosphere value.
xs: Without the atmosphere, the surface would be about **-18 °C instead of +15 °C** — option **(3)**.
Trapped heat from **greenhouse gases** keeps the average temperature up (UPSC **2025**: all three statements correct).
Option (4) reverses the two figures.
xa: Atmosphere is **transparent to short-wave** sunlight, **opaque to long-wave** terrestrial radiation.
Greenhouse gases: **CO2, CH4, water vapour, N2O** (APPSC **2025**).
Global land temperature up **1.59 °C** since pre-industrial (UNEP Emissions Gap **2025**).

15.s: Which one of the following gases is correctly matched with its approximate share of the greenhouse effect?
15.x: In the stated estimates, CFCs account for approximately 15 percent; methane accounts for about 20 percent, nitrous oxide 5 percent and carbon dioxide 60 percent.
15.tq: Check the gas-share pair directly and use the remaining shares as distractors.
xs: **CFCs — ~15%** of the greenhouse effect is correctly matched — option **(1)**.
Correct shares: **CO2 ~60%**, **methane ~20%**, **N2O ~5%** — so the other pairs are wrong.
xa: CFC source: **refrigeration, aerosols**.
**Water vapour** is the most abundant greenhouse gas (a feedback).

15.s: With reference to the January isotherms in the Northern Hemisphere, which one of the following is correct?
o: They bend equatorward over both land and oceans because January is a winter month.
They run exactly along the parallels because land and oceans have equal temperatures.
They bend poleward over land and equatorward over oceans because land remains warmer than oceans.
They bend equatorward over land and poleward over oceans because oceans are warmer than land.
15.x: In January, Northern Hemisphere isotherms bend equatorward over colder landmasses and poleward over relatively warmer oceans.
15.tq: Use the land-sea contrast to distinguish the direction of the January bends.
xs: In January, NH isotherms **bend equatorward over land** and **poleward over oceans** because **oceans are warmer than land** — option **(4)**.
Land heats and cools faster than water, so winter land is colder (UPSC **2025**: both statements correct, II explains I).
In **July** the pattern **reverses** — poleward over land.
xa: **Isotherms** join places of equal temperature, running roughly **east-west**.
Southern Hemisphere isotherms are **more regular** (mostly ocean).
**Thermal equator** lies mostly **north of the equator** (more land in the NH).

15.s:
Consider the following statements regarding isotherms:
1. Isotherms join places having equal temperature.
2. They generally run east-west, parallel to latitudes.
3. They are more regular in the Southern Hemisphere because it has a greater oceanic area.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
15.x: All three statements are correct. Isotherms connect places of equal temperature, generally follow an east-west direction, and are more regular in the ocean-dominated Southern Hemisphere.
15.tq: Check each definition, orientation and hemispheric comparison separately.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4)** (**1, 2 and 3**).
Isotherms **join places of equal temperature** and run roughly **east-west, parallel to latitudes**.
They are **more regular in the Southern Hemisphere** because it is mostly **ocean**.
xa: January: isotherms bend **equatorward over land**, **poleward over oceans**; July reverses.
**Thermal equator** = line of highest mean temperature, mostly north of the equator.
India winter: **20°C isotherm** runs from the **Tapti** mouth to the **Mahanadi delta**.

15.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the winter temperature pattern in India?
o: Temperature rises from north to south only in coastal areas.
Temperature remains uniform from north to south because the 20°C isotherm is straight.
Temperature generally rises from north to south.
Temperature generally falls from north to south because the south is farther from the Equator.
15.x: During Indian winter, temperature generally increases from north to south, consistent with the southward decrease in latitude.
15.tq: Use the north-south temperature trend rather than the location of one isotherm alone.
xs: In Indian winter, temperature **generally rises from north to south** — option **(3)**.
The **20°C isotherm** runs from the mouth of the **Tapti (Tapi)** to the **Mahanadi delta**; places south of it are warmer.
xa: Winter diurnal range is highest in the **north-west**: **14-18°C**.
India coldest: **Dras** (Ladakh), **-45°C** (1908).
North Indian winter mornings: **inversion** + heavy moisture + **fog**.

15.s: The thermal equator is best defined as the
o: line joining places of highest mean temperature, generally lying north of the geographical Equator.
boundary between the tropical and polar zones, fixed at 23½° latitude.
line joining the coldest places in both hemispheres.
geographical Equator, which never shifts seasonally.
15.x: The thermal equator is the line of highest mean temperature. It lies mostly north of the geographical Equator and shifts with the apparent movement of the Sun.
15.tq: Distinguish the shifting thermal equator from the fixed geographical Equator.
xs: The **thermal equator** is the line of **highest mean temperature**, lying mostly **north of the geographical equator** — option **(1)**.
It lies north because the **NH has more land**, and it **shifts** with the sun's apparent movement — so it is not fixed.
xa: **Isotherms** run roughly east-west; in January they bend **equatorward over land**.
Southern Hemisphere isotherms are **more regular** (mostly ocean).
Annual range is **minimum at the equator**.

15.s: The winter 20°C isotherm in India runs approximately from:
o: The Sabarmati mouth to the Godavari delta
The Tapi mouth to the Mahanadi delta
The Tapi mouth to the Kaveri delta
The Narmada mouth to the Krishna delta
15.x: In winter, the 20°C isotherm extends from the mouth of the Tapi to the Mahanadi delta.
15.tq: Use the two-endpoint method for a geographical line or isotherm.
xs: In winter the **20°C isotherm** runs from the **mouth of the Tapi** to the **Mahanadi delta** — option **(2)**.
Temperature in winter rises from **north to south**.
xa: Winter diurnal range highest in the **north-west**: **14-18°C**.
Isotherms join places of **equal temperature**.
**Thermal equator** lies mostly north of the equator.

15.s:
Consider the following statements about the range of temperature:
1. The annual range of temperature is minimum at the equator.
2. The annual range is largest in continental interiors of high latitudes such as Siberia.
3. Coastal areas have a continental climate with a large annual range.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
15.x: Statement 1 is correct: the annual range is minimum at the equator. Statement 2 is correct: it is largest in high-latitude continental interiors like Siberia. Statement 3 is wrong: coasts are equable/maritime with a small range. Hence 1 and 2 only.
15.tq: Sea moderates; interiors swing.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: the annual range is **minimum at the equator**.
Statement 2 correct: largest annual range in **continental interiors of high latitudes** (**Siberia**).
Statement 3 wrong: coasts are **equable/maritime** with a **small range**, moderated by the sea.
xa: **Seasonal differences are maximum in high latitudes** (APPSC-G1 **2023**).
**Continentality** = large annual and daily ranges (northern interiors of India).
AP: coast low diurnal range; **Rayalaseema** high.

15.s: Which one of the following statements about diurnal temperature range in Andhra Pradesh is correct?
o: The coast and Rayalaseema have identical diurnal ranges.
Rayalaseema generally has a higher diurnal range than the coast.
The coast generally has a higher diurnal range than Rayalaseema.
The diurnal range is lowest in all interior areas of Andhra Pradesh.
15.x: The maritime influence reduces the coastal diurnal range, whereas the interior Rayalaseema region generally has a higher range.
15.tq: Compare coastal moderation with interior continental conditions.
xs: **Rayalaseema** has a **higher diurnal range** than the coast — option **(2)**.
The AP **coast** has a **low** diurnal range, moderated by the sea (maritime influence).
xa: **Visakhapatnam & Kakinada** get **sea-breeze relief**, while **Palnadu** bakes.
AP hottest: **Rentachintala** (Palnadu), above **47°C**; AP coldest: **Lambasingi** (ASR).
India: winter diurnal range highest in the **north-west** (**14-18°C**).

15.s: Clear nights are generally colder than cloudy nights because clear skies
o: increase incoming short-wave radiation at night.
prevent the Earth from emitting long-wave radiation.
permit greater loss of heat by terrestrial radiation.
create strong convection from the upper atmosphere.
15.x: Clear skies allow greater radiational loss of heat from the Earth, whereas clouds send some outgoing heat back toward the surface.
15.tq: Link night-time temperature to outgoing terrestrial radiation.
xs: **Clear skies** permit **greater loss of heat by terrestrial radiation** — option **(3)**.
**Cloudy nights** stay warmer because clouds **trap outgoing radiation** and send heat back.
The earth keeps emitting long-wave radiation at night; there is no incoming short-wave at night.
xa: Clear nights bring **cold nights and frost**.
**Clear skies, calm dry air** and long winter nights favour **temperature inversion**.
**High, thin clouds** trap heat; **low, thick clouds** reflect sunlight.

15.s: The large annual and daily ranges of temperature found in continental interiors are primarily associated with which of the following?
15.x: Continentality causes large annual and daily temperature ranges in continental interiors, while maritime influence moderates temperature near coasts.
15.tq: Test the precise geographical term associated with a distinctive climatic characteristic.
xs: Large annual and daily ranges in continental interiors come from **continentality** — option **(1)**.
Interiors have **hot summers, cold winters** (e.g. northern interiors of India).
**Maritime influence** does the opposite: coasts are **equable**, with a small range.
xa: Largest annual range: continental interiors of high latitudes (**Siberia**).
Annual range is **minimum at the equator**.
Land heats and cools faster than water.

15.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Coastal areas generally experience moderation of temperature by the sea.
2. Visakhapatnam and Kakinada receive relief from sea breezes.
3. Palnadu is cited as an example of an area that experiences the same maritime moderation as Visakhapatnam.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
15.x: The sea moderates coastal temperatures, and Visakhapatnam and Kakinada receive sea-breeze relief. Palnadu is cited as an interior area that bakes, not as a maritime location.
15.tq: Find the one wrong comparison in a group of closely related geographical statements.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: **coasts** are **equable/maritime**, moderated by the sea.
Statement 2 correct: **Visakhapatnam & Kakinada** get **sea-breeze relief**.
Statement 3 wrong: **Palnadu** **bakes** — it is an interior area, not maritime.
xa: AP coast = low diurnal range; **Rayalaseema** = high.
AP hottest: **Rentachintala** (Palnadu), above **47°C**.
**48.1 °C at Piduguralla** (Palnadu) on 21 May **2026** — the 2026 peak.

15.s: Which one of the following regions of India records the highest diurnal range of temperature in winter?
15.x: The diurnal range is highest in north-western India during winter, where it is about 14°–18°C.
15.tq: Identify the correct region before matching it with the associated numerical range.
xs: Winter diurnal range is highest in **north-western India** — **14-18°C** — option **(3)**.
Coasts and deltas have a **small range** due to sea moderation.
xa: **Continentality** gives large annual and daily ranges in northern interiors of India.
**Clear nights** lose more heat — cold nights and frost.
India coldest: **Dras** (Ladakh), **-45°C** (**1908**).

15.s: Why does temperature normally decrease with increasing altitude?
o: Higher air receives more long-wave radiation from the Sun.
The ground heats the air from below, while higher air is thinner and contains less water vapour and dust.
The Earth stops emitting radiation above the lower atmosphere.
The atmosphere is heated mainly from above by direct solar radiation.
15.x: The ground heats the atmosphere from below. At higher levels the air is thinner and contains less water vapour and dust, so it absorbs less heat.
15.tq: Identify the heating source and the properties of higher air.
xs: The **ground heats the air from below**, while higher air is **thinner** with **less water vapour and dust** — option **(2)**.
So higher air absorbs less heat, and temperature falls at the normal lapse rate of **6.5 °C/km**.
The atmosphere is not heated mainly from above by direct sunlight, and the earth does not stop emitting radiation.
xa: The sun emits **short-wave**; earth re-emits **long-wave infra-red** (**8,000-25,000 nm**), absorbed by CO2 and water vapour.
**Temperature inversion** is when this reverses and temperature **rises** with height.
**Terrestrial radiation** is the main source heating the atmosphere.

15.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the radiation processes involved in atmospheric heating?
o: The Sun emits long-wave radiation and the Earth re-emits short-wave radiation.
The Sun emits short-wave radiation and the Earth re-emits long-wave infrared radiation.
Both the Sun and the Earth emit only short-wave radiation.
Both the Sun and the Earth emit only long-wave radiation.
15.x: Solar radiation is primarily short-wave, while the Earth re-emits absorbed energy as long-wave infrared radiation.
15.tq: Avoid the common reversal of solar and terrestrial radiation.
xs: The **sun emits short-wave** radiation and the **earth re-emits long-wave infra-red** — option **(2)**.
The earth's long waves (**8,000-25,000 nm**) are absorbed by **CO2 and water vapour**, so air is heated **from below**.
xa: Atmosphere: **transparent to short-wave**, **opaque to long-wave** — the greenhouse effect.
Normal lapse rate: **6.5 °C/km**.
⚠ "Heated more by incoming solar radiation" is **wrong** (UPSC **2024**).

15.s: The long-wave infrared radiation re-emitted by the Earth lies approximately in the range of
15.x: Earth's outgoing long-wave infrared radiation is approximately in the 8,000–25,000 nanometre range.
15.tq: Recall the radiation wavelength range stated for terrestrial emission.
xs: Earth's re-emitted long-wave infra-red lies in **8,000-25,000 nm** — option **(4)**.
It is absorbed by **CO2 and water vapour**, heating the air **from below**.
xa: The sun emits **short-wave** radiation; earth emits **long-wave**.
Higher air is thinner with less water vapour and dust, so absorbs less heat.
Normal lapse rate: **6.5 °C/km**.

15.s: The normal lapse rate, at which temperature falls with increasing height in the troposphere, is about:
15.x: Temperature normally falls with height at about 6.5 °C per km, because the air is heated from below and higher air absorbs less heat.
15.tq: Normal lapse = 6.5 per km (about 1 °C per 165 m).
xs: The normal lapse rate is about **6.5 °C per km** — option **(3)**.
Air is heated **from below**; higher air is thinner with less water vapour and dust, so it absorbs less heat.
xa: **Convection** (vertical transfer by rising warm air) is **confined to the troposphere**.
In a **temperature inversion**, temperature **rises** with height instead.
The stratosphere is a **permanent inversion** layer.

15.s: Temperature inversion refers to a condition in which
o: temperature remains constant at all heights.
temperature rises with height instead of falling.
temperature falls more rapidly with height than under normal conditions.
temperature rises only over oceans during summer.
15.x: During an inversion, the normal lapse relationship is reversed and temperature increases with height.
15.tq: Use the reversal of the normal lapse rate as the defining feature.
xs: In a **temperature inversion**, the normal lapse reverses and **temperature rises with height** — option **(2)**.
Normally temperature falls at **6.5 °C/km**.
xa: Conditions: **long winter nights, clear skies, calm dry air, snow cover**.
Effects: **fog, frost, smog**; pollutants trapped in the planetary boundary layer.
Types: **ground/radiation**, **valley (air-drainage)**, **frontal/advection**, and **permanent** (polar areas; stratosphere).

15.s: Which combination of conditions is most favourable for the development of a temperature inversion?
o: Short summer nights, cloudy skies, strong winds and humid air
Long winter nights, clear skies, calm dry air and snow cover
Long summer days, heavy rainfall, strong convection and moist air
Cloudy nights, strong turbulence and high surface temperatures
15.x: Long winter nights, clear skies, calm and dry air, and snow cover favour rapid surface cooling and inversion formation.
15.tq: Select the complete set of inversion-producing conditions.
xs: **Long winter nights, clear skies, calm dry air and snow cover** favour inversion — option **(2)**.
These allow rapid **night cooling** of the ground; clouds, wind, turbulence or convection would prevent it.
xa: Effects: **fog, frost, smog**; pollutants trapped in the **planetary boundary layer**.
North Indian winter mornings: inversion + heavy moisture + **fog**.
**Ground/radiation inversion** = surface, night cooling.

15.s: In a valley inversion, the valley floor is colder than the slopes because
o: warm air flows downslope and accumulates at the valley floor.
the valley floor is always nearer to the Sun.
cold air drains downslope and settles in the valley.
the slopes receive no solar radiation in winter.
15.x: Cold, dense air flows downslope and accumulates in valleys, producing frost pockets while the slopes remain relatively warmer.
15.tq: Follow the movement of dense cold air to determine the colder location.
xs: In a **valley inversion**, **cold air drains downslope** and settles in the valley — option **(3)**.
This creates **frost pockets** on valley floors while **slopes stay warmer**.
xa: Hence **orchards/plantations** are placed on **upper slopes**.
It is also called **air-drainage inversion**.
Other types: **ground/radiation**, **frontal/advection**, **permanent** (polar areas).

15.s: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: Frontal inversion — association with a frontal boundary
Valley inversion — downslope drainage of cold air
Surface or radiation inversion — night-time cooling of the ground
Stratosphere — absence of any inversion condition
15.x: The stratosphere is a permanent inversion layer, so it is incorrect to associate it with the absence of inversion.
15.tq: Find the single reversed or denied relationship in the list.
xs: **Stratosphere — absence of any inversion** is wrongly matched — option **(4)**.
The **stratosphere** is a **permanent inversion layer**; permanent inversions also occur in **polar areas**.
Others are correct: **frontal** inversion at fronts; **valley** = cold-air drainage; **ground/radiation** = night cooling.
xa: Inversion conditions: **long winter nights, clear skies, calm dry air, snow cover**.
Effects: **fog, frost, smog**.
Valley inversion → **frost pockets** on floors, orchards on upper slopes.

15.s:
Which of the following are effects of temperature inversion?
1. Fog
2. Frost
3. Smog
4. Trapping of pollutants in the planetary boundary layer
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
15.x: Inversions can produce fog, frost and smog and can trap pollutants within the planetary boundary layer.
15.tq: Recognise the common atmospheric and pollution effects as one complete group.
xs: All four — **fog**, **frost**, **smog** and **pollutants trapped in the planetary boundary layer** — are effects of inversion: option **(4)**.
In an inversion, temperature **rises with height**, so cold surface air stays put and pollutants cannot rise.
North Indian winter mornings: inversion + heavy moisture + **fog**.
xa: Conditions: **long winter nights, clear skies, calm dry air, snow cover**.
**Valley inversion**: cold air drains downslope → **frost pockets** on valley floors; **orchards** on upper slopes.
Permanent inversion: **polar areas**; the **stratosphere** is a permanent inversion layer.

15.s: An urban heat island is primarily produced because
o: cities receive no long-wave radiation at night.
rural vegetation reflects all incoming radiation toward cities.
urban areas are always located at lower latitudes than rural areas.
concrete and asphalt store heat and make cities warmer than surrounding rural areas.
15.x: Concrete and asphalt absorb and retain heat, causing urban areas to be warmer than their rural surroundings.
15.tq: Identify the physical surface property responsible for the urban-rural temperature contrast.
xs: **Concrete and asphalt** absorb and **store heat**, making cities **warmer than the surrounding rural** countryside — option **(4)**: the **urban heat island**.
It is not a matter of latitude, nor of cities receiving no long-wave radiation.
xa: **Hyderabad** UHI intensity: **5.74-6.82 °C**.
**Chennai**: vegetation fell **25% (2014) → 10% (2024)**; built-up area rose **36% → 67%**.
**Data centres** add ~**2 °C** to land-surface temperature within **10 km**.
**TRISHNA** (ISRO-CNES) will map **urban heat islands**; PSLV launch due **2027**.

15.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
15.x: Dras in Ladakh recorded approximately −45°C in 1908. Death Valley is associated with 56.7°C, while Vostok is associated with −89.2°C.
15.tq: Start with the sure place-temperature pair and eliminate swapped extremes.
xs: **Dras** (Ladakh) — about **-45°C** in **1908** is correctly matched — option **(1)**; it is India's coldest place.
**Death Valley** is the world's hottest (**56.7°C**), and **Vostok** the world's coldest (**-89.2°C**) — options (2) and (3) swap them.
**Lambasingi** is AP's coldest at about **2°C**, not -45°C.
xa: AP hottest: **Rentachintala** (Palnadu), above **47°C**.
Lambasingi (ASR) is called the "**Kashmir of AP**".
AP's 2026 peak: **48.1 °C at Piduguralla** (Palnadu) on **21 May 2026**.

15.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched with respect to temperature extremes in Andhra Pradesh?
15.x: Rentachintala in Palnadu is identified as the hottest place, while Lambasingi is the coolest place in Andhra Pradesh.
15.tq: Guard against reversing the two extreme-temperature locations.
xs: AP **hottest — Rentachintala**; **coolest — Lambasingi** — option **(1)**.
**Rentachintala** (Palnadu) goes above **47°C**; **Lambasingi** (ASR) is about **2°C**, the "**Kashmir of AP**".
Option (4) reverses them; Palnadu is a hot interior district, not the coolest.
xa: 2026 peak: **48.1 °C at Piduguralla** (Palnadu), **21 May 2026**; **45 °C** crossed in **18** districts.
India coldest: **Dras** (**-45°C**, 1908); world hottest **Death Valley** (**56.7°C**).
AP coast has a low diurnal range; **Rayalaseema** high.

15.s: Which of the following correctly represents the IMD threshold maximum temperatures for heat-wave qualification in plains, coastal areas and hills, respectively?
15.x: The threshold maximum temperatures are 40°C for plains, 37°C for coasts and 30°C for hills.
15.tq: Match each geographical setting with its specific numerical threshold.
xs: IMD thresholds: **40°C plains**, **37°C coast**, **30°C hills** — option **(1)**.
⚠ Memory aid: **40 – 37 – 30** = **plains – coast – hills**; option (2) swaps plains and coast.
xa: Heat wave: departure of **4.5 to 6.4 °C** from normal; severe: **above 6.4 °C**.
Plains only: an actual max of **45 °C** or more = heat wave; **47 °C** or more = severe.
**NDMA** heat-wave guidelines: **2019**.

15.s: A heat wave is classified as a severe heat wave on the basis of departure from normal when the departure is:
15.x: A departure above 6.4°C from the normal temperature constitutes a severe heat wave; 4.5°C to 6.4°C corresponds to a heat wave.
15.tq: Discriminate between adjacent numerical categories by focusing on the boundary value.
xs: A **severe heat wave** is a departure from normal **above 6.4°C** — option **(3)**.
A departure of **4.5 to 6.4 °C** is an ordinary **heat wave**, so option (2) describes the lower category.
xa: Thresholds to qualify: **40 °C plains**, **37 °C coast**, **30 °C hills**.
Actual max (plains): **45 °C** or more = heat wave; **47 °C** or more = severe heat wave.
**NDMA** heat-wave guidelines: **2019**; AP **Heat Wave Action Plan** since **2016**.

15.s: Which of the following statements about Andhra Pradesh’s heat-wave management is correct?
o: Andhra Pradesh has no district-level heat-wave warning system.
The Heat Wave Action Plan has operated in Andhra Pradesh since 2016.
The plan was introduced after the 2026 heat season ended.
The Heat Wave Action Plan was introduced in Andhra Pradesh only in 2026.
15.x: Andhra Pradesh has had a Heat Wave Action Plan since 2016. APSDMA also sends district-wise SMS heat-wave alerts.
15.tq: Test the exact year of establishment while rejecting recent-year substitution traps.
xs: AP's **Heat Wave Action Plan** has operated **since 2016** — option **(2)**.
So it was not introduced in **2026**; and AP does have district-level warnings — **APSDMA** sends **district-wise SMS** heatwave alerts.
xa: HAP **2026** severe-heatwave-prone districts include **Tirupati, Prakasam, SPSR Nellore, Guntur, Bapatla, Palnadu**, **Srikakulam**.
**IMD Amaravati** warned South Coastal AP (**Kavali, Ongole, Bapatla, Nellore**) as early as **8-9 March 2026**.
**NDMA** heat-wave guidelines: **2019**.

15.s: Which one of the following districts is included among the severe-heatwave-prone districts identified in the Heatwave Action Plan 2026?
15.x: Palnadu is included in the listed severe-heatwave-prone districts. The other districts are not included in the specified list.
15.tq: Select the listed district by distinguishing included and nearby plausible alternatives.
xs: **Palnadu** is among the severe-heatwave-prone districts of **HAP 2026** — option **(4)**.
The notes' list does not include Anantapuramu, Kadapa or Kurnool.
xa: Full list: **Tirupati, Prakasam, SPSR Nellore, Markapuram, Guntur, Bapatla, Palnadu**.
Also: **Eluru, NTR, Kakinada, East Godavari, Alluri Sitharama Raju, Srikakulam**.
Palnadu peaks: **48.1 °C at Piduguralla** (2026); **Rentachintala** is AP's hottest place.

15.s: On 21 May 2026, the peak temperature of 48.1°C in Andhra Pradesh was recorded at:
15.x: Piduguralla in Palnadu recorded 48.1°C on 21 May 2026. The event was part of the 2026 peak heat episode.
15.tq: Test the exact place-date-temperature combination without confusing it with the usual hottest-place reference.
