22.tq: Shelf (gentle, to 200 m) → slope (steep, canyons) → rise (sediment apron) → abyssal plain.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 is correct: the **continental shelf** goes to about **200 m**.
Statement 2 is correct: it is the gently sloping, **"submerged prolongation of land"**.
Statement 3 is wrong: the steep drop is the **continental slope**; the **continental rise** is an **apron of sediment** at the slope's foot.
xa: **Continental slope:** ~**200-3,000 m**, with **canyons and trenches**.
**Deep sea plain:** about **3,000-6,000 m**, the flattest surface on earth.
Shelf holds the **richest fishing grounds**, **oil and gas**.

22.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the continental shelf:
1. It contains some of the richest fishing grounds.
2. It is an important zone for oil and natural gas resources.
3. It is the deepest and steepest part of the ocean floor.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
22.x: The continental shelf is important for fisheries, oil and gas. It is not the deepest and steepest part of the ocean floor; that description relates to oceanic deeps and trenches.
22.tq: Find the statement that reverses the comparison between the shallow shelf and the deepest relief.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
The **continental shelf** has the **richest fishing grounds** and **oil and gas**.
Statement 3 is wrong: the shelf is the **shallowest**, gently sloping part; the deepest, steep-sided features are the **oceanic deeps** (trenches).
xa: Shelf extends to about **200 m**.
**Mumbai High** oilfield lies on India's wide **western shelf**.
**40th Amendment, 1976** vests shelf minerals in the **Union**.

22.s:
Arrange the following ocean-floor divisions in descending order of their usual depth:
A. Continental shelf
B. Continental slope
C. Deep-sea plain
D. Oceanic deeps
Select the correct sequence.
22.x: Oceanic deeps are deepest, followed by deep-sea plains, continental slopes and continental shelves.
22.tq: Apply the depth sequence from the continental margin towards the deepest oceanic relief.
xs: Descending depth: **oceanic deeps > deep-sea plain > continental slope > continental shelf** — option **(2) D, C, B, A**.
**Deeps** are the deepest; **deep sea plain** about **3,000-6,000 m**; **slope** ~**200-3,000 m**; **shelf** to about **200 m**.
xa: **Continental rise:** apron of sediment at the foot of the slope.
**Deep sea plain** is the **most extensive part** of the ocean floor.
⚠ **Canyons and trenches** = slope; **volcanoes and earthquakes** = deeps.

22.s: Which one of the following statements about the deep-sea or abyssal plain is correct?
o: It is generally confined to the first 200 metres below sea level.
It forms the flattest and smoothest extensive surface on the Earth's surface.
It is the steepest section between the shelf and the continental rise.
It consists exclusively of active volcanoes and earthquake zones.
22.x: The deep-sea plain, generally about 3,000–6,000 metres deep, is the flattest and smoothest extensive surface on Earth and is the most extensive part of the ocean floor.
22.tq: Reject extreme words such as ‘exclusively’ and identify the defining comparison.
xs: The **deep sea (abyssal) plain** is the **flattest, smoothest** surface on earth — option **(2)**.
It lies at about **3,000-6,000 m**, not within the first **200 m**, which is the shelf.
The steep drop is the **slope**; **volcanoes and earthquakes** belong to the **deeps**.
xa: It is the **most extensive part of the ocean floor**, covered by fine **clays/oozes**.
**Polymetallic nodules** lie here.
**Pelagic deposits** (oozes, red clay) cover the deep-sea plains and deeps.

22.s: Polymetallic nodules are particularly associated with which part of the ocean floor?
22.x: Polymetallic nodules occur on the deep-sea plains.
22.tq: Link a resource to its characteristic ocean-floor environment.
xs: **Polymetallic nodules** lie on the **deep sea (abyssal) plain** — option **(3)**.
The plain lies at about **3,000-6,000 m** and is the **most extensive part** of the ocean floor.
xa: **Seamounts** carry **cobalt-rich crusts** (LENS Apr 2025).
India holds a **polymetallic sulphide** licence on the **Indian Ocean Ridge** valid to **Sept 2031**.
**Varaha** mining machine trialled at **5,270 m** in the Central Indian Ocean.

22.s:
With reference to oceanic deeps and trenches, consider the following statements:
1. They are generally long, narrow and steep-sided.
2. They are associated with active volcanoes and strong earthquakes.
3. They occur mostly in the Pacific Ocean.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
22.x: Oceanic deeps or trenches are long, narrow and steep-sided, commonly occur at plate-convergence zones, and are associated with volcanoes and strong earthquakes. Most are located in the Pacific Ocean.
22.tq: Use the all-inclusive option only when each characteristic belongs to the same relief feature.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
**Oceanic deeps (trenches)** are **long, narrow, steep-sided** and the deepest parts, at **plate convergence**.
They are tied to **active volcanoes and strong earthquakes** (APPSC G2 2023) and lie **mostly in the Pacific**.
xa: Trenches mark **subduction zones**, where one plate dives under another.
**Mariana Trench (Challenger Deep)** is the **deepest point on earth**, about **11 km**.
⚠ **Canyons and trenches** = slope feature in the APPSC G2 2023 match.

22.s: The deep sea below about 200 metres is described as the:
22.x: The deep sea below 200 metres is described as the oldest and largest biome, occupying about 90–95 per cent of Earth's habitable space.
22.tq: Pair the numerical extent with the correct superlative description.
xs: The **deep sea (below 200 m)** is the **oldest and largest biome** — option **(2)**.
It makes up about **90-95%** of earth's **habitable space**.
xa: **Mesopelagic ("twilight zone")** lies at **200-1,000 m**.
The **deep sea plain** is the most extensive part of the ocean floor.
**Deep Ocean Mission** surveys found about **39** potentially new species.

22.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below:
List-I (Ocean-floor feature)
a. Continental shelf
b. Continental slope
c. Deep-sea plain
d. Oceanic deeps

List-II (Characteristic)
i. Active volcanoes and strong earthquakes
ii. Canyons and trenches
iii. Rich fishing grounds and oil and gas
iv. Flattest and smoothest extensive surface

Codes:
22.x: The continental shelf is rich in fisheries and hydrocarbons; the slope has canyons and trenches; the deep-sea plain is the flattest surface; and oceanic deeps are associated with volcanoes and earthquakes.
22.tq: Start from the sure pair—shelf with fishing grounds and oil—and eliminate incompatible codes.
xs: **a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i** — option **(1)**, the **APPSC G2 2023** pattern.
**Shelf** = rich **fishing grounds, oil and gas**; **slope** = **canyons and trenches**.
**Deep-sea plain** = **flattest, smoothest** surface; **deeps** = **active volcanoes and strong earthquakes**.
xa: ⚠ **Most extensive** part of the floor = **deep sea plain**.
**Polymetallic nodules** lie on the deep sea plain.

22.s: Which one of the following statements correctly describes the continental shelf along the Indian coast?
o: It is broad along the east coast and narrow off Gujarat.
It is uniformly broad along both the eastern and western coasts.
It is broadest off Gujarat and parts of Maharashtra and narrow along the eastern coast.
It is absent off the western coast because of deep ocean trenches.
22.x: India's continental shelf is broadest off Gujarat and parts of Maharashtra, while it is relatively narrow along the east coast.
22.tq: Use the east-versus-west comparison instead of treating the coastline as uniform.
xs: India's shelf is **broadest off Gujarat and part of Maharashtra** and **narrow along the east coast** — option **(3)**.
The shelf is **wide off the west coast**, so options saying the east is broad or the west is absent are wrong.
xa: **Mumbai High (Bombay High)** oilfield lies on the wide **western shelf**.
AP's shelf covers about **33,000 sq km**.
AP's **1,053 km** coast (**3rd longest**) fronts the narrow east-coast shelf.

22.s: The Mumbai High oil field is situated on:
o: The continental slope off the Bay of Bengal
22.x: Mumbai High lies on the wide western continental shelf, particularly in the Gujarat-Mumbai sector.
22.tq: Associate the resource location with the correct coastal shelf sector.
xs: **Mumbai High** lies on the **wide western continental shelf** — option **(3)**.
The western shelf is **broadest off Gujarat and part of Maharashtra** (Gujarat-Mumbai).
xa: Shelf resources: **oil and gas** (Bombay High, **KG basin**), placer minerals, fisheries.
The **east coast** shelf is **narrow**.
**40th Amendment, 1976** vests shelf minerals in the **Union**.

22.s: Under the Constitution (Fortieth Amendment) Act, 1976, minerals of the continental shelf and the EEZ are vested in the:
22.x: The Constitution (Fortieth Amendment) Act, 1976 vests minerals of the continental shelf and the EEZ in the Union.
22.tq: Apply the authority-identification method to a constitutional resource provision.
xs: The **Constitution (40th Amendment) Act, 1976** vests minerals of the **continental shelf and EEZ** in the **Union** — option **(3)**.
So neither **State Governments** nor port authorities own them.
xa: **Territorial sea:** **12 nm / 22 km**, largely overlapping the productive shelf.
**2025:** India widened its shelf claim by **~10,000 sq km** in the central Arabian Sea before the **CLCS**.
Data for the claim came from **NCPOR Goa**.

22.s: Which of the following is NOT a resource associated with India's continental shelf?
o: Coal deposits of the Himalayan ranges
22.x: Oil and gas, placer minerals and fisheries are resources associated with the continental shelf. Himalayan coal deposits are not listed as a shelf resource.
22.tq: Find the geographically unrelated resource among shelf-based resources.
xs: **Coal deposits of the Himalayan ranges** are not a shelf resource — option **(3)**.
India's shelf resources are **oil and gas** (Bombay High, KG basin), **placer minerals** and **fisheries**.
xa: **Mumbai High** lies on the wide **western shelf**.
Shelf minerals are vested in the **Union** by the **40th Amendment, 1976**.
AP's shelf covers about **33,000 sq km**.

22.s: In 2025, India added approximately how much area in the central Arabian Sea to its extended-shelf claim before the UN Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf?
22.x: In 2025, India added about 10,000 square kilometres in the central Arabian Sea to its extended-shelf claim before the UN CLCS.
22.tq: Separate the newly added claim from the much larger total EEZ area.
xs: In **2025** India widened its extended-shelf claim by **~10,000 sq km** in the **central Arabian Sea** — option **(1)**.
The claim went before the **UN Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf (CLCS)**, with data by **NCPOR Goa**.
xa: **40th Amendment, 1976** vests shelf and EEZ minerals in the **Union**.
India applied for the **Afanasy-Nikitin Seamount**, contested by **Sri Lanka**.
India sought exploration rights in the **Carlsberg Ridge** in **2024**.

22.s:
Consider the following statements regarding guyots:
1. A guyot is a flat-topped seamount.
2. Its top is planed by waves before the feature sinks below the sea surface.
3. It is a ring-shaped coral reef around a central lagoon.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
22.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. A ring-shaped coral reef around a central lagoon is an atoll, not a guyot.
22.tq: Separate the correct statements from a swapped definition of an atoll.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
A **guyot** is a **flat-topped seamount**, **planed by waves**, then **sunk**.
Statement 3 is wrong: a ring-shaped reef around a lagoon is an **atoll**.
xa: ⚠ **Seamount** = does not reach surface; **Guyot** = flat-topped seamount.
**Atolls:** e.g. **Lakshadweep**, **Maldives**.
**CMS COP15** declared seamounts **critical habitat**.

22.s: An atoll is best described as a:
o: Ring- or horseshoe-shaped coral reef enclosing a central lagoon
Deep gorge cut across the continental slope
Flat-topped submarine mountain formed only by tectonic uplift
Submarine volcanic peak with a pointed summit
22.x: An atoll is a ring- or horseshoe-shaped coral reef surrounding a central lagoon. Lakshadweep and Maldives provide examples.
22.tq: Apply the characteristic-shape clue to identify the landform.
xs: An **atoll** is a **ring- or horseshoe-shaped coral reef** around a **central lagoon** — option **(1)**.
Examples: **Lakshadweep** and **Maldives**.
A gorge across the slope is a **submarine canyon**; a flat-topped seamount is a **guyot**; a volcanic peak is a **seamount**.
xa: **Guyot:** planed by waves, then sunk.
**Mahadevan Canyon** lies off **Visakhapatnam**.

22.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Submarine canyon — Deep, steep-sided valley cut across the shelf and slope
Guyot — Coral reef surrounding a lagoon
Atoll — Flat-topped seamount planed by waves
Seamount — Valley formed off a river mouth
22.x: A submarine canyon is a deep, steep-sided valley that cuts across the continental shelf and slope, often near river mouths.
22.tq: Start with the sure definition and eliminate the options with swapped landforms.
xs: A **submarine canyon** is a **deep, steep-sided valley** cut across the **shelf and slope** — option **(1)**.
A **guyot** is a flat-topped seamount, and an **atoll** is the reef around a lagoon — so (2) and (3) are swapped.
A **seamount** is an undersea volcanic peak, not a valley.
xa: Canyons lie often off **river mouths**; e.g. **Hudson Canyon**, **Mahadevan Canyon off Visakhapatnam**.
The **continental slope** is marked by **canyons and trenches** (APPSC G2 2023).

22.s: The Mahadevan Canyon, mentioned in relation to submarine canyons, is located off the coast of:
22.x: Mahadevan Canyon is a submarine canyon located off Visakhapatnam.
22.tq: Test the location attached to a named geographical feature.
xs: **Mahadevan Canyon** is a submarine canyon **off Visakhapatnam** — option **(2)**.
Submarine canyons are deep, steep-sided valleys across the **shelf and slope**, often off **river mouths**.
xa: Another example: **Hudson Canyon**.
**Visakhapatnam** is AP's only **major port**.
AP's coast is **1,053 km** long, the **3rd longest**.

22.s: Which one of the following was declared a critical habitat by CMS COP15?
22.x: CMS COP15 declared seamounts to be critical habitat.
22.tq: Use the named-organisation and feature association to avoid a location-based distractor.
xs: **CMS COP15** declared **seamounts** **critical habitat** — option **(2)**.
A seamount is an undersea **volcanic** peak that **does not reach the surface**.
xa: Seamounts carry **cobalt-rich crusts** (LENS Apr 2025).
**Deep Ocean Mission** surveys found about **25 seamounts** in the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal.
They also found **2 active + 2 inactive hydrothermal vents**.

22.s: Which one of the following best describes a seamount?
o: A flat-topped submarine mountain planed by waves
A submarine volcanic mountain that does not reach the sea surface
A ring-shaped coral reef enclosing a lagoon
A deep, steep-sided valley cut across the continental slope
22.x: A seamount is an undersea volcanic mountain or peak that does not reach the surface; seamounts carry cobalt-rich crusts. A flat-topped, wave-planed seamount is a guyot; a ring reef around a lagoon is an atoll; a steep valley across the shelf and slope is a submarine canyon.
22.tq: Seamount pointed and submerged; guyot flat-topped.
xs: A **seamount** is a submarine **volcanic mountain** that **does not reach the surface** — option **(2)**.
A flat-topped wave-planed one is a **guyot**; a ring reef is an **atoll**; a steep valley is a **submarine canyon**.
xa: Seamounts carry **cobalt-rich crusts**; **CMS COP15** declared them **critical habitat**.
India applied for the **Afanasy-Nikitin Seamount**, contested by **Sri Lanka**.
**Deep Ocean Mission** surveys: about **25 seamounts** found.

22.s: Trenches in the ocean floor primarily mark:
o: Locations where ocean water freezes permanently
The margins of stable continental interiors
Zones where one tectonic plate dives beneath another
22.x: Oceanic trenches commonly occur at subduction zones, where one plate descends beneath another.
22.tq: Apply the landform-process relationship rather than recalling only a name.
xs: **Trenches** mark **subduction zones**, where **one plate dives under another** — option **(4)**.
They are the **oceanic deeps**, at **plate convergence**, with active volcanoes and strong earthquakes.
xa: **Mariana Trench (Challenger Deep)** is the **deepest point on earth**.
Most trenches lie in the **Pacific**.
**Sunda (Java)** is the Indian Ocean's deepest trench.

22.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
22.x: The Puerto Rico Trench is the deepest point of the Atlantic Ocean. The Mariana, South Sandwich and Sunda trenches belong to the Pacific, Southern and Indian Oceans respectively.
22.tq: Use ocean-wise elimination of wrongly paired trenches.
xs: The **Puerto Rico Trench** is in the **Atlantic**, its deepest point — option **(2)**.
**Mariana** is in the **Pacific**, **South Sandwich** in the **Southern Ocean**, **Sunda** in the **Indian Ocean**.
xa: ⚠ Deepest: Pacific = **Mariana**, Indian = **Sunda (Java)**, Atlantic = **Puerto Rico**.
**Diamantina Deep:** south-east Indian Ocean, south-west of Australia.
**Aleutian:** North Pacific.

22.s: The deepest point on Earth, the Challenger Deep, is located in the:
22.x: The Challenger Deep lies in the Mariana Trench in the Pacific Ocean and is about 11 km deep.
22.tq: Match the superlative with its exact geographical feature.
xs: **Challenger Deep** lies in the **Mariana Trench** — option **(3)**.
It is in the **Pacific**, the **deepest point on earth**, about **11 km**, next to the **Northern Mariana Islands**.
**Tonga** and **Kermadec** are in the south-west Pacific; **Aleutian** in the North Pacific.
xa: Indian Ocean's deepest: **Sunda (Java)**; Atlantic's: **Puerto Rico**.
Trenches mark **subduction zones**.

22.s: The Tonga and Kermadec trenches are situated in the:
22.x: Both the Tonga and Kermadec trenches occur in the south-western Pacific Ocean.
22.tq: Discriminate between nearby trench groups by their oceanic sector.
xs: The **Tonga** and **Kermadec** trenches lie in the **south-west Pacific** — option **(1)**.
**South Sandwich** is the **Southern Ocean** trench; **Diamantina Deep** is in the **south-east Indian Ocean**.
xa: **Aleutian Trench:** North Pacific.
**Mariana (Challenger Deep):** deepest point on earth.
Oceanic deeps lie **mostly in the Pacific**.

22.s: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is characterised by which one of the following features?
o: It is S-shaped, with Iceland and the Azores rising above it.
It is a straight ridge extending only along the eastern Pacific.
It lies south of Iceland and carries transatlantic cables.
It is situated off Namibia in the South Atlantic.
22.x: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is S-shaped, and Iceland and the Azores rise above parts of it. The other descriptions refer to different features.
22.tq: Use the distinctive shape and associated islands as identifying clues.
xs: The **Mid-Atlantic Ridge** is **S-shaped**, with **Iceland and Azores** rising above it — option **(1)**.
South of Iceland carrying cables is the **Telegraph Plateau**; off Namibia is the **Walvis Ridge**.
xa: **East Pacific Rise:** Pacific.
**Ninety East Ridge:** Indian Ocean, along **90 deg E**.
**Carlsberg Ridge:** north-west Indian Ocean (**Arabian Sea**).

22.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Cocos Ridge — East Pacific, off Central America
Walvis Ridge — South Atlantic, off Namibia
Carlsberg Ridge — South Atlantic, off Namibia
22.x: The Carlsberg Ridge is located in the north-western Indian Ocean, in the Arabian Sea. The Walvis Ridge is the feature off Namibia.
22.tq: Find the swapped location among otherwise familiar ridge-ocean pairs.
xs: **Carlsberg Ridge — South Atlantic, off Namibia** is wrongly matched — option **(4)**.
The **Carlsberg Ridge** lies in the **north-west Indian Ocean (Arabian Sea)**; the ridge off **Namibia** is the **Walvis Ridge**.
**Cocos Ridge** (East Pacific, off Central America) and **East Pacific Rise** (Pacific) are correct.
xa: India sought exploration rights in the **Carlsberg Ridge** in **2024**.
**Mid-Atlantic Ridge** is S-shaped; **Iceland** and **Azores** rise above it.

22.s: The Telegraph Plateau is located in the North Atlantic, south of Iceland, and is associated with:
o: The deepest point of the Atlantic Ocean
22.x: The Telegraph Plateau lies south of Iceland in the North Atlantic and was used as a route for transatlantic cables.
22.tq: Link a geographical feature with its distinctive human-use association.
xs: The **Telegraph Plateau** carried the **route of the transatlantic cable** — option **(4)**.
It lies in the **North Atlantic, south of Iceland**.
The Atlantic's deepest point is the **Puerto Rico Trench**, not this plateau.
xa: **Mid-Atlantic Ridge:** S-shaped; **Iceland** and **Azores** rise above it.
**Walvis Ridge:** South Atlantic, off **Namibia**.

22.s: India sought exploration rights in 2024 in respect of the:
22.x: India sought exploration rights in the Carlsberg Ridge in 2024.
22.tq: Connect the policy action with the correct marine geographical feature.
xs: India sought exploration rights in the **Carlsberg Ridge** in **2024** — option **(4)**.
The ridge lies in the **north-west Indian Ocean (Arabian Sea)**.
xa: India holds a **polymetallic sulphide** licence on the **Indian Ocean Ridge** valid to **Sept 2031**.
India applied for the **Afanasy-Nikitin Seamount**, contested by **Sri Lanka**.
**Telegraph Plateau** (cables) and **Walvis Ridge** (off Namibia) are in the Atlantic.

22.s:
With reference to the floor of the Indian Ocean, consider the following statements:
1. The Sunda (Java) Trench is the deepest trench of the Indian Ocean.
2. The Ninety East Ridge runs along about 90 degrees East longitude.
3. India's application for the Afanasy-Nikitin Seamount is contested by Sri Lanka.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
22.x: All three are correct: the Sunda (Java) Trench is the Indian Ocean's deepest trench, the Ninety East Ridge runs along 90 degrees E, and India's claim to the Afanasy-Nikitin Seamount is contested by Sri Lanka. Options A, B and C each leave out one true statement.
22.tq: Indian Ocean: Sunda Trench deepest; Ninety East Ridge on 90 deg E.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: the **Sunda (Java) Trench** is the Indian Ocean's **deepest trench**.
Statement 2: the **Ninety East Ridge** runs along **90 deg E**.
Statement 3: India's claim to the **Afanasy-Nikitin Seamount** is **contested by Sri Lanka**.
xa: **Diamantina Deep:** south-east Indian Ocean, south-west of Australia.
**Carlsberg Ridge:** Arabian Sea; India sought rights in **2024**.
Polymetallic sulphide licence on the **Indian Ocean Ridge** valid to **Sept 2031**.

22.s:
Consider the following statements about terrigenous deposits:
1. They may include gravel, sand, silt and mud.
2. Their coarseness generally decreases away from the shore.
3. They become coarser as the distance from the shore increases.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
22.x: Terrigenous material may consist of gravel, sand, silt and mud. Coarser material is deposited near the coast, while finer material settles farther offshore; therefore statement 3 is false.
22.tq: Spot the reversed trend in a comparison statement about distance from the coast.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 is correct: **terrigenous** deposits are **gravel, sand, silt, mud** from land.
Statement 2 is correct: **coarseness decreases** away from shore — coarse near the coast, fine mud farther out.
Statement 3 is wrong: ⚠ **"coarseness increases seaward"** was the wrong statement in **APPSC G1 2024**.
xa: They settle **mainly on the continental shelves** and slopes.
**Pelagic deposits** (oozes + **red clay**) cover the deep-sea plains and deeps.

22.s: Which one of the following is NOT a pelagic deposit?
22.x: Calcareous ooze, siliceous ooze and red clay are pelagic deposits. Coastal gravel is a land-derived terrigenous deposit.
22.tq: Find the exception by separating deep-sea deposits from coarse coastal material.
xs: **Coastal gravel** is not pelagic — it is a land-derived **terrigenous** deposit — option **(1)**.
**Pelagic** deposits are deep-sea **oozes** (calcareous, siliceous) and **red clay**.
xa: **Calcareous ooze:** **lime shells** (globigerina, pteropod).
**Siliceous ooze:** **silica skeletons** (diatom, radiolarian), colder or deeper water.
**Red clay:** the **most widespread** deep-sea deposit.

22.s: Calcareous ooze is primarily composed of:
o: Fine inorganic clay and volcanic dust alone
Gravel and sand transported from continental rivers
Silica skeletons of diatoms and radiolarians
Lime shells of tiny organisms such as globigerina and pteropods
22.x: Calcareous ooze consists mainly of the lime shells of tiny organisms, including globigerina and pteropods.
22.tq: Match each ooze type with its distinctive biological composition.
xs: **Calcareous ooze** is made of **lime shells** of tiny organisms such as **globigerina and pteropods** — option **(4)**.
**Silica skeletons** of diatoms and radiolarians form **siliceous ooze**; clay and volcanic dust form **red clay**.
**Gravel and sand** from land are **terrigenous** deposits.
xa: Siliceous ooze forms in **colder or deeper water**.
**Red clay** is largest in the **deep Pacific**.

22.s: Which one of the following statements about red clay is correct?
o: It is restricted to river mouths and estuaries.
It is the most widespread deep-sea deposit and is largest in the deep Pacific.
It is formed exclusively from lime shells in warm shallow seas.
It occurs only on continental shelves and consists mainly of gravel.
22.x: Red clay consists of fine inorganic clay and volcanic dust. It is the most widespread deep-sea deposit and is particularly extensive in the deep Pacific.
22.tq: Use the superlative and location together to identify the correct deposit.
xs: **Red clay** is the **most widespread deep-sea deposit**, **largest in the deep Pacific** — option **(2)**.
It is **fine inorganic clay and volcanic dust**, not lime shells or gravel.
xa: **Pelagic** deposits cover the **deep-sea plains and deeps**.
**Calcareous ooze** = lime shells; **siliceous ooze** = silica skeletons.
**Terrigenous** deposits settle mainly on the **shelves** and slopes.

22.s: Terrigenous deposits derived from the land are laid down mainly on the:
22.x: Terrigenous deposits (gravel, sand, silt, mud from land) settle mainly on the continental shelves and slopes (APPSC G1 2024, statement I correct). Deep-sea plains and deeps, including trench floors, are covered by pelagic oozes and red clay; mid-ocean ridges are far from land-derived supply.
22.tq: Terrigenous = shelf/slope; pelagic = deep plains.
xs: **Terrigenous** deposits settle **mainly on the continental shelves and slopes** — option **(3)**.
This was the correct statement I in **APPSC G1 2024**.
**Deep-sea plains and deeps** are covered by **pelagic** oozes and **red clay**.
xa: Terrigenous deposits get **finer away from the shore**.
⚠ "Coarseness increases seaward" was the **wrong** statement.
**Red clay** is the most widespread deep-sea deposit.

22.s: Which one of the following statements best explains the temperature contrast between the western and eastern sides of tropical oceans?
o: The western side is warmer because warm currents generally flow along the eastern coasts of continents, whereas the eastern side is cooled by cold currents and upwelling along western continental coasts.
The western side is cooler because cold currents flow along the eastern coasts of continents.
The eastern side is warmer because upwelling brings warm deep water to the surface.
Both sides have the same temperature because ocean currents do not affect tropical waters.
22.x: In the tropics, the western side of an ocean is warmer because warm currents flow along the eastern coasts of continents. The eastern side is cooler due to cold currents and upwelling along western continental coasts.
22.tq: Use the reversed coast and current relationships as the principal trap.
xs: In the tropics the **western side is warmer**: **warm currents** run along continents' **east coasts** — option **(1)**.
**Trade winds** also pile warm water **westward**.
The **eastern side is cooler** due to **cold currents + upwelling** on continents' west coasts.
xa: ⚠ Tropics: **west warmer**; temperate: **east warmer** (westerlies, e.g. **North Atlantic Drift**).
The **annual range** is smaller in the **Pacific** than in the **Atlantic**.
**Northern hemisphere** oceans are warmer than southern (more land).

22.s: The higher-latitude reversal of the usual tropical ocean-temperature pattern is associated with the:
22.x: In the tropics the western sides of oceans are warmer, but in temperate latitudes the westerlies reverse this and make the eastern sections warmer, as the North Atlantic Drift does off NW Europe. Humboldt, Labrador and Benguela are cold currents.
22.tq: Match the exceptional higher-latitude pattern with its named current.
xs: In the **temperate zone** the **westerlies** reverse the tropical pattern and make **eastern sections warmer**, as with the **North Atlantic Drift** — option **(4)**.
In the **tropics**, by contrast, the **western** side is warmer.
The tropical eastern side is cooled by **cold currents + upwelling** on continents' west coasts.
xa: ⚠ Tropics: **west warmer**; temperate: **east warmer** — both statements correct (**UPSC 2021**).
Tropical west is warm because **trade winds** pile warm water **westward**.
The **annual range** is smaller in the vast **Pacific** than in the **Atlantic**.

22.s: Oceans absorb approximately what proportion of the excess heat associated with current global warming?
22.x: Oceans take up more than 90% of the excess heat. Ocean heat content reached a record in 2025, increasing by 23 zettajoules.
22.tq: Use the magnitude distinction between a minor and overwhelming share.
xs: Oceans take up **more than 90%** of the **excess heat** — option **(1)**.
This makes the ocean the main store of global-warming heat, far above the other options.
xa: **Marine heatwave:** SST **3-4 deg C** above average for at least **5 days**.
Vertical layers: warm surface layer to **~500 m** → **thermocline** (~**500-1,000 m**) → cold deep layer near **0-4 deg C**.
**CTD sensors** were fitted even to **sharks** in **2026** for hurricane forecasting.

22.s: A marine heatwave is conventionally identified when sea-surface temperature remains approximately how much above average for at least five days?
22.x: A marine heatwave is defined here as sea-surface temperature about 3–4°C above average for at least five days.
22.tq: Identify the event using both its temperature threshold and duration.
xs: A **marine heatwave** is SST **3-4 deg C above average** for **at least 5 days** — option **(3)**.
It is listed under ocean **temperature and heat**.
xa: Oceans take up **>90%** of excess heat.
**Mesopelagic ("twilight zone")** lies at **200-1,000 m**.
Tropical warm surface layer: **20-25 degC**, to about **500 m**.

22.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the temperature of ocean water:
1. Surface temperature generally falls from the equator towards the poles.
2. Northern Hemisphere oceans are generally warmer than Southern Hemisphere oceans.
3. Greater land area in the Northern Hemisphere contributes to this temperature difference.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
22.x: All three statements are correct. Surface temperature decreases poleward, and the greater land area in the Northern Hemisphere contributes to its relatively warmer oceans.
22.tq: Link the observed geographical pattern with its stated physical explanation.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: surface temperature **falls from the equator to the poles**.
Statements 2 and 3: **northern hemisphere** oceans are **warmer than southern** because of **more land**.
xa: **Enclosed tropical seas** are the **warmest**.
⚠ Tropics: **west warmer**; temperate: **east warmer**.
The **annual range** is smaller in the **Pacific** than in the **Atlantic**.

22.s: The annual range of ocean temperature is generally smaller in the Pacific Ocean than in the Atlantic Ocean because the Pacific is:
o: Deeper only in its eastern part
Located entirely in the Southern Hemisphere
22.x: The annual range of ocean temperature is smaller in the vast Pacific than in the Atlantic: a larger, more extensive body of water heats and cools more slowly, so its temperature varies less over the year.
22.tq: Test the direct comparison and avoid confusing ocean size with hemispheric location.
xs: The annual temperature range is **smaller in the vast Pacific** than in the **Atlantic** — option **(3) Vast and more extensive**.
Its sheer size makes its temperature vary less over the year.
xa: The **Pacific** is the **largest** ocean: **Pacific > Atlantic > Indian > Southern > Arctic**.
**Northern hemisphere** oceans are warmer than southern (more land).
**Enclosed tropical seas** are warmest.

22.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the vertical temperature structure of tropical ocean water?
o: Warm surface layer up to 1,000 m; thermocline from 1,000–2,000 m; deep layer near 20°C
Thermocline at the surface; warm layer below 1,000 m; deep layer near 10°C
Warm surface layer up to about 500 m; thermocline from about 500–1,000 m; deep layer near 0°C
A single uniform layer from the surface to the ocean floor
22.x: Tropical oceans have a warm surface layer to about 500 m (20-25 degC), a thermocline from about 500-1,000 m where temperature falls fast, and a cold deep layer near 0-4 degC. A, B and D misplace or omit these layers.
22.tq: Match each vertical layer with both its depth range and temperature characteristic.
xs: Tropical oceans: **warm surface layer to ~500 m** → **thermocline ~500-1,000 m** → **cold deep layer near 0 deg C** — option **(3)**.
The surface layer is **20-25 degC**; in the thermocline temperature **drops fast with depth**; the deep layer is **0-4 deg C**.
So options placing the warm layer to **1,000 m** or giving one uniform layer are wrong.
xa: **Polar seas** have **only the single cold layer**.
In **mid-latitudes** the warm layer forms **only in summer**.

22.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. In polar seas, generally only a single cold layer exists.
2. In mid-latitudes, the warm surface layer forms only during summer.
3. The tropical thermocline is a zone in which temperature falls rapidly with depth.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
22.x: All three are correct: polar seas have only a single cold layer, in mid-latitudes the warm surface layer forms only in summer, and the tropical thermocline (about 500-1,000 m) is where temperature drops fast with depth.
22.tq: Combine spatial and seasonal qualifiers carefully; none of the three statements is contradictory.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: **polar seas** have **only the single cold layer**.
Statement 2: in **mid-latitudes** the warm layer forms **only in summer**.
Statement 3: the **thermocline** (~**500-1,000 m**) is where temperature **drops fast with depth**.
xa: Tropical warm surface layer reaches about **500 m** (**20-25 degC**).
Deep layer: near **0-4 deg C**.

22.s:
Consider the following statements about salinity:
1. Salinity is expressed as grams of dissolved salt per 1,000 g of water (per mille or ppt).
2. Marine water has a salinity of about 35 ppt.
3. Brackish water has a salinity higher than that of marine water.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
22.x: Statement 1 is correct: salinity is grams of salt per 1,000 g of water. Statement 2 is correct: marine water is about 35 ppt. Statement 3 is wrong: brackish water is 5-35 ppt, i.e. less saline than marine water. So 1 and 2 only (B); A misses statement 2, and C and D include the false statement 3.
22.tq: Per mille = per 1,000 g; sea ~35, brackish 5-35 (below sea).
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 is correct: salinity = **grams of dissolved salt per 1,000 g** of water (**per mille / ppt**).
Statement 2 is correct: **marine water ~35 ppt**.
Statement 3 is wrong: **brackish water** is **5-35 ppt**, less saline than marine water.
xa: **Raised by** evaporation + freezing; **lowered by** precipitation, river inflow + ice melt.
Salinity is **highest in the subtropics** (~**20-30 deg**).

22.s: Which combination contains only processes that generally increase salinity?
22.x: Evaporation and freezing increase salinity because they remove freshwater. Precipitation, river inflow and ice melt generally lower salinity.
22.tq: Classify processes according to whether freshwater is removed or added.
xs: **Evaporation and freezing** raise salinity — option **(4)**.
**Precipitation, river inflow** and **ice melt** lower it, so options (1), (2) and (3) are wrong.
xa: **Currents and winds** redistribute salinity.
Highest in the **subtropics** (~**20-30 deg**); lower at the **rainy equator**.
Marine water **~35 ppt**; brackish **5-35 ppt**.

22.s: The highest oceanic salinity is generally found in the subtropical belt approximately between:
22.x: Oceanic salinity is generally highest in the subtropics, around 20°–30° latitude, because of high evaporation and relatively lower rainfall.
22.tq: Use the latitude range as the decisive geographical clue.
xs: Salinity is **highest in the subtropics**, about **20-30 deg** latitude — option **(4)**.
It is **lower at the rainy equator** (option 2's belt).
xa: Salinity is **raised by evaporation** + freezing; **lowered by precipitation** and river inflow.
**Red Sea** (~**41**) is among the saltiest seas; **Baltic** among the least saline.
Marine water averages **~35 ppt**.

22.s: The very high salinity of the Dead Sea is mainly associated with its:
o: Open connection to the Arctic Ocean
22.x: The Dead Sea is a closed basin with intense evaporation, producing salinity of about 238 per mille.
22.tq: Identify the cause-effect pair behind an extreme numerical value.
xs: The **Dead Sea** (**238** per mille) owes its salinity to a **closed basin** and **intense evaporation** — option **(4)**.
Rainfall, tributaries and open connections would lower salinity, not raise it.
xa: Ranking (APPSC G2 2023): **Lake Van (330) > Dead Sea (238) > Great Salt Lake (220)**.
**Great Salt Lake** (Utah) is also a **closed basin**.
**Black Sea** is **17-18 ppt**, about half the ocean average.

22.s: Which one of the following water bodies is a closed soda lake and the world's largest alkaline lake?
22.x: Lake Van in Turkey is a closed soda lake and the world's largest alkaline lake, with salinity of about 330 per mille.
22.tq: Use the unique descriptive identity of the water body.
xs: **Lake Van** (Turkey) is a **closed soda lake** and the **world's largest alkaline lake** — option **(4)**.
Its salinity is **330** per mille, the highest in the table.
**Great Salt Lake** (**220**) is a closed basin in Utah; the **Red Sea** (~**41**) and **Baltic** are seas.
xa: ⚠ APPSC G2 2023 key: **Lake Van > Dead Sea > Great Salt Lake** (NCERT figures).
**Dead Sea:** **238**, closed basin with intense evaporation.

22.s: The high salinity of the Red Sea is primarily related to:
o: High evaporation and little river inflow
Its location in a humid equatorial belt
22.x: The Red Sea has relatively high salinity, about 41 per mille, because of high evaporation and little river inflow.
22.tq: Match the salinity pattern with the controlling climatic and drainage factors.
xs: The **Red Sea** (~**41** per mille) is salty due to **high evaporation** and **little river inflow** — option **(1)**.
It is **among the saltiest seas**.
**Many rivers and low evaporation** describe the **Baltic**, the opposite case.
xa: **Mediterranean:** ~**37-39**.
**Black Sea:** **17-18 ppt**.
Marine water averages **~35 ppt**.

22.s: Which one of the following explains the lowest salinity of the Baltic Sea among the listed water bodies?
o: High evaporation and little river inflow
Many rivers, low evaporation and cold conditions
22.x: The Baltic Sea has salinity below about 10 per mille because it receives many rivers and has low evaporation in cold conditions.
22.tq: Infer the low-salinity cause from freshwater input and evaporation conditions.
xs: The **Baltic Sea** has the **lowest** salinity (under ~**10**) because of **many rivers, low evaporation** and **cold** — option **(4)**.
A closed basin with intense evaporation describes the **Dead Sea**; high evaporation with little inflow the **Red Sea**; soda lake is **Lake Van**.
xa: **Black Sea:** **17-18 ppt**, about half the ocean average.
Salinity is **lowered by precipitation, river inflow** and ice melt.
**Mediterranean:** ~**37-39**.

22.s: Which one of the following sequences represents the correct descending order of salinity among the listed water bodies?
o: Lake Van > Dead Sea > Great Salt Lake
Great Salt Lake > Lake Van > Dead Sea
Dead Sea > Lake Van > Great Salt Lake
Lake Van > Great Salt Lake > Dead Sea
22.x: Lake Van has a salinity of approximately 330 per mille, followed by the Dead Sea at about 238 per mille and the Great Salt Lake at about 220 per mille.
22.tq: Use the ranking method by comparing the numerical values before considering familiar names.
xs: **Lake Van (330) > Dead Sea (238) > Great Salt Lake (220)** — option **(1)**.
This is the **APPSC G2 2023** key, using **NCERT** figures.
xa: **Lake Van:** closed **soda lake**, world's largest **alkaline** lake.
**Dead Sea:** **closed basin**, intense evaporation; **Great Salt Lake** (Utah): closed basin.
**Red Sea** ~**41**; **Baltic** under ~**10**.

22.s: The first National Report on Deep-Sea and Distant-Water Fishery Resources of India's EEZ was released by the:
o: Centre for Marine Living Resources and Ecology
Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
National Centre for Polar and Ocean Research
22.x: The Centre for Marine Living Resources and Ecology (CMLRE) released the first National Report on Deep-Sea and Distant-Water Fishery Resources of the EEZ.
22.tq: Use the ‘which institution released it’ institutional trap.
xs: The **CMLRE** (Centre for Marine Living Resources and Ecology) released the **first National Report** on **Deep-Sea and Distant-Water Fishery Resources** of the EEZ — option **(2)**.
**NIOT** runs the **Nellore** seafront facility; **NCPOR Goa** supplied data for the shelf claim.
xa: A **CMLRE report** (Aug 2026) says the **mesopelagic** zone drives the biological carbon pump.
**Deep Ocean Mission:** approved **June 2021**, **Rs 4,077 crore**, **MoES**.

22.s: Which one of the following statements about Andhra Pradesh's maritime geography is correct?
o: Andhra Pradesh has a 1,053 km coast, the third-longest among Indian states, and Visakhapatnam is its only major port.
Andhra Pradesh has a 5,270 km coast, the third-longest among Indian states, and Machilipatnam is its only major port.
Andhra Pradesh has a 2,300 km coast, the longest among Indian states, and Nellore is its only major port.
Andhra Pradesh has a 1,053 km coast, the second-longest among Indian states, and Kakinada is its only major port.
22.x: Andhra Pradesh has a 1,053 km coast, described as the third-longest, and Visakhapatnam is the state's only major port. Its east-coast shelf is narrow.
22.tq: Combine the coastline figure, rank and port instead of relying on one familiar location.
xs: AP has a **1,053 km** coast, the **3rd longest**, and **Visakhapatnam** is its **only major port** — option **(1)**.
That coast fronts the **narrow east-coast shelf**.
xa: AP's shelf covers about **33,000 sq km**.
**Mahadevan Canyon** lies **off Visakhapatnam**.
**NIOT** has a **Nellore seafront facility**.

22.s: MATSYA-6000, mentioned in the context of India's deep-ocean capabilities, has:
o: Been withdrawn from the Deep Ocean Mission
Been used only for coral-reef mapping
22.x: MATSYA-6000 has passed its tests as part of India's deep-ocean exploration capabilities.
22.tq: Use the status-word distinction between a tested system and a proposed or withdrawn one.
xs: **MATSYA-6000** has **passed its tests** — option **(4) Completed its tests**.
It is part of the **Deep Ocean Mission**, approved **June 2021** (**Rs 4,077 crore**, MoES).
xa: Indian scientists reached **5,002 m** in an **Atlantic** dive.
Mining machine **Varaha** was trialled at **5,270 m** in the **Central Indian Ocean**.
DOM surveys found about **25 seamounts** and about **39** potentially new species.

22.s: Which one of the following facilities is associated with NIOT's Nellore seafront station?
o: Testing deep-sea mining and LTTD desalination equipment, along with deployment of new deep-sea buoys
Researching only coral-reef bleaching in the Gulf of Mannar
Operating India's first major commercial fishing harbour
Manufacturing aircraft carriers and testing satellite launch vehicles
22.x: NIOT's Nellore seafront facility tests deep-sea mining and LTTD desalination equipment, and its station has also started new deep-sea buoys.
22.tq: Identify the facility by linking its functions rather than its location alone.
xs: **NIOT's Nellore seafront facility** tests **deep-sea mining** and **LTTD desalination** kit — option **(1)**.
The question adds that it deploys new **deep-sea buoys**; coral, fishing harbour and aircraft carriers are not its work.
xa: **Varaha** mining machine trialled at **5,270 m**.
AP angle: **east-coast shelf, ports, NIOT**.
**Visakhapatnam** is AP's only **major port**.

22.s: With reference to India's Deep Ocean Mission, which one of the following is correct?
o: It was approved in June 2021 with an outlay of Rs 4,077 crore under the Ministry of Earth Sciences
It was approved in 2018 with an outlay of Rs 40,770 crore under the Ministry of Environment
It was approved in June 2021 with an outlay of Rs 4,077 crore under the Ministry of Shipping
It was approved in 2023 with an outlay of Rs 407 crore under ISRO
22.x: The Deep Ocean Mission was approved in June 2021 at Rs 4,077 crore and is run by the Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES). Option B has the wrong year, amount and ministry; C has the wrong ministry; D has the wrong year, amount and agency.
22.tq: DOM: 2021, Rs 4,077 cr, MoES.
xs: The **Deep Ocean Mission** was approved in **June 2021**, **Rs 4,077 crore**, under **MoES** (Ministry of Earth Sciences) — option **(1)**.
Options (2), (3) and (4) get the year, amount or ministry wrong.
xa: **MATSYA-6000** has **passed its tests**.
Scientists reached **5,002 m** in an Atlantic dive; **Varaha** trialled at **5,270 m**.
DOM surveys: **2 active + 2 inactive hydrothermal vents**.

23.s:
Arrange the following stores of the Earth's water in descending order of their share:
A. Groundwater
B. Oceans
C. Rivers and streams
D. Polar ice caps and glaciers
23.x: The descending order is oceans, polar ice caps and glaciers, groundwater, and rivers and streams.
23.tq: Apply the first-and-last method using the largest and smallest stores before placing the middle items.
xs: **Oceans > polar ice and glaciers > groundwater > rivers** — option **(1) B, D, A, C**.
Oceans **~97%**, ice caps and glaciers **~2%**, groundwater **~0.7%**, rivers and streams **smallest** (UPPSC 2025).
xa: **Lakes, soil moisture, atmosphere** hold only **tiny fractions**.
Ocean average salinity: about **35 per mille**.

23.s: Approximately what proportion of the Earth's water is present in the oceans?
23.x: Approximately 97 percent of the Earth's water is stored in the oceans.
23.tq: Distinguish the share of the oceans from the percentage of Earth’s surface covered by water.
xs: About **97 percent** of earth's water is in the **oceans** — option **(4)**.
Asked in **APPSC GS 2025**.
xa: **Ice caps and glaciers:** ~**2%**; **groundwater:** ~**0.7%**.
Order: **Oceans > polar ice and glaciers > groundwater > rivers** (UPPSC 2025).
**Rivers and streams** are the **smallest** store.

23.s: Which one of the following is the smallest major store among the listed components of the Earth's water resources?
23.x: Rivers and streams constitute the smallest share among the listed major water stores.
23.tq: Use the size comparison rather than confusing visible availability with total storage.
xs: **Rivers and streams** are the **smallest** store — option **(2)**.
Order: **oceans (~97%) > ice caps and glaciers (~2%) > groundwater (~0.7%) > rivers**.
xa: This order was asked in **UPPSC 2025**.
**Lakes, soil moisture, atmosphere** are **tiny fractions**.

23.s: Salinity of ocean water is generally expressed in which of the following units?
o: Parts per thousand, per mille or PSU
Parts per hundred or percentage only
23.x: Salinity is expressed in parts per thousand, called per mille or ppt, and also in Practical Salinity Units (PSU).
23.tq: Test the exact scientific unit rather than an approximate everyday measure.
xs: Salinity is expressed in **parts per thousand (per mille, ppt)** or **PSU** — option **(2)**.
It is the **total dissolved salts** in sea water.
xa: **Ocean average:** about **35 per mille** (**35 g per kg**).
Salts come from **weathered rock** carried by rivers and **volcanic/hydrothermal** emissions.
Salinity **reduces evaporation** (APPSC GS 2018).

23.s: The average salinity of ocean water is approximately:
23.x: The average salinity of ocean water is about 35 per mille, equivalent to approximately 35 grams of dissolved salts per kilogram of water.
23.tq: Distinguish the decimal scale from the standard per-mille value.
xs: Average ocean salinity is about **35 per mille** — option **(1)**.
That equals **35 g per kg** of sea water.
xa: Units: **per mille, ppt** or **PSU**.
**Sodium chloride** is ~**77.8%** of dissolved salts.
Highest salinity: **subtropics**; lower at the **equator** and near the **poles**.

23.s:
Which of the following are important sources of salts in ocean water?
1. Weathered rock material carried by rivers
2. Volcanic emissions on the sea floor
3. Hydrothermal emissions on the sea floor
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
23.x: Ocean salts are supplied by weathered materials transported by rivers and by volcanic and hydrothermal emissions from the sea floor.
23.tq: Combine independent source statements and select the inclusive code when all are supported.
xs: All three are sources — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Salts come from **weathered rock material carried by rivers**.
And from **volcanic/hydrothermal emissions** on the sea floor.
xa: **Sodium chloride** ~**77.8%**, **magnesium chloride** ~**10.9%** of dissolved salts.
By ions: **chloride + sodium** dominate.
Ocean average: about **35 per mille**.

23.s: Which one of the following combinations is correctly matched?
23.x: River inflow adds fresh water and lowers salinity. Evaporation and freezing generally raise salinity, while precipitation and melting lower it.
23.tq: Match each process with its direct effect on salt concentration.
xs: **River inflow lowers salinity** — option **(3)** — e.g. the **Black Sea** fed by the **Danube, Dnieper, Dniester**.
**Evaporation raises** it, **precipitation lowers** it, and **freezing raises** it, so (1), (2) and (4) are reversed.
xa: **Melting** lowers salinity; **currents and winds** redistribute saline water.
Salinity **reduces evaporation** (APPSC GS 2018).
**Baltic** and **Black Sea** are low-salinity because rivers pour in.

23.s: What is the effect of salinity on the evaporation of sea water?
o: Salinity has no effect on evaporation
23.x: Salinity reduces evaporation (APPSC GS 2018). Evaporation raises salinity, but salinity itself lowers the rate of evaporation, so it does not increase it. It does affect evaporation, but it does not stop it altogether.
23.tq: Evaporation raises salinity; salinity lowers evaporation.
xs: **Salinity reduces evaporation** — option **(2)** (APPSC GS 2018).
⚠ Do not reverse it: **evaporation raises salinity**, but salinity itself **lowers** evaporation.
xa: **Precipitation** and **river inflow** lower salinity.
Ocean average: about **35 per mille**.
Subtropics are saltiest due to **high evaporation, low rain**.

23.s: Which salt constitutes the largest approximate share of the dissolved salts in seawater?
23.x: Sodium chloride accounts for approximately 77.8 percent of the dissolved salts in seawater.
23.tq: Select the dominant constituent by comparing percentage shares.
xs: **Sodium chloride** is the largest share, about **77.8%** of dissolved salts — option **(1)**.
**Magnesium chloride** ~**10.9%**, **magnesium sulphate** ~**4.7%**, **calcium sulphate** ~**3.6%**.
xa: **Potassium sulphate:** ~**2.5%**.
By ions: **chloride + sodium** dominate, then **sulphate** and **magnesium**.

23.s: Which of the following correctly describes the relative abundance of ions in seawater?
o: Magnesium and sulphate dominate, followed by sodium and chloride.
Calcium and potassium dominate, followed by chloride and sodium.
Potassium and calcium dominate, followed by magnesium and sulphate.
Chloride and sodium dominate, followed by sulphate and magnesium.
23.x: By ions, chloride and sodium are the dominant constituents of seawater, followed by sulphate and magnesium.
23.tq: Distinguish the ranking of ions from the ranking of complete salts.
xs: By ions, **chloride and sodium dominate**, followed by **sulphate and magnesium** — option **(4)**.
This matches **sodium chloride** being ~**77.8%** of dissolved salts.
xa: **Magnesium chloride** ~**10.9%** is the second-largest salt.
Ocean average: about **35 per mille**.

23.s:
Arrange the following salts according to their approximate share of dissolved salts in seawater, from highest to lowest:
A. Magnesium sulphate
B. Potassium sulphate
C. Sodium chloride
D. Calcium sulphate
23.x: The correct order is sodium chloride, magnesium sulphate, calcium sulphate and potassium sulphate, corresponding approximately to 77.8%, 4.7%, 3.6% and 2.5%.
23.tq: Arrange percentage values rather than relying on the chemical names.
xs: **Sodium chloride > magnesium sulphate > calcium sulphate > potassium sulphate** — option **(1) C, A, D, B**.
xa: **Magnesium chloride** (~**10.9%**) ranks second overall.
By ions: **chloride + sodium** dominate.

23.s: The highest open-ocean salinity is generally observed in the subtropical regions mainly because of:
o: Heavy river discharge and melting ice
High evaporation and relatively low rainfall
23.x: Subtropical regions generally have high evaporation and low rainfall, resulting in relatively high surface salinity.
23.tq: Connect the salinity pattern with the balance between evaporation and freshwater input.
xs: Subtropics have the highest salinity due to **high evaporation and low rain** — option **(4)**.
⚠ Highest = **subtropics**, not the **equator**.
xa: **Equator:** lower (heavy rain); **poles:** lower (melting ice, low evaporation).
**Red Sea, Persian Gulf, Mediterranean:** high (hot, dry areas).
**Baltic, Black Sea:** low (rivers pour in).

23.s: Which one of the following correctly explains the comparatively low salinity near the equator and the poles?
o: High evaporation near the equator and freezing near the poles
Heavy rainfall near the equator and ice melting near the poles
River inflow near the equator and high evaporation near the poles
Low rainfall near the equator and absence of ice near the poles
23.x: Heavy equatorial rainfall lowers salinity near the equator, while melting ice and low evaporation lower salinity near the poles.
23.tq: Match each latitude belt with its characteristic freshwater process.
xs: Salinity is lower at the **equator** due to **heavy rain** and near the **poles** due to **melting ice** and low evaporation — option **(2)**.
High evaporation raises salinity, which is why the **subtropics** are highest.
xa: ⚠ Highest = **subtropics**, not the **equator**.
**Freezing** raises salinity; **melting** lowers it.
Ocean average: about **35 per mille**.

23.s: Which of the following pairs of enclosed seas and salinity conditions is correctly matched?
o: Red Sea — low salinity due to heavy river inflow
Persian Gulf — high salinity in a hot and dry setting
Baltic Sea — high salinity due to intense evaporation
Black Sea — high salinity due to absence of rivers
23.x: The Persian Gulf has high salinity because it is situated in a hot and dry region. The Baltic and Black Seas have lower salinity where freshwater input is important.
23.tq: Use the environmental setting and freshwater inflow as the deciding clues.
xs: **Persian Gulf** — **high** salinity in a **hot, dry** setting — option **(2)**.
The **Red Sea** is **high**, not low; the **Baltic** and **Black Sea** are **low** because **rivers pour in**.
xa: The **Mediterranean** is also high (hot, dry area).
**Arabian Sea** is saltier than the **Bay of Bengal**.
Black Sea is fed by the **Danube, Dnieper, Dniester**.

23.s: Which one of the following statements is correct regarding the salinity of the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal?
o: The Arabian Sea is saltier because the Bay of Bengal receives Ganga–Brahmaputra water.
The Arabian Sea is less saline because it receives more river water.
The Bay of Bengal is saltier because it receives major rivers.
Both have exactly the same salinity throughout the year.
23.x: The Arabian Sea is saltier than the Bay of Bengal, where the discharge of the Ganga and Brahmaputra supplies substantial fresh water.
23.tq: Watch for the reversed comparison trap involving river discharge and salinity.
xs: The **Arabian Sea is saltier** because the **Bay of Bengal** gets **Ganga-Brahmaputra** water — option **(1)**.
River inflow **lowers** salinity, so the Bay of Bengal is the less saline one.
xa: **Baltic** and **Black Sea:** low (rivers pour in).
**Red Sea, Persian Gulf, Mediterranean:** high (hot, dry).
Highest belt: **subtropics**.

23.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
23.x: A pycnocline is a zone of rapid change in water density. A thermocline concerns temperature, a halocline salinity, and a chemocline chemical characteristics.
23.tq: Discriminate among look-alike scientific terms by identifying their root meaning.
xs: **Pycnocline** = rapid change in **density** — option **(1)**.
**Thermocline** = temperature; **halocline** = salinity; **chemocline** = chemistry, so (2), (3), (4) are wrong.
xa: ⚠ **Halocline** = salinity; **Pycnocline** = density.
Each cline acts as a **barrier to vertical mixing**.
Chemoclines are typical of **meromictic** basins like the **Black Sea**.

23.s:
Consider the following statements about oceanic clines:
1. A thermocline denotes a rapid change in temperature.
2. A halocline denotes a rapid change in salinity.
3. A chemocline denotes a rapid change in chemical characteristics.
4. Each cline can act as a barrier to vertical mixing.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
23.x: All four statements are correct. Clines mark sharp vertical changes and impede the vertical mixing of water.
23.tq: Identify the common functional feature after matching each technical term with its gradient.
xs: All four are correct — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
**Thermocline** = temperature; **halocline** = salinity; **chemocline** = chemistry (oxygen/hydrogen sulphide).
Each cline acts as a **barrier to vertical mixing**.
xa: **Pycnocline** = rapid change in **density**.
Density rises as **temperature falls** and **salinity rises**.

23.s: The Black Sea is cited as an example of a basin where a chemocline is associated with:
o: Complete mixing of upper and lower layers
Uniform temperature from surface to bottom
Rare mixing between upper and lower layers due to chemical differences
Absence of dissolved gases in all layers
23.x: The Black Sea is a meromictic basin in which upper and lower layers rarely mix, and chemical differences such as oxygen and hydrogen sulphide are important.
23.tq: Apply the definition of a chemocline to the characteristic structure of a meromictic basin.
xs: The **Black Sea** is **meromictic**: upper and lower layers **rarely mix**, with a **chemocline** — option **(3)**.
The chemocline marks a change in **chemistry** (e.g. **oxygen/hydrogen sulphide**).
xa: The Black Sea is fed by the **Danube, Dnieper, Dniester**, so its salinity is **low**.
Clines act as **barriers to vertical mixing**.
⚠ **Halocline** = salinity; **Pycnocline** = density.

23.s:
Consider the following statements about the density of ocean water:
1. Density rises as temperature falls.
2. Density rises as salinity rises.
3. Increased pressure with depth raises density.
4. Denser water tends to sink while lighter water rises.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
23.x: All four statements are correct. Temperature, salinity and pressure influence density, and density differences cause sinking and rising movements of water.
23.tq: Check each listed factor independently before selecting the complete combination.
xs: All four are correct — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
Density rises as **temperature falls** and as **salinity rises**; **pressure (depth)** also raises it.
**Denser water sinks**, lighter water rises → this **drives currents**.
xa: **Cold polar water sinks** and creeps towards the **equator**.
**Pycnocline** = zone of rapid density change.

23.s: Cold polar water sinking and moving towards lower latitudes is primarily an example of the role of:
o: Density differences in driving ocean circulation
Uniform surface heating in all latitudes
Absence of pressure at great depth
23.x: Cold polar water is denser and sinks; the resulting density-driven movement contributes to ocean currents and carries water towards the equator.
23.tq: Infer the controlling mechanism from the sequence of cooling, sinking and horizontal movement.
xs: Cold polar water sinking and creeping to the equator shows **density differences** driving **ocean circulation** — option **(1)**.
Cold water is **denser**, so it **sinks**; lighter water rises.
xa: Density rises with **falling temperature**, **rising salinity** and **pressure**.
**Pycnocline** = rapid change in **density**, a barrier to mixing.

23.s: Approximately what proportion of the ocean surface experienced marine heatwaves in 2025?
23.x: About 90 percent of the ocean surface experienced marine heatwaves in 2025.
23.tq: Identify the correct percentage without confusing it with the ocean’s heat-absorption share.
xs: About **90 percent** of the ocean surface saw **marine heatwaves** in **2025** — option **(3)** (WMO 2025).
2025 also set an **ocean heat content record**: about **23 zettajoules** more heat.
xa: Oceans absorb **over 90%** of excess heat.
They also absorb about **a quarter** of human CO2 → **acidification** (pH ~**8.1** falling).

23.s: Which of the following correctly describes the proposed use of sharks fitted with CTD tags?
o: They are being trained to measure only coastal salinity.
They are being tested as ocean-data collectors for hurricane forecasting.
They are being used to replace all ocean buoys.
They are being used to desalinate seawater.
23.x: Sharks carrying CTD tags are being tested as mobile ocean-data collectors to support hurricane forecasts.
23.tq: Identify the specific technological application and reject exaggerated replacement claims.
xs: Sharks fitted with **CTD tags** are tested as **ocean-data collectors** for **hurricane forecasts** — option **(2)**.
**CTD** measures conductivity (salinity), temperature and depth.
xa: **NIOT**'s **Nellore** station operationalised **OMNI** deep-sea buoys.
About **90%** of the ocean surface saw marine heatwaves in **2025**.

23.s: The OMNI deep-sea buoys operationalised through the NIOT satellite station at Nellore record which set of parameters in real time?
o: Rainfall, humidity and wind speed only
Only wave height and atmospheric pressure
23.x: The OMNI deep-sea buoys record temperature, salinity and ocean currents in real time for cyclone and Indian Ocean Dipole forecasting.
23.tq: Match the observing system with its exact parameter set and purpose.
xs: **OMNI** buoys give real-time **temperature, salinity, currents** — option **(4)**.
They are run through **NIOT's satellite station at Nellore** for **cyclone** and **IOD** forecasting.
xa: Sharks with **CTD tags** are tested for hurricane forecasts.
Ocean heat content record in **2025**: about **23 zettajoules**.

23.s:
Consider the following statements about the role of oceans in climate change:
1. Oceans absorb over 90 percent of excess heat.
2. Oceans absorb about one-fourth of human carbon dioxide emissions.
3. Absorption of carbon dioxide contributes to ocean acidification.
4. Ocean pH is approximately 8.1 and is declining.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
23.x: All four statements are correct. Ocean uptake of excess heat and carbon dioxide produces warming effects and contributes to declining pH, with ocean pH around 8.1.
23.tq: Combine quantitative climate facts with the associated cause-and-effect relationship.
xs: All four are correct — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
Oceans absorb **over 90%** of excess heat and about **a quarter of human CO2**.
The CO2 causes **acidification**, with **pH ~8.1** and falling.
xa: About **90%** of the ocean surface saw marine heatwaves in **2025** (WMO 2025).
Ocean heat content record in **2025**: about **23 zettajoules** more heat.

24.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Crest — lowest part of a wave
Trough — highest part of a wave
Wavelength — distance from one crest to the next crest
Wave period — vertical distance from crest to trough
24.x: Wavelength is the distance between successive crests. The crest is the top, the trough is the bottom, wave height is crest-to-trough distance, and period is the time between successive crests.
24.tq: Match each technical term with its precise definition.
xs: **Wavelength** is the distance from **one crest to the next crest** — so option **(3)** is correct.
The **crest** is the **top** of a wave, not the lowest part; the **trough** is the **bottom**, not the highest part.
The vertical distance from crest to trough is the wave **height**; the wave **period** is the **time between crests**.
xa: Waves carry **energy, not water**; water particles move in small **circles**, with **wind** supplying the energy.
⚠ **Wavelength** = crest to crest; **height** = crest to trough.
**Swells** are slow, steady, **long-period** waves from distant storms; steep waves are young, from a **local wind**.

24.s: Which of the following statements about waves is correct?
o: Wave motion is caused exclusively by the rotation of the Earth.
Deep water is strongly affected by every ordinary wind wave.
Waves transport large quantities of water permanently in the direction of travel.
Water particles in a wave generally move in small circles and wind supplies the energy.
24.x: Waves mainly carry energy, not water. Water particles move in small circular motions, wind supplies the energy, and deep water is comparatively little affected.
24.tq: Distinguish energy transfer from mass transport in physical geography.
xs: In a wave, **water particles move in small circles** and **wind supplies the energy** — option **(4)**.
Waves carry **energy, not water**, so they do not transport water permanently in the direction of travel.
**Deep water** is barely affected by ordinary waves; and the energy comes from **wind**, not the Earth's rotation.
xa: **Largest waves** occur in the **open ocean**.
**Breakers**: near shore, waves slow by **friction** and break when **depth < half the wavelength**.
A **tsunami** is different: it comes from a **sudden vertical displacement of the sea floor** (quake, landslide, volcano).

24.s: Which one of the following statements regarding swells is correct?
o: They are short, steep waves produced immediately by local winds.
They are narrow channels of water flowing away from the shore.
They occur only when the sea floor is vertically displaced.
They are slow, steady, long-period waves that originate from distant storms.
24.x: Swells are long-period waves generated by storms far from the place where they are observed. Narrow channels flowing away from shore are rip currents.
24.tq: Use the origin and period of a wave to identify a swell.
xs: **Swells** are **slow, steady, long-period waves** that come from **distant storms** — option **(4)**.
Short, steep waves from **local winds** are young wind waves, not swells.
Narrow channels flowing **away from shore** are **rip currents**; sea-floor displacement produces a **tsunami**.
xa: **Kallakkadal** (Kerala swell surge): long-period swells (**30-300 s**) from southern Indian Ocean storms ~**10,000 km** away.
Kallakkadal is most frequent in the **pre-monsoon** season.
**INCOIS** set up a second **Coastal Flood Monitoring System** at **Kollam** harbour for Kallakkadal forecasts.

24.s: A wave approaching a shore generally breaks when:
o: Its crest becomes equal to its trough
The wind ceases in the open ocean
The water depth becomes less than half the wavelength
The water depth becomes greater than the wavelength
24.x: Near the shore, friction slows the wave. It breaks when the water depth is less than half its wavelength.
24.tq: Recall the threshold ratio used to identify the formation of breakers.
xs: A wave breaks when the **water depth becomes less than half the wavelength** — option **(3)**.
Near the shore, waves **slow by friction** with the sea floor; these are **breakers**.
Crest and trough are the **top** and **bottom** of a wave; they never become "equal", so option (1) is meaningless.
xa: **Wavelength** = crest to crest; wave **height** = crest to trough; **period** = time between crests.
**Rip currents**: narrow, fast channels flowing **away from shore** as shoreward water escapes through a narrow path.
**ISRO** project: **AI + satellite** tools to detect **rip currents** for beach safety.

24.s: Kallakkadal, observed along the Kerala coast, is associated with:
o: A tidal bore caused by the full Moon
Long-period swell surges from storms in the southern Indian Ocean
Short wind waves generated within the Arabian Sea
A sudden vertical displacement of the sea floor near Kerala
24.x: Kallakkadal is a swell surge produced by long-period swells generated by storms in the southern Indian Ocean.
24.tq: Link the regional term with its specific wave phenomenon and source.
xs: **Kallakkadal** is caused by **long-period swell surges** from **storms in the southern Indian Ocean** — option **(2)**.
These swells (**30-300 s**) travel ~**10,000 km** to reach the **Kerala** coast; most frequent **pre-monsoon**.
It is not local wind waves (those are short and steep) nor a sea-floor displacement (that is a **tsunami**).
xa: **Swells** = slow, steady, **long-period** waves from **distant storms**.
**INCOIS** (Hyderabad) issues **swell-surge** alerts and has a **Coastal Flood Monitoring System** at **Kollam** harbour.
⚠ A **storm surge** is different: a weather-driven rise from **winds + pressure changes**.

24.s: The term 'tsunami' literally refers to a:
24.x: Tsunami is a Japanese term meaning 'harbour wave'. It has a very long wavelength and may travel at up to 800 km/h in the deep ocean.
24.tq: Test the exact meaning of a look-alike geographical term.
xs: **Tsunami** is a **Japanese** word meaning **"harbour wave"** — option **(1)**.
A tsunami is caused by a **sudden vertical displacement of the sea floor** (quake, landslide, volcano).
It has an **extremely long wavelength** and travels up to **800 km/h** in the deep ocean.
xa: **INCOIS, Hyderabad** runs the **Indian Tsunami Early Warning System (ITEWS)**.
ITEWS is a **UNESCO regional tsunami service provider** for **25** Indian Ocean countries; warns within **10 minutes**.
ITEWS parts: seismic network, deep-ocean **Bottom Pressure Recorders**, coastal **tide gauges**, satellite link, **Decision Support System**.

24.s: Which one of the following correctly compares wind waves and tsunamis?
o: Wind waves are caused by sea-floor displacement, whereas tsunamis are caused by ordinary surface winds.
Wind waves have extremely long wavelengths, whereas tsunamis have short wavelengths.
Wind waves are caused by surface winds, whereas tsunamis may result from sudden vertical displacement of the sea floor.
Both have the same cause, wavelength and speed.
24.x: Wind waves are generated by wind acting on the sea surface. Tsunamis may result from sudden vertical displacement of the sea floor due to an earthquake, landslide or volcanic activity.
24.tq: Compare the cause column first, then eliminate options that reverse the two phenomena.
xs: **Wind waves** come from **wind on the surface**; a **tsunami** may come from a **sudden vertical displacement of the sea floor** — option **(3)**.
Option (1) reverses the causes; option (2) reverses wavelengths — wind waves are **short**, tsunamis **extremely long**.
Speed also differs: wind waves are **slow**, a tsunami reaches **800 km/h** in deep ocean — so option (4) is wrong.
xa: Tsunami = Japanese **"harbour wave"**; triggers: **quake, landslide, volcano**.
**ITEWS** monitored **32** major earthquakes in **2025**.
**NIOT, Chennai** OMNI buoys feed **tsunami** and **IOD** monitoring.

24.s: Which one of the following correctly describes a rip current?
o: A tidal current flowing only towards the beach
A broad current flowing parallel to the coastline
A deep-ocean current caused exclusively by salinity differences
A narrow, fast channel flowing away from the shore
24.x: A rip current is a narrow and fast-moving channel of water flowing away from the shore.
24.tq: Discriminate the exact direction and form of a rip current from other coastal currents.
xs: A **rip current** is a **narrow, fast channel flowing away from the shore** — option **(4)**.
It forms when **shoreward water escapes through a narrow path**, so it flows seaward, not towards the beach.
Density/salinity-driven flow is the deep **thermohaline** circulation, not a rip current.
xa: **ISRO** project uses **AI + satellite** tools to detect **rip currents** for **beach safety**.
**Breakers**: waves break near shore when **depth < half the wavelength**.
**Tidal currents** form when tidal water is channelled into **bays/estuaries**.

24.s: Which one of the following best describes a tide?
o: An irregular rise of sea level caused by storm winds
A permanent increase in sea level caused by melting ice
A circular movement of ocean water caused by the Coriolis force
A periodic rise and fall of sea level occurring once or twice a day
24.x: A tide is the periodic rise and fall of sea level, generally occurring once or twice a day. Storm surges are irregular and weather-driven phenomena.
24.tq: Use the precise definition and distinguish tides from storm surges.
xs: A **tide** is the **periodic rise and fall of sea level once or twice a day** — option **(4)**.
It is caused by the **gravitational pull of the moon** (greater) and **sun** (lesser), countered by **centrifugal force**.
An irregular rise from storm winds is a **storm surge** — weather-driven, irregular, **unlike tides**.
xa: High tides recur about every **12 h 25 min**.
**Semi-diurnal** (two highs + two lows a day) is the **most common** type.
Tidal energy: **tidal range** (barrage across an estuary) vs **tidal stream** (underwater turbines).

24.s:
With reference to the causes of tides, consider the following statements:
1. The gravitational pull of the Moon is greater than that of the Sun in producing tides.
2. Centrifugal force acts in opposition to gravitational attraction.
3. The vertical component of tide-generating force is more important than the horizontal component.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
24.x: The Moon has the greater tidal influence, and centrifugal force counters gravitational attraction. The horizontal components of the tide-generating force are more significant than the vertical component, making statement 3 false.
24.tq: Identify the incorrect comparison of horizontal and vertical components.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 correct: the **moon's** pull is **greater**, the **sun's** lesser.
Statement 2 correct: **centrifugal force counters gravity**.
Statement 3 wrong: the **horizontal components** of tide-generating force matter **more than the vertical**.
xa: **Tide-generating force** = gravitational attraction − centrifugal force.
⚠ **Direct tide** = gravity (moon side); **indirect tide** = centrifugal force (opposite side).
**Perigean tides**: moon **closest** to the earth → unusually high tides.

24.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The tidal bulge on the side opposite to the Moon is associated with centrifugal force.
2. The bulge facing the Moon is called the indirect tide.
3. Two tidal bulges are formed on opposite sides of the Earth.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
24.x: The opposite-side bulge is associated with centrifugal force and the two bulges occur on opposite sides. The bulge facing the Moon is the direct tide, not the indirect tide.
24.tq: Spot the swapped meaning in a confusable pair.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2) 1 and 3 only**.
Statement 1 correct: the bulge on the **opposite side** comes from **centrifugal force** (the **indirect tide**).
Statement 2 wrong: the bulge **facing the moon** is the **direct tide** (gravitational attraction).
Statement 3 correct: there are **two tidal bulges** on opposite sides of the earth.
xa: **Bulge height** is higher over **wide continental shelves**, lower at **mid-ocean islands**.
**Spring tide**: sun, moon and earth **in a line** (**new moon and full moon**) — highest range.
**Neap tide**: sun and moon at **right angles** (first/third quarter) — lowest range.

24.s: The tide-generating force is best represented by the
o: sum of wind force and atmospheric pressure
difference between gravitational attraction and centrifugal force
sum of vertical and horizontal components of wind
difference between ocean temperature and salinity
24.x: Tide-generating force results from the difference between gravitational attraction and centrifugal force.
24.tq: Test the exact relationship in a definition.
xs: **Tide-generating force** = **gravitational attraction − centrifugal force** — option **(2)**.
Gravity comes from the **moon** (greater) and **sun** (lesser); **centrifugal force** counters it.
Wind, pressure, temperature and salinity do not generate tides; **winds + pressure** cause **storm surges**.
xa: Its **horizontal components** matter more than the vertical.
Moon side bulge = **direct tide**; opposite side = **indirect tide**.
Tidal water channelled into **bays/estuaries** forms **tidal currents**.

24.s:
Consider the following statements about tides and related sea-level changes:
1. Tidal bulges are higher over wide continental shelves than at mid-ocean islands.
2. Tidal water channelled into bays and estuaries forms tidal currents.
3. Storm surges are periodic rises of sea level caused by the pull of the moon and sun.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
24.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: storm surges are caused by winds and pressure changes; they are weather-driven and irregular, unlike tides. So 1 and 2 only (A); options B, C and D each include the false statement 3.
