25.s: The Dipole Mode Index (DMI) is used for monitoring which of the following ocean-atmosphere phenomena?
25.x: The Indian Ocean Dipole is monitored through the Dipole Mode Index, or DMI.
25.tq: Match the specialised index with the phenomenon it monitors.
xs: The **Dipole Mode Index (DMI)** measures the **Indian Ocean Dipole** — option **(4)**.
The **Southern Oscillation** is measured by the **SOI** (Tahiti minus Darwin), not the DMI.
xa: Late **May 2026** DMI value **-0.34 °C** = **neutral**.
IOD discovered in **1999**; develops **April-May**, peaks in **October**.
⚠ **Positive IOD** = more rain (offsets El Nino).

25.s: Which of the following statements regarding the Madden–Julian Oscillation is correct?
o: It is a westward-moving belt of clouds beginning over the Pacific Ocean and recurring every 5–10 days.
It is a seasonal reversal of winds confined to the Arabian Sea.
It is an eastward-moving belt of clouds and rain beginning over the tropical Indian Ocean and recurring every 30–60 days.
It is a stationary pressure belt over the subtropical Atlantic Ocean.
25.x: The MJO is an eastward-moving belt of clouds and rain that starts over the tropical Indian Ocean and recurs every 30–60 days.
25.tq: Combine movement, place of origin and recurrence interval to identify the exact phenomenon.
xs: The **MJO** is an **eastward-moving** belt of clouds and rain that starts over the **tropical Indian Ocean** and recurs every **30-60 days** — option **(3)**.
It is not westward, not from the Pacific, and not every 5-10 days; it is not a seasonal Arabian Sea wind reversal.
xa: Identified by **Madden and Julian, 1971-72**.
Convection rises up to **10 km**; it fades in the **eastern Pacific** but circles the globe aloft.
It shifts the heavy-rain zone eastward → **active/break spells** of the monsoon.

25.s: Madden and Julian identified the oscillation named after them during
25.x: Madden and Julian identified the MJO in 1971–72.
25.tq: Use the close decade options to test precise historical recall.
xs: **Madden and Julian** identified the oscillation in **1971-72** — option **(4)**.
The **MJO** is an **eastward-moving** pulse of clouds, convection and rain, starting as a warm pool in the tropical **Indian Ocean**.
xa: **Walker** described the Southern Oscillation in the **1920s**.
MJO convection reaches up to **10 km**.

25.s:
Which of the following correctly describes the vertical and horizontal behaviour of the Madden-Julian Oscillation?
1. Its convection can rise up to 10 km.
2. It fades in the eastern Pacific but circles the globe aloft.
3. It shifts the heavy-rain zone eastward.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
25.x: The MJO convection rises up to 10 km, weakens in the eastern Pacific while continuing aloft around the globe, and shifts the heavy-rain zone eastward.
25.tq: Combine vertical extent, movement and rainfall-zone displacement.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: MJO convection rises up to **10 km**.
Statement 2: it **fades in the eastern Pacific** but **circles the globe aloft**.
Statement 3: it **shifts the heavy-rain zone eastward**.
xa: The shift produces **active/break spells** of the monsoon.
Periodicity: every **30-60 days**.
Identified by **Madden and Julian, 1971-72**.

25.s: The Madden-Julian Oscillation is associated with which monsoon pattern?
o: The complete absence of monsoon variability
Only winter snowfall in North India
Active and break spells of the monsoon
25.x: By shifting the zone of heavy rain eastward, the MJO contributes to active and break spells of the monsoon.
25.tq: Connect a moving atmospheric pulse with its practical weather effect.
xs: The **MJO** causes **active and break spells** of the monsoon — option **(4)**.
It does this by **shifting the heavy-rain zone eastward**.
xa: MJO recurs every **30-60 days** and moves **eastward**.
It begins as a warm pool in the tropical **Indian Ocean**.
Convection up to **10 km**; fades in the **eastern Pacific** but circles the globe aloft.

25.s: In its April 2026 forecast, the India Meteorological Department projected the southwest monsoon at what level of the Long Period Average?
25.x: The IMD forecast projected a below-normal monsoon at 92% of the Long Period Average, whose reference value was stated as 87 cm.
25.tq: Distinguish closely spaced percentage figures in a forecast question.
xs: IMD's **April 2026** forecast put the monsoon at **92% of LPA** — option **(1)**.
The **LPA** is **87 cm**; the forecast was **below normal** due to a developing **El Nino**.
xa: It was the first "below normal" April warning in **11 years**.
El Nino gives a **delayed/weak Indian monsoon** via high pressure over the Indian Ocean.
Weak monsoon years hit **rain-fed Rayalaseema** farming.

25.s: Which inference regarding El Nino and Bay of Bengal cyclones is supported by the INCOIS study?
o: El Nino may reduce post-monsoon Bay of Bengal cyclones.
El Nino always increases post-monsoon Bay of Bengal cyclones.
El Nino shifts all Bay of Bengal cyclones to the Arabian Sea.
El Nino has no relationship with Bay of Bengal cyclones.
25.x: The study indicated that El Nino may reduce the number of post-monsoon Bay of Bengal cyclones.
25.tq: Use the cautious wording ‘may’ and distinguish a possible tendency from an absolute rule.
xs: The **INCOIS** study says **El Nino may reduce** post-monsoon Bay of Bengal cyclones — option **(1)**.
ENSO governs the number of **post-monsoon (Oct-Dec)** Bay of Bengal cyclones.
**La Nina** goes the other way: **more floods and severe cyclones** in the Bay of Bengal.
xa: INCOIS is in **Hyderabad**.
Fewer/more Bay of Bengal cyclones affect **coastal AP**.
El Nino weakens the **Walker circulation** and shifts it eastward.

25.s: Which of the following correctly describes the relevance of ENSO-related cyclone and monsoon changes to Andhra Pradesh?
o: They are unrelated to agricultural conditions in Andhra Pradesh.
They influence only irrigation-fed agriculture in Rayalaseema.
They can affect coastal Andhra Pradesh and rain-fed farming in Rayalaseema.
They affect only the inland districts and not coastal Andhra Pradesh.
25.x: Fewer or more Bay of Bengal cyclones and weak monsoon years directly affect coastal Andhra Pradesh and rain-fed Rayalaseema farming.
25.tq: Translate a broad climate relationship into its regional agricultural and hazard consequences.
xs: ENSO-linked cyclone and monsoon changes hit **coastal AP** and **rain-fed Rayalaseema** farming — option **(3)**.
**Fewer/more Bay of Bengal cyclones** affect the coast; **weak monsoon years** hit rain-fed Rayalaseema.
So they affect both coast and interior — options (1), (2) and (4) are wrong.
xa: **NIOT OMNI buoys** off **Nellore** support **IOD** monitoring.
IMD **April 2026**: below-normal monsoon, **92% of LPA (87 cm)**.
El Nino impacts: **drought**, lower **rice, sugarcane** yields, **food inflation**.

25.s: The NIOT OMNI buoys located off Nellore are relevant primarily to which activity?
o: Monitoring volcanic activity in the Pacific
25.x: NIOT OMNI buoys off Nellore support monitoring of the Indian Ocean Dipole.
25.tq: Match the regional observing platform with its stated monitoring purpose.
xs: **NIOT OMNI buoys** off **Nellore** support **IOD monitoring** — option **(2)**.
The **IOD** is the SST difference between the **Arabian Sea** and the eastern Indian Ocean **south of Indonesia**.
xa: IOD measured by the **Dipole Mode Index (DMI)**; late **May 2026** value **-0.34 °C** = neutral.
IOD develops **April-May**, peaks in **October**.
ENSO monitoring uses the **Nino 3.4 region** and NASA's **Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich**.

25.s:
Arrange the following developments in chronological order:
A. Identification of the Indian Ocean Dipole
B. Last El Nino mentioned in the record
C. First description of the Southern Oscillation by Walker

Choose the correct sequence.
25.x: Walker first described the Southern Oscillation in the 1920s, the Indian Ocean Dipole was identified in 1999, and the last El Nino mentioned was in 2023–24.
25.tq: Anchor the sequence using the 1920s, 1999 and 2023–24 time markers.
xs: Order: **C, A, B** — option **(2)**.
**C**: **Walker** described the **Southern Oscillation** in the **1920s**.
**A**: the **IOD** was identified in **1999**; **B**: the last El Nino was **2023-24**.
xa: **Madden and Julian** identified the **MJO** in **1971-72** — between Walker and the IOD.
**2025** was the **warmest La Nina year on record**.
IMD's **April 2026** forecast was the first "below normal" April warning in **11 years**.

25.s: Which ocean-atmosphere condition was cited as the reason for the IMD's April 2026 below-normal monsoon forecast?
o: A reduction in Bay of Bengal sea-surface temperature
25.x: The below-normal monsoon forecast was attributed to a developing El Nino.
25.tq: Apply the stated cause-effect relationship between ENSO conditions and monsoon prospects.
xs: IMD's **April 2026** below-normal forecast was due to a **developing El Nino** — option **(3)**.
The forecast was **92% of LPA (87 cm)**, the first "below normal" April warning in **11 years**.
A **neutral** IOD (DMI **-0.34 °C**, late May 2026) was not the cited cause.
xa: El Nino → air descends over the Indian Ocean → **high pressure** → **delayed/weak monsoon**.
A **positive IOD** could **offset** El Nino, as in **1997**.
**6 of 10** El Nino years brought depressed Indian rainfall.

26.s: Marine ecosystems cover approximately what proportion of the Earth’s surface?
26.x: Marine ecosystems cover about 71 per cent of the Earth’s surface.
26.tq: Separate the surface-area figure from the water-volume figure.
xs: Marine ecosystems cover about **71 per cent** of Earth's surface — option **(3)**.
**97%** is their share of Earth's **water**, not of the surface.
xa: Marine ecosystems include **coral reefs, hydrothermal vents, estuaries, salt marshes, mangroves, seagrass beds, kelp forests**.
**Rivers and freshwater lakes** are **not** marine (lentic/lotic freshwater ecosystems).
Oceans, mainly **phytoplankton**, produce **about half (50%+)** of Earth's oxygen.

26.s: Approximately what proportion of the Earth’s water is held by marine ecosystems?
26.x: Marine ecosystems hold approximately 97 per cent of the Earth’s water.
26.tq: Use the paired percentage distinction between surface coverage and water storage.
xs: Marine ecosystems hold about **97 per cent** of Earth's water — option **(4)**.
**71%** is the share of Earth's **surface** they cover.
xa: The **epipelagic (sunlit)** zone holds the **highest percentage** of marine habitats/life.
The **neritic shelf zone** is the **richest fishing zone**.
Coral reefs cover **< 1% of the ocean floor** yet support **> 25%** of marine species.

26.s: Which one of the following is a marine ecosystem associated with chemosynthetic life?
26.x: Hydrothermal vents are marine ecosystems that support chemosynthetic life, unlike rivers and freshwater lakes.
26.tq: Use the distinctive biological process to identify the ecosystem.
xs: **Hydrothermal vents** are marine ecosystems with **chemosynthetic** life — option **(3)**.
**Rivers** and **freshwater lakes** are freshwater (lotic/lentic) ecosystems, **not marine**; a glacial pond is freshwater too.
xa: Other marine ecosystems: **coral reefs, intertidal zone, estuaries, salt marshes, mangroves, seagrass beds, kelp forests**.
Ocean **primary producers** are **phytoplankton** (diatoms, dinoflagellates, cyanobacteria).
The **aphotic** zone is dark with **no photosynthesis**.

26.s:
Which of the following are marine ecosystems?
1. Estuaries
2. Salt marshes
3. Mangroves
4. Kelp forests

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
26.x: Estuaries, salt marshes, mangroves and kelp forests are all marine or coastal marine ecosystems.
26.tq: Test recognition of a group of related ecosystem types.
xs: All four are marine ecosystems — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
**Estuaries, salt marshes, mangroves** and **kelp forests** are all listed as marine.
xa: Also marine: **coral reefs, hydrothermal vents, tidal/intertidal zone, seagrass beds**.
⚠ **Rivers** and **freshwater lakes** are **not marine**.
The **Gulf of Mannar Biosphere Reserve** combines estuaries, salt marshes, mangroves, coral reefs and seagrass beds.

26.s: The littoral or intertidal zone lies between the
o: sunlit and dark zones of the ocean
sea floor and the deepest ocean trench
continental shelf and the open ocean
26.x: The littoral or intertidal zone is the area between the high-tide and low-tide marks.
26.tq: Recall the physical boundaries of the intertidal zone.
xs: The **littoral / intertidal** zone lies between the **high-tide and low-tide marks** — option **(4)**.
Sunlit vs dark is the **photic/aphotic** divide; shelf vs open ocean is the **neritic/oceanic** divide.
xa: **Neritic** zone: from the **high-water line** over the continental shelf to about **200 m**.
**Benthic** = the **sea floor** and its organisms.
**Oceanic** = open ocean **beyond the shelf**.

26.s: The neritic zone extends from the high-water line over the continental shelf to approximately
26.x: The neritic zone extends from the high-water line across the continental shelf to about 200 metres depth.
26.tq: Associate the neritic zone with the continental shelf and its approximate depth.
xs: The **neritic zone** reaches about **200 m** depth over the **continental shelf** — option **(4)**.
It starts at the **high-water line**.
xa: The neritic shelf zone is the **richest fishing zone**.
The **photic (euphotic)** zone is the sunlit upper layer (~**200 m**) where photosynthesis occurs.
Corals grow in **clear, shallow, sunlit** water, usually < ~**50 m**.

26.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes the oceanic zone from the neritic zone?
o: The oceanic zone is the open ocean beyond the continental shelf, whereas the neritic zone overlies the shelf
The oceanic zone is sunlit, whereas the neritic zone is permanently dark
The oceanic zone is the sea floor, whereas the neritic zone is the water column
The oceanic zone lies over the continental shelf, whereas the neritic zone is beyond it
26.x: The neritic zone overlies the continental shelf, while the oceanic zone refers to the open ocean beyond the shelf.
26.tq: Discriminate between two zones using their relation to the continental shelf.
xs: **Oceanic** zone = **open ocean beyond the shelf**; **neritic** zone = **over the continental shelf** — option **(1)**.
Option (4) swaps them; the **sea floor** is the **benthic** zone, not the oceanic zone.
Sunlit vs dark is the **photic/aphotic** distinction, not oceanic/neritic.
xa: Neritic zone extends to about **200 m** depth.
**Neritic shelf zone** = richest fishing zone.
**Littoral/intertidal** = between high- and low-tide marks.

26.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: Pelagic — sea floor and its organisms
26.x: The photic or euphotic zone is the sunlit upper layer in which photosynthesis occurs. The pelagic zone is the open water column, the benthic zone is the sea floor, and the aphotic zone is dark.
26.tq: Match each oceanic term with its precise spatial meaning.
xs: **Photic — zone where photosynthesis occurs** is correctly matched — option **(3)**.
**Benthic** is the **sea floor** and its organisms (not the water column); the **aphotic** zone is **dark**, not sunlit.
So "pelagic — sea floor" and "aphotic — sunlit" are wrong pairings.
xa: Photic (euphotic) = sunlit upper layer, about **200 m**.
**Epipelagic (sunlit)** zone holds the **highest percentage** of marine life.
**Aphotic** = dark zone below, **no photosynthesis**.

26.s: The richest fishing zone among the following is generally the
26.x: The neritic zone over the continental shelf is generally the richest fishing zone.
26.tq: Link shallow continental-shelf waters with high fisheries productivity.
xs: The **neritic shelf zone** is the richest fishing zone — option **(3)**.
It extends from the **high-water line** over the **continental shelf** to about **200 m**.
The **aphotic** zone is dark with no photosynthesis, so it cannot be the richest.
xa: **Upwelling** zones (Peru-Chile, California, Namibia, Somalia, Kerala) are also rich fisheries.
**Epipelagic (sunlit)** zone holds the most marine habitats/life.
**Phytoplankton** are the ocean's main **primary producers**.

26.s: Which ocean zone holds the highest percentage of marine habitats and life?
26.x: The epipelagic (sunlit) zone holds the highest percentage of marine habitats and life, because light there allows photosynthesis. The aphotic zone is dark with no photosynthesis, and the abyssal and hadal zones on the deep sea floor and in trenches support far less life.
26.tq: Sunlit epipelagic = most marine life.
xs: The **epipelagic (sunlit)** zone holds the **highest percentage** of marine habitats/life — option **(1)**.
Light there allows **photosynthesis**; the **aphotic** zone is dark with **no photosynthesis**.
xa: The **photic (euphotic)** layer is about **200 m** deep.
**Phytoplankton** (diatoms, dinoflagellates, cyanobacteria) are the main primary producers.
The **neritic shelf zone** is the richest fishing zone.

26.s: Which of the following are the principal primary producers in the ocean?
o: Phytoplankton such as diatoms, dinoflagellates and cyanobacteria
26.x: Phytoplankton, including diatoms, dinoflagellates and cyanobacteria, constitute the main primary producers of the ocean.
26.tq: Distinguish primary producers from consumers in a marine food web.
xs: **Phytoplankton** — **diatoms, dinoflagellates, cyanobacteria** — are the ocean's main **primary producers** — option **(4)**.
Fish, crustaceans, shellfish, mammals and turtles are consumers, not primary producers.
xa: Oceans, mainly phytoplankton, produce **about half (50%+)** of Earth's oxygen — more than all rainforests combined.
**Upwelling** brings nutrients → **plankton boom** → rich fisheries.
**Red tide** = toxic bloom of mostly **dinoflagellates**.

26.s: Approximately how much of Earth’s oxygen is produced by the oceans, mainly through phytoplankton?
26.x: The oceans, mainly through phytoplankton, produce about half or more than half of Earth’s oxygen, exceeding the contribution of all rainforests combined.
26.tq: Select the approximate share rather than confusing oceanic production with rainforest production.
xs: Oceans, mainly via **phytoplankton**, produce **about half (50%+)** of Earth's oxygen — option **(2)**.
That is **more than all rainforests combined**.
xa: Phytoplankton = **diatoms, dinoflagellates, cyanobacteria**.
**El Nino** suppresses Peru upwelling → **fewer phytoplankton**, fishery collapse.
Marine ecosystems cover about **71%** of Earth's surface.

26.s: Upwelling along a coast generally occurs when:
o: Tides permanently stop vertical movement of seawater
Warm surface water sinks because of intense evaporation
River water pushes all subsurface water into the open ocean
Winds push surface water offshore and cold, nutrient-rich subsurface water rises
26.x: Coastal upwelling occurs when winds drive surface water away from the coast, allowing cold, nutrient-rich subsurface water to rise.
26.tq: Use the direction of surface-water movement to identify the upwelling mechanism.
xs: **Upwelling**: winds push **surface water offshore** and **cold, nutrient-rich subsurface water rises** — option **(4)**.
Result: a **plankton boom** and **rich fisheries**.
xa: Upwelling zones: **Peru-Chile** (Humboldt), **California**, **Namibia** (Benguela), **Somalia** (Findlater), **Kerala**.
**El Nino** **suppresses** the Peru upwelling.
Kerala upwelling supports **oil sardine and mackerel**.

26.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Upwelling zone)
a. Peru–Chile
b. California
c. Namibia
 d. Somalia/Horn of Africa

List-II (Associated current or season)
i. Benguela Current
 ii. Findlater Current and southwest monsoon
 iii. Humboldt Current
 iv. California Current

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
26.x: Peru–Chile is associated with the Humboldt Current, California with the California Current, Namibia with the Benguela Current, and Somalia with the Findlater Current and southwest monsoon.
26.tq: Start from the sure current–coast pairs and eliminate codes containing a wrong association.
xs: Correct code: **a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii** — option **(1)**.
**Peru-Chile** — **Humboldt** (anchoveta fishery); **California** — **California current**.
**Namibia** — **Benguela**; **Somalia/Horn of Africa** — **Findlater current, SW monsoon**.
xa: **Kerala / SW India** upwelling: **SW monsoon** — **oil sardine and mackerel**.
Upwelling: winds push surface water offshore → cold, nutrient-rich water rises.
**El Nino** suppresses Peru upwelling → fishery collapse.

26.s:
Consider the following statements about upwelling off Kerala and southwest India:
1. It is associated with the southwest monsoon.
2. It supports oil sardine and mackerel fisheries.
3. It is caused by the Benguela Current.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
26.x: Kerala and southwest India experience upwelling associated with the southwest monsoon, supporting oil sardine and mackerel fisheries. The Benguela Current is associated with Namibia.
26.tq: Separate the correct seasonal and fisheries links from the swapped-current statement.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: Kerala/SW India upwelling comes with the **SW monsoon**.
Statement 2: it supports **oil sardine and mackerel** fisheries.
Statement 3 wrong: the **Benguela** current is linked to **Namibia (SW Africa)**, not Kerala.
xa: **Somalia/Horn of Africa** upwelling: **Findlater** current, SW monsoon.
**Peru-Chile** upwelling: **Humboldt** (anchoveta fishery).
AP fisheries depend on **Bay of Bengal plankton** productivity, now threatened by **marine heatwaves**.

26.s: El Niño can cause a collapse of the Peru fishery because it:
o: Strengthens Peru upwelling and eliminates all nutrients
Suppresses Peru upwelling, reducing phytoplankton and fish food
Stops all ocean circulation in the Pacific Ocean
Increases cold-water upwelling and causes excessive shell formation
26.x: El Niño suppresses the Peru upwelling system, reducing phytoplankton abundance and thereby contributing to fishery collapse.
26.tq: Trace the sequence from climate event to upwelling, phytoplankton and fisheries.
xs: **El Nino suppresses Peru upwelling**, reducing **phytoplankton** and fish food — option **(2)**.
No upwelling → no nutrient-rich water → **fewer phytoplankton** → **fishery collapse**.
It does not strengthen upwelling or increase cold water — that is the opposite of El Nino.
xa: The Peru-Chile upwelling is tied to the **Humboldt** current — the **anchoveta** fishery.
Since **1998** every strong El Nino has coincided with a **global bleaching event**.
Phytoplankton are the ocean's main **primary producers**.

26.s: Coral reefs are primarily built from the skeletons of which organisms?
26.x: Coral reefs are built from the calcium carbonate skeletons secreted by coral polyps.
26.tq: Use the direct organism–formation association.
xs: Coral reefs are built from skeletons of tiny **coral polyps** — option **(4)**.
Polyps are **colonial marine invertebrates**; their skeleton is **calcium carbonate (aragonite)**.
xa: Polyps live in **mutualistic symbiosis** with **zooxanthellae** (single-celled algae).
**Ocean acidification** makes it harder for corals to build **calcium carbonate** skeletons.
Reef types: **fringing**, **barrier**, **atoll**.

26.s:
Consider the following statements regarding coral reef distribution:
1. Coral reefs are generally found between about 30°N and 30°S.
2. Zooxanthellae live in symbiotic association with corals.
3. Coral reefs generally require water temperatures below 20°C.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
26.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because coral reefs generally require warm water above about 20°C.
26.tq: Reject the reversed temperature condition while retaining the latitude and symbiosis facts.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: reefs lie mostly within the **tropics**, roughly **30°N-30°S**.
Statement 2: **zooxanthellae** live in **mutualistic symbiosis** with corals.
Statement 3 wrong: corals need **warm water above ~20°C**, not below.
xa: Minimum about **20-21 °C**; optimum **23-25 °C**.
Water must be **clear, shallow, sunlit** (usually < ~**50 m**), sediment-free, normal salinity.
Reefs avoid **muddy river mouths**.

26.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Type of reef)
a. Fringing reef
b. Barrier reef
c. Atoll

List-II (Characteristic)
i. Ring reef enclosing a central lagoon
ii. Grows close to the shore
iii. Runs parallel to the coast and is separated from it by a lagoon

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
26.x: A fringing reef grows close to the shore, a barrier reef is separated from the coast by a lagoon, and an atoll encloses a central lagoon.
26.tq: Start with the sure pair and eliminate codes containing a wrong reef characteristic.
xs: Correct code: **a-ii, b-iii, c-i** — option **(1)**.
**Fringing reef** grows **close to the shore**; **barrier reef** runs **parallel to the coast**, separated by a wide, deep **lagoon**.
**Atoll** = **ring-shaped reef** enclosing a lagoon, with no central island.
xa: Fringing: **Gulf of Mannar**, **Gulf of Kutch**.
Barrier: **Great Barrier Reef** (Australia) — Queensland, Coral Sea.
Atoll: **Lakshadweep** — India's only true atolls.

26.s: The Great Barrier Reef is correctly described as a:
o: Fringing reef in the Gulf of Mannar
Barrier reef off Queensland in the Coral Sea
Fringing reef off the coast of Maharashtra
26.x: The Great Barrier Reef is a barrier reef located off Queensland in the Coral Sea and extends for about 2,300 km.
26.tq: Discriminate among reef types by matching the named example with its location.
xs: The **Great Barrier Reef** is a **barrier reef** off **Queensland** in the **Coral Sea** — option **(3)**.
**Lakshadweep** has **atolls**; the **Gulf of Mannar** has **fringing** reefs; **Malvan** (Maharashtra) has patchy reefs.
xa: **UNESCO World Heritage Site 1981**.
World's **largest** reef, followed by the **Mesoamerican Barrier Reef**.

26.s: The mutualistic association between coral polyps and zooxanthellae is correctly described by which one of the following?
o: Zooxanthellae destroy coral tissues and prevent calcification
Corals provide food and colour, while zooxanthellae provide calcium carbonate
Zooxanthellae provide food and colour, while corals provide shelter and nutrients
Both organisms independently obtain all their nutrients from seawater
26.x: Zooxanthellae photosynthesise and supply food and colour to corals. The coral provides them with shelter and nutrients.
26.tq: Test the reciprocal benefits in a symbiotic relationship.
xs: **Zooxanthellae** supply **food and colour**; the **coral** gives **shelter and nutrients** — option **(3)**.
The algae **photosynthesise** to supply food/energy; option (2) reverses the roles.
The coral, not the algae, builds the **calcium carbonate** skeleton.
xa: This is **mutualistic symbiosis** (**mutualism**).
**Bleaching** = corals turn **white after expelling zooxanthellae** and lose pigments.
Bleached coral is **stressed, not necessarily dead**.

26.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
26.x: Lakshadweep contains India’s only true atolls. The Great Barrier Reef is a barrier reef, while the Gulf of Kutch is associated with fringing reefs.
26.tq: Use the example to distinguish similar reef types.
xs: **Atoll — Lakshadweep** is correctly matched — option **(4)**.
Lakshadweep has **India's only true atolls**.
**Gulf of Kutch** has **fringing** reefs; the **Great Barrier Reef** is a **barrier** reef.
xa: Atoll = **ring-shaped** reef enclosing a lagoon, no central island.
A giant **Pavona clavus** (potato patch coral) colony was found near **Kadmat Island, Lakshadweep**.
⚠ Highest diversity = **Andaman & Nicobar**; only atolls = **Lakshadweep**.

26.s:
With reference to coral reef growth conditions, consider the following statements:
1. Coral reefs generally require warm water, with a minimum temperature of about 20–21°C.
2. The optimum temperature for coral growth is approximately 23–25°C.
3. Coral reefs generally flourish in clear, shallow and sunlit water.
4. Heavy sediment deposition at muddy river mouths favours coral reef growth.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
26.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Heavy sediment and freshwater from muddy river mouths generally inhibit coral reef growth.
26.tq: Identify the environmental requirement and reject the reversed condition.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(1) 1, 2 and 3 only**.
Statements 1-2: minimum about **20-21 °C**, optimum **23-25 °C**.
Statement 3: corals need **clear, shallow, sunlit** water.
Statement 4 wrong: corals **avoid muddy river mouths**; they need **sediment-free** water.
xa: That is why most of India's **east coast** (West Bengal, Odisha, **Andhra Pradesh**) has **no reefs**.
Depth usually < ~**50 m**; normal salinity.
Location: mostly within **30°N-30°S**.

26.s: Coral reefs are called the ‘Rainforests of the Sea’ primarily because they
o: support exceptionally high marine species richness despite occupying less than one per cent of the ocean floor
are found only near tropical rainforests
receive the highest rainfall among all marine ecosystems
cover most of the ocean floor and contain only tropical plants
26.x: Coral reefs cover less than one per cent of the ocean floor but support more than 25 per cent of all marine species, giving them exceptionally high species richness.
26.tq: Distinguish an ecological epithet from a literal geographical association.
xs: Reefs are **"Rainforests of the Sea"** because they cover **< 1% of the ocean floor** yet support **> 25% of all marine species** — option **(1)**.
The epithet is about **species richness**, not rainfall or being near rainforests.
xa: With tropical rainforests, reefs have the **highest species richness**.
Roles: **break wave power during storms**, preventing **coastal erosion**.
**APPSC 2024** paired the epithet with "breaks wave power" — both true, but the second does not explain the first.

26.s: Which one of the following is NOT a role of coral reefs?
o: Increasing coastal erosion by amplifying storm waves
26.x: Coral reefs break storm waves and thereby help prevent coastal erosion. They also provide nursery grounds and support fisheries and tourism.
26.tq: Find the option that reverses a stated ecological function.
xs: **Increasing coastal erosion by amplifying storm waves** is **not** a reef role — option **(3)**.
Reefs do the opposite: they **break wave power during storms**, **preventing coastal erosion**.
They also provide **nursery/spawning grounds**, **fisheries**, **tourism** and biodiversity.
xa: Reefs protect coasts from **storm surges**.
NGT cleared the **₹92,000-crore Great Nicobar project** (Feb 2026) — **coral loss** is the core objection.
**MPAs**, no-fishing zones and sanctuaries help reefs **recover**.

26.s: The association between coral polyps and zooxanthellae is best described as:
o: Predation, because corals consume the algae
Parasitism, because the algae destroy coral tissue
Mutualism, because both partners derive benefits
Commensalism, because only the algae benefit
26.x: Zooxanthellae provide photosynthetic energy, while corals provide shelter and nutrients. Therefore, the relationship is mutualistic.
26.tq: Infer the ecological relationship from the benefits received by both partners.
xs: The coral-zooxanthellae relationship is **mutualism** — both partners **benefit** — option **(3)**.
Algae **photosynthesise** → supply food/energy and colour; coral gives **shelter and nutrients**.
It is not predation, parasitism or commensalism, since neither harms nor gains alone.
xa: Zooxanthellae are **single-celled algae**.
Stressed corals **expel** zooxanthellae → **bleaching**.
**Rising SST / marine heatwaves** are now the **strongest global driver** of coral loss.

26.s:
Assertion (A): Coral reefs are called the 'Rainforests of the Sea'.
Reason (R): Coral reefs break wave power during storms and prevent coastal erosion.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
26.x: Both statements are true (APPSC 2024). Reefs are called 'Rainforests of the Sea' because they cover under 1% of the ocean floor yet support over 25% of marine species, i.e. their species richness, not their wave-breaking role. So R does not explain A; options C and D are wrong because both A and R are true.
26.tq: Rainforest epithet = biodiversity, not storm protection.
xs: **Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation** — option **(2)**.
A is true because reefs cover **< 1% of the ocean floor** yet hold **> 25%** of marine species — **species richness**.
R is true (reefs **break wave power**, preventing **coastal erosion**) but it does not explain the epithet (**APPSC 2024**).
xa: Other services: **nurseries/spawning grounds**, fisheries, tourism, protection from **storm surges**.
With tropical rainforests, reefs have the **highest species richness**.

26.s: Which one of the following sets contains only recognised true coral reef areas in India?
o: Godavari Delta, Mahanadi Delta, Malvan and West Bengal
Sundarbans, Krishna Delta, Chilika and Gulf of Kutch
West Bengal, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh and Lakshadweep
Gulf of Mannar, Gulf of Kutch, Lakshadweep and Andaman and Nicobar Islands
26.x: India’s recognised true reef areas include the Gulf of Mannar, Gulf of Kutch, Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Lakshadweep. Patchy reefs also occur at Malvan in Maharashtra.
26.tq: Select the complete valid geographical set while rejecting sediment-rich east-coast locations.
xs: **Gulf of Mannar, Gulf of Kutch, Lakshadweep, Andaman & Nicobar** are true reef areas — option **(4)**.
Most of the **east coast** (**West Bengal, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh**) has **no reefs** — heavy river sediment + freshwater.
**Malvan** (Maharashtra) has only **patchy reefs**.
xa: **Andaman & Nicobar** = **highest diversity**; **Lakshadweep** = only true **atolls**.
**Gulf of Mannar** (TN), **Gulf of Kutch** (Gujarat) = true reefs.
⚠ **AP** has **no true coral reefs**.

26.s: Coral reefs are absent along most parts of the east coast of India mainly because of
o: absence of sunlight throughout the year
excessively high salinity near all river mouths
heavy river sediment and freshwater input
extremely cold ocean currents and permanent sea ice
26.x: Most of the east coast, including West Bengal, Odisha and Andhra Pradesh, lacks reefs because heavy river sediment and freshwater inhibit coral growth.
26.tq: Connect a physical coastal condition with the geographical distribution of reefs.
xs: Most of India's **east coast** lacks reefs because of **heavy river sediment and freshwater** — option **(3)**.
Corals need **clear, sediment-free** water of **normal salinity** and avoid **muddy river mouths**.
xa: No-reef states: **West Bengal, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh**.
AP fisheries depend on **Bay of Bengal plankton** productivity, threatened by **marine heatwaves**.
The east coast exception: **Gulf of Mannar** (TN) has true reefs.

26.s: Which one of the following is correctly associated with the Gulf of Mannar Biosphere Reserve?
o: It is India’s only true atoll system and has no islands
It is India’s first national coral reef research institute
It is located on the Andhra coast and consists only of freshwater wetlands
It is India’s first marine biosphere reserve and includes coral reefs, mangroves and seagrass beds
26.x: The Gulf of Mannar Biosphere Reserve is India’s first marine biosphere reserve. It includes islands, estuaries, beaches, coral reefs, salt marshes, mangroves, seagrass beds and dugongs.
26.tq: Match the reserve with its status and ecosystem composition.
xs: The **Gulf of Mannar Biosphere Reserve** is India's **first marine biosphere reserve**, with **coral reefs, mangroves, seagrass beds** — option **(4)**.
It also has islands, estuaries, beaches, salt marshes, and **dugongs** in its seagrass beds.
India's **only true atolls** are in **Lakshadweep**; the **first coral reef research institute** is at **Chidiyatapu**; it is in **TN**, not AP.
xa: Gulf of Mannar is a **true reef** of the **fringing** type.
**Feb 2025** bleaching hit the **Gulf of Mannar** and **Palk Bay**.
**National Coral Reef Research Institute** = **Chidiyatapu, South Andaman**.

26.s:
Which of the following statements about the Great Barrier Reef is correct?
1. It is situated along the north-eastern coast of Australia.
2. It is approximately 2,300 km long.
3. It contains about 3,000 reefs and 900 islands.
4. It was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1981.

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
26.x: All four statements are correct. The Great Barrier Reef lies off north-eastern Australia, is about 2,300 km long, includes approximately 3,000 reefs and 900 islands, and became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1981.
26.tq: Combine location, scale, composition and heritage-status facts in one coded question.
xs: All four statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
The **Great Barrier Reef** lies off **Queensland, Australia** (Coral Sea), ~**2,300 km** long.
It has ~**3,000 reefs + 900 islands** and became a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** in **1981**.
xa: Area ~**344,400 sq km**; ~**1,500** fish + **400+** coral species.
It is the **world's largest** reef, followed by the **Mesoamerican Barrier Reef**.
Type: **barrier reef** — parallel to the coast, separated by a wide, deep lagoon.

26.s: Which is the correct order of the largest coral reef systems mentioned below?
o: Gulf of Mannar, Mesoamerican Barrier Reef
Great Barrier Reef, Mesoamerican Barrier Reef
Mesoamerican Barrier Reef, Great Barrier Reef
26.x: The Great Barrier Reef of Australia is the largest system, followed by the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef.
26.tq: Read the comparison as a ranked pair and avoid reversing the order.
xs: **Great Barrier Reef** first, then the **Mesoamerican Barrier Reef** — option **(2)**.
Option (3) reverses the order; the **Gulf of Mannar** and **Lakshadweep** are Indian reefs, not the largest systems.
xa: Great Barrier Reef: ~**2,300 km**, **UNESCO WHS 1981**.
It lies off **Queensland** in the **Coral Sea**.
⚠ In India: highest diversity = **Andaman & Nicobar**; only atolls = **Lakshadweep**.

26.s:
With reference to coral reefs in India, consider the following statements:
1. The Andaman and Nicobar region has the highest diversity among the Indian reef regions listed.
2. Coral reefs occur in the Gulf of Mannar and the Gulf of Kutch.
3. Malvan is a coral-reef region in Maharashtra.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
26.x: All three statements are correct. Indian reef regions include the Gulf of Mannar, Gulf of Kutch, Andaman and Nicobar, Lakshadweep and Malvan; the Andaman and Nicobar region has the highest diversity among them.
26.tq: Test a complete regional list through the ‘all statements’ option.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: **Andaman & Nicobar** has the **highest diversity**.
Statement 2: **Gulf of Mannar** (TN) and **Gulf of Kutch** (Gujarat) have **true reefs**.
Statement 3: **Malvan** (Maharashtra) has **patchy reefs**.
xa: **Lakshadweep** = India's only true **atolls**.
India's first **National Coral Reef Research Institute**: **Chidiyatapu, South Andaman**.
**Andaman** mass bleaching was linked to about a **2°C rise** in Indian Ocean temperature.

26.s: India's first National Coral Reef Research Institute is located at:
26.x: India's first National Coral Reef Research Institute is located at Chidiyatapu in South Andaman.
26.tq: Apply the location-based institutional association.
xs: India's first **National Coral Reef Research Institute** is at **Chidiyatapu, South Andaman** — option **(4)**.
**Malvan** (Maharashtra) has patchy reefs; **Lakshadweep** has India's only atolls; **Gulf of Mannar** has India's first **marine biosphere reserve**.
xa: **Andaman & Nicobar** has the **highest reef diversity** in India.
**CMLRE Kochi** studies **EEZ** living resources.
Andaman mass bleaching: about a **2°C rise** in Indian Ocean temperature (**UPPSC 2024** key).

26.s: Which one of the following is regarded as the strongest global driver of coral loss in the context of coral bleaching?
o: Rising sea-surface temperature and marine heatwaves
26.x: Rising sea-surface temperature and marine heatwaves are currently the strongest global drivers of coral loss associated with bleaching.
26.tq: Identify the dominant driver among several environmental factors.
xs: **Rising SST and marine heatwaves** are now the **strongest global driver** of coral loss — option **(3)**.
They are the **primary cause** of bleaching.
Normal tides are not a driver — though **extremely low tides** are listed as a trigger.
xa: Other triggers: **pollution and runoff, high UV, disease, storms/cyclones, ocean acidification**.
Also: **crown-of-thorns starfish**, coral mining, tourism.
GCRMN 2026: in **2024**, **87%** of reefs faced unprecedented heat stress.

26.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I: Global bleaching event

a. First
b. Second
c. Third
d. Fourth

List-II: Year or period

i. 1998
ii. 2010
iii. 2014–2017
iv. 2023–mid-2025

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
26.x: The first global event occurred in 1998, the second in 2010, the third during 2014–2017, and the fourth from 2023 to about mid-2025.
26.tq: Start with the certain year-event pair and complete the chronological matching.
xs: Correct code: **a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv** — option **(1)**.
1st **1998** (strong El Nino); 2nd **2010**; 3rd **2014-2017** (**68.2%** of reef areas hit).
4th: **2023 - ended ~mid-2025** — the fastest and most extensive.
xa: The 4th hit **84%** of reef areas in **83** countries (NOAA).
Since **1998** every strong **El Nino** has coincided with a global bleaching event.
Large-scale bleaching takes **more than 15 years** to recover from.

26.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the fourth global coral bleaching event?
o: It occurred from 2014 to 2017 and affected reefs in 21 countries
It occurred from 2023 and ended around mid-2025, affecting 84 per cent of reef areas in 83 countries
It occurred from 2010 to 2012 and affected 68.2 per cent of reef areas
It began in 1998, lasted one year and was linked only to El Niño
26.x: The fourth global bleaching event began in 2023, ended around mid-2025, and was the fastest and most extensive, affecting 84 per cent of reef areas in 83 countries.
26.tq: Use the year, scale and country count together to identify the event.
xs: The **4th** global event ran from **2023** to **~mid-2025**, hitting **84%** of reef areas in **83** countries — option **(2)**.
xa: The 4th was the **fastest, most extensive** (NOAA).
Since **2010**, major disturbances recur every **4-6 years** vs once a decade earlier (GCRMN 2026).
GCRMN 2026: hard-coral cover down **9.5%** vs 1980-2009.

26.s: Since 1998, every strong El Niño has coincided with
o: the disappearance of all marine heatwaves
the formation of new atolls in the Pacific Ocean
the complete recovery of coral reefs
26.x: Every strong El Niño since 1998 has coincided with a global coral bleaching event.
26.tq: Identify the stated recurring relationship between El Niño and bleaching.
xs: Since **1998**, every strong **El Nino** has coincided with a **global coral bleaching event** — option **(4)**.
The first global event (**1998**) itself came with a **strong El Nino**.
xa: Recovery from large-scale bleaching takes **more than 15 years**.
El Nino also suppresses **Peru upwelling** → fishery collapse.

26.s: Major disturbances to coral reefs are now occurring approximately every:
26.x: The reported interval for major coral-reef disturbances has shortened to approximately every 4–6 years.
26.tq: Identify the correct interval from closely spaced time-range options.
xs: Major reef disturbances now recur every **4-6 years** — option **(1)**.
Since **2010** (GCRMN 2026), versus **once a decade** earlier.
xa: Recovery from large-scale bleaching takes **more than 15 years** — so reefs get no time to recover.
GCRMN **7th** Status report: hard-coral cover down **9.5%** vs 1980-2009.
In **2024**, **87%** of reefs faced unprecedented heat stress.

26.s:
With reference to coral bleaching, consider the following statements:
1. Bleaching occurs when coral polyps expel their symbiotic zooxanthellae.
2. A bleached coral is necessarily dead.
3. Loss of pigments accompanies bleaching.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
26.x: Coral bleaching involves expulsion of zooxanthellae and loss of pigments. A bleached coral is stressed but is not necessarily dead.
26.tq: Find the false absolute statement; ‘necessarily dead’ reverses the distinction between stress and death.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2) 1 and 3 only**.
Statement 1: bleaching = polyps **expel symbiotic zooxanthellae** (**APPSC-G2 2017**).
Statement 2 wrong: bleached coral is **stressed, not necessarily dead** (but prone to starvation/disease).
Statement 3: corals turn **white** and **lose pigments**.
xa: Primary cause: **rising SST / marine heatwaves**.
**INCOIS** issues **coral bleaching** and algal bloom alerts.
Zooxanthellae normally supply the coral's **food and colour**.

26.s: Which one of the following is NOT identified as a factor that can contribute to coral bleaching?
26.x: Pollution, extreme low tides and ocean acidification are recognised contributors to coral bleaching. Increased carbonate availability is not listed as a bleaching factor.
26.tq: Eliminate the three recognised stressors and identify the reversed carbonate claim.
xs: **Increase in carbonate availability** is **not** a bleaching factor — option **(3)**.
In fact **ocean acidification** **lowers** carbonate ions, which harms corals — and acidification **is** a trigger.
**Extremely low tides** and **pollution and runoff** are listed triggers.
xa: Other triggers: **high UV, disease, storms/cyclones, crown-of-thorns starfish, coral mining, tourism**.
Primary cause: **rising SST and marine heatwaves**.
**Harmful algal blooms** also block sunlight for corals and seagrass.

26.s:
In February 2025, coral bleaching was reported from which of the following groups of Indian regions?
1. Gulf of Mannar and Palk Bay
2. Lakshadweep and Andaman and Nicobar Islands
3. Gulf of Kachchh
4. Sundarbans and Chilika
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
26.x: The reported Indian sites were the Gulf of Mannar, Palk Bay, Lakshadweep, Andaman and Nicobar Islands and the Gulf of Kachchh. Sundarbans and Chilika were not included.
26.tq: Build the answer by identifying the listed Indian sites and rejecting the added locations.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(2) 1, 2 and 3 only**.
**Feb 2025** bleaching hit the **Gulf of Mannar, Palk Bay, Lakshadweep, Andaman & Nicobar** and **Gulf of Kachchh**.
**Sundarbans and Chilika** were not on the list (the east coast mostly has **no reefs**).
xa: **Andaman** mass bleaching linked to about a **2°C rise** in Indian Ocean temperature.
The **4th global event** (2023-mid-2025) covered **84%** of reef areas.
NGT directed the Environment Ministry to **protect and regenerate** reefs in the **Great Nicobar** project.

26.s: The mass coral bleaching in the Andaman region was linked to approximately what rise in Indian Ocean temperature?
26.x: The Andaman mass bleaching was linked to an approximately 2°C rise in Indian Ocean temperature.
26.tq: Use the specific temperature figure rather than the general marine-heatwave threshold.
xs: The **Andaman** mass bleaching was linked to about a **2°C** rise in Indian Ocean temperature — option **(3)**.
This was the **UPPSC 2024** key; rising SST is the **primary cause** of bleaching.
xa: **Andaman & Nicobar** has India's **highest reef diversity**.
**Feb 2025** bleaching also hit the **Gulf of Mannar, Palk Bay, Lakshadweep, Gulf of Kachchh**.
India's first **National Coral Reef Research Institute** is at **Chidiyatapu, South Andaman**.

26.s: Ocean acidification is best described as:
o: An increase in carbonate ions due to the decomposition of plankton
A fall in the pH of seawater caused mainly by uptake of atmospheric carbon dioxide
A fall in ocean temperature caused by increasing salinity
A rise in the pH of seawater due to oxygen absorption
26.x: Ocean acidification refers to the falling pH of seawater, which is normally alkaline with a pH of about 8.1, owing mainly to the absorption of carbon dioxide.
26.tq: Use the precise definition to distinguish acidification from changes in temperature or salinity.
xs: **Ocean acidification** = **falling seawater pH** from **CO2 uptake** — option **(2)**.
Seawater is **alkaline** (**pH ~8.1**); CO2 + water → **carbonic acid** → bicarbonate + hydronium ions, and **carbonate ions fall**.
So carbonate ions decrease, not increase; and pH falls, not rises.
xa: Corals, plankton and shellfish then **struggle to build calcium carbonate shells**.
Oceans absorb about **30-40%** of anthropogenic CO2; acidity up **30%** since the Industrial Revolution.
Worst areas: **cold temperate seas** (higher CO2 solubility) + **melting Arctic**.

26.s: The terms ‘evil twin of global warming’ and ‘the other CO2 problem’ refer to:
26.x: Ocean acidification is popularly described as the ‘evil twin of global warming’ or ‘the other CO2 problem’.
26.tq: Identify the exact popular expressions associated with the environmental process.
xs: **"Evil twin of global warming"** and **"the other CO2 problem"** = **ocean acidification** — option **(3)**.
It is the fall in ocean **pH** (normally ~**8.1**) as seas absorb **CO2**.
xa: Acidity may rise **150%** by **2100**.
It weakens **calcifiers** — corals, plankton, shellfish.
⚠ **Eutrophication** is different: excess **nitrogen and phosphorus** → algal blooms → **dead zones** (e.g. **Gulf of Mexico**).

26.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the chemical basis of ocean acidification:
1. Carbon dioxide reacts with water to form carbonic acid.
2. Carbonic acid yields bicarbonate and hydronium ions.
3. The concentration of carbonate ions declines.
4. Calcifying organisms find it easier to build calcium carbonate shells.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
26.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is false because declining carbonate ions make calcium carbonate shell formation more difficult for corals, plankton and shellfish.
26.tq: Find the statement that reverses the effect of declining carbonate ions.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(1) 1, 2 and 3 only**.
Statement 1: **CO2 + water → carbonic acid**.
Statement 2: carbonic acid yields **bicarbonate + hydronium ions**.
Statement 3: **carbonate ions fall**; so statement 4 is wrong — calcifiers find it **harder** to build **calcium carbonate** shells.
xa: Calcifiers hit: **corals, plankton and shellfish**.
Seawater is **alkaline**, **pH ~8.1**; acidification = falling pH from **CO2** uptake.
Epithets: **"evil twin of global warming"** / **"the other CO2 problem"**.

26.s: Approximately what proportion of anthropogenic carbon dioxide is absorbed by the oceans?
26.x: The oceans absorb approximately 30–40% of anthropogenic carbon dioxide; another cited estimate places the uptake above 25%.
26.tq: Use the middle numerical range carefully rather than confusing it with the alternative lower estimate.
xs: Oceans absorb about **30-40 percent** of anthropogenic **CO2** — option **(3)**.
Some notes put it at **>25%**.
xa: Ocean acidity is up **30%** since the **Industrial Revolution**.
Acidity may rise **150%** by **2100**.
Worst areas: **cold temperate seas** and the **melting Arctic**.

26.s: Ocean acidification is expected to be more severe in cold temperate seas primarily because:
o: Cold water contains no carbonate ions
Cold seas have permanently higher salinity than tropical seas
Cold water has higher carbon dioxide solubility
26.x: Carbon dioxide is more soluble in cold water, making cold temperate seas particularly vulnerable to acidification. The melting Arctic is also identified as a region of concern.
26.tq: Link the regional pattern to the physical property of gas solubility.
xs: Cold temperate seas acidify more because **cold water has higher CO2 solubility** — option **(4)**.
The **melting Arctic** is the other worst-hit area.
Salinity, sunlight or an absence of carbonate ions are not the reasons given.
xa: Chemistry: **CO2 + water → carbonic acid → bicarbonate + hydronium**; **carbonate ions fall**.
Normal seawater **pH ~8.1** (alkaline).
Oceans absorb about **30-40%** of anthropogenic CO2.

26.s: Which of the following combinations correctly explains the formation of harmful algal blooms?
o: Farm runoff and sewage introduce excess nitrogen and phosphorus, causing eutrophication.
Ocean cooling removes nutrients and directly produces toxic blooms.
Reduced nutrient supply prevents the growth of algae and causes eutrophication.
Increased carbonate ions convert shellfish into phytoplankton.
26.x: Excess nitrogen and phosphorus from farm runoff and sewage cause eutrophication, which can produce harmful algal blooms.
26.tq: Trace the cause-effect chain from nutrient enrichment to algal blooming.
xs: **Farm runoff and sewage** add excess **nitrogen and phosphorus**, causing **eutrophication** — option **(1)**.
Eutrophication drives **harmful algal blooms**; it comes from **more** nutrients, not fewer or from cooling.
Carbonate ions do not turn shellfish into phytoplankton — option (4) is nonsense.
xa: When the bloom **dies and decomposes**, oxygen is stripped → **dead zones**.
Blooms **block sunlight** for corals and seagrass.
Dead zones: **Gulf of Mexico** (Mississippi runoff), **Chesapeake Bay**.

26.s:
Consider the following statements about harmful algal blooms:
1. When a bloom dies and decomposes, oxygen is stripped from the water, creating dead zones.
2. The Gulf of Mexico dead zone is linked to runoff from the Mississippi.
3. Blooms increase sunlight reaching corals and seagrass, aiding their growth.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
26.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: blooms block sunlight for corals and seagrass. Hence 1 and 2 only (A); B, C and D include the false statement 3.
26.tq: Nutrients -> bloom -> decay -> no oxygen -> dead zone; blooms shade the seabed.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: a dying, decomposing bloom **strips oxygen** → **dead zones**.
Statement 2: the **Gulf of Mexico** dead zone comes from **Mississippi** runoff.
Statement 3 wrong: blooms **block sunlight** for corals and seagrass.
xa: Another dead zone: **Chesapeake Bay**.
Cause: excess **nitrogen and phosphorus** (farm runoff, sewage) → **eutrophication**.
**INCOIS** issues **algal bloom** and coral bleaching alerts.

26.s:
With reference to red tides, consider the following statements:
1. They are toxic algal blooms.
2. They are mostly associated with dinoflagellates.
3. They may discolour water.
4. They may kill fish and contaminate shellfish.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
26.x: Red tides are toxic blooms, mostly involving dinoflagellates, that can discolour water, kill fish and contaminate shellfish.
26.tq: Use the inclusive option when every listed characteristic belongs to the same phenomenon.
xs: All four statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
A **red tide** is a **toxic bloom**, mostly of **dinoflagellates**.
It **discolours water**, **kills fish** and **contaminates shellfish**.
xa: Dinoflagellates are also among the ocean's **primary producers** (phytoplankton).
Harmful algal blooms → decomposition → **dead zones**.
**INCOIS** issues algal bloom alerts.

26.s: Which organisation issues alerts relating to algal blooms and coral bleaching?
26.x: The Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS) issues alerts on algal blooms and coral bleaching.
26.tq: Distinguish the alert-issuing institution from organisations engaged in monitoring or research.
xs: **INCOIS** issues **algal bloom and coral bleaching alerts** — option **(4)**.
**CMLRE Kochi** studies **EEZ living resources**; **GCRMN** publishes the **Status of the World's Coral Reefs** report.
xa: GCRMN **7th** report (2026): hard-coral cover down **9.5%** vs 1980-2009.
In **2024**, **87%** of reefs faced unprecedented heat stress.
Primary bleaching cause: **rising SST and marine heatwaves**.

26.s: The Aichi Target 11 under the Convention on Biological Diversity envisaged protection of what proportion of coastal and marine areas by 2020?
26.x: Aichi Target 11 set the goal of protecting 10 per cent of coastal and marine areas by 2020.
26.tq: Distinguish the Aichi target from the later 30x30 framework.
xs: **Aichi Target 11** (CBD, **2011-2020**) aimed to protect **10 per cent** of coastal and marine areas by **2020** — option **(2)**.
**30%** belongs to the later **30x30** target (by **2030**).
xa: 30x30: **30%** of land + **30%** of oceans by 2030 — **Kunming-Montreal GBF**, **COP15**, **Dec 2022**, **Target 3**.
**MPAs**, no-fishing zones and sanctuaries help reefs **recover**.
Recovery from large-scale bleaching takes **more than 15 years**.

26.s: The 30x30 target under Target 3 of the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework seeks to protect by 2030
26.x: The 30x30 target seeks protection of 30 per cent of land and 30 per cent of oceans by 2030. It was adopted under the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework at COP15 in December 2022.
26.tq: Use the numerical phrase itself to distinguish the target’s two components.
xs: **30x30** = protect **30% of land and 30% of oceans** by **2030** — option **(4)**.
It is **Target 3** of the **Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework**, adopted at **COP15**, **Dec 2022**.
xa: Earlier target: **Aichi Target 11** — **10%** of coastal and marine areas by **2020**.
**MPAs**, no-fishing zones and sanctuaries help reefs recover.
Since **2010** major reef disturbances recur every **4-6 years**.

26.s:
Which of the following measures can help coral reefs recover?
1. Marine protected areas
2. No-fishing zones
3. Marine sanctuaries

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
26.x: Marine protected areas, no-fishing zones and sanctuaries reduce pressures on reefs and help them recover.
26.tq: Apply the conservation principle to a reef-management scenario.
xs: All three help reefs recover — option **(1) 1, 2 and 3**.
**MPAs**, **no-fishing zones** and **sanctuaries** are all listed as aiding reef recovery.
xa: **Aichi Target 11**: **10%** of coastal/marine areas protected by **2020**.
**30x30**: **30%** of land + oceans by **2030** (Kunming-Montreal GBF, Target 3).
Recovery from large-scale bleaching takes **more than 15 years**.

26.s: According to the 7th Status of the World’s Coral Reefs report of GCRMN, hard-coral cover has:
26.x: The report records a 9.5% decline in hard-coral cover compared with the 1980–2009 reference period.
26.tq: Match the direction, magnitude and reference period together.
xs: **GCRMN's 7th** report: hard-coral cover **declined 9.5%** vs **1980-2009** — option **(4)**.
It is a decline, not an increase — option (2) gets the direction wrong.
xa: In **2024**, **87%** of reefs faced unprecedented heat stress.
Since **2010** major disturbances recur every **4-6 years** vs once a decade earlier.
4th global bleaching event (2023-mid-2025) hit **84%** of reef areas in **83** countries.

26.s: The principal mandate associated with CMLRE, Kochi, is the study of:
o: Living resources of the Exclusive Economic Zone
Only atmospheric ozone over the Indian Ocean
Terrestrial forest fires in the Western Ghats
26.x: The Centre for Marine Living Resources and Ecology (CMLRE), Kochi, studies living resources in the Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ).
26.tq: Decode the institutional role from the organisation’s marine-resource focus.
xs: **CMLRE Kochi** studies **EEZ living resources** — option **(2)**.
Global coral-reef statistics come from **GCRMN**, not CMLRE.
xa: **INCOIS** issues algal bloom and coral bleaching alerts.
India's first **National Coral Reef Research Institute**: **Chidiyatapu, South Andaman**.
**Kerala** upwelling supports **oil sardine and mackerel**.

26.s: Which one of the following current-affairs pairs is correctly matched?
o: Pavona clavus — artificial reef modules off Ramanathapuram
D-COIN — oil sardine fishery off Kerala
PMMSY — coral colony near Kadmat Island
Pavona clavus — giant potato patch coral colony near Kadmat Island, Lakshadweep
26.x: A giant Pavona clavus (potato patch coral) colony was reported near Kadmat Island, Lakshadweep. Options A and C mismatch Pavona clavus and PMMSY, and B wrongly pairs D-COIN with the oil sardine fishery.
26.tq: Separate the species-location pair from the programme-location pair.
xs: **Pavona clavus** — giant **potato patch coral** colony near **Kadmat Island, Lakshadweep** — option **(4)**.
Option (1) gives Pavona clavus the wrong place; option (3) pairs the Kadmat colony with the wrong name.
xa: **Lakshadweep** has India's **only true atolls**.
**Feb 2025** bleaching also hit **Lakshadweep**.
Atoll = **ring-shaped** reef enclosing a lagoon, no central island.

26.s: The National Green Tribunal’s clearance of the ₹92,000-crore Great Nicobar project included a direction to:
o: Protect and regenerate coral reefs through the Environment Ministry
Remove all coral reefs before project construction
Suspend all marine research in the Nicobar Islands
Transfer coral-reef protection exclusively to the Fisheries Ministry
26.x: The NGT clearance directed the Environment Ministry to protect and regenerate coral reefs; coral loss remained a central objection to the project.
26.tq: Identify the authority’s actual environmental direction instead of an extreme or transferred power.
xs: The NGT directed the **Environment Ministry** to **protect and regenerate coral reefs** — option **(1)**.
The **₹92,000-crore Great Nicobar project** was cleared in **Feb 2026**; **coral loss** remains the core objection.
xa: **Andaman & Nicobar** has India's **highest reef diversity**.
**Andaman** mass bleaching was linked to about a **2°C rise** in Indian Ocean temperature.
Reefs **break wave power**, preventing coastal erosion.

26.s:
With reference to Andhra Pradesh, consider the following statements:
1. Andhra Pradesh has no true coral reefs.
2. Its fisheries depend partly on plankton productivity in the Bay of Bengal.
3. Marine heatwaves threaten this plankton-supported fisheries base.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
26.x: All three statements are correct: Andhra Pradesh has no true coral reefs, while its fisheries rely on Bay of Bengal plankton productivity that is threatened by marine heatwaves.
26.tq: Combine the regional exception with the linked fisheries and climate relationship.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: **AP has no true coral reefs** — **heavy river sediment + freshwater** on the east coast.
Statements 2-3: AP fisheries depend on **Bay of Bengal plankton productivity**, now threatened by **marine heatwaves**.
xa: Other east-coast states without reefs: **West Bengal, Odisha**.
**Phytoplankton** are the ocean's main **primary producers**.
⚠ Highest diversity = **Andaman & Nicobar**; only atolls = **Lakshadweep**; AP = **no reefs**.

27.s:
Consider the following statements regarding India's disaster vulnerability:
1. About 58.6% of India's landmass faces moderate-to-very-high earthquake risk.
2. More than 40 million hectares, approximately 12% of the area, is flood-prone.
3. About 68% of the cultivable area is vulnerable to drought.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
27.x: All three are correct: about 58.6% of the landmass faces moderate-to-very-high earthquake risk, over 40 million ha (~12%) is flood-prone, and about 68% of the cultivable area is drought-vulnerable.
27.tq: Check each numerical statement independently before selecting the coded combination.
xs: All three statements are correct — so option **(4) 1, 2 and 3** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: about **58.6%** of India's landmass faces **moderate-to-very-high earthquakes** (NDMA).
Statement 2 is correct: more than **40 million ha (~12%)** of India is **flood-prone**.
Statement 3 is correct: about **68%** of the **cultivable area** is drought-vulnerable.
xa: About **5,700 km** of the old **7,516.6 km** coastline is exposed to **cyclones and tsunamis**.
**Assam** alone has **31.05 lakh ha** of flood-prone area.
⚠ The coastline was remeasured to **11,098.81 km** (MHA, **Dec 2024**) — older hazard shares still use the old base.
**World Risk Index 2025:** India is the **2nd most vulnerable** country, after the **Philippines**.

27.s: According to the older coastline base used for the hazard estimates, approximately how much of India's coastline faces cyclones and tsunamis?
27.x: Approximately 5,700 km of the old 7,516.6 km coastline was considered exposed to cyclones and tsunamis.
27.tq: Separate the exposed length from the total and revised coastline figures.
xs: About **5,700 km** of India's coastline faces **cyclones and tsunamis** — so option **(2)** is correct.
This share is measured on the **old coastline base of 7,516.6 km** (NDMA hazard shares).
**7,516.6 km** is the whole old coastline and **11,098.81 km** is the remeasured coastline (MHA, **Dec 2024**) — neither is the exposed share.
xa: The remeasurement was done by the **National Hydrographic Office** with the **Survey of India**; only the method changed, not the land.
**Gujarat** has the longest revised coastline (**2,340.62 km**); **Andhra Pradesh** is **3rd** with **1,053.07 km**.
Hazard → region: **cyclones** hit mainly the **east coast**.
Cyclones affect **13 coastal states/UTs** and **84 coastal districts**.

27.s: According to the World Risk Index 2025, India is the world's second most vulnerable country after which country?
27.x: The World Risk Index 2025 places India as the second most vulnerable country, after the Philippines.
27.tq: Direct ranking recall.
xs: In the **World Risk Index 2025**, India is the **2nd most vulnerable** country, after **the Philippines** — so option **(4)** is correct.
India's risk is dominated by **floods and storms**, while **China and Indonesia** face higher **seismic** risk.
xa: India loses about **0.4% of GDP every year** to disasters (1990-2024).
About **58.6%** of the landmass faces moderate-to-very-high earthquakes; ~**68%** of cultivable area is drought-vulnerable.
Core formula: **Hazard x Vulnerability = Disaster**.

27.s: Which of the following hazard-to-region associations is correctly matched?
o: Cyclones — east coast; drought — Rajasthan and the Deccan interior
Drought — Western Ghats; earthquakes — east coast only
27.x: Cyclones are especially associated with the east coast, while drought is prominent in Rajasthan and the Deccan interior. Floods affect the Brahmaputra-Ganga plains, earthquakes the Himalaya and Kutch, and landslides the Himalaya and Western Ghats.
27.tq: Check both hazard and regional setting in each pair.
xs: **Cyclones — east coast** and **drought — Rajasthan + Deccan interior** are both correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
Option (1) is wrong: **earthquakes** belong to the **Himalaya + Kutch**, and the **Brahmaputra-Ganga plains** are the **flood** region.
Option (3) is wrong: **landslides** occur in the **Himalaya + Western Ghats**; **Kutch** is an earthquake zone.
Option (4) is wrong: the **Western Ghats** are a landslide zone, and earthquakes are not tied to the east coast.
xa: Full NDMA map: **Floods** → Brahmaputra-Ganga plains; **Earthquakes** → Himalaya + Kutch; **Landslides** → Himalaya + Western Ghats.
The **east coast** gets far more cyclones than the west; **Andhra Pradesh** is the most cyclone-prone state.
**Drought-prone regions** also include Kutch-Saurashtra, Marathwada-Vidarbha, interior Karnataka and **Rayalaseema** (AP).

27.s: Which organisation publishes the annual Global Report on Internal Displacement?
27.x: The Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre, headquartered in Geneva, publishes the annual Global Report on Internal Displacement.
27.tq: Match the report with its specialised international institution.
xs: The **Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre (IDMC)**, based in **Geneva**, publishes the annual **Global Report on Internal Displacement** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The IDMC tracks people displaced within their own countries; disasters displace **millions** every year.
xa: **Water-related disasters worldwide (2025):** about **5,000 deaths** and **8 million** displaced.
**Emerging Asia (OECD):** about **100 disasters a year** affecting about **80 million** people.
India's main risk drivers are **floods and storms**.

27.s: India loses approximately what share of its GDP every year to natural disasters during 1990–2024?
27.x: India lost approximately 0.4% of its GDP annually to natural disasters during 1990–2024.
27.tq: Place the decimal correctly by distinguishing percentage scale.
xs: India loses about **0.4% of GDP every year** to natural disasters (**1990-2024**) — so option **(2)** is correct.
The main **risk drivers** behind these losses are **floods and storms**.
xa: **2025 toll:** about **331 days** of climate impacts and **over 4,000 deaths** from climate-induced disasters.
The heaviest 2025 toll was in **Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand**.
**World Risk Index 2025:** India **2nd most vulnerable**, after the Philippines.

27.s: Which two hazards are identified as the principal drivers of India's disaster risk?
27.x: Floods and storms are identified as India's main disaster-risk drivers.
27.tq: Select the paired dominant hazards rather than a single hazard or a broader list.
xs: **Floods and storms** are the principal drivers of India's disaster risk — so option **(1)** is correct.
Unlike India, **China and Indonesia** face higher **seismic** risk; earthquakes are not India's main risk driver.
xa: More than **40 million ha (~12%)** of India is flood-prone.
Cyclones affect **13 coastal states/UTs** and **84 coastal districts**.
India loses about **0.4% of GDP** a year to disasters (1990-2024).

27.s: In 2025, the heaviest toll from climate-induced disasters in India was reported in:
27.x: More than 4,000 deaths were reported in India from climate-induced disasters in 2025, with the heaviest toll in Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand.
27.tq: Link the national figure with the specifically identified regional concentration.
xs: The heaviest 2025 toll from climate-induced disasters was in **Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand** — so option **(2)** is correct.
In **2025**, India saw about **331 days** of climate impacts and **over 4,000 deaths** from climate-induced disasters.
xa: **2025 flash floods** at **Dharali and Harsil** (Uttarkashi) diverted the **Bhagirathi**.
**Mandi (HP)** got nearly **20 times** its normal rain in 2025.
The **Dharali flood (5 Aug 2025)** came from an **ice-patch collapse on the Srikanta glacier** (ISRO study).

27.s:
Consider the following statements about floods:
1. A flood occurs when water exceeds channel capacity and spills onto normally dry land.
2. Floods are generally sudden-onset events that cannot be predicted by region or season.
3. Riverine, flash, coastal and urban floods are recognised types of floods.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
27.x: Statement 1 is correct: this is the definition of a flood. Statement 2 is wrong: ordinary floods are slow-onset and predictable by region and season (it is flash floods that are sudden). Statement 3 is correct: the four types are riverine, flash, coastal and urban. So '1 only' misses 3; '2 and 3 only' and '1, 2 and 3' include the false statement 2.
27.tq: Ordinary floods = slow-onset and seasonal; flash floods are the sudden ones.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — so option **(2) 1 and 3 only** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: a flood is when water **exceeds channel capacity** and spills onto normally dry land.
Statement 2 is wrong: floods are **slow-onset** and **predictable by region and season**.
Statement 3 is correct: the types are **riverine, flash, coastal and urban** floods.
xa: **Causes (APPSC 2025 key):** **heavy/prolonged rainfall, poor drainage, deforestation, dam failure**.
**Structural** measures: channel and drainage improvement, diversion; **non-structural**: flood-proofing, flood fighting, flood insurance.
Flood control is a **state subject**; the Centre supports states through **FMBAP**.

27.s:
Which of the following sets contains only causes of floods identified for India?
1. Heavy or prolonged rainfall
2. Poor drainage and low infiltration
3. Deforestation and dam failure
4. Siltation resulting from soil erosion
27.x: Heavy rainfall, poor drainage, low infiltration, deforestation, dam failure and siltation from soil erosion are all recognised causes of floods.
27.tq: Check whether each listed causal factor belongs to the same hazard rather than selecting a partial combination.
xs: All four are recognised causes of floods — so option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4** is correct.
**Heavy/prolonged rainfall, poor drainage, deforestation and dam failure** are the APPSC 2025 key causes.
**Low infiltration** and **siltation from soil erosion** are further causes, along with storm surges and snow/ice melt.
xa: **Assam:** **800 sq km** of upstream **Nagaland** forest was cleared in **2013-23**, causing faster runoff.
**Rashtriya Barh Ayog** assessed about **40 million ha** as flood-prone.
Flood types: **riverine, flash, coastal, urban**.

27.s: Riverine flooding in the Krishna-Godavari region may become particularly severe when water is released simultaneously from:
27.x: Flooding in the Krishna-Godavari region can be especially severe when Srisailam, Nagarjuna Sagar and Hirakud release water together.
27.tq: Test the linked dam names through a same-basin and downstream-impact association.
xs: Krishna-Godavari delta floods are worst when **Srisailam, Nagarjuna Sagar and Hirakud** release water together — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Hirakud** is in **Odisha**; the **Krishna-Godavari deltas** are AP's main riverine-flood zone.
xa: AP faces three hazards: **coastal cyclones, delta floods and Rayalaseema drought**.
**Urban flooding** in AP hits **Vijayawada** (Budameru rivulet), Visakhapatnam and Guntur.
Flood control is a **state subject**, supported by the Centre through **FMBAP**.

27.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Rashtriya Barh Ayog is the National Flood Commission.
2. The Rashtriya Barh Ayog assessed about 40 million hectares as flood-prone.
3. Flood control is a Union subject, with States only implementing central schemes.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
27.x: Statement 1 is correct: Rashtriya Barh Ayog = National Flood Commission. Statement 2 is correct: it assessed about 40 million ha as flood-prone. Statement 3 is wrong: flood control is a State subject; the Centre only supports States through FMBAP. So '1 only' misses 2, while '2 and 3 only' and '1, 2 and 3' include the false statement 3.
27.tq: Flood control = State subject; Centre helps via FMBAP.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — so option **(2) 1 and 2 only** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: **Rashtriya Barh Ayog** is the **National Flood Commission** (set up **1976**; some notes give **1980**).
Statement 2 is correct: it assessed about **40 million ha** as flood-prone.
Statement 3 is wrong: flood control is a **state subject**; the Centre only supports states through **FMBAP**.
xa: The **Expert Committee for Scientific Assessment of Flood-Prone Areas** was set up in **2012** by the **Ministry of Water Resources**.
**India-China ELM** on flood data held its **16th meeting** in **Apr 2025**.
**India-Bhutan JGE** held its **11th meeting** in **May 2025**.

27.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
27.x: Flood insurance is a non-structural measure. Dams and reservoirs, and channel and drainage improvement are structural measures, while flood-plain zoning is non-structural.
27.tq: Find the classification reversal by comparing physical construction with policy and financial tools.
xs: **Flood insurance** is a **non-structural** measure, so "Flood insurance—structural measure" is wrongly matched — option **(1)** is correct.
**Channel and drainage improvement** and diversion are **structural** measures, so option (2) is correctly matched.
Non-structural measures are **flood-proofing, flood fighting and flood insurance**.
xa: Flood control is a **state subject**; the Centre supports states via **FMBAP**.
**Rashtriya Barh Ayog** (National Flood Commission) assessed about **40 million ha** as flood-prone.
Flood types: **riverine, flash, coastal and urban**.

27.s: The Expert Committee for Scientific Assessment of Flood-Prone Areas was set up in 2012 by which Ministry?
27.x: The Ministry of Water Resources set up the Expert Committee in 2012. MHA is the nodal ministry for disaster management generally, Earth Sciences runs IMD/INCOIS, and Agriculture handles drought - none of them set up this committee.
27.tq: Flood-prone area assessment = Water Resources (RBA 40 Mha; Expert Committee 2012).
xs: The **Ministry of Water Resources** set up the Expert Committee for Scientific Assessment of Flood-Prone Areas in **2012** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It followed the earlier **Rashtriya Barh Ayog (National Flood Commission)**, set up in **1976**.
xa: The Rashtriya Barh Ayog assessed about **40 million ha** as flood-prone.
Flood control is a **state subject**; the Centre helps through **FMBAP**.
⚠ Drought, hailstorms, frost and pest attacks go to the **Agriculture Ministry**; other notified disasters go to the **MHA**.

27.s: Which sequence correctly explains the formation of a glacial lake outburst flood?
o: Glacier retreat → enlargement of a proglacial lake → bursting of the lake → flood
Deforestation → oceanic tide → lake freezing → flood
River siltation → volcanic eruption → glacier advance → flood
Rain shadow → soil erosion → sea-level fall → flood
27.x: Glacier retreat can enlarge proglacial lakes; when the lake bursts, the stored water produces a glacial lake outburst flood.
27.tq: Arrange the causal chain from environmental change to disaster occurrence.
xs: A GLOF forms by **glacier retreat → enlargement of a proglacial lake → bursting of the lake → flood** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**GLOF** = **glacial lake outburst flood**: glacier retreat enlarges proglacial lakes that later burst.
xa: **Nepal** saw catastrophic GLOF flash floods on **26 Aug 2026**; UNDP counts **26 GLOFs since the 1970s**.
The world has lost **9,500+ Gt** of glacier mass since **1975**.
**Central Himalaya** glacier area is down **>20%** in three decades.

27.s: The catastrophic flash floods reported in Nepal on 26 August 2026 were associated with which hazard?
o: Tsunami generated in the Indian Ocean
27.x: The Nepal flash floods of 26 August 2026 are a GLOF case: glacier retreat enlarges proglacial lakes that then burst; UNDP counts 26 GLOFs in Nepal since the 1970s. A tsunami, storm surge or urban drainage failure has nothing to do with a Himalayan flash flood.
27.tq: Match the dated event with its specific hydrological-disaster category.
xs: The Nepal flash floods of **26 Aug 2026** were a **glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF)** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**UNDP** counts **26 GLOFs** in Nepal **since the 1970s**.
