**Baglihar** and **Salal** (Chenab) sluices were closed after **Pahalgam** (2025).

37.s:
Consider the following statements about the Indus Waters Treaty:
1. India has held the treaty in abeyance since 2025.
2. India accepted the Court of Arbitration's award in May 2026.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
37.x: Statement 1 is correct: the treaty has been in abeyance since 2025. Statement 2 is wrong: in May 2026 India rejected the Court of Arbitration's award as 'null and void'. So 1 only (A); B and C wrongly accept statement 2, D wrongly rejects statement 1.
37.tq: Abeyance (2025) and rejection of the award go together - India did not accept it.
xs: Only statement 1 is correct — option **(1) 1 only**.
Statement 1 correct: the **IWT** has been **in abeyance** since **2025**.
Statement 2 wrong: India **rejected** the **Court of Arbitration**'s award as "**null and void**" (May 2026).
xa: Eastern rivers **Ravi, Beas, Sutlej** → India.
Western rivers **Indus, Jhelum, Chenab** → mainly Pakistan.
**Indus** flows are rising vs **Ganga** flows falling.

37.s: A study reported that Indus flows were rising while Ganga flows were falling. Which factor was identified as the main explanation for this contrast?
o: Tidal action in the Arabian Sea
37.x: The reported contrast in river flows was attributed mainly to groundwater pumping.
37.tq: Link the observed trend with its stated causal factor.
xs: The contrast is mainly due to **groundwater pumping** — option **(3)**.
**Indus** flows are **rising**, **Ganga** flows **falling**.
xa: The **IWT** has been in **abeyance** since **2025**.
The **Gandak** is India's **2nd largest gharial habitat**.
The **Ganga-Brahmaputra-Meghna** is the largest basin.

37.s: The Gandak is regarded as India's second-largest habitat for gharials after which river?
37.x: The Gandak is India's second-largest gharial habitat, after the Chambal.
37.tq: Use the ranking clue and identify the river placed first.
xs: The **Gandak** is India's **2nd largest gharial habitat** after the **Chambal** — option **(3)**.
The **Chambal** rises at **Mhow** and joins the **Yamuna**.
xa: City: **Chambal-Kota**.
The **Gandak** is a **left-bank** Ganga tributary.
The **Kosi** is also left-bank; the **Son** is right-bank.

37.s: Which one of the following statements regarding Andhra Pradesh's river systems is correct?
o: All the rivers of Andhra Pradesh are wholly within the State.
About 15 of the approximately 40 rivers of Andhra Pradesh are inter-state rivers.
The State has fewer than ten rivers associated with neighbouring States.
Only the Pennar is governed by an inter-state tribunal award.
37.x: Andhra Pradesh has about 40 rivers, of which approximately 15 are inter-state rivers. Krishna and Godavari waters are also shared through tribunal awards.
37.tq: Reject absolute statements and retain the option matching the stated count and relationship.
xs: AP has ~**40 rivers**, **15 of them inter-state** — option **(2)**.
So not all rivers are wholly within AP, and more than ten are shared.
Several, not only the Pennar, have tribunal awards — e.g. **Vamsadhara** (**2017**) and **Krishna**.
xa: Interstate rivers: **Godavari, Krishna, Pennar, Vamsadhara, Nagavali**.
~**75%** of AP lies in the Godavari, Krishna and Pennar basins.
**Pennar** = lifeline of **Rayalaseema**.

37.s: The Godavari reaches the sea in Andhra Pradesh at which place through seven distributaries?
37.x: The Godavari meets the sea at Antarvedi through seven distributaries forming the Konaseema delta.
37.tq: Distinguish the Godavari mouth from the Krishna mouth and from an upstream barrage.
xs: The Godavari meets the sea at **Antarvedi** through **7 distributaries** — option **(2)**.
**Dowleswaram** is the **Sir Arthur Cotton Barrage**; **Hamsaladeevi** is the **Krishna**'s mouth; **Sangameswaram** is the Krishna-Tungabhadra confluence.
xa: The delta is **Konaseema**.
Distributaries: **Gautami, Vasishta, Vainateya, Tulya, Bharadwaja, Kaushika, Athreya**.
Godavari in AP: ~**250 km**.

37.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Pennar — forms the Konaseema delta through seven distributaries
Godavari — meets the sea at Hamsaladeevi
Krishna — meets the Tungabhadra at Sangameswaram
Krishna — runs 536 km out of 597 km in Andhra Pradesh
37.x: The Krishna meets the Tungabhadra at Sangameswaram (Nandyal). The Konaseema delta with seven distributaries belongs to the Godavari, Hamsaladeevi is the Krishna's sea outlet (the Godavari reaches the sea at Antarvedi), and the Krishna's course in AP is about 485 km, not 536 km.
37.tq: Use the correctly matched river-location relationship and expose swapped river facts.
xs: The **Krishna** meets the **Tungabhadra** at **Sangameswaram** — option **(3)**.
**Konaseema** with **7 distributaries** is the **Godavari**'s delta, not the Pennar's.
**Hamsaladeevi** is the **Krishna**'s mouth; the Godavari reaches the sea at **Antarvedi**.
The Krishna runs ~**485 km** in AP.
xa: Sangameswaram is in **Nandyal**.
The **Tungabhadra** is the **largest** Krishna tributary.
**Raichur doab** lies between the **Krishna and Tungabhadra**.

37.s: Under the National Perspective Plan (1980) for interlinking of rivers, the links identified are
37.x: The NPP 1980 identified 30 links, 14 in the Himalayan component and 16 in the peninsular component. Option B reverses the split, and C and D give wrong totals.
37.tq: NPP 1980: 30 = 14 Himalayan + 16 peninsular.
xs: NPP 1980 identified **30 links**: **14 Himalayan** + **16 peninsular** — option **(1)**.
Option (2) reverses the split; (3) and (4) give wrong totals.
xa: The NPP is implemented via the **NWDA**.
**Ken-Betwa** is the **flagship ILR project**.
ILR was first proposed by **Sir Arthur Cotton**.

38.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the winds called monsoons?
o: Local winds confined to the coastal districts of India
Primary planetary winds that blow permanently in one direction
Upper-air winds that never reach the land surface
Seasonal or periodic secondary winds that reverse direction with the season
38.x: Monsoons are seasonal or periodic secondary winds. Their direction reverses with the change of season; they are not primary planetary winds.
38.tq: Distinguish monsoons from primary winds by their periodic reversal and classification.
xs: Monsoons are **seasonal/periodic secondary winds** that **reverse direction** with the season — option **(4)**.
They are **not primary (planetary)** winds — ⚠ "primary winds" was the false statement in PYQ G2 2023.
They blow **sea → land in summer** and **land → sea in winter**.
xa: The word comes from Arabic **"Mausim"** (season).
Monsoons lie mainly in the tropics between **20°N and 20°S**.
Their distribution is controlled mainly by **relief**.

38.s:
Consider the following statements about the monsoon:
1. Monsoons are confined mainly to the tropics between 20°N and 20°S.
2. Monsoon rainfall in India is steady and equally distributed.
3. The distribution of monsoon rainfall is controlled mainly by relief.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
38.x: Statement 1 is correct: monsoons lie mainly within 20°N-20°S. Statement 2 is wrong: the monsoon is not steady and is unequally distributed, with breaks and variability. Statement 3 is correct: relief mainly controls its distribution. So 1 and 3 only (B); A leaves out true statement 3, C and D include the false statement 2.
38.tq: 'Equally distributed' is the classic false statement (PYQ 2022).
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 3 only**.
Statement 1 correct: monsoons lie mainly between **20°N and 20°S**.
Statement 2 wrong: the monsoon is **not steady** and is **unequally distributed** (⚠ PYQ 2022 trap).
Statement 3 correct: distribution is controlled mainly by **relief**.
xa: The monsoon is marked by **breaks** and **variability**.
Its sudden onset is the "**burst**" (first week of June).
PYQ G2 2023/2024: statements II and III correct.

38.s: The sudden onset of the south-west monsoon, generally noticed in the first week of June, is known as the:
38.x: The sudden onset of the south-west monsoon in the first week of June is called the monsoon burst.
38.tq: Match the climatic event with its standard technical term.
xs: The sudden onset in the **first week of June** is the **monsoon burst** — option **(3)**.
The monsoon is **not steady**: it has **breaks** and uncertainty.
xa: Onset over **Kerala ~1 June**, the first state; A&N Islands ~**25 May**.
During a **break**, the trough shifts to the **Himalayan foothills**.
The **retreating** monsoon comes in **Oct-Nov**.

38.s: Who noted the seasonal winds in the tenth century?
38.x: Al Masudi, a tenth-century scholar, noted the seasonal winds associated with the monsoon system.
38.tq: Identify the historical observer associated with the climatic phenomenon.
xs: **Al Masudi** (**10th c.**) noted the seasonal winds — option **(2)**.
The **thermal theory** came later from Sir Edmund **Halley** (**1686**).
xa: A modern (complex) explanation is dated **1957** in some notes.
Without the monsoons north India would be **desert**.
"Monsoon" comes from Arabic **"Mausim"** (season).

38.s: The word 'monsoon' is derived from the Arabic word 'Mausim', which means
38.x: 'Mausim' is Arabic for season, reflecting the seasonal reversal of these winds. The word does not mean rain, wind or sea, though monsoons bring rain and are winds that blow from the sea in summer.
38.tq: Monsoon < Mausim = season.
xs: Arabic **"Mausim"** means **season** — option **(3)**.
⚠ Some notes give Urdu 'mausin' or Malay 'monsin'.
xa: Monsoons are **seasonal/periodic secondary** winds that reverse with the season.
Sea → land in **summer**; land → sea in **winter**.
**Al Masudi** (**10th c.**) noted the seasonal winds.

38.s: According to the classical thermal theory of the monsoon, the summer monsoon is produced primarily because:
o: The ITCZ remains fixed south of the equator throughout the year.
Land heats faster than the sea, creating a low-pressure area over land that draws moist winds from the sea.
The Himalayas generate a cold high-pressure area over northern India in summer.
The sea heats faster than the land, creating a permanent low over the ocean.
38.x: Sir Edmund Halley's thermal theory, proposed in 1686, attributes the monsoon to differential heating of land and sea. Summer heating creates a low over land that attracts moist maritime winds.
38.tq: Apply the pressure-gradient logic of differential heating rather than memorising only the theory’s name.
xs: **Land heats faster than sea**, creating a **summer low over land** that draws moist sea winds — option **(2)**.
This is the classical **thermal** theory of Sir Edmund **Halley** (**1686**); the pattern reverses in winter.
The sea does not heat faster; in summer the **high** lies over the sea.
xa: The **dynamic theory** explains the monsoon by the northward shift of the **ITCZ**.
**Tibetan plateau** heating creates an upper-air anticyclone and a stronger **TEJ**.
**Mascarene High** near **Madagascar** drives **cross-equatorial flow**.

38.s: The dynamic or ITCZ theory explains the southwest monsoon mainly through:
o: The cooling of the Tibetan Plateau during the summer months.
The northward shift of the ITCZ over the Ganga plain, drawing south-east trade winds across the equator as south-westerlies.
The southward shift of the ITCZ over the Indian Ocean during summer.
The permanent eastward movement of the subtropical westerly jet over peninsular India.
38.x: In summer, the ITCZ shifts northward over the Ganga plain as the monsoon trough. South-east trades cross the equator and are deflected to become south-westerly winds.
38.tq: Follow the movement of the pressure belt and the cross-equatorial wind path.
xs: The **ITCZ** shifts **north** over the **Ganga plain** as the **monsoon trough**, pulling **SE trades** across the equator as **SW winds** — option **(2)**.
Its **N-S swings** set the rainfall (UPSC CSAT).
A **southward** ITCZ shift is the opposite of the summer pattern.
xa: During **breaks**, the trough shifts to the **Himalayan foothills**.
**STJ** north of the Himalayas → **onset**; back south → **withdrawal**.
Thermal theory: Sir Edmund **Halley**, **1686**.

38.s:
Consider the following statements about jet streams and the Indian monsoon:
1. The subtropical westerly jet shifts north of the Himalayas during summer.
2. The tropical easterly jet extends from the South China Sea towards East Africa.
3. The return of the subtropical westerly jet south of the Himalayas is associated with monsoon withdrawal.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
38.x: All three statements are correct. The northward shift of the subtropical westerly jet is associated with onset, while its return south of the Himalayas accompanies withdrawal; the tropical easterly jet extends from the South China Sea to East Africa.
38.tq: Combine onset, withdrawal and jet-stream path statements before selecting the coded option.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
The **subtropical westerly jet (STJ)** shifts **north of the Himalayas** in summer → **onset** — correct.
The **TEJ** runs from the **South China Sea to East Africa** — correct.
The STJ's return **south** → **withdrawal** — correct.
xa: The **TEJ** coincides with the **SW monsoon**.
**Tibetan plateau** heating strengthens the **TEJ**.
In the retreating monsoon the **TEJ disappears**.

38.s: The heating of the Tibetan Plateau contributes to the southwest monsoon by:
o: Creating an upper-air anticyclone and strengthening the tropical easterly jet
Blocking all cross-equatorial winds in the Arabian Sea
Creating a permanent surface high and weakening the tropical easterly jet
Producing the subtropical westerly jet south of the Himalayas in summer
38.x: The Tibetan Plateau, at about 5,000 m, acts as a heat island in summer. Its intense heating produces an upper-air anticyclone and strengthens the tropical easterly jet.
38.tq: Connect plateau heating with its upper-air circulation effects.
xs: Tibetan heating creates an **upper-air anticyclone** and a **stronger Tropical Easterly Jet** — option **(1)**.
The plateau (~**5,000 m**) acts as a **heat island**, producing **low pressure**, not a surface high.
xa: A **permanent high** lies in the **S Indian Ocean** (UPSC).
The **TEJ** runs from the **South China Sea to East Africa**.
**Dust aerosols** heat the mid-troposphere over the **Indo-Gangetic plain**.

38.s:
Consider the following statements about factors influencing the Indian monsoon:
1. El Niño generally weakens the monsoon, while La Niña strengthens it.
2. A positive Indian Ocean Dipole can offset the effect of El Niño.
3. An unfavourable phase of the Madden-Julian Oscillation strengthens the monsoon.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
38.x: Statement 1 is correct: El Niño weakens, La Niña aids the monsoon. Statement 2 is correct: a positive IOD can offset El Niño. Statement 3 is wrong: an unfavourable MJO phase stalls the monsoon. So 1 and 2 only (B); A leaves out true statement 2, C and D include the false statement 3.
38.tq: 'Unfavourable' can only mean bad for the monsoon - it stalls it.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 correct: **El Nino weakens**; **La Nina strengthens/aids** the monsoon.
Statement 2 correct: a **positive IOD** can offset El Nino.
Statement 3 wrong: an **unfavourable MJO** phase **stalls** the monsoon.
xa: 2026: WMO gave ~**80%** chance of **El Nino** in Jul-Aug; a "**Super El Nino**" year was feared.
Monsoon set in over **Kerala on 4 June**, **three days late**, under a strengthening El Nino.
IMD forecast ~**90% of LPA** (Jun 2026).

38.s: The Mascarene High is best described as:
o: A permanent high-pressure cell in the southern Indian Ocean near Madagascar
A seasonal low-pressure cell over north-western India
A high-pressure cell over the Tibetan Plateau
A temperate cyclone over the Mediterranean Sea
38.x: The Mascarene High is a permanent high-pressure cell in the southern Indian Ocean near Madagascar and helps drive cross-equatorial flow.
38.tq: Distinguish a pressure cell by location and pressure character.
xs: The **Mascarene High** is a **permanent high-pressure cell** in the **south Indian Ocean** near **Madagascar** — option **(1)**.
A **Mediterranean** temperate cyclone describes **western disturbances**, not the Mascarene High.
xa: It drives **cross-equatorial flow** — a SW monsoon formation factor.
The **Somali jet** with the **Somalia current** intensifies monsoon winds.
Tibetan heating gives a **low** (heat island), not a high.

38.s: The principal role of the Mascarene High in the south-west monsoon mechanism is to:
o: Block the north-east monsoon over Tamil Nadu
Drive cross-equatorial flow towards the Indian subcontinent
Generate western disturbances over the Mediterranean
Cause snowfall in the Himalayan region
38.x: The Mascarene High drives the cross-equatorial flow that contributes to the formation of the south-west monsoon.
38.tq: Link a pressure cell to the wind movement it generates.
xs: The Mascarene High drives **cross-equatorial flow** — option **(2)**.
It is listed among the **SW monsoon's formation factors**.
**Western disturbances** come from the **Mediterranean** and bring Himalayan **snow** — not the Mascarene High.
xa: It lies near **Madagascar**.
SE trades cross the equator as **SW winds** (ITCZ theory).
**Somali jet**: low-level jet along the **East African coast**.

38.s: The Somali jet intensifies the Indian monsoon in association with the:
38.x: The Somali jet, together with the Somalia Current, intensifies the monsoon winds.
38.tq: Match the atmospheric jet with its associated ocean current.
xs: The **Somali jet** works with the **Somalia current** — option **(3)**.
It is a **low-level jet** along the **East African coast** that intensifies monsoon winds.
xa: The **Mascarene High** drives **cross-equatorial flow**.
The **TEJ** extends from the **South China Sea to East Africa**.
**Dust aerosols** help pull the monsoon inland.

38.s:
Consider the following statements about the IMD classification of seasons:
1. Winter comprises January and February.
2. The pre-monsoon (summer) season extends from February to April.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
38.x: Statement 1 is correct: IMD winter is January-February. Statement 2 is wrong: the pre-monsoon/summer season is March-May. So 1 only (A); B and C accept the false statement 2, D rejects the true statement 1.
38.tq: IMD: Jan-Feb, Mar-May, Jun-Sep, Oct-Dec.
xs: Only statement 1 is correct — option **(1) 1 only**.
Statement 1 correct: IMD winter = **January-February**.
Statement 2 wrong: pre-monsoon/summer = **March-May**.
xa: SW monsoon **June-September**; post-monsoon/NE monsoon **October-December**.
⚠ Older notes use **Dec-Feb** for winter (table per IYB 2026).
Coldest: **Dec-Jan**.

38.s: The south-west monsoon season in the IMD classification covers:
38.x: The IMD south-west monsoon season extends from June to September.
38.tq: Recall the precise four-month seasonal block.
xs: The IMD **south-west monsoon** season runs from **June to September** — option **(2)**.
**October-December** is the **post-monsoon / NE monsoon**.
xa: The SW monsoon gives about **75%** of annual rain.
Pre-monsoon: **March-May**; winter: **January-February**.

38.s: Which of the following statements regarding heat conditions in India is correct?
o: Heat waves generally peak in January and February.
North-western and central India are hottest mainly from April to June, with heat waves peaking in May-June.
The hottest period in north-western India is restricted to October-November.
Heat waves peak only during the south-west monsoon season.
38.x: North-western and central India experience their hottest conditions from April to June, and heat waves generally peak in May-June.
38.tq: Combine the season, region and peak-period clues.
xs: NW and central India are hottest in **April-June**, with heat waves peaking in **May-June** — option **(2)**.
**January-February** is **winter**; **October-November** is the **retreating** monsoon with "October heat".
xa: Record: **Ganganagar** (Rajasthan) ~**50°C** in **1935**.
**Nautapa**: a **nine-day** peak of summer heat before the monsoon.
**Loo**: hot, dry, dust-laden afternoon wind of the north plains.

38.s: Which one of the following is NOT one of the six traditional Indian seasons?
38.x: The six traditional seasons are Vasanta, Grishma, Varsha, Sharad, Hemanta and Shishira. Pravaha is not included in this list.
38.tq: Identify the outsider from a fixed traditional list.
xs: **Pravaha** is not one of the six traditional seasons — option **(1)**.
The six: **Vasanta, Grishma, Varsha, Sharad, Hemanta, Shishira**.
xa: IMD uses **four** seasons: winter, pre-monsoon, SW monsoon, post-monsoon.
**Varsha** corresponds to the rainy season.
Coldest months: **Dec-Jan**.

38.s: Mango showers are associated mainly with which of the following regions?
38.x: Mango showers are characteristic of Kerala and coastal Karnataka; they also occur in Andhra Pradesh during April–May.
38.tq: Use the region–phenomenon association to distinguish closely related pre-monsoon events.
xs: **Mango showers** fall on the coasts of **Kerala and Karnataka** — option **(1)** (coastal Karnataka: PYQ G2 2024).
They also occur in **AP** in **Apr-May** and help **early ripening of mangoes**.
**West Bengal, Odisha, Assam** get the **Kaal Baisakhi**; Rajasthan-Punjab get **Loo** and **Andhi**.
xa: **Blossom showers** aid **coffee** flowering in Kerala and nearby Karnataka.
Local convective storms give about **10%** of annual rainfall.
APPSC G2 2024 key: **mango showers → Karnataka**.

38.s:
Consider the following pairs (local pre-monsoon phenomenon : region):
1. Blossom (coffee) showers : Kerala and nearby coffee areas of Karnataka
2. Kaal Baisakhi : Rajasthan and Punjab
3. Bardoli Chheerha : Assam
Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched?
38.x: Pair 1 is correct: blossom showers aid coffee flowering in Kerala and nearby Karnataka. Pair 2 is wrong: Kaal Baisakhi (Nor'westers) strike West Bengal, Odisha and Assam, not Rajasthan. Pair 3 is correct: Bardoli Chheerha is Assam's name for the Kaal Baisakhi thunderstorm ('tea showers'). So 1 and 3 only (B); A leaves out pair 3, C and D include the wrong pair 2.
38.tq: Kaal Baisakhi = east (West Bengal, PYQ 2025); the north-west gets Loo and Andhi.
xs: Pairs 1 and 3 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 3 only**.
Pair 1 correct: **blossom showers** aid **coffee** in Kerala and nearby Karnataka.
Pair 2 wrong: **Kaal Baisakhi** hits **West Bengal**, Odisha, Assam — not Rajasthan and Punjab.
Pair 3 correct: **Bardoli Chheerha** is **Assam**'s name for the Kaal Baisakhi.
xa: In Assam these storms are called "**tea showers**".
Kaal Baisakhi = **Nor'westers**: violent **evening thunderstorms**.
APPSC GS 2025 key: **Kaal Baisakhi → West Bengal**.

38.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Loo:
1. It is a hot, dry and dust-laden afternoon wind.
2. It is mainly experienced over the northern and north-western plains.
3. In Andhra Pradesh, it is locally associated with Rayalaseema.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
38.x: All three statements are correct. The Loo is a hot, dry and dusty afternoon wind of the northern and north-western plains and is also locally experienced in Rayalaseema.
38.tq: Combine definition and regional-distribution statements, checking all three independently.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
The **Loo** is a **hot, dry, dust-laden afternoon wind** — correct.
It blows over the **north and north-west plains**, **Punjab to Bihar** — correct.
In AP it is felt locally in **Rayalaseema** — correct.
xa: **Andhi** dust storms run from **Rajasthan (Thar)** into Punjab, Haryana, Delhi, W UP.
Hottest place in AP: **Rentachintala** (Palnadu).
**Nautapa**: nine-day peak heat before the monsoon.

38.s:
Consider the following statements about Andhi (pre-monsoon dust storms):
1. They move from Rajasthan (Thar) into Punjab, Haryana, Delhi and western Uttar Pradesh.
2. They occur mainly in December and January.
3. Such dust and hail storms are now becoming more frequent in central India.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
38.x: Statement 1 is correct: Andhi spreads from the Thar into Punjab, Haryana, Delhi and western UP. Statement 2 is wrong: they are pre-monsoon storms of March to June. Statement 3 is correct: they are now more frequent in central India. So 1 and 3 only (B); A leaves out true statement 3, C and D include the false statement 2.
38.tq: Pre-monsoon means March-June, never mid-winter.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 3 only**.
Statement 1 correct: **Andhi** moves from **Rajasthan (Thar)** into **Punjab, Haryana, Delhi, W UP**.
Statement 2 wrong: they are **pre-monsoon** storms of **March to June**.
Statement 3 correct: dust and hail storms are now **more frequent in central India**.
xa: The **Loo** is the hot, dry afternoon wind of the same plains.
Hot season: **March-May**.
Pre-monsoon local storms give about **10%** of annual rain.

38.s:
Consider the following statements about the hot season in India:
1. It generally extends from March to May.
2. Local convective storms during this period contribute about 10 per cent of the annual rainfall as pre-monsoon rain.
3. Pre-monsoon rain is useful for rice, jute, coffee, mango and tea.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
38.x: The hot season generally lasts from March to May. Local convective storms produce about 10 per cent of annual rainfall as pre-monsoon rain, which benefits rice, jute, coffee, mango and tea.
38.tq: Test a season, a quantitative figure and its agricultural significance together.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
The hot season runs **March-May** — correct.
Local convective storms give about **10%** of annual rainfall — correct.
This rain helps **rice, jute, coffee, mango, tea** — correct.
xa: Examples: **mango showers**, **blossom showers**, **Kaal Baisakhi**.
Record heat: **Ganganagar** ~**50°C** (**1935**).
Heat waves peak in **May-June**.

38.s: Which one of the following places recorded approximately 50°C during 1935 in the context of the hot season?
38.x: Ganganagar in Rajasthan recorded approximately 50°C in 1935, illustrating the intensity of the hot season in north-western India.
38.tq: Recall the location linked with a distinctive historical temperature record.
xs: **Ganganagar** (Rajasthan) recorded ~**50°C** in **1935** — option **(4)**.
NW and central India are hottest in **April-June**.
xa: **Nautapa** is the **nine-day** peak heat of north India before the monsoon.
The **Loo** blows over the north and north-west plains.
**Rajasthan** is the **lowest-rainfall** state.

38.s: Dust aerosols over the Indo-Gangetic Plain assist the advance of the monsoon inland because they:
o: Reverse the direction of ocean currents
Heat the mid-troposphere and help pull the monsoon inland
Cool the lower troposphere and suppress convection
Eliminate pressure differences between land and sea
38.x: Dust aerosols heat the mid-troposphere over the Indo-Gangetic Plain. This heating helps pull the monsoon inland.
38.tq: Apply the stated cause-and-effect relationship rather than merely recalling a definition.
xs: **Dust aerosols** heat the **mid-troposphere** over the **Indo-Gangetic plain**, helping pull the monsoon inland — option **(2)**.
They do not cool the lower troposphere or reverse currents.
xa: **Mascarene High** (near Madagascar) drives **cross-equatorial flow**.
The **Somali jet** and **Somalia current** intensify monsoon winds.
**Tibetan plateau** heating strengthens the **TEJ**.

38.s: ‘Nautapa’ refers to:
o: A prolonged break in the northeast monsoon
A nine-day period of winter rainfall in south India
The first week of the southwest monsoon in Kerala
A nine-day period of peak summer heat in north India before the monsoon
38.x: Nautapa is the traditional nine-day peak of summer heat in north India and occurs just before the arrival of the monsoon.
38.tq: Identify a traditional climatic term by its duration, season and region.
xs: **Nautapa** is the traditional **nine-day** peak of **summer heat** in **north India**, just before the monsoon — option **(4)**.
It is not a rainy spell or a monsoon break.
xa: Heat waves peak in **May-June**.
Record: **Ganganagar** ~**50°C** (**1935**).
Onset over **Kerala ~1 June**.

38.s: Kaal Baisakhi (Nor'westers), the violent evening thunderstorms of the hot-weather season, are associated mainly with
38.x: Kaal Baisakhi strikes West Bengal (also Odisha and Assam) in the hot season (APPSC GS 2025 key). Kerala gets mango showers, while Rajasthan and Punjab get the Loo and Andhi dust storms.
38.tq: Kaal Baisakhi = West Bengal; mango showers = Kerala/Karnataka.
xs: **Kaal Baisakhi** strikes **West Bengal** — option **(2)** (APPSC GS 2025 key).
It also hits **Odisha and Assam**; **Kerala** gets **mango showers**; Rajasthan and Punjab get **Loo** and **Andhi**.
xa: They are **violent evening thunderstorms / squalls** with torrential rain.
In Assam: "**tea showers**", locally **Bardoli Chheerha**.
**Blossom showers** aid **coffee** flowering.

38.s:
Consider the following statements about the normal onset and advance of the south-west monsoon:
1. It normally sets in over Kerala on 1 June.
2. It reaches the Andaman and Nicobar Islands about 25 May, roughly a week before Kerala.
3. As per IMD's revised normal dates, it covers the whole country by 15 June.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
38.x: Statement 1 is correct: normal onset over Kerala is 1 June. Statement 2 is correct: the A&N Islands get it around 25 May, about a week earlier. Statement 3 is wrong: IMD's revised normal date for covering the whole country is 8 July (15 June is roughly when it reaches Bhopal). So 1 and 2 only (B); A leaves out true statement 2, C and D include the false statement 3.
38.tq: A&N 25 May -> Kerala 1 June -> whole country 8 July.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 correct: onset over **Kerala ~1 June**, the first state.
Statement 2 correct: the **A&N Islands** get it ~**25 May**, about a week earlier.
Statement 3 wrong: IMD's revised full-coverage date is **8 July**; ~**15 June** is when it reaches **Bhopal**.
xa: IMD declares onset after **10 May** when **60% of 14** stations get **2.5 mm** for two days.
**Delhi** is reached ~**25 June**.
2026: onset on **4 June**, **three days late**.

38.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the duration of the southwest monsoon in India:
1. It lasts for less than 75 days in western Rajasthan.
2. It lasts for more than 120 days in the south-western peninsula.
3. Its duration is uniform throughout the country.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
38.x: The duration is less than 75 days in western Rajasthan and more than 120 days in the south-western peninsula. It is not uniform throughout India.
38.tq: Compare regional extremes and reject the absolute statement about uniformity.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 correct: **<75 days** in **W Rajasthan**.
Statement 2 correct: **>120 days** in the **SW peninsula**.
Statement 3 wrong: the duration is **not uniform**.
xa: Withdrawal begins from the **NW** in **October** and ends by **end-November**.
Full coverage: IMD revised normal date **8 July**.
The SW monsoon gives about **75%** of annual rain.

38.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the approximate advance of the southwest monsoon?
o: Bhopal by 15 June and Delhi by 25 June
Bhopal by 25 May and Delhi by 1 June
Bhopal by 1 July and Delhi by 8 July
Bhopal by 25 June and Delhi by 15 July
38.x: The southwest monsoon normally reaches Bhopal around 15 June and Delhi around 25 June.
38.tq: Use the sequence and paired dates to distinguish advance dates from onset and withdrawal dates.
xs: The monsoon reaches **Bhopal ~15 June** and **Delhi ~25 June** — option **(1)**.
The country is covered in about a month; IMD's revised full-coverage date is **8 July**.
xa: Kerala onset ~**1 June**; A&N ~**25 May**.
⚠ Some notes say full coverage "by **end of July**", others "by **end of June**".
IMD uses rainfall over **5-day pentads**.

38.s: During a ‘break’ in the southwest monsoon, which one of the following conditions generally occurs?
o: The Arabian Sea branch reverses into a winter monsoon over the west coast.
The tropical easterly jet disappears and the westerly jet moves south of the Himalayas.
The monsoon trough shifts permanently to the Indian Ocean and all rainfall stops.
The monsoon trough shifts to the Himalayan foothills, leaving the plains relatively dry.
38.x: During a monsoon break, the trough shifts towards the Himalayan foothills. The plains consequently experience dry conditions while the Himalayan region receives heavy rainfall.
38.tq: Apply the cause-and-effect relationship between trough position and regional rainfall.
xs: During a **break**, the trough shifts to the **Himalayan foothills**, leaving the plains **dry** — option **(4)**.
The hills meanwhile get **heavy rain**.
**TEJ disappearing** and the **westerly jet returning south** describe the **retreating** monsoon, not a break.
xa: The monsoon is marked by **breaks** and **variability**.
The **monsoon trough** is the ITCZ over the **Ganga plain**.
An **unfavourable MJO** phase stalls the monsoon.

38.s: The withdrawal of the southwest monsoon from India normally:
o: Begins in the south in May and ends in August
Begins in the north-west in October and ends by the end of November
Begins in the east in September and ends by mid-October
Begins simultaneously throughout India in November
38.x: Withdrawal begins from north-western India in October and is generally complete by the end of November.
38.tq: Remember the direction and time span of withdrawal rather than the onset sequence.
xs: Withdrawal **begins from the NW in October** and **ends by end-November** — option **(2)**.
It follows the **STJ** returning **south** of the Himalayas.
xa: Retreating monsoon (**Oct-Nov**): clear skies + "**October heat**".
**Bay of Bengal cyclones** bring heavy rain to the south then.
Duration: **<75 days** (W Rajasthan) to **>120 days** (SW peninsula).

38.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Bay of Bengal branch — moves north along the western coast after crossing the Western Ghats
Arabian Sea branch — Agumbe and Hulikal receive very heavy rainfall
Arabian Sea branch — first strikes the Meghalaya hills
Bay of Bengal branch — produces a rain-shadow region immediately east of the Western Ghats
38.x: The Arabian Sea branch strikes the Western Ghats first, giving very heavy rain at Agumbe and Hulikal on the Ghats crest. It is this branch (not the Bay branch) that moves north along the west coast and leaves a rain shadow east of the Ghats, while the Bay of Bengal branch (not the Arabian Sea branch) strikes the Meghalaya hills.
38.tq: Use branch-specific routes and locations to eliminate swapped descriptions.
xs: **Arabian Sea branch — Agumbe and Hulikal** get very heavy rain — option **(2)**.
It is the **Arabian Sea** branch that moves north along the **west coast** and leaves a **rain-shadow** east of the Ghats.
The **Bay of Bengal** branch strikes **Meghalaya** (Mawsynram).
xa: Agumbe and Hulikal lie on the **Ghats crest** in **Karnataka**.
The Arabian Sea branch misses **Rajasthan** (winds parallel to the **Aravallis**).
The Bay branch is deflected west by the **Himalayas** along the **Ganga plain**.

38.s: The rain-shadow region associated with the Arabian Sea branch of the southwest monsoon lies mainly:
o: To the west of the Malabar Coast
To the east of the Western Ghats
38.x: The Western Ghats force uplift on their windward side, leaving a rain-shadow region to their east.
38.tq: Use the windward-leeward comparison to identify the rain-shadow location.
xs: The Arabian Sea branch's **rain shadow** lies **east of the Western Ghats** — option **(3)**.
It covers the **interior peninsula**: interior **Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana, AP Rayalaseema, Tamil Nadu**.
xa: The windward **Malabar coast** gets rain first.
Driest in AP: **Hagari valley** (**< 51 cm**).
**Ladakh/Leh** lies in the rain shadow of the **Himalaya**.

38.s: The southwest monsoon season contributes approximately what proportion of India's annual rainfall?
38.x: The southwest monsoon season provides about 75 per cent of India's annual rainfall.
38.tq: Select the stated national share without confusing it with regional rainfall percentages.
xs: The **SW monsoon** gives about **75 per cent** (**75%**) of annual rain — option **(3)**.
The rest comes mainly from **pre-monsoon** storms (about **10%**), the **NE monsoon** and **western disturbances**.
xa: Season: **June-September**.
Western disturbances give NW India **10-15 cm** winter rain.
The **NE monsoon** (Oct-Dec) waters the **Coromandel coast**.

38.s:
Consider the following statements about the Bay of Bengal branch of the southwest monsoon:
1. It strikes the Myanmar and north-eastern hills at nearly right angles.
2. It is subsequently turned westward by the Himalayas along the Ganga plain.
3. It produces an east-to-west decline of rainfall over the northern plains.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
38.x: All three statements correctly describe the path and rainfall effect of the Bay of Bengal branch.
38.tq: Follow the sequence of wind movement before judging the resulting rainfall pattern.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
The **Bay of Bengal branch** strikes the **Myanmar coast and NE hills** at **right angles** — correct.
The **Himalayas** deflect it **west** along the **Ganga plain** — correct.
Rain falls **E → W**, so the **NW stays dry** — correct.
xa: It soaks **Meghalaya — Mawsynram** (APPSC GS 2024).
**Mawsynram** mean ~**1,187 cm**, then **Cherrapunji (Sohra)**.
The **Arabian Sea branch** strikes the **Western Ghats** first.

38.s: The long-period average (LPA) of south-west monsoon rainfall over India, based on 1971–2020, is
38.x: The LPA of the south-west monsoon for 1971–2020 is 868.6 mm (about 87 cm). 668.6 and 768.6 mm are distractors, and about 1,187 cm (not mm) is Mawsynram's mean annual rainfall.
38.tq: SW monsoon LPA = 868.6 mm ~ 87 cm.
xs: ~**1,187 cm** is **Mawsynram**'s mean rainfall, not the LPA.
xa: 2026 April forecast: **92% of LPA** (LPA **87 cm**), first "below normal" April forecast in **11 years**.
Later revision: **90%** (Jun 2026).
**OMT** predicts monsoon rain better than **SST**.

38.s: Which one of the following places is recognised as the wettest place in India, receiving a mean annual rainfall of approximately 1,187 cm?
38.x: Mawsynram in the Khasi Hills of Meghalaya receives a mean annual rainfall of approximately 1,187 cm and is the wettest place in India.
38.tq: Use the exact place–figure association rather than confusing nearby high-rainfall places.
xs: **Mawsynram** (Khasi Hills, Meghalaya), ~**1,187 cm**, is the **wettest** place — option **(1)**.
**Cherrapunji (Sohra)** comes next; **Agumbe** and **Hulikal** are the Western Ghats' wettest.
xa: Mawsynram is the wettest place on Earth: **467.4 inches** a year (PYQ 2021 key).
It is watered by the **Bay of Bengal branch**.
Driest: **Ruyli** (Jaisalmer), ~**8.33 cm**.

38.s:
Consider the following statements regarding exceptionally high rainfall locations in India:
1. Mawsynram is located in the Khasi Hills of Meghalaya.
2. Cherrapunji is also known as Sohra.
3. Agumbe and Hulikal are wettest locations on the crest of the Western Ghats.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
38.x: All three statements are correct. Mawsynram and Cherrapunji are in Meghalaya, while Agumbe and Hulikal in Karnataka are notable wet locations on the Western Ghats crest.
38.tq: Check each place–region pair separately before selecting the combination.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
**Mawsynram** is in the **Khasi Hills, Meghalaya**; **Cherrapunji** is **Sohra** — correct.
**Agumbe** and **Hulikal** (Karnataka) get the heaviest rain on the **Ghats crest** — correct.
xa: Highest-rainfall state: **Meghalaya**; lowest: **Rajasthan**.
Mawsynram mean ~**1,187 cm**.
Agumbe-Hulikal rain comes from the **Arabian Sea branch**.

38.s: Which one of the following correctly identifies the states with the highest and lowest rainfall in India respectively?
38.x: Meghalaya is identified as the highest-rainfall state, whereas Rajasthan is the lowest-rainfall state in the stated comparison.
38.tq: Split the pair and verify the direction of the comparison.
xs: Highest **Meghalaya**, lowest **Rajasthan** — option **(4)**.
Option **(1)** reverses them.
xa: Wettest place: **Mawsynram** (Meghalaya); driest: **Ruyli** (Jaisalmer).
Rajasthan is dry because the Arabian Sea branch runs **parallel to the Aravallis**.
The Bay branch reaches Rajasthan **exhausted**.

38.s:
Which of the following regions are included in the low-rainfall zone receiving less than 60 cm of rainfall?
1. Thar Desert
2. Punjab-Haryana region
3. Kutch
4. Ladakh-Karakoram
5. Interior Peninsula
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
38.x: The low-rainfall zone receiving less than 60 cm covers the Thar, Punjab-Haryana, Kutch, Ladakh-Karakoram and the interior peninsula.
38.tq: Treat a listed geographical classification as a checklist and test every member.
xs: All five lie in the **<60 cm** zone — option **(4) 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5**.
The low zone: **Thar, Punjab-Haryana, Kutch, Ladakh-Karakoram, interior peninsula**.
xa: It is one of **three** rainfall zones.
Interior peninsula is dry as the **rain shadow** of the Western Ghats.
Driest place: **Ruyli** (~**8.33 cm**).

38.s:
Which of the following areas are situated in rain-shadow regions associated with the Western Ghats or the Himalayas?
1. Interior Maharashtra
2. Karnataka interior
3. Telangana
4. Rayalaseema
5. Ladakh
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
38.x: The lee of the Western Ghats includes interior Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana, Rayalaseema and parts of Tamil Nadu; Ladakh lies in the rain shadow behind the Himalayas.
38.tq: Use the physical barrier and its lee-side effect to identify all applicable regions.
xs: All five are rain-shadow areas — option **(3) 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5**.
Lee of the **Western Ghats**: interior **Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana, AP Rayalaseema**, Tamil Nadu.
**Ladakh / Leh** lies behind the **Great Himalaya** — rain shadow of the Himalaya, a **cold desert**.
xa: AP's driest: **Hagari valley** (**< 51 cm**), Rayalaseema rain shadow.
**Rayalaseema** depends on the **NE monsoon**, with Nellore and Prakasam.
The **Tamil Nadu coast** stays relatively dry in the SW monsoon.

38.s: Why does Rajasthan receive very little rainfall from the Arabian Sea branch of the southwest monsoon?
o: The Aravalli Range lies parallel to the branch and therefore does not provide significant uplift.
The branch is diverted completely towards the Bay of Bengal by the Himalayas.
The branch loses all its moisture over the Western Ghats before reaching Rajasthan.
The branch reaches Rajasthan only after crossing the Khasi Hills.
38.x: The Arabian Sea branch runs parallel to the Aravallis, so the range does not act as a barrier to force the air upward and produce substantial rainfall.
38.tq: Ask whether the mountain range is perpendicular or parallel to the moisture-bearing winds.
xs: The Arabian Sea branch runs **parallel to the Aravallis**, so there is **no barrier to lift it** — option **(1)**.
The **Bay branch** arrives **exhausted**, and Rajasthan is **far from the sea**.
xa: Rajasthan is the **lowest-rainfall** state.
**Western disturbances** give NW India **10-15 cm** winter rain for **rabi**.
Koeppen: extreme western Rajasthan = **BWhw** (hot desert).

38.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
38.x: Ruyli in Jaisalmer district receives about 8.33 cm of rainfall and is identified as the driest place in India. Bellary and Leh are low-rainfall areas, whereas Cherrapunji is in Meghalaya.
38.tq: Start from the sure place–attribute pair and reject reversed extremes.
xs: **Ruyli** (Jaisalmer), ~**8.33 cm**, is the **driest** place — option **(1)**.
The wettest is **Mawsynram**; **Leh** has very low rain; **Cherrapunji** is in **Meghalaya**, not the Thar.
xa: Lowest-rainfall state: **Rajasthan**.
Leh is a **cold desert** behind the Great Himalaya.
The Thar lies in the **<60 cm** zone.

38.s:
Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
1. Leeward Deccan—rain shadow of the Western Ghats
2. Ladakh—region behind the Great Himalaya and cold desert
3. Hagari valley—lowest rainfall region in Andhra Pradesh
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
38.x: The leeward Deccan lies in the Western Ghats’ rain shadow, Ladakh lies behind the Great Himalaya and is a cold desert, and the Hagari valley has the lowest rainfall in Andhra Pradesh, below 51 cm.
38.tq: Verify each region–cause pair, paying special attention to the Andhra Pradesh exception.
xs: All three pairs are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
The leeward Deccan is the **rain shadow of the Western Ghats** — correct.
**Ladakh** lies **behind the Great Himalaya**, a **cold desert** — correct.
**Hagari valley** is AP's **lowest-rainfall** area (**< 51 cm**) — correct.
xa: AP's wettest: **Sileru-Sabari valleys** (**140-152 cm**).
AP climate: **Aw**, with both SW and NE monsoons.
AP's coolest place: **Lambasingi**.

38.s:
Which of the following phenomena are associated with the retreating southwest monsoon?
1. The Sun moves southward and the north-western low-pressure area weakens.
2. The westerly jet returns south of the Himalayas.
3. The tropical easterly jet disappears.
4. Clear skies and ‘October heat’ are experienced.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
38.x: All four conditions accompany the retreating monsoon. The weakening of the north-western low, jet-stream changes and clear, hot weather are characteristic of October–November.
38.tq: Test a complete cluster of associated seasonal characteristics.
xs: All four are correct — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
The **Sun moves south** and the **NW low vanishes** — correct.
The **westerly jet returns** south of the Himalayas; the **TEJ disappears** — correct.
Clear skies and "**October heat**" follow — correct.
xa: The retreating monsoon runs **Oct-Nov**.
**Bay of Bengal cyclones** bring heavy rain to the south (**bimodal**).
**NE monsoon** winds pick up Bay moisture for the **Coromandel coast**.

38.s: The bimodal rainfall received by parts of southern India during the retreating monsoon is mainly associated with:
o: The permanent high over the South Indian Ocean
38.x: Bay of Bengal cyclones bring bimodal rainfall to the south during the October–November retreating monsoon season.
38.tq: Match the seasonal rainfall feature with its immediate weather system.
xs: The bimodal rainfall of parts of south India in the retreating monsoon comes from **Bay of Bengal cyclones** — option **(2)**.
In the **retreating monsoon (Oct-Nov)** the sun moves south and the NW low vanishes; **Bay of Bengal cyclones** then bring heavy rain to the south.
**Western disturbances** are **Mediterranean** cyclones that rain on **NW India** in winter, not the south.
The **permanent high** in the S Indian Ocean (Mascarene High) drives the SW monsoon's cross-equatorial flow; **dust storms** (Andhi) are pre-monsoon storms of **Rajasthan**.
xa: In the retreat the **westerly jet returns** south of the Himalayas and the **tropical easterly jet disappears**.
Clear skies + hot, humid weather of the retreat = **"October heat"**.
**NE monsoon (Oct-Dec)** rains on the **Coromandel coast (Tamil Nadu)**, **Rayalaseema, Nellore, Prakasam**.
SW monsoon withdrawal begins from the **NW in October** and ends by **end-November**.

38.s: Western disturbances affecting north-western India are best described as:
o: Mediterranean temperate cyclones reaching India through Iran, Afghanistan and Pakistan
Tropical cyclones originating in the Bay of Bengal
Local convectional storms originating over the Thar Desert
Retreating monsoon winds originating over the Arabian Sea
38.x: Western disturbances are temperate cyclones originating in the Mediterranean region and reaching north-western India through Iran, Afghanistan and Pakistan.
38.tq: Identify the origin and pathway of the weather system.
xs: Western disturbances are **Mediterranean temperate cyclones** reaching India via **Iran, Afghanistan and Pakistan** — option **(1)**.
They are temperate, not **tropical cyclones of the Bay of Bengal** (those cause the south's retreating-monsoon rain).
They are not local convective storms like the **Andhi** of the Thar, nor **retreating monsoon** winds.
xa: They give **NW India 10-15 cm** of winter rain, vital for **rabi** crops.
They bring **snow** to the hills of **J&K, HP and Uttarakhand**.
Fewer western disturbances → reduced winter rain and snow in north India.
IMD winter season = **January-February** (older notes: **Dec-Feb**); coldest months **Dec-Jan**.

38.s: The term ‘October heat’ refers to:
o: A heat wave occurring exclusively in north-western India in April
Extreme heat caused by western disturbances
Hot and humid weather during the retreat of the monsoon
Cold and dry weather after the winter monsoon
38.x: October heat denotes the hot and humid conditions experienced in October as the south-west monsoon retreats.
38.tq: Discriminate between a named climatic phenomenon and nearby seasonal conditions.
xs: **'October heat'** is the **hot and humid weather** with clear skies during the **retreat of the monsoon** — option **(3)**.
It belongs to the **retreating monsoon (Oct-Nov)**, when the sun moves south and the NW low vanishes — not April, and not caused by **western disturbances**.
It is hot and humid, not cold and dry.
xa: IMD's **post-monsoon / NE monsoon** season is **October-December**.
During the retreat the **westerly jet returns** south of the Himalayas and the **tropical easterly jet disappears**.
**Bay of Bengal cyclones** in this period give the south heavy, **bimodal** rain.
**Nautapa** = the traditional **nine-day** peak of summer heat in north India just before the monsoon.

38.s: The relative dryness of the Tamil Nadu coast during the south-west monsoon is mainly due to:
o: The permanent dominance of western disturbances
Its location on the leeward side and the winds blowing parallel to the coast
Its location north of the Tropic of Cancer
The absence of the Bay of Bengal
38.x: The Tamil Nadu coast lies in a rain-shadow position during the south-west monsoon, while the winds largely blow parallel to the coast.
38.tq: Apply the rain-shadow and wind-direction concepts to a regional example.
xs: The Tamil Nadu coast stays relatively dry in the SW monsoon because it lies in the **rain-shadow (leeward side)** and the **winds blow parallel to the coast** — option **(2)**.
So it gets little SW-monsoon rain and **depends on the NE monsoon** (Oct-Dec).
**Western disturbances** affect NW India, and Tamil Nadu is far south of the **Tropic of Cancer**, on the Bay of Bengal itself.
xa: The **Coromandel coast** is Koeppen **As** — monsoon with **dry summer** (winter rain).
The NE monsoon's retreating winds pick up **Bay of Bengal** moisture and rain on **Coromandel, Rayalaseema, Nellore, Prakasam**.
Rain-shadow lee of the **Western Ghats**: interior Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana, **AP Rayalaseema**, Tamil Nadu.
⚠ **Rajasthan** stays dry for a similar reason — the Arabian Sea branch runs **parallel to the Aravallis**.

38.s:
Consider the following statements about the north-east monsoon:
1. Its retreating winds pick up moisture over the Bay of Bengal.
2. It brings rain to the Coromandel (Tamil Nadu) coast during October-December.
3. Because of this winter rain, the Coromandel coast falls under the Köppen climate type Aw.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
38.x: Statement 1 is correct: retreating winds gain Bay of Bengal moisture. Statement 2 is correct: the NE monsoon (Oct-Dec) rains on the Coromandel coast, Rayalaseema, Nellore and Prakasam. Statement 3 is wrong: the Coromandel coast is 'As' (monsoon with dry summer); Aw is tropical savanna of most of the peninsula, including AP. So 1 and 2 only (B); A leaves out true statement 2, C and D include the false statement 3.
38.tq: As = dry Summer, wet winter -> Coromandel.
xs: Statement 1 **correct**: the NE monsoon's **retreating winds pick up Bay of Bengal moisture**.
Statement 2 **correct**: it rains on the **Coromandel coast (Tamil Nadu)** in **October-December**.
Statement 3 **wrong**: the Coromandel coast is Koeppen **As** (monsoon, dry summer); **Aw** is tropical savanna of most of the peninsula.
So **1 and 2 only** — option **(2)**.
xa: The NE monsoon also rains on **Rayalaseema, Nellore and Prakasam**.
**AP is Aw** and receives both the SW and NE monsoons.
**Amw** = west coast south of **Goa**; **Cwg** = **Ganga plain** (dry winter).
The Tamil Nadu coast stays dry in the SW monsoon: rain-shadow and winds **parallel to the coast**.

38.s: Which group of regions is specifically identified as receiving rainfall from the north-east monsoon?
o: Coromandel coast, Rayalaseema, Nellore and Prakasam
Punjab, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh and Kashmir
Gujarat, western Rajasthan, Punjab and Ladakh
Konkan, Malabar, Goa and coastal Karnataka
38.x: The north-east monsoon brings rainfall to the Coromandel coast, Rayalaseema, Nellore and Prakasam.
38.tq: Test the complete regional distribution rather than a single location.
xs: The NE monsoon rains on the **Coromandel coast, Rayalaseema, Nellore and Prakasam** — option **(1)**.
Its **retreating winds pick up Bay of Bengal moisture** in **Oct-Dec** and shed it on the south-east.
**Punjab, Haryana, HP, Kashmir** get winter rain/snow from **western disturbances**; **Konkan-Malabar-Goa** get the **Arabian Sea branch** of the SW monsoon.
xa: The Coromandel coast is Koeppen **As** (monsoon with dry summer / winter rain).
AP gets both the SW and NE monsoons; its climate is **Aw**.
**Bay of Bengal cyclones** in **Oct-Nov** make southern rainfall **bimodal**.
IMD's **post-monsoon / NE monsoon** season runs **October-December**.

38.s: Western disturbances originating from the Mediterranean are associated with:
o: 3–8 cm rain in coastal Andhra Pradesh and snowfall in the Nilgiris
South-west monsoon rain over the entire Indian peninsula
10–15 cm rain in north-west India and snowfall in Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand
Only dry winds over north-west India without agricultural significance
38.x: Mediterranean western disturbances bring about 10–15 cm of rain to north-west India, benefit rabi crops and produce snowfall in Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand.
38.tq: Keep the rainfall range, crop effect and snowfall region together.
xs: Mediterranean **western disturbances** bring **10-15 cm** of winter rain to **NW India** and **snow** in **J&K, HP and Uttarakhand** — option **(3)**.
This rain is vital for **rabi** crops, so they are not "without agricultural significance".
They affect NW India in winter, not coastal AP, the Nilgiris or the SW-monsoon peninsula.
xa: Route: **Mediterranean** → **Iran-Afghanistan-Pakistan** → NW India.
Fewer western disturbances → reduced winter rain and snow in north India.
Local pre-monsoon convective storms give about **10%** of annual rainfall; the **SW monsoon** about **75%**.

38.s: Which of the following climate-type codes is correctly matched with its region?
o: Amw — West coast south of Goa
BWhw — Most of the peninsula south of the Tropic of Cancer
38.x: Amw denotes a monsoon climate with a short dry season and occurs on the west coast south of Goa.
38.tq: Start from the sure climate-code and region pair.
xs: **Amw** (monsoon, short dry season) is correctly matched with the **west coast south of Goa** — option **(1)**.
**BWhw** (hot desert) belongs to **extreme western Rajasthan**, not the peninsula.
**Aw** (tropical savanna) is **most of the peninsula** south of the Tropic of Cancer, not Rajasthan.
**Dfc** is **Arunachal Pradesh**; the Coromandel coast is **As**.
xa: **Cwg** (dry winter) → **Ganga plain**, E Rajasthan, N MP, most of NE India.
**BShw** (semi-arid steppe) → NW Gujarat, W Rajasthan, parts of Punjab.
**E / ET** (polar / tundra) → J&K, Ladakh, Himachal, Uttarakhand highlands.
**AP is Aw**.

38.s: The climate type BShw is associated with:
o: A cold humid climate with a short summer in Arunachal Pradesh
A semi-arid steppe climate in north-western Gujarat, western Rajasthan and parts of Punjab
A monsoon climate with dry summer on the Coromandel coast
A hot desert climate in extreme western Rajasthan
38.x: BShw represents a semi-arid steppe climate found in north-western Gujarat, western Rajasthan and parts of Punjab.
38.tq: Distinguish between similar Koppen climate codes by region and climate character.
xs: **BShw** is the **semi-arid steppe** climate of **NW Gujarat, W Rajasthan and parts of Punjab** — option **(2)**.
Cold humid with a short summer in Arunachal is **Dfc**; dry summer on the Coromandel coast is **As**.
Hot desert of **extreme western Rajasthan** is **BWhw**, not BShw.
xa: ⚠ **BShw** (steppe) vs **BWhw** (hot desert) — both in Rajasthan.
APPSC **G1 2024** key: short dry season → west coast; dry summer → Coromandel; dry winter → Ganga plain; steppe → NW.
**Amw** = west coast south of **Goa**; **Cwg** = **Ganga plain**.

38.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Aw — Most of the peninsula south of the Tropic of Cancer
As — Coromandel coast and Tamil Nadu
Cwg — Ganga plain, eastern Rajasthan and northern Madhya Pradesh
38.x: ET denotes a polar or tundra climate found in the highlands of Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand, not coastal Andhra Pradesh.
38.tq: Find the wrong location attached to an otherwise familiar climate code.
xs: **ET — Coastal Andhra Pradesh** is wrongly matched — option **(4)**.
**E / ET** (polar / tundra) belongs to the highlands of **J&K, Ladakh, Himachal and Uttarakhand**; **AP is Aw**.
The rest are correct: **Aw** → most of the peninsula; **As** → **Coromandel coast**; **Cwg** → **Ganga plain**, E Rajasthan, N MP.
xa: **Dfc** (cold humid winter, short summer) → **Arunachal Pradesh**.
**BWhw** (hot desert) → **extreme western Rajasthan**; **BShw** (steppe) → NW Gujarat, W Rajasthan, parts of Punjab.
**Amw** (short dry season) → **west coast south of Goa**.

38.s: The climate type Dfc is characteristic of:
o: The west coast south of Goa
38.x: Dfc denotes a cold humid climate with a short summer and is associated with Arunachal Pradesh.
38.tq: Use the distinctive climate-region association.
xs: **Dfc** — cold humid winter with a short summer — is characteristic of **Arunachal Pradesh** — option **(1)**.
West coast south of Goa is **Amw**; extreme western Rajasthan is **BWhw**; the Coromandel coast is **As**.
xa: **Cwg** covers **most of NE India** along with the Ganga plain.
**E / ET** (polar / tundra) → J&K, Ladakh, Himachal, Uttarakhand highlands.
**AP is Aw** (tropical savanna).

38.s:
Match the Koeppen climate code with its region:
a. As
b. Cwg
c. BWhw
d. Amw

i. Ganga plain
ii. Coromandel coast
iii. Extreme western Rajasthan
iv. West coast south of Goa
38.x: As (monsoon with dry summer) is the Coromandel coast; Cwg (monsoon with dry winter) is the Ganga plain; BWhw (hot desert) is extreme western Rajasthan; Amw (short dry season) is the west coast south of Goa. B swaps As and Cwg, C swaps the desert and west-coast codes, and D is wrong throughout.
38.tq: Dry summer = Coromandel (As); dry winter = Ganga plain (Cwg).
xs: Correct code **a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv** — **As → Coromandel coast (ii)**, **Cwg → Ganga plain (i)**, **BWhw → extreme western Rajasthan (iii)**, **Amw → west coast south of Goa (iv)**: option **(1)**.
**As** = monsoon with **dry summer**; **Cwg** = monsoon with **dry winter**; **BWhw** = **hot desert**; **Amw** = monsoon with **short dry season**.
Option (2) swaps As and Cwg; option (3) swaps the desert and west-coast codes.
xa: **BShw** (semi-arid steppe) → NW Gujarat, W Rajasthan, parts of Punjab.
**Dfc** → **Arunachal Pradesh**; **E / ET** → J&K, Ladakh, Himachal, Uttarakhand highlands.
This mirrors the APPSC **G1 2024** matching key.

38.s:
Consider the following statements about the National Monsoon Mission:
1. It was launched in 2012 by the Ministry of Earth Sciences.
2. It is implemented through IITM Pune and the IMD.
3. Its second phase ran from 2017 to 2030.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
38.x: Statement 1 is correct: MoES launched it in 2012. Statement 2 is correct: IITM Pune and IMD run it. Statement 3 is wrong: Phase 1 was 2012-17 and Phase 2 was 2017-25. So 1 and 2 only (B); A leaves out true statement 2, C and D include the false statement 3.
38.tq: 2012 launch, 2017 and 2025 phase ends.
xs: Statement 1 **correct**: the **National Monsoon Mission** was launched in **2012** by **MoES**.
Statement 2 **correct**: it is run through **IITM Pune** and **IMD**.
Statement 3 **wrong**: Phase 2 ran **2017-25** (Phase 1: **2012-17**).
So **1 and 2 only** — option **(2)**.
xa: Investment about **Rs 1,000 crore** (Mission + HPC) → third-party audit return **Rs 50,000 crore**.
**Mission Mausam** followed on **14 Jan 2025** (**Rs 2,000 crore**).
**IMD** is under the **Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES)**.
Models: **SEFS 2007**, **Coupled Forecasting System 2012**, **Multi-Model Ensemble 2021**.

38.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. SEFS statistical ensemble — 2007
2. Monsoon Mission Coupled Forecasting System — 2012
3. Multi-Model Ensemble — 2021
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
38.x: SEFS was associated with 2007, the Monsoon Mission Coupled Forecasting System with 2012 and the Multi-Model Ensemble with 2021.
38.tq: Match each technical model with its introduction year.
xs: All three pairs are correct — option **(4)** **1, 2 and 3**.
**SEFS** statistical ensemble — **2007**; **Monsoon Mission Coupled Forecasting System** — **2012** (dynamic ocean-atmosphere-land); **Multi-Model Ensemble** — **2021**.
xa: **Block-level model** unveiled **May 2026**: blends AI with nearly a century of data from the Kerala onset date.
**National Monsoon Mission** launched **2012** by **MoES** (**IITM Pune** + **IMD**).
**Doppler radars**: **47** now vs **14** in **2014**.
⚠ The **2026** onset forecast (26 May ± **4** days) failed — first miss since **2015**.

38.s:
Consider the following statements about Mission Mausam:
1. It was launched on 14 January 2025 along with IMD Vision 2047.
2. It is implemented by the IMD, NCMRWF and ISRO.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
38.x: Statement 1 is correct: Mission Mausam was launched on 14 January 2025 with IMD Vision 2047. Statement 2 is wrong: it is implemented by the IMD, NCMRWF and IITM, not ISRO. So 1 only (A); B and C accept the false statement 2, D rejects the true statement 1.
38.tq: Same MoES trio as always: IMD, NCMRWF, IITM.
xs: Statement 1 **correct**: **Mission Mausam** was launched on **14 Jan 2025** with **IMD Vision 2047**.
Statement 2 **wrong**: it is implemented by **IMD, NCMRWF and IITM** — not ISRO.
So **1 only** — option **(1)**.
xa: Outlay **Rs 2,000 crore**.
It built the **Bharat Forecast System** — **6 km** resolution, **10-day** rain forecasts.
IMD DG: **M. Mohapatra**; MoES Secretary: **M. Ravichandran** (Apr 2026).

38.s: The Bharat Forecast System developed under Mission Mausam provides:
o: 10 km resolution and one-year drought forecasts
26 km resolution and seasonal snowfall forecasts
1 km resolution and one-month temperature forecasts
38.x: The Bharat Forecast System provides forecasts at 6 km resolution, including 10-day rainfall forecasts.
38.tq: Match the technical system with both its resolution and forecast period.
xs: The **Bharat Forecast System** gives **6 km resolution** and **10-day rainfall forecasts** — option **(3)**.
It was built under **Mission Mausam** (launched **14 Jan 2025**).
xa: Mission Mausam: **Rs 2,000 crore**; implemented by **IMD, NCMRWF, IITM**.
**Doppler radars** rose to **47** from **14** in **2014**.
**Block-level model** (**May 2026**) blends AI with nearly a century of Kerala-onset data.

38.s: The number of Doppler weather radars in India increased from 14 in 2014 to approximately:
38.x: India had 47 Doppler weather radars, compared with 14 in 2014.
38.tq: Test a before-and-after infrastructure figure.
xs: India now has **47** Doppler weather radars, up from **14** in **2014** — option **(3)**.
The expansion sits alongside **IMD**'s modernisation under **MoES**.
xa: **Mission Mausam** (**14 Jan 2025**, **Rs 2,000 crore**) built the **Bharat Forecast System** (**6 km**, **10-day** rain forecasts).
**National Monsoon Mission** (**2012**): Phase 1 **2012-17**, Phase 2 **2017-25**.
IMD DG (Apr 2026): **M. Mohapatra**.

38.s: Ocean Mean Temperature is measured as the average temperature of the upper Indian Ocean up to the:
38.x: OMT is the average temperature of the upper Indian Ocean down to the 26°C isotherm.
38.tq: Recall the defining threshold of a specialised ocean indicator.
xs: **Ocean Mean Temperature (OMT)** is the average temperature of the upper Indian Ocean down to the **26°C isotherm** — option **(4)**.
It is measured in **Jan-Mar** and predicts monsoon rain better than **SST**.
xa: **Mascarene High**: permanent high near **Madagascar** driving the **cross-equatorial flow**.
**Somali jet** + **Somalia current** intensify monsoon winds.

38.s: Which statement about Ocean Mean Temperature is correct?
o: It is measured in January-March and predicts monsoon rainfall better than SST.
It is measured in June-September and is less useful than SST for monsoon prediction.
It is measured only in October and predicts snowfall in the Himalayas.
It refers to the temperature of the entire Indian Ocean basin throughout the year.
38.x: OMT is measured during January-March and has been identified as a better predictor of monsoon rainfall than sea-surface temperature.
38.tq: Distinguish a specialised indicator from the related SST concept.
xs: **OMT** is measured in **January-March** and **predicts monsoon rainfall better than SST** — option **(1)**.
It covers only the **upper** Indian Ocean down to the **26 deg C isotherm**, not the whole basin all year.
xa: **Dust aerosols** heat the mid-troposphere over the **Indo-Gangetic plain** → help pull the monsoon inland.
**Breaks**: the trough shifts to the Himalayan foothills — plains dry, hills get heavy rain.

38.s: In 2026, the southwest monsoon set in over Kerala on
38.x: In 2026, the monsoon reached Kerala on 4 June, which was three days later than the normal date.
38.tq: Distinguish the Kerala onset date from the later Andhra Pradesh onset date.
xs: In **2026** the monsoon set in over Kerala on **4 June** — option **(1)** — **three days late** under a strengthening **El Nino**.
**1 June** is the normal Kerala onset date; **6 June** is when it reached **AP**.
xa: **17 of 28** AP districts were deficient by **14 June**.
The onset forecast (26 May ± **4** days) failed — first miss since **2015**.
Normally **A&N Islands ~25 May**, then **Kerala ~1 June**; full coverage by **8 July** (revised normal).

38.s: Which phenomenon was being watched in 2026 as a possible offset to El Nino's adverse influence on the Indian monsoon?
38.x: The Indian Ocean Dipole was being monitored as a possible offset to the influence of El Nino.
38.tq: Identify the associated climate oscillation rather than a general atmospheric circulation feature.
xs: The **Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD)** was watched as a possible offset to **El Nino** in 2026 — option **(4)**.
A **positive IOD** can offset El Nino, which **weakens** the monsoon.
**La Nina** strengthens the monsoon but was not the 2026 offset; **western disturbances** bring winter rain to NW India.
xa: WMO gave ~**80%** chance of El Nino in Jul-Aug; a **"Super El Nino"** year was feared.
An unfavourable **MJO** phase stalls the monsoon.
IMD forecast ~**90% of LPA**; June deficit **43%**.

38.s:
With reference to the 2026 monsoon forecast, consider the following statements:
1. The IMD forecast was about 90% of the long-period average.
2. A June rainfall deficit of 43% led the Centre to activate contingency plans.
3. The forecast was issued in the absence of any El Nino concern.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
38.x: The forecast was about 90% of the long-period average, and the 43% June deficit led to contingency planning. Statement 3 is false because a developing super El Nino was a concern.
38.tq: Reject the statement that reverses the reported climate concern.
xs: Statement 1 **correct**: IMD forecast about **90% of LPA**.
Statement 2 **correct**: the **43%** June deficit made the Centre activate **contingency plans**.
Statement 3 **wrong**: a strengthening **El Nino** (feared **"Super El Nino"**) was the key concern.
So **1 and 2 only** — option **(1)**.
xa: April forecast was **92% of LPA** — first "below normal" April forecast in **11 years**.
**August 2026** was the hottest August; four Bay lows lasted **26 days** (normal **16.3**).
Onset over Kerala on **4 June**, **3** days late.

38.s: The rainfall deficit in Andhra Pradesh during 1 June–25 August 2026 was reported as
38.x: Andhra Pradesh recorded a 51.2% rainfall deficit during 1 June–25 August 2026.
38.tq: Match the percentage with its period and geographical unit before considering district figures.
xs: AP's rainfall deficit for **1 Jun-25 Aug 2026** was **51.2 percent** — option **(2)**; **all 28 districts** were deficient.
**43%** was the all-India **June** deficit; **67.5%** was **Prakasam** and **75.9%** **Annamayya**.
xa: Worst districts: **Annamayya 75.9%**, **Prakasam 67.5%**, **Chittoor 65%**.
All **seven** Bay systems formed at the head of the Bay.
**Kurnool** promoted **pre-monsoon dry sowing** on **92,000** acres.

38.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched with respect to rainfall extremes in Andhra Pradesh?
o: Sileru-Sabari valleys — 140–152 cm; Hagari valley — less than 51 cm
Sileru-Sabari valleys — less than 51 cm; Hagari valley — 140–152 cm
Sileru-Sabari valleys — about 966 cm; Hagari valley — 75.9 cm
Sileru-Sabari valleys — 51–75 cm; Hagari valley — 90–100 cm
38.x: The Sileru-Sabari valleys are the wettest parts of Andhra Pradesh, receiving about 140–152 cm, while the Hagari valley is the driest, receiving less than 51 cm.
38.tq: Use the wettest–driest contrast and verify both the region and range.
xs: Wettest **Sileru-Sabari valleys** get **140-152 cm**; driest **Hagari valley** gets **less than 51 cm** — option **(1)**.
Option (2) reverses them; **75.9** is Annamayya's **2026 deficit %**, not a rainfall figure.
xa: **Hagari valley** lies in the **Rayalaseema rain-shadow**.
Temperature extremes: hottest **Rentachintala** (Palnadu); coolest **Lambasingi**.
India's wettest: **Mawsynram** (~**1,187 cm**); driest: **Ruyli** (Jaisalmer, ~**8.33 cm**).

38.s: In Andhra Pradesh, the hottest and the coolest places are respectively
38.x: Rentachintala (Palnadu) is the hottest place in AP and Lambasingi the coolest. Option A reverses them; the Hagari and Sileru valleys are AP's rainfall extremes (driest and wettest), not temperature extremes, and Antarvedi is the Godavari's mouth.
38.tq: Hot Rentachintala, cool Lambasingi.
xs: AP's hottest place is **Rentachintala** (Palnadu) and coolest **Lambasingi** — option **(2)**.
Option (1) reverses them; **Hagari** and **Sileru** valleys are AP's **rainfall** extremes (driest and wettest).
xa: **Sileru-Sabari** valleys: **140-152 cm**; **Hagari**: **<51 cm**.
**AP climate: Aw**; gets both SW and NE monsoons.
India's record heat: **Ganganagar** (Rajasthan) ~**50°C** in **1935**.

39.s: Which of the following correctly represents the east-to-west decrease of rainfall across the northern plains?
39.x: Rainfall decreases eastward to westward across the northern plains in the sequence Kolkata, Patna, Prayagraj, Delhi and Bikaner.
39.tq: Read the spatial gradient as a directional sequence rather than a time sequence.
xs: Rainfall across the northern plains decreases east to west: **Kolkata > Patna > Prayagraj > Delhi > Bikaner** — option **(2)**.
**Kolkata** in the east is wettest; **Bikaner** in the Thar is driest.
Option (3) is the reverse (west-to-east increase order); options (1) and (4) break the sequence.
xa: In the **peninsula** rainfall decreases **west to east** because of the Western Ghats' **rain-shadow**.
Monsoon lasts **< 75 days** in **western Rajasthan** vs **> 120 days** in the **south-west peninsula**.
**High CV (> 50%)**: western Rajasthan, Kutch, Ladakh.

39.s: The broad pattern of rainfall distribution across the northern plains and the peninsular region is respectively
o: from east to west and from west to east
uniform from east to west and from west to east
from west to east and from east to west
from north to south and from south to north
39.x: Rainfall decreases from east to west along the northern plains, while across the peninsula it generally decreases from west to east.
39.tq: Compare the two directional trends without reversing their order.
xs: Rainfall decreases **from east to west** in the **northern plains** and **from west to east** in the **peninsula** — option **(1)**.
Northern plains: **Kolkata > Patna > Prayagraj > Delhi > Bikaner**.
Peninsula: the east lies in the **rain-shadow** of the Western Ghats.
Option (3) reverses both; rainfall is not uniform.
xa: **Low CV (< 25%)**: west coast, Western Ghats, NE, eastern peninsula.
**Rain-shadow Deccan** is a chronic **drought** region.
Monsoon duration: **< 75 days** (W Rajasthan) to **> 120 days** (SW peninsula).

39.s: The south-west monsoon lasts less than 75 days in ____ and more than 120 days in ____.
39.x: The monsoon lasts less than 75 days in western Rajasthan, where it arrives late and leaves early, and more than 120 days in the south-west peninsula, where it arrives first. Option B reverses the two; the others name regions that do not mark these limits.
39.tq: <75 days W Rajasthan; >120 days SW peninsula.
xs: The SW monsoon lasts **less than 75 days** in **western Rajasthan** and **more than 120 days** in the **south-west peninsula** — option **(1)**.
Option (2) reverses the two regions.
xa: **Western Rajasthan** also has **high rainfall variability (CV > 50%)**.
Onset and withdrawal dates show **large inter-annual variability**.
**Western India — Rajasthan, Gujarat** is chronically **drought**-prone (PYQ 2025).

39.s: Which of the following regions generally have a high coefficient of variation of rainfall, above 50 percent?
39.x: Western Rajasthan, Kutch and Ladakh generally have a high rainfall coefficient of variation above 50 percent. The west coast, Western Ghats, north-east and eastern peninsula generally have low variability below 25 percent.
39.tq: Separate high-variability dry regions from low-variability humid regions.
xs: **Western Rajasthan, Kutch and Ladakh** have a **high CV (> 50%)** — option **(2)**.
The **west coast, Western Ghats, NE** and **eastern peninsula** have **low CV (< 25%)** — so options (3) and (4) are wrong.
xa: **CV = (standard deviation / mean) x 100**; higher CV = less dependable rain.
Low-rainfall areas tend to have high variability; high-rainfall areas low variability.
Chronic drought: **Rajasthan, Gujarat**, rain-shadow Deccan, **Rayalaseema** and south **Prakasam**.

39.s: Which statement about Indian rainfall variability is correct?
o: Only the withdrawal date varies, while onset is fixed
The onset and withdrawal dates are fixed every year
Only the onset date varies, while withdrawal is fixed
The dates of monsoon onset and withdrawal show large inter-annual variability
39.x: There is large inter-annual variability in both the onset and withdrawal dates of the monsoon.
39.tq: Watch for reversed or exclusive wording when two linked dates are involved.
xs: Both monsoon **onset and withdrawal** dates show **large inter-annual variability** — option **(4)**.
So neither date is fixed — options (1), (2) and (3) are wrong.
xa: Variability is measured by **CV = (standard deviation / mean) x 100**.
**Low CV (< 25%)**: west coast, Western Ghats, NE, eastern peninsula; **high CV (> 50%)**: W Rajasthan, Kutch, Ladakh.
**6 of 10** El Nino years brought weak Indian monsoons.

39.s: A district records rainfall 65 percent above its normal rainfall. Under the IMD departure classification, it would be placed in which category?
39.x: Rainfall departure of +60 percent or more is classified as large excess for a state or district. The separate all-India season categories use different percentage bands.
39.tq: Apply the correct state or district departure band rather than the all-India seasonal band.
xs: **+65%** falls in **+60% or more**, so the district is **large excess** — option **(1)**.
**"Above normal"** is an all-India season band (**105-110%** of LPA), not a district category.
xa: **Deficient**: **-20% to -59%**; **large deficient**: **-60% to -99%**.
⚠ District "normal" = **-19% to +19%**; all-India "normal" = **96-104%** of LPA.

39.s: Which of the following correctly represents the IMD rainfall departure bands for a state or district?
o: Large excess: +50% or more; Excess: +10% to +49%; Normal: 0% to +20%
Large excess: +60% or more; Excess: +20% to +59%; Normal: -19% to +19%
Large excess: above +110%; Excess: +60% to +100%; Normal: -20% to +20%
Large excess: -60% to -99%; Excess: -20% to -59%; Normal: -19% to +19%
39.x: For a state or district, large excess is +60 percent or more, excess is +20 to +59 percent, and normal is -19 to +19 percent. Deficient is -20 to -59 percent and large deficient is -60 to -99 percent.
39.tq: Compare adjacent departure bands and detect reversed positive and negative ranges.
xs: State/district bands: **large excess +60% or more**, **excess +20% to +59%**, **normal -19% to +19%** — option **(2)**.
Option (4) gives the minus bands, which are **deficient (-20% to -59%)** and **large deficient (-60% to -99%)**.
**Above 110%** is the all-India **excess** band (% of LPA), not a district departure.
xa: All-India: deficient **< 90%**, below normal **90-95%**, normal **96-104%**, above normal **105-110%**, excess **> 110%**.
**2015**: actual rain **86%** of LPA — one of the worst droughts.

39.s: For the all-India season, rainfall below 90 percent of the Long Period Average is classified as:
39.x: For the all-India season, rainfall below 90 percent of the LPA is classified as deficient. Below normal is 90–95 percent, normal is 96–104 percent, above normal is 105–110 percent and excess is above 110 percent.
39.tq: Keep the all-India seasonal classification separate from state and district departure categories.
xs: All-India season rainfall **below 90%** of LPA is **deficient** — option **(1)**.
**"Large deficient"** is a state/district category (**-60% to -99%**), not an all-India band.
xa: **Above normal** = **105-110%**; **excess** = **> 110%** of LPA.
**2015** got **86%** of LPA — a deficient year, one of the worst droughts.

39.s: The coefficient of variation (CV) used to measure rainfall variability is calculated as
39.x: CV = (standard deviation / mean) x 100. Option A inverts the ratio, and the range or mean deviation are other measures of spread. A higher CV means more variable rainfall, as in western Rajasthan (>50%).
39.tq: CV = SD/mean x 100; high CV = unreliable rain.
xs: **CV = (standard deviation / mean) x 100** — option **(2)**.
Option (1) inverts the ratio; range and mean deviation are not used in the CV.
