xa: **Low CV (< 25%)**: west coast, Western Ghats, NE, eastern peninsula.
**High CV (> 50%)**: western Rajasthan, Kutch, Ladakh.
Onset and withdrawal dates also show large inter-annual variability.

39.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. El Niño is identified when the central/east equatorial Pacific is at least 0.5°C warmer for five consecutive overlapping 3-month periods.
2. Every El Niño year has produced a weak Indian monsoon.
3. A positive Indian Ocean Dipole can offset the effect of El Niño.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
39.x: Statement 1 is correct: that is the stated El Niño threshold. Statement 2 is wrong: only about 6 of 10 El Niño years brought weak Indian monsoons. Statement 3 is correct: a positive IOD can offset El Niño. So 1 and 3 only (B); A leaves out true statement 3, C and D include the false statement 2.
39.tq: 'Every' / 'always' with El Niño is a trap - it is 6 out of 10.
xs: Statement 1 **correct**: El Nino = central/east equatorial Pacific at least **0.5°C** warmer for **five consecutive overlapping 3-month periods**.
Statement 2 **wrong**: only **6 of 10** El Nino years brought weak Indian monsoons.
Statement 3 **correct**: a **positive IOD** can offset El Nino.
So **1 and 3 only** — option **(2)**.
xa: ⚠ **El Nino weakens**, **La Nina strengthens** the monsoon.
La Nina also brings colder winters and more **Bay cyclones**.
**2023** was deficient under the **2023-24 El Nino**.

39.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. La Niña generally strengthens the Indian monsoon.
2. La Niña is associated with colder winters.
3. La Niña can bring more Bay of Bengal cyclones.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
39.x: La Niña generally strengthens the monsoon and is associated with colder winters and more Bay of Bengal cyclones. All three statements are correct.
39.tq: Test the complete set of effects associated with La Niña.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4)** **1, 2 and 3**.
**La Nina** generally **strengthens the monsoon**, brings **colder winters** and **more Bay cyclones**.
xa: **El Nino** weakens the monsoon: **6 of 10** El Nino years → weak Indian monsoons.
A **positive IOD** can offset El Nino.
El Nino threshold: at least **0.5°C** warmer for **five** overlapping 3-month periods.

39.s: Which pair of years is cited as deficient southwest monsoon years in the stated rainfall record?
39.x: The cited deficient years are 2015, when actual rainfall was 86 percent of LPA, and 2023, associated with the 2023–24 El Niño.
39.tq: Link the years with the deficient-rainfall description instead of inferring from a general climate cycle.
xs: The cited deficient years are **2015 and 2023** — option **(2)**.
**2015**: actual rain **86%** of LPA — one of the worst droughts.
**2023**: linked to the **2023-24 El Nino**.
xa: All-India **deficient** = **< 90%** of LPA.
**6 of 10** El Nino years → weak Indian monsoons.
AP had a **-16.5%** deficit in **2023-24**.

39.s: About what proportion of India’s agricultural or cultivable land is drought-prone in varying degrees?
39.x: About 68 percent of India’s agricultural or cultivable land is drought-prone in varying degrees.
39.tq: Use the numerical figure directly and distinguish cultivable land from total geographical area.
xs: About **68 percent** of India's agricultural (cultivable) land is **drought-prone** in varying degrees — option **(4)** (PYQ 2023 key).
⚠ The flood figure is different: **~12%** of India's land is prone to floods and river erosion.
xa: Chronic drought: **Rajasthan, Gujarat**, rain-shadow Deccan, **Rayalaseema** and south **Prakasam**.
Drought types: **meteorological** (rain), **agricultural** (soil moisture), **hydrological** (river/groundwater), **flash** (sudden heat + no rain).
Declaration: **Manual for Drought Management** (**2016**, revised **2020**).

39.s:
Which of the following regions are identified as chronically drought-prone?
1. Western Rajasthan and Gujarat
2. The rain-shadow Deccan
3. Rayalaseema and southern Prakasam
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
39.x: Chronic drought-prone regions include western Rajasthan, Gujarat, the rain-shadow Deccan, Rayalaseema and southern Prakasam. In Rayalaseema and southern Prakasam, failure of the north-east monsoon and groundwater depletion contribute to chronic drought.
39.tq: Combine the national and Andhra Pradesh examples before selecting the inclusive code.
xs: All three are chronically drought-prone — option **(4)** **1, 2 and 3**.
**Western India — Rajasthan, Gujarat** (PYQ 2025); the **rain-shadow Deccan**; AP's **Rayalaseema** and south **Prakasam**.
In Rayalaseema and south Prakasam the causes are **NE monsoon failure** and **groundwater depletion**.
xa: About **68%** of India's cultivable land is drought-prone.
**Kurnool** promoted **Pre-Monsoon Dry Sowing** on **92,000** acres (Jul 2026).
**High CV (> 50%)** in western Rajasthan, Kutch, Ladakh.

39.s:
Consider the following pairs (type of drought : basis):
1. Meteorological drought : rainfall deficit
2. Agricultural drought : river flow and groundwater levels
3. Flash drought : sudden heat with no rain
Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched?
39.x: Pair 1 is correct: meteorological drought = rain deficit. Pair 2 is wrong: agricultural drought is about soil moisture; river and groundwater define hydrological drought. Pair 3 is correct: flash drought = sudden heat plus no rain. So 1 and 3 only (B); A leaves out pair 3, C and D include the wrong pair 2.
39.tq: Meteorological-rain, agricultural-soil, hydrological-water bodies.
xs: Pair 1 **correct**: **meteorological** drought = **rain deficit**.
Pair 2 **wrong**: **agricultural** drought is about **soil moisture**; river/groundwater defines **hydrological** drought.
Pair 3 **correct**: **flash drought** = **sudden heat + no rain**.
So **1 and 3 only** — option **(2)**.
xa: About **68%** of cultivable land is drought-prone.
Declaration under the **Manual for Drought Management** (**2016**, revised **2020**).
Chronic drought in AP: **Rayalaseema** and south **Prakasam**.

39.s: The Manual for Drought Management, 2016, revised in 2020, uses which combination of indicators for drought declaration?
o: Rainfall deficit, vegetation, soil moisture and water indicators
Cloud cover, humidity, pressure and sunshine duration only
River length, crop export, population and forest area
Temperature, latitude, altitude and wind speed only
39.x: The Manual for Drought Management uses rainfall deficit, vegetation, soil moisture and water indicators for declaring drought. Exact current trigger thresholds are not specified here.
39.tq: Identify the responsible indicators instead of assuming rainfall alone determines declaration.
xs: The Manual uses **rainfall deficit, vegetation, soil moisture and water indicators** — option **(1)**.
These match the drought types: **meteorological** (rain), **agricultural** (soil moisture), **hydrological** (river/groundwater).
Cloud cover, latitude or population are not its declaration indicators.
xa: Manual for Drought Management: **2016**, revised **2020**.
**Flash drought** = sudden heat + no rain.
About **68%** of India's cultivable land is drought-prone.

39.s: Approximately what share of India’s land is prone to floods and river erosion?
39.x: Approximately 12 percent of India’s land is prone to floods and river erosion.
39.tq: Recall the area proportion and distinguish it from drought-prone cultivable land.
xs: About **12 percent** of India's land is prone to **floods and river erosion** — option **(2)** (NIDM Annual Report **2023-24**; PYQ 2025).
⚠ Do not confuse with **68%** — the share of cultivable land that is **drought**-prone.
xa: Worst flood areas: **Brahmaputra** valley, **Kosi** and Ganga plains, coastal deltas.
Mitigation: **embankments**, drainage channels, sea dykes, real-time flood forecasting.
**37,760 sq km** of flood-prone area protected in **West Bengal**.

39.s:
Which of the following areas are among the worst affected by floods in India?
1. Brahmaputra valley
2. Kosi and Ganga plains of Bihar and Uttar Pradesh
3. Coastal deltas of the Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri, Odisha and West Bengal
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
39.x: The Brahmaputra valley, the Kosi and Ganga plains, and several eastern and southern coastal deltas are major flood-affected areas. The Brahmaputra valley is popularly associated with the ‘sorrow of Assam’.
39.tq: Group the major flood basins and deltas without omitting the Himalayan valley.
xs: All three are among the worst flood-hit areas — option **(4)** **1, 2 and 3**.
**Brahmaputra** valley ("**sorrow of Assam**"); **Kosi** and Ganga plains (Bihar, UP); coastal deltas of **Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri**, Odisha and WB.
The deltas are hit by **Andaman Sea depressions**.
xa: About **12%** of India's land is flood-prone (NIDM **2023-24**).
Himalayan rivers swell in the monsoon; **cloudburst** flash floods are rising in the Himalaya and NE.
**37,760 sq km** of flood-prone area protected in West Bengal.

39.s: Which one of the following is NOT a flood-mitigation measure identified for flood-prone areas?
o: Complete removal of all river channels
39.x: Embankments, drainage channels, sea dykes and real-time flood forecasting are recognised mitigation measures. Complete removal of river channels is not a flood-mitigation measure.
39.tq: Find the option that is not a practical mitigation measure among the listed interventions.
xs: **Complete removal of all river channels** is not a flood-mitigation measure — option **(3)**.
Listed measures: **embankments**, **drainage channels**, **sea dykes** and **real-time flood forecasting**.
xa: e.g. **37,760 sq km** flood-prone area protected in **West Bengal**.
About **12%** of India's land is prone to floods and river erosion.
**Brahmaputra** valley = "**sorrow of Assam**".

39.s: Why do Himalayan rivers frequently cause floods during the monsoon season?
o: They are unaffected by intense rainfall events
They flow only through desert regions
They swell during the monsoon, while cloudburst flash floods are also increasing in the Himalaya and the north-east
They receive no monsoon rainfall but are fed only by groundwater
39.x: Himalayan rivers swell during the monsoon, and cloudburst-induced flash floods are increasing in the Himalaya and the north-east.
39.tq: Connect the physical cause with the resulting flood hazard.
xs: Himalayan rivers **swell during the monsoon**, and **cloudburst flash floods** are increasing in the **Himalaya and the north-east** — option **(3)**.
They are rain-fed in the monsoon, not desert rivers or groundwater-only.
xa: Worst flood zones: **Brahmaputra** valley, **Kosi** and Ganga plains of Bihar and UP.
About **12%** of India's land is flood-prone.
Mitigation includes **real-time flood forecasting** and **embankments**.

39.s:
Consider the following statements regarding rainfall deficiency reported by 16 September 2026:
1. Meghalaya recorded the highest rainfall deficiency among the regions mentioned.
2. Manipur recorded a rainfall deficiency of 43 per cent.
3. Andhra Pradesh recorded a rainfall deficiency of 42 per cent and was the third worst-affected region.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
39.x: All three statements are correct. Meghalaya recorded the worst deficiency at 59 per cent, Manipur recorded 43 per cent deficiency, and Andhra Pradesh recorded 42 per cent deficiency, ranking third worst.
39.tq: Check each percentage independently before selecting the coded combination.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4)** **1, 2 and 3**.
**Meghalaya -59%** was the worst; **Manipur -43%**; **AP -42%** was third worst (**255.3 mm** vs **442.3 mm** normal) — by **16 Sep 2026**.
xa: **17 of 36** States/UTs were normal; **16** deficient; **2** excess; **1** large excess.
District **deficient** band = **-20% to -59%**.

39.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the broad rainfall pattern of Andhra Pradesh?
o: The State receives about 278.7 mm of average annual rainfall, with almost all rainfall from the Northeast Monsoon.
The State receives about 681.6 mm of average annual rainfall, divided equally between the two monsoons.
The State receives about 966 mm of average annual rainfall, of which the Southwest Monsoon contributes about two-thirds and the Northeast Monsoon about one-third.
The State receives about 966 mm of average annual rainfall, of which the Northeast Monsoon contributes about two-thirds and the Southwest Monsoon about one-third.
39.x: Andhra Pradesh has an average annual rainfall of about 966 mm. Approximately two-thirds is received from the Southwest Monsoon and one-third from the Northeast Monsoon.
39.tq: Use the relative-share comparison to distinguish the dominant monsoon from the subordinate one.
xs: AP gets about **966 mm** a year, **Southwest Monsoon about two-thirds**, **Northeast Monsoon about one-third** — option **(3)**.
Option (4) reverses the shares; **278.7 mm** and **681.6 mm** are the **2024-25** NE and SW figures, not the average.
xa: That followed a **-16.5%** deficit in **2023-24**.
Highest rain: **Sileru-Sabari valleys** (**140-152 cm**).

39.s: The highest rainfall in Andhra Pradesh, ranging from approximately 140 to 152 cm, is associated with which of the following areas?
39.x: The highest rainfall in Andhra Pradesh occurs in the Sileru–Sabari valleys, where it ranges from about 140 to 152 cm.
39.tq: Identify the precise geographical location linked with the stated rainfall range.
xs: AP's highest rainfall, about **140-152 cm**, is in the **Sileru-Sabari valleys** — option **(1)**.
**Kurnool** is an interior Rayalaseema district, not a coastal plain; Rayalaseema is AP's chronic **drought** zone.
xa: **Rayalaseema** and south **Prakasam**: NE monsoon failure + groundwater depletion.
By **16 Sep 2026** AP was **-42%** (third worst).

40.s: The classification of Indian forest types associated with H.G. Champion and G.S. Puri comprises how many major types and sub-types?
40.x: The classification associated with H.G. Champion and G.S. Puri recognises 5 major types and 15 sub-types.
40.tq: Directly distinguish the paired numerical classification figures.
xs: **H.G. Champion and G.S. Puri** classify Indian forests into **5 major types and 15 sub-types** — option **(2)**.
The 5 major types: **Moist Tropical, Dry Tropical, Montane Subtropical, Montane Temperate, Alpine**.
xa: Most widespread: **tropical deciduous** forests = **65.6%** of forest area (PYQ G2 2025).
Single largest type: **moist deciduous 37%**; second **dry deciduous 28.6%**.
Tallest trees: **tropical wet evergreen** (> **45 m**).

40.s: Which one of the following forest types is correctly matched with its characteristic rainfall?
o: Tropical wet evergreen — less than 25 cm
40.x: Tropical thorn forests occur in areas receiving about 25–75 cm of rainfall. Wet evergreen forests require more than 250 cm, semi-evergreen forests 200–250 cm, and dry deciduous forests 75–100 cm.
40.tq: Use the rainfall range to eliminate reversed forest-type pairs.
xs: **Tropical thorn — 25-75 cm** is correctly matched — option **(3)**.
**Wet evergreen** needs **> 250 cm** (not < 25 cm); **moist deciduous** is **100-200 cm** (200-250 cm is **semi-evergreen**).
**Dry deciduous** gets **75-100 cm**, not > 250 cm.
xa: **Desert vegetation** (xerophytes) grows below **25 cm** — western Rajasthan, adjoining Punjab/Gujarat.
Thorn forests: **Rajasthan, Gujarat, Rayalaseema**; species **Acacia, Ziziphus, Prosopis, babul**, cacti.
⚠ Rainfall ladder: thorn **25-75** → dry deciduous **75-100** → moist deciduous **100-200** → semi-evergreen **200-250** → evergreen **> 250 cm**.

40.s:
Consider the following statements regarding tropical wet evergreen forests:
1. They generally occur in areas receiving more than 250 cm of rainfall.
2. They are found in parts of the Western Ghats and North-Eastern India.
3. They account for approximately 37% of India’s forest area.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
40.x: Tropical wet evergreen forests require more than 250 cm of rainfall and occur in the Western Ghats, Assam, Meghalaya, Manipur, Tripura, Nagaland and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Their share is about 8%, not 37%.
40.tq: Identify the false percentage while retaining the correct distribution statements.
xs: Statement 1 **correct**: wet evergreen forests need **> 250 cm** rain.
Statement 2 **correct**: they occur in the **Western Ghats**, Assam, Meghalaya, Manipur, Tripura, Nagaland and **A&N**.
Statement 3 **wrong**: their share is **~8%**; **37%** is **moist deciduous**.
So **1 and 2 only** — option **(1)**.
xa: Species: **rosewood, ebony, mahogany** (PYQ 2023), gurjan, ironwood.
Tallest trees of India's forests: > **45 m**.
**Semi-evergreen** (**200-250 cm**) fringes the evergreen belts, **4.1%** of forest area.

40.s: Which of the following groups contains only important species of tropical wet evergreen forests in India?
40.x: Rosewood, ebony, mahogany, gurjan and ironwood are among the important species of tropical wet evergreen forests.
40.tq: Group species by the forest type in which they naturally occur.
xs: **Rosewood, ebony, mahogany and ironwood** are wet evergreen species — option **(4)**.
**Teak, sal, arjun, mahua** = **moist deciduous**; **juniper, birch, fir, rhododendron** = **Himalayan sub-alpine/alpine**; **Acacia, babul, Prosopis, Ziziphus** = **thorn** forests.
xa: Wet evergreen also has **gurjan, jamun** and **canes** (PYQ 2023 asked rosewood-ebony-mahogany).
Rainfall **> 250 cm**; share **~8%** (51,249 sq km).
Found in **Western Ghats**, NE states and **A&N**.

40.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below the lists:

List-I (Forest type)
a. Moist deciduous
b. Dry deciduous
c. Thorn

d. Littoral or tidal

List-II (Characteristic species)
i. Rhizophora and Avicennia
ii. Teak, sal and mahua
iii. Acacia, Ziziphus and Prosopis
iv. Teak, sandalwood and Terminalia

Codes:
40.x: Moist deciduous forests include teak, sal and mahua; dry deciduous forests include teak, sandalwood and Terminalia; thorn forests include Acacia, Ziziphus and Prosopis; tidal forests include Rhizophora and Avicennia.
40.tq: Start from the sure mangrove pair and complete the species associations.
xs: Correct code **a–ii, b–iv, c–iii, d–i** — option **(1)**.
**Moist deciduous → teak, sal, mahua**; **dry deciduous → teak, sandalwood, Terminalia**; **thorn → Acacia, Ziziphus, Prosopis**; **littoral/tidal → Rhizophora, Avicennia**.
xa: ⚠ **Teak** occurs in both moist and dry deciduous forests; **sal** marks moist deciduous, **sandalwood** dry deciduous (south).
Mangroves also have **Sonneratia**; Sundarbans has the **Sundari** tree.
Dry deciduous also has **red sanders** (AP).

40.s:
Consider the following statements about the distribution of natural vegetation in India:
1. Dry deciduous forests of Andhra Pradesh are associated with the Nallamala and Eastern Ghats.
2. Tropical thorn forests occur in Rajasthan, Gujarat and Rayalaseema.
3. Desert (xerophytic) vegetation is found in areas receiving 25-75 cm of rainfall.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
40.x: Statement 1 is correct: AP's dry deciduous forests lie in the Nallamala and Eastern Ghats. Statement 2 is correct: thorn forests occur in Rajasthan, Gujarat and Rayalaseema. Statement 3 is wrong: desert vegetation occurs below 25 cm; 25-75 cm is the thorn-forest range. So '1 only' misses statement 2, and '2 and 3 only' and '1, 2 and 3' wrongly include statement 3.
40.tq: Thorn = 25-75 cm; desert = below 25 cm.
xs: Statement 1 **correct**: AP's **dry deciduous** forests lie in the **Nallamala** and **Eastern Ghats**.
Statement 2 **correct**: **thorn** forests occur in **Rajasthan, Gujarat, Rayalaseema**.
Statement 3 **wrong**: desert vegetation grows below **25 cm**; **25-75 cm** is the **thorn** range.
So **1 and 2 only** — option **(2)**.
xa: Desert vegetation = **xerophytes** of western Rajasthan; **date palms** in oases.
**Nallamala** = AP's biggest forest; AP is mainly **dry deciduous**.
Dry deciduous = **28.6%** of India's forest area.

40.s: Shola forests are best described as:
o: Temperate forests of the Nilgiris, Anaimalai and Palani hills
Alpine meadows above the Himalayan tree line
Tropical thorn forests of the north-western plains
40.x: Sholas are temperate forest formations of the Nilgiris, Anaimalai and Palani hills, generally occurring as stunted evergreen patches with grasslands in the Western Ghats.
40.tq: Discriminate the regional meaning of the term ‘Shola’ from alpine and mangrove formations.
xs: **Sholas** are the **temperate forests of the Nilgiris, Anaimalai and Palani hills** — option **(1)** (PYQ G1 2024).
They are **stunted evergreen** patches with **grassland** in the Western Ghats — not alpine, thorn or mangrove.
xa: Montane wet temperate (shola) forests need high hill rainfall.
**Alpine** meadows lie above the Himalayan tree line, up to **4,750 m**.
**Mangroves** grow on tidal coasts — deltas, creeks, **A&N**.

40.s:
Consider the following statements about alpine vegetation in India:
1. It occurs above the tree line in the Himalaya.
2. Alpine meadows may extend up to about 4,750 metres.
3. It is principally a tidal-coast formation.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
40.x: Alpine vegetation occurs above the tree line in the Himalaya, and alpine meadows may extend up to about 4,750 metres. It is not a tidal-coast formation.
40.tq: Reject the geographically incompatible statement.
xs: Statement 1 **correct**: alpine vegetation occurs **above the tree line** in the **Himalaya**.
Statement 2 **correct**: alpine meadows extend up to about **4,750 m**.
Statement 3 **wrong**: tidal coasts carry **littoral/mangrove** forests.
So **1 and 2 only** — option **(2)**.
xa: Local names: **Bugyals** (Uttarakhand), **Margs** (Kashmir).
Alpine meadows zone: **2,900-6,000 m**; **dry alpine scrub** (juniper) above **4,000 m**.
**Deschampsia-Deyeuxia** grasses grow in the **alpine** region.

40.s:
Arrange the following forest types in descending order of their share in India’s forest area:
A. Tropical dry deciduous
B. Tropical wet evergreen
C. Tropical moist deciduous
40.x: Tropical moist deciduous forests account for about 37%, tropical dry deciduous forests about 28.6%, and tropical wet evergreen forests about 8%.
40.tq: Rank the categories by percentage before selecting the sequence.
xs: Descending share: **moist deciduous (37%) > dry deciduous (28.6%) > wet evergreen (~8%)** — **C, A, B**, option **(1)**.
Moist and dry **deciduous** together make the tropical deciduous forests, the **most widespread** type; **wet evergreen** forests are much smaller.
xa: ⚠ 37% + 28.6% = **65.6%** — tropical deciduous forests together.
Moist deciduous ~**2,36,794 sq km**; dry deciduous ~**1,86,620 sq km**.
**Semi-evergreen** = **4.1%**.

40.s: The tropical deciduous forests of India together account for approximately what share of the country’s forest area?
40.x: Tropical moist deciduous and tropical dry deciduous forests together account for approximately 65.6% of India’s forest area.
40.tq: Add the two deciduous forest shares rather than selecting the larger individual category.
xs: **Tropical deciduous (monsoon) forests** together cover **65.6%** of India's forest area — option **(3)**.
**Moist deciduous 37%** + **dry deciduous 28.6%** = 65.6%; so **37.0%** is only the moist type.
xa: They are the **most widespread** forests (PYQ G2 2025).
Moist deciduous: **teak, sal**, sandalwood, arjun, mahua (**100-200 cm**).
Dry deciduous (**75-100 cm**) is the forest **most vulnerable to fire**.

40.s: Tidal forests in India are found not only in deltaic and creek regions but also in the:
40.x: Tidal or mangrove forests occur in deltas and creeks and also in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
40.tq: Use the coastal-island association to identify the additional distribution area.
xs: Besides deltas and creeks, **tidal forests** occur in the **Andaman and Nicobar Islands** — option **(2)** (PYQ 2025).
Lakshadweep, the **Aravallis** and **Ladakh** are not listed for tidal forests.
xa: Features: **stilt and knee roots**; submerged at high tide.
Largest mangrove: **Sundarbans** (West Bengal).
Older shares: **WB 50%**, **Gujarat 21%**, **A&N 14%** of India's mangroves.

40.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched with its Himalayan altitude zone?
40.x: Sub-tropical chir pine occurs around 1,000–1,800 metres. Moist temperate forests occur around 1,500–3,000 metres, alpine meadows around 2,900–6,000 metres, and dry alpine scrub above 4,000 metres.
40.tq: Match the vegetation zone with its altitude range without reversing the sequence.
xs: **Sub-tropical chir pine — 1,000-1,800 m** is correct — option **(3)**.
**Moist temperate** forests lie at **1,500-3,000 m**; **alpine meadows** at **2,900-6,000 m**; **dry alpine scrub** above **4,000 m**.
xa: Moist temperate trees: **oak, deodar, fir**.
Sub-alpine: **fir, birch, rhododendron**.
Dry alpine scrub is dominated by **juniper**.

40.s:
Consider the following statements about Himalayan altitude zones:
1. Moist temperate forests include oak, deodar and fir.
2. Sub-alpine vegetation includes fir, birch and rhododendron.
3. Dry alpine scrub dominated by juniper occurs above about 4,000 metres.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
40.x: All three statements correctly describe Himalayan vegetation zones and their characteristic species or altitude.
40.tq: Verify each altitude-zone and species association separately.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4)** **1, 2 and 3**.
**Moist temperate** = **oak, deodar, fir**; **sub-alpine** = **fir, birch, rhododendron**; **dry alpine scrub** (juniper) above **4,000 m**.
xa: Moist temperate zone: **1,500-3,000 m**; chir pine **1,000-1,800 m**.
Alpine meadows: **2,900-6,000 m**.
Southern (windward) slopes carry **denser forest** than northern slopes.

40.s:
Arrange the following Himalayan vegetation zones from lower to higher elevation:
A. Temperate forests
B. Alpine meadows
C. Tropical sal forests
D. Subtropical chir-pine forests
E. Subalpine birch-rhododendron forests
40.x: The sequence upward is tropical sal foothills, subtropical chir pine, temperate forests, subalpine birch-rhododendron forests and alpine meadows.
40.tq: Use the lower-to-higher elevation sequence and check the first and last zones.
xs: Upward order: **tropical sal → subtropical chir pine → temperate → subalpine birch-rhododendron → alpine meadows** — **C, D, A, E, B**, option **(1)**.
**Sal** marks the tropical foothills, **chir pine** the subtropical zone (**1,000-1,800 m**) and **alpine meadows** the top, above the tree line.
xa: Temperate trees: **oak, deodar, blue pine, silver fir**.
Alpine meadows reach **4,750 m+**.
⚠ Some notes give a shorter order: subtropical-temperate-alpine.

40.s: Which one of the following combinations is associated with temperate Himalayan forests?
o: Mangrove, sundari, stilt root and knee root
Oak, deodar, blue pine and silver fir
40.x: Temperate Himalayan forests include oak, deodar, blue pine and silver fir.
40.tq: Identify a vegetation belt from its characteristic species.
xs: **Oak, deodar, blue pine and silver fir** are temperate Himalayan trees — option **(3)**.
Stilt/knee roots and sundari = **mangroves**; **sal, teak, sandalwood, mahua** = **deciduous**; **acacia, babul**, cactus = **thorn**.
xa: **Deodar** is a temperate conifer of the **Western Himalaya**.
Eastern Himalaya: **oaks, laurels, maples, rhododendrons, alder, birch**.
Below the temperate belt lies **chir pine** (**1,000-1,800 m**).

40.s:
Consider the following statements about Himalayan vegetation:
1. Eastern Himalayan forests include oaks, laurels, maples, rhododendrons, alder and birch.
2. The tree line is lower in the Eastern Himalaya than in the Western Himalaya.
3. The northern slopes generally carry denser forests than the southern slopes.
40.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false: the southern or windward slopes generally carry denser forests than the northern slopes.
40.tq: Use a reversed-slope comparison as the main distractor.
xs: Statement 1 **correct**: Eastern Himalaya has **oaks, laurels, maples, rhododendrons, alder, birch**.
Statement 2 **correct**: the **tree line is lower in the east** than in the west.
Statement 3 **wrong**: the **southern (windward) slopes** carry denser forest.
So **1 and 2 only** — option **(1)**.
xa: Sequence up the slope: sal → **chir pine** → temperate → subalpine → **alpine meadows**.
**Dry alpine scrub** (juniper) lies above **4,000 m**.
**Deodar** = Western Himalaya.

40.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Sal — Moist deciduous forests of the Terai and Indo-Gangetic plains
Jackfruit — Alpine meadows of the Himalaya
40.x: Jackfruit is an evergreen tree associated with the Western Ghats, not with Himalayan alpine meadows. Sal, teak and deodar are correctly matched with their stated regions.
40.tq: Find the species placed in a clearly unsuitable ecological region.
xs: **Jackfruit — alpine meadows** is wrong — option **(4)**; jackfruit is an **evergreen** tree of the **Western Ghats**.
The rest are correct: **deodar → Western Himalaya**; **sal → moist deciduous** of the Terai and Indo-Gangetic plain; **teak → central and peninsular India**.
xa: **Sandalwood** → dry deciduous, **South India**.
**Mahua** → deciduous, **Central India**.
Teak also grows in AP's **Eastern Ghats**.

40.s:
Which of the following statements regarding sal and teak is correct?
1. Sal is associated with moist deciduous forests.
2. Sal occurs in the Terai, Indo-Gangetic plain, Chota Nagpur and parts of the Northeast.
3. Teak is associated with central and peninsular India and also occurs in the Eastern Ghats of Andhra Pradesh.
40.x: Sal is a moist deciduous species with the listed distribution, while teak occurs in central and peninsular India, including the Eastern Ghats of Andhra Pradesh. All three statements are correct.
40.tq: Test a species through a combined type-and-distribution statement set.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4)** **1, 2 and 3**.
**Sal** = **moist deciduous**, in the **Terai, Indo-Gangetic plain, Chota Nagpur, NE**.
**Teak** = central and peninsular India, including AP's **Eastern Ghats**.
xa: Teak grows in both **moist and dry deciduous** forests.
**Deodar** = temperate conifer of the **Western Himalaya**.
Moist deciduous = **37%** of forest area — the single most widespread type.

40.s: Which one of the following correctly matches the tree with its forest type and region?
o: Sandalwood — Dry deciduous forests of South India
Deodar — Tropical mangrove forests of Odisha
40.x: Sandalwood is associated with dry deciduous forests of South India. Deodar occurs in the Western Himalaya, mahua in Central India and jackfruit in the Western Ghats.
40.tq: Use the forest-type and region pair together to reject mismatches.
xs: **Sandalwood — dry deciduous forests of South India** is correct — option **(1)**.
**Deodar** is a temperate conifer of the **Western Himalaya**; **mahua** a deciduous tree of **Central India**; **jackfruit** an evergreen of the **Western Ghats**.
xa: Dry deciduous also has **teak, Terminalia, red sanders**.
Dry deciduous forests get **75-100 cm** rain and cover **28.6%** of forest area.
AP's dry deciduous forests: **Nallamala**, Eastern Ghats.

40.s:
Which of the following statements regarding mangrove vegetation is correct?
1. Mangroves commonly possess stilt and knee roots.
2. Their roots may remain submerged during high tide.
3. They generally occur at the fringes of river deltas on both coasts of India.
40.x: Mangroves possess specialised stilt and knee roots, occur in intertidal deltaic areas and may be submerged during high tide. All three statements are correct.
40.tq: Combine related ecological adaptations and distribution facts in a statement-based question.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4)** **1, 2 and 3**.
Mangroves have **stilt and knee roots**, are **submerged at high tide**, and grow at **delta fringes on both coasts**.
xa: Species: **Rhizophora, Avicennia, Sonneratia**.
Sites: **Sundarbans** (WB), **Bhitarkanika** (Odisha), **Pichavaram** (TN), **Coringa** (AP).
AP mangroves: **421.43 sq km** (ISFR 2023).

40.s:
Consider the following statements about mangrove cover in Andhra Pradesh:
1. Andhra Pradesh had 421.43 sq km of mangrove cover according to ISFR 2023.
2. Its mangrove cover increased by 13.01 sq km.
3. The mangrove cover includes a very dense class.
40.x: Andhra Pradesh had 421.43 sq km of mangrove cover in ISFR 2023, showing an increase of 13.01 sq km. It had no very dense mangrove class.
40.tq: Use a numerical statement pair with one reversed or unsupported classification.
xs: Statement 1 **correct**: AP had **421.43 sq km** of mangroves (ISFR 2023).
Statement 2 **correct**: an increase of **13.01 sq km**.
Statement 3 **wrong**: AP has **no very dense class** of mangroves.
So **1 and 2 only** — option **(1)**.
xa: ⚠ ISFR 2023 ranks **Gujarat second**; AP SES **2025-26** calls AP's mangroves second-largest.
**Coringa** WLS (Kakinada): **Godavari-Krishna** delta mangroves.
AP mangroves + littoral: **418 sq km** (another figure in the notes).

40.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the conflicting claims regarding the rank of Andhra Pradesh in mangrove cover?
o: The State Economic Survey places Andhra Pradesh third, whereas ISFR 2023 places Odisha second.
AP State Economic Survey describes Andhra Pradesh as having the second-largest mangrove cover, whereas ISFR 2023 places Gujarat second.
ISFR 2023 places Andhra Pradesh first, whereas the State Economic Survey places West Bengal second.
Both sources place Andhra Pradesh first in mangrove cover.
40.x: The Andhra Pradesh SES 2025–26 describes AP as having the second-largest mangrove cover, while ISFR 2023 places Gujarat second. This is identified as a data discrepancy.
40.tq: Compare two authorities instead of relying on a single rank claim.
xs: The AP **State Economic Survey** calls AP's mangroves the **second-largest**, while **ISFR 2023** places **Gujarat second** — option **(2)**.
The notes flag this as a **discrepancy**.
xa: AP mangroves: **421.43 sq km**, **+13.01 sq km**, no very dense class.
Older shares: **WB 50%**, **Gujarat 21%**, **A&N 14%**.
**Sundarbans** (WB) is the largest mangrove.

40.s: According to the older distributional estimate cited for India’s mangroves, which of the following is the correct descending order of shares?
o: West Bengal, Gujarat, Andaman and Nicobar Islands
Gujarat, West Bengal, Andaman and Nicobar Islands
Andaman and Nicobar Islands, West Bengal, Gujarat
West Bengal, Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Gujarat
40.x: The older estimate gives West Bengal about 50%, Gujarat about 21% and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands about 14% of India’s mangroves.
40.tq: Use the relative percentages to establish descending order.
xs: Older shares: **West Bengal 50%**, **Gujarat 21%**, **A&N 14%** — option **(1)**.
So the order is **West Bengal > Gujarat > A&N**; option (2) swaps the first two.
xa: **Sundarbans** (WB): largest mangrove; **Sundari** tree; Sundarbans BR **9,630 sq km**.
**A&N** tidal forests (PYQ 2025).
⚠ ISFR 2023 still puts **Gujarat second**.

40.s:
Consider the following pairs (mangrove site : State):
1. Bhitarkanika : Odisha
2. Pichavaram : Tamil Nadu
3. Coringa : Andhra Pradesh
4. Sundarbans : Gujarat
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
40.x: Pairs 1-3 are correct: Bhitarkanika (saltwater crocodiles) is in Odisha, Pichavaram near Chidambaram in Tamil Nadu, and Coringa WLS near Kakinada in AP. Pair 4 is wrong: the Sundarbans, India's largest mangrove, is in West Bengal. So 1, 2 and 3 only.
40.tq: Sundarbans WB, Bhitarkanika Odisha, Pichavaram TN, Coringa AP.
xs: Pairs 1, 2, 3 **correct**: **Bhitarkanika → Odisha** (saltwater crocodiles), **Pichavaram → Tamil Nadu** (near Chidambaram), **Coringa → AP** (Kakinada).
Pair 4 **wrong**: the **Sundarbans** is in **West Bengal**.
So **1, 2 and 3 only** — option **(2)**.
xa: Sundarbans = largest mangrove; **Sundari** tree.
Bhitarkanika is a **national park**; Coringa a **WLS**.
**A&N** has tidal forests.

40.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Grass type)
a. Sehima-Dichanthium
b. Phragmites-Saccharum
c. Deschampsia-Deyeuxia
d. Bothriochloa

List-II (Habitat)
i. Alpine region
ii. High-rainfall paddy tracts
iii. Black-soil regions
iv. Marshy localities

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
40.x: Sehima-Dichanthium occurs on black soils; Phragmites-Saccharum in marshy localities; Deschampsia-Deyeuxia in alpine regions; and Bothriochloa in high-rainfall paddy tracts.
40.tq: Start with the sure habitat association and eliminate incompatible codes.
xs: Correct code **a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii** — option **(1)** (matches the PYQ 2024 key).
**Sehima-Dichanthium → black soils**; **Phragmites-Saccharum → marshy** localities; **Deschampsia-Deyeuxia → alpine**; **Bothriochloa → high-rainfall paddy tracts**.
xa: **Banni** = vast tropical grassland of **Kutch, Gujarat**.
Alpine meadows: **Bugyals** (Uttarakhand), **Margs** (Kashmir).
**Sabai grass** is used for rope and paper.

40.s: Banni grassland, one of the vast tropical grasslands of India, is located in:
40.x: Banni is a vast tropical grassland situated in the Kutch region of Gujarat.
40.tq: Use a distinctive landscape-place association.
xs: **Banni** grassland lies in **Kutch, Gujarat** — option **(2)**.
The **Terai** has marshy **Phragmites-Saccharum** grass; the **Nilgiris** have **sholas**.
xa: **Bugyals** = Uttarakhand alpine meadows; **Margs** = Kashmir.
**Sehima-Dichanthium** grows on **black soils**.
**Sabai grass** → rope and paper.

40.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Sabai grass — rope and paper manufacture
Banni — alpine meadow of Himachal Pradesh
40.x: Sabai grass is used for making rope and paper. Bugyals are alpine meadows of Uttarakhand, while margs are associated with Kashmir; Banni is in Kutch, Gujarat.
40.tq: Find the correctly matched item among closely related grassland terms.
xs: **Sabai grass — rope and paper** is correct — option **(2)**.
**Margs** are Kashmir's alpine meadows, **Bugyals** Uttarakhand's; **Banni** is a tropical grassland of **Kutch, Gujarat**.
xa: ⚠ **Bugyals** (Uttarakhand) vs **Margs** (Kashmir) — a common swap trap.
Alpine grass: **Deschampsia-Deyeuxia**.
Marshy grass: **Phragmites-Saccharum**.

40.s: For the purpose of the India State of Forest Report, forest cover refers to land of more than one hectare having canopy density of at least:
40.x: Forest cover includes land exceeding one hectare with canopy density of 10% or more, regardless of ownership.
40.tq: Separate the area criterion from the canopy-density criterion.
xs: Forest cover = land over **1 ha** with canopy density **≥ 10%**, **regardless of ownership** — option **(1)**.
Ownership and recorded-forest status do not matter.
xa: Classes: **VDF ≥ 70%**, **MDF 40-70%**, **OF 10-40%**; **scrub < 10%** is not forest cover.
ISFR is published **biennially** by the **Forest Survey of India** (**1981**, **Dehradun**).
ISFR 2023 forest cover: **21.76%**.

40.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the density classes used in the India State of Forest Report?
o: Very Dense Forest: 40% or more; Moderately Dense Forest: 20–40%; Open Forest: below 20%
Very Dense Forest: 80% or more; Moderately Dense Forest: 50–80%; Open Forest: 20–50%
Very Dense Forest: 60% or more; Moderately Dense Forest: 30–60%; Open Forest: 10–30%
Very Dense Forest: 70% or more; Moderately Dense Forest: 40–70%; Open Forest: 10–40%
40.x: The classes are Very Dense Forest at 70% or more, Moderately Dense Forest at 40–70%, and Open Forest at 10–40% canopy density.
40.tq: Compare the adjacent canopy-density ranges without reversing their order.
xs: **Scrub** (< **10%**) is not counted as forest cover.
xa: Forest cover = land > **1 ha** with canopy **≥ 10%**, any ownership.
⚠ AP's "**38,436.58 sq km**" figure wrongly adds **8,351.62 sq km** scrub.

40.s: Which one of the following statements regarding scrub is correct?
o: Scrub has canopy density below 10% and is not counted as forest cover.
Scrub has canopy density between 40% and 70% and is counted as moderately dense forest.
Scrub has canopy density of 70% or more and is counted as very dense forest.
Scrub has canopy density between 10% and 40% and is counted as open forest.
40.x: Scrub is assigned to areas with canopy density below 10% and is excluded from the forest-cover category.
40.tq: Distinguish the lower threshold of scrub from the open-forest range.
xs: **Scrub** has canopy density **below 10%** and is **not counted as forest cover** — option **(1)**.
xa: ⚠ Trap: AP "**38,436.58 sq km / 23.59%**" includes **8,351.62 sq km** scrub; true forest cover is **30,084.96 sq km**.
ISFR 2023 notes **dense canopy thinning into scrub**.
Forest cover threshold: **≥ 10%** canopy on land > **1 ha**.

40.s: According to ISFR 2023, which of the following combinations is correct for India’s forest cover, tree cover and their combined extent?
o: Forest cover 25.17%, tree cover 3.41%, combined cover 28.58%
Forest cover 21.76%, tree cover 3.41%, combined cover 25.17%
Forest cover 24.62%, tree cover 2.14%, combined cover 26.76%
Forest cover 20.00%, tree cover 5.17%, combined cover 25.17%
40.x: ISFR 2023 reported forest cover of 7,15,343 sq km or 21.76%, tree cover of 1,12,014 sq km or 3.41%, and combined forest and tree cover of 25.17%.
40.tq: Match the three related percentages rather than treating them as interchangeable.
xs: ISFR 2023: **forest cover 21.76%**, **tree cover 3.41%**, **combined 25.17%** — option **(2)**.
Areas: forest **7,15,343 sq km**; tree **1,12,014 sq km**; total **8,27,357 sq km**.
⚠ **25.17%** is the combined figure, not forest cover alone.
xa: Net gain **2021-23**: **1,445.81 sq km** — only **156 sq km** forest + **1,289 sq km** tree cover outside recorded forests.
**NFP 1988** target: **33%** (India's status: **25.17%**).
Publisher: **Forest Survey of India** (**1981**, **Dehradun**; MoEFCC).

40.s: What was the net gain in India’s forest and tree cover between 2021 and 2023 as reported in ISFR 2023?
40.x: The net gain in forest and tree cover between 2021 and 2023 was reported as 1,445.81 sq km.
40.tq: Distinguish the net gain from its separate forest-cover and tree-cover components.
xs: Net gain in forest and tree cover, **2021-23**: **1,445.81 sq km** — option **(1)**.
Of this, only **156 sq km** was forest and **1,289 sq km** tree cover outside recorded forests.
xa: Critics: "**Planting more, foresting less**" — **140 crore** saplings vs **156 sq km** true forest gain.
ISFR 2023 total forest + tree cover: **25.17%**.
Dense canopy was **thinning into scrub**.

40.s: Which State had the third-largest forest cover in India according to the figures provided for ISFR 2023?
40.x: Chhattisgarh had the third-largest forest cover, measuring about 55,812 sq km. Odisha had about 61,204 sq km, while Meghalaya was notable for the share of its geographical area under forest.
40.tq: Separate ranking by absolute forest area from ranking by percentage of geographical area.
xs: **Chhattisgarh** had the **3rd largest** forest cover (**55,812 sq km**) — option **(1)**.
**Odisha** had **61,204 sq km**; **Meghalaya** is notable for **~76%** of its area under forest.
xa: SDG India Index **2023-24**: AP **18.28%**; best **Mizoram 84.53%**.
**Guru Ghasidas-Tamor Pingla** (Chhattisgarh) = **56th Tiger Reserve**.

40.s: Which one of the following correctly states Meghalaya’s position in relation to forest cover?
o: About 56% of its geographical area is under forest
About 36% of its geographical area is under forest
About 96% of its geographical area is under forest
About 76% of its geographical area is under forest
40.x: Approximately 76% of Meghalaya’s geographical area is under forest, according to the figures cited.
40.tq: Test percentage of geographical area rather than absolute forest-cover ranking.
xs: About **76%** of **Meghalaya**'s area is under forest — option **(4)**.
**36%** is the share of India's forest cover prone to frequent **fires**.
xa: **Mizoram 84.53%** tops the SDG India Index **2023-24** on forest cover.
**Chhattisgarh** = **3rd largest** forest cover (**55,812 sq km**).
India forest cover (ISFR 2023) = **21.76%**.

40.s: Which type of forest is considered most vulnerable to forest fires?
40.x: Dry deciduous forests are especially vulnerable to fires because of their seasonal dryness and accumulation of dry biomass.
40.tq: Associate fire vulnerability with the seasonally dry forest type.
xs: **Dry deciduous** forests are the most vulnerable to fire — option **(2)**.
About **36%** of forest cover is prone to frequent fires (ISFR **2015**).
xa: AP: **largest fire-affected area in 2023-24** (**5,286.76 sq km**); **3rd** in large-fire events.
AP is mainly dry deciduous; fire risk in **Chittoor and Annamayya** forests (Apr-May 2026).
Dry deciduous rain: **75-100 cm**.

40.s: With reference to forest fires during 2023–24, which one of the following is correct regarding Andhra Pradesh?
o: It had the smallest fire-affected area and ranked first in large-fire events.
It had the largest fire-affected area, about 5,286.76 sq km, and ranked third in large-fire events.
It ranked third in fire-affected area, with about 2,856.76 sq km affected.
It had the largest fire-affected area, but recorded no large-fire events.
40.x: Andhra Pradesh had the largest fire-affected area in 2023–24, measuring about 5,286.76 sq km, and ranked third in large-fire events.
40.tq: Check both the absolute area figure and the separate event ranking.
xs: AP had the **largest fire-affected area** in **2023-24**, about **5,286.76 sq km**, and ranked **third** in large-fire events — option **(2)**.
Options (1) and (4) contradict this, and option (3) has the wrong rank and area.
xa: ~**36%** of India's forest cover is fire-prone (ISFR 2015; APPSC 2025 key).
**Dry deciduous** forests are most vulnerable — AP's dominant type.
Fire risk flagged in **Chittoor and Annamayya** forests (Apr-May 2026).

40.s:
Consider the following statements about the Forest Survey of India:
1. ISFR is published biennially.
2. The Forest Survey of India was established in 1981.
3. Its headquarters is at Dehradun.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
40.x: ISFR is a biennial assessment by the Forest Survey of India, established in 1981 and headquartered at Dehradun.
40.tq: Verify the periodicity, establishment year and location separately.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4)** **1, 2 and 3**.
**ISFR** is **biennial**; the **Forest Survey of India** was set up in **1981**, headquartered at **Dehradun**, under **MoEFCC**.
xa: ISFR 2023: forest cover **21.76%**, tree cover **3.41%**, total **25.17%**.
Forest cover = land > **1 ha**, canopy **≥ 10%**.

40.s: Which State has the highest forest cover percentage among the following?
40.x: Mizoram has the highest forest cover percentage mentioned, at 84.53%; Andhra Pradesh is reported at 18.28%.
40.tq: Use the highest-value comparison rather than the state-specific figure.
xs: **Mizoram** has the highest forest-cover share — **84.53%** — option **(4)**.
**AP** is far lower at **18.28%** (SDG India Index **2023-24**).
xa: **Meghalaya**: **~76%** of its area.
NFP 1988 target: **33%**; **66%** in hills.

40.s: According to ISFR 2015, about what share of India's forest cover is prone to frequent forest fires?
40.x: About 36% of India's forest cover is prone to frequent fires (ISFR 2015; APPSC 2025 key), and dry deciduous forests are the most vulnerable. 16%, 26% and 46% are distractors.
40.tq: ~36% fire-prone; dry deciduous most at risk.
xs: About **36%** of India's forest cover is prone to frequent fires (ISFR **2015**) — option **(3)** (APPSC 2025 key).
**Dry deciduous** forests are the most vulnerable.
xa: AP: largest fire-affected area in **2023-24** (**5,286.76 sq km**).
AP ranked **3rd** in large-fire events.
Fire risk flagged in **Chittoor and Annamayya** forests (Apr-May 2026).

40.s: The National Forest Policy, 1988 envisages forest and tree cover over what percentage of India’s total area?
40.x: The National Forest Policy, 1988 set a target of 33% of the total area under forest and tree cover.
40.tq: Distinguish the national target from the separate hill-and-mountain target.
xs: **NFP 1988** targets **33%** of area under forest and tree cover — option **(2)**.
**66%** is the target for **hills and mountains**; India's status is **25.17%**.
xa: **Forest (Conservation) Act 1980**: central approval to divert forest land.
**CAMPA** manages compensatory afforestation funds.
ISFR 2023 forest cover alone: **21.76%**.

40.s: Under the National Forest Policy, 1988, the target for forest and tree cover in hills and mountains is:
40.x: The National Forest Policy, 1988 prescribed a target of 66% forest and tree cover in hills and mountains.
40.tq: Compare the general 33% target with the higher physiographic-region target.
xs: In **hills and mountains** the NFP 1988 target is **66%** — option **(3)**.
**33%** is the national target for the whole country.
xa: India's status: **25.17%** forest + tree cover.
**Meghalaya ~76%**; **Mizoram 84.53%**.

40.s: The Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 requires which of the following before forest land is diverted for non-forest purposes?
o: Approval only of the district collector
Approval only of the State Legislature
Approval of the National Tiger Conservation Authority
40.x: Diversion of forest land under the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 requires central approval.
40.tq: Ask which authority exercises the decisive approval power.
xs: Under the **Forest (Conservation) Act 1980**, diverting forest land needs **Central Government approval** — option **(2)**.
AP diverted **149.57 ha** under the FCA in Apr-Dec **2025** (SES **2025-26**).
xa: **CAMPA** manages compensatory afforestation funds.
**NTCA** is a statutory body under **WPA 1972**, headed by the Environment Minister.
SC bars mining within **1 km** of every NP/WLS unless a larger ESZ is notified.

40.s: Which institution manages the compensatory afforestation funds generated under the forest conservation framework?
40.x: CAMPA manages the compensatory afforestation funds.
40.tq: Match the environmental institution with its specific financial function.
xs: **CAMPA** manages the **compensatory afforestation funds** — option **(4)**.
**NTCA** is the tiger authority under **WPA 1972**.
xa: **Forest (Conservation) Act 1980**: central approval for diversion.

40.s:
Consider the following statements regarding forest classifications:
1. In a protected forest, rights are recorded and activities are allowed unless specifically prohibited.
2. A village forest is a reserved forest assigned to a village community.
3. In a reserved forest, all activities are freely permitted unless prohibited by a specific notification.
40.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because activities in reserved forests are barred unless expressly permitted.
40.tq: Test the reversal between permitted activities in protected and reserved forests.
xs: Statement 1 **correct**: in a **protected forest** rights are recorded and activities are **allowed unless prohibited**.
Statement 2 **correct**: a **village forest** is a reserved forest **assigned to a village community**.
Statement 3 **wrong**: in a **reserved forest** everything is **barred unless expressly permitted**.
So **1 and 2 only** — option **(1)**.
xa: All three classes come from the **Indian Forest Act 1927**.
**Conservation / community reserves** came by the **WPA amendment 2002**.
AP: **Reserved ~85.8%**, **Protected ~13.6%**, **Unclassed ~0.6%**.

40.s: What was the approximate distribution of Andhra Pradesh forests among Reserved, Protected and Unclassed categories respectively?
40.x: In Andhra Pradesh, approximately 85.8% of forests are Reserved, 13.6% Protected and 0.6% Unclassed.
40.tq: Recall the three-part percentage distribution in the stated order.
xs: AP forests: **Reserved 85.8%**, **Protected 13.6%**, **Unclassed 0.6%** — option **(4)**.
Option (1) swaps Protected and Unclassed; option (2) swaps Reserved and Protected.
xa: Reserved = **grazing/felling prohibited** (strictest).
**Sri Venkateswara** = AP's first NP (**1989**); **Papikonda** largest; **Rajiv Gandhi** smallest.

40.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched with the applicable law or regime?
o: National Park — Indian Forest Act, 1927 only
Conservation reserve — Wildlife Protection Act amendment, 2002
40.x: Conservation and community reserves were provided under the Wildlife Protection Act amendment of 2002. Reserved, protected and village forests are categories under the Indian Forest Act, 1927.
40.tq: Identify the correct statute attached to each legal category.
xs: **Conservation reserve — WPA amendment 2002** is correct — option **(2)**.
**National Parks** fall under **WPA 1972**, not the Indian Forest Act.
**Reserved forests** and **village forests** come under the **Indian Forest Act 1927**; **community reserves** came with the **2002** WPA amendment.
xa: Conservation reserve = **govt land** buffers or corridors; community reserve = **community or private land**.
⚠ Reserved = **barred unless permitted**; Protected = **allowed unless prohibited**.
PA network (2026): **127 conservation reserves**, **75 community reserves**; **1,134 PAs** in all.

40.s: With reference to mining near protected areas, which of the following statements is correct?
o: Mining is prohibited only within 100 metres of a National Park.
The 1 km restriction applies only to Biosphere Reserves.
The Supreme Court has barred mining within 1 km of every National Park and Wildlife Sanctuary unless a larger eco-sensitive zone is notified.
Mining is permitted inside every National Park if approved by the State Government.
40.x: Mining is banned inside National Parks and Sanctuaries, and the Supreme Court has barred mining within 1 km of every such area unless a larger eco-sensitive zone is notified.
40.tq: Apply the legal rule to a protected-area boundary scenario.
xs: The **Supreme Court** has barred **mining within 1 km** of every **NP and WLS** unless a larger **ESZ** is notified — option **(3)**.
Mining is **banned inside** NPs and sanctuaries (WPA 1972), so option (4) is wrong; the rule covers NPs/WLS, not only biosphere reserves.
xa: NPs and sanctuaries are created under **WPA 1972**.
**Forest (Conservation) Act 1980** needs central approval to divert forest land.

40.s: Regeneration from stool shoots after felling, generally maintained on a short rotation for fuelwood, is known as:
40.x: Coppice regeneration arises from stool shoots after felling and is generally managed on a short rotation, particularly for fuelwood.
40.tq: Discriminate silvicultural terms by their regeneration method.
xs: Regeneration from **stool shoots** after felling on a **short rotation** for **fuelwood** is **coppice** — option **(3)**.
**High forest** is raised from **seed** on a long rotation; the **selection system** removes mature trees singly or in groups.
xa: ⚠ **Coppice** = shoots, short rotation; **High forest** = seed, long rotation (timber).
Selection system keeps an **uneven-aged** forest.

40.s: In the selection system of silviculture, the forest is maintained as:
o: A plantation harvested completely at one time
An uneven-aged forest by removing mature trees singly or in groups
An even-aged crop regenerated only by stool shoots
40.x: The selection system removes mature trees singly or in groups and maintains an uneven-aged forest.
40.tq: Apply the definition to identify the correct forest-management outcome.
xs: The **selection system** keeps an **uneven-aged forest** by removing **mature trees singly or in groups** — option **(2)**.
Regeneration only by **stool shoots** is **coppice**; complete one-time harvest is not selection.
xa: **High forest**: crop raised from **seed**, **long rotation** (timber).
**Coppice**: stool shoots, **short rotation** (fuelwood).

40.s: A forest manager wants a long-rotation timber crop raised from seed, while avoiding complete clearance of the forest and retaining trees of different ages. Which combination of silvicultural concepts is most appropriate?
o: Village forest and protected forest classification
Coppice and short-rotation fuelwood management only
40.x: High forest provides a seed-raised, long-rotation timber crop, while the selection system retains an uneven-aged forest by removing mature trees singly or in groups.
40.tq: Combine two definitions in a practical forest-management scenario.
xs: **High forest** (seed-raised, **long-rotation timber**) + **selection system** (uneven-aged, trees removed singly or in groups) — option **(4)**.
**Coppice** is short-rotation fuelwood from stool shoots; **village/protected forest** are legal classes, not silviculture.
xa: ⚠ **Coppice** = shoots, short rotation; **High forest** = seed, long rotation.
Legal classes (**Indian Forest Act 1927**): reserved, protected, village forest.

40.s: Jim Corbett National Park was originally established in 1936 under which name?
40.x: Jim Corbett National Park was established in 1936 as Hailey National Park and is recognised as India’s first national park.
40.tq: Use the direct year–name association for the first national park.
xs: **Jim Corbett NP** began in **1936** as **Hailey National Park** — option **(1)** — India's first NP.
**Bharatpur** is the other name of **Keoladeo NP** (Rajasthan); **Palamau** is a Jharkhand tiger reserve.
xa: Corbett lies in **Uttarakhand**.
**Amangarh TR** (UP) is the **Corbett buffer**.
**Askot WLS** (Pithoragarh, Uttarakhand) — musk deer habitat.

40.s: Keoladeo National Park, also known as Bharatpur, is located in which State?
40.x: Keoladeo National Park is situated at Bharatpur in Rajasthan and is also a Ramsar site.
40.tq: Test the protected-area–State association directly.
xs: **Keoladeo NP (Bharatpur)** is in **Rajasthan** — option **(2)**.
It is also a **Ramsar site**.
xa: **Nelapattu** (AP) is a bird sanctuary — AP's smallest WLS.
**Jim Corbett** (Uttarakhand) = India's first NP (**1936**, as Hailey NP).
**Great Indian Bustard** lives in **Rajasthan and Gujarat**.

40.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Kanha Tiger Reserve — Madhya Pradesh
2. Askot Wildlife Sanctuary — Uttarakhand
3. Palamau Tiger Reserve — Jharkhand
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
40.x: All three pairs are correctly matched. Kanha is in Madhya Pradesh, Askot is in Uttarakhand, and Palamau is in Jharkhand.
40.tq: Check each protected-area–State pair independently before selecting the code.
xs: All three pairs are correct — option **(4)** **1, 2 and 3**.
**Kanha TR → Madhya Pradesh**; **Askot WLS → Uttarakhand** (Pithoragarh); **Palamau TR → Jharkhand**.
xa: Palamau was one of the **original 9** (**1973**); **Betla NP** is its core.
Askot is a **musk deer** habitat.
Kanha is linked to **Guru Ghasidas-Tamor Pingla** (Chhattisgarh).

40.s: Madhav Tiger Reserve, recognised as India’s 58th tiger reserve, is located in which State?
40.x: Madhav Tiger Reserve is situated in Shivpuri, Madhya Pradesh, and is the 58th tiger reserve.
40.tq: Link the ordinal number with the corresponding reserve and State.
xs: **Madhav TR**, the **58th** tiger reserve, is in **Madhya Pradesh** (**Shivpuri**) — option **(3)**.
The **Sakhya Sagar** Ramsar site lies inside it.
xa: ⚠ Order: **56th** Guru Ghasidas-Tamor Pingla (Chhattisgarh) → **57th** Ratapani (MP) → **58th** Madhav.
**MP has 9 tiger reserves**, the most of any state.
Project Tiger: **58 reserves** (**84,488 sq km**, ~**2.6%** of India's land).

40.s: Which State has the highest number of tiger reserves in India?
40.x: Madhya Pradesh has 9 tiger reserves, the highest number among Indian States.
40.tq: Use the superlative State–number association.
xs: **Madhya Pradesh** has the most tiger reserves — **9** — option **(1)**.
MP's reserves include **Kanha**, **Ratapani** (57th) and **Madhav** (58th).
xa: Project Tiger (**1973**): **9** reserves → **58** reserves across **18** states.
**Veerangana Durgavati TR** is Project Cheetah's 3rd home.
About **30%** of tigers live outside reserves.

40.s: The National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA) is correctly described as which of the following?
o: A constitutional body headed by the Chief Justice of India
A statutory body under the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972, headed by the Environment Minister
A non-statutory body headed by the Prime Minister
A statutory body under the Forest Conservation Act, 1980, headed by the Home Minister

40.tq: Ask who created the body and who heads it to avoid authority-based traps.
xs: **NTCA** is a **statutory body under WPA 1972**, headed by the **Environment Minister** — option **(2)**.
It is not constitutional, not under the **Forest (Conservation) Act 1980**, and not headed by the PM or Home Minister.
xa: **Project Tiger** began in **1973** with **9 reserves (18,278 sq km)**.
**CAMPA** manages compensatory afforestation funds.

40.s: Satkosia Tiger Reserve comprises which of the following protected areas?
o: Satkosia Gorge and Debrigarh Wildlife Sanctuary
Satkosia Gorge and Baisipalli Wildlife Sanctuary
40.x: Satkosia Tiger Reserve comprises Satkosia Gorge and Baisipalli Wildlife Sanctuary; Debrigarh is not part of its stated composition.

**Debrigarh** is not part of it, so option (1) is the trap.

**Buxa TR** is in **West Bengal**; **Palamau TR** in **Jharkhand**.

40.s: Which of the following tiger reserves is located in Uttar Pradesh and forms the buffer of Corbett Tiger Reserve?
40.x: Amangarh Tiger Reserve is in Uttar Pradesh and serves as the buffer of Corbett Tiger Reserve.

o: It was the 58th tiger reserve and lies in Madhya Pradesh.

xs: **Panna** became a **UNESCO Biosphere Reserve** in **2020** — option **(3)**.

40.s:
Consider the following statements:

xs: Statement 1 **correct**: India has **58** tiger reserves.
Statement 2 **correct**: they grew from **9** in **1973** to **58**.

40.s: India's wild tiger population in 2022 and its approximate share of the world's wild tigers were

40.s: Nelapattu Bird Sanctuary, noted as the smallest wildlife sanctuary in Andhra Pradesh, is located in:

40.s: Project Cheetah was launched in India on 17 September 2022 and involved which distinctive conservation activity?
o: The world’s first intercontinental translocation of a large carnivore
The first captive breeding of the Great Indian Bustard
The first reintroduction of tigers into India
The first translocation of elephants from Africa to India

xs: **Project Cheetah** (**17 Sep 2022**) was the **world's first intercontinental large-carnivore translocation** — option **(1)**.
GIB breeding and tiger reintroduction are other projects, not Project Cheetah.

Gandhi Sagar Wildlife Sanctuary as the second home and Veerangana Durgavati Tiger Reserve as the third
Veerangana Durgavati Tiger Reserve as the second home and Palamau Tiger Reserve as the third
Kanha Tiger Reserve as the second home and Gandhi Sagar Wildlife Sanctuary as the third

xa: Project Cheetah launched **17 Sep 2022**.
Population: **53**.

40.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Great Indian Bustard:

o: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India
Wildlife First v. State of Rajasthan
T.N. Godavarman v. Union of India
M.K. Ranjitsinh v. Union of India

xs: The GIB power-line case is **M.K. Ranjitsinh v. Union of India** — option **(4)**.

xa: SC's **2021** underground-lines order was **modified in 2024**.
GIB: fewer than **150** birds, in **Rajasthan and Gujarat**.
First artificial-insemination breeding at **Jaisalmer**.

40.s: The first artificial-insemination breeding of the Great Indian Bustard was conducted at:

xs: The first **artificial-insemination** breeding of the **Great Indian Bustard** was at **Jaisalmer** — option **(2)**.
**Bharatpur** is the Keoladeo bird sanctuary.
xa: GIB: **Rajasthan, Gujarat**; fewer than **150** birds.
Case: **M.K. Ranjitsinh v. UoI**; SC order **2021**, modified **2024**.

40.s: The “Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam” campaign claimed the planting of approximately how many saplings?
40.x: The campaign claimed that 140 crore saplings had been planted.

xs: **Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam** claimed **140 crore** saplings — option **(3)**.

xa: Net forest + tree cover gain **2021-23**: **1,445.81 sq km**, mostly **1,289 sq km** tree cover outside recorded forests.
**Aravalli** "**Green Wall**" vs mining damage is another debate.

40.s: Which one of the following best describes the dominant natural vegetation and principal forest tract of Andhra Pradesh?
o: Tropical evergreen forests, with the Eastern Ghats as the largest forest tract
Alpine forests, with the Papikonda hills as the biggest forest tract
Mangrove forests, with the Godavari delta as the biggest forest tract
Dry deciduous forests, with Nallamala as the biggest forest tract

xs: AP's forests are mainly **dry deciduous**, and **Nallamala** is the **biggest forest** — option **(4)**.
**Papikonda** is AP's largest NP, not an alpine forest; mangroves cover only about **418 sq km** (with littoral).

**NSTR** = India's largest TR by area.

40.s: The proposed translocation programme for Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam Tiger Reserve (NSTR) includes
o: gaur from Maharashtra and tigresses from Gujarat and Rajasthan
gaur from Central India and tigresses from Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh
elephants from Central India and lions from Gujarat
blackbuck from Madhya Pradesh and tigers from Karnataka
40.x: The plan proposes bringing gaur from Central India and tigresses from Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh to NSTR.

xs: AP plans to bring **gaur from Central India** to **NSTR** from **Sep 2026**, with **tigresses from Maharashtra and MP** — option **(2)**.
Options (1), (3) and (4) name the wrong animals or source states.
xa: **NSTR** = India's largest TR by area, with **63-67** tigers.
**Satpura-Melghat** corridor is being cut by railway lines.
Fire risk: **Chittoor and Annamayya** forests (Apr-May 2026).

40.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the three National Parks of Andhra Pradesh?
o: Sri Venkateswara was the first, Rajiv Gandhi is the largest and Papikonda is the smallest.
Rajiv Gandhi was the first, Sri Venkateswara is the largest and Papikonda is the smallest.

40.s: Which of the following environmental issues is associated with the Satpura–Melghat tiger corridor?
o: Translocation of gaur from Central India
Expansion of mangrove vegetation into the corridor
Eviction of tribal communities by a biosphere-reserve order
Construction of railway lines through the corridor

40.s: The Supreme Court-ordered eviction in Agasthyamalai Biosphere Reserve has raised concerns primarily relating to
40.x: The eviction issue in Agasthyamalai Biosphere Reserve has raised concerns regarding tribal rights.
40.tq: Identify the social dimension linked to a conservation action.
xs: The SC-ordered eviction in **Agasthyamalai BR** raises **tribal rights** concerns — option **(3)**.

40.s: As per ISFR 2023, Andhra Pradesh's forest cover (VDF + MDF + OF) is about 30,085 sq km. The figure of 38,436.58 sq km (23.59%) sometimes quoted is wrong as 'forest cover' because it
o: adds tree cover outside recorded forests
adds about 8,351.62 sq km of scrub, which ISFR does not count as forest cover
40.x: 38,436.58 sq km = 30,084.96 sq km of forest cover + 8,351.62 sq km of scrub. Scrub (canopy below 10%) is not forest cover in ISFR, so the right figure is about 30,085 sq km (~18.46%). The other options do not account for the difference.
40.tq: AP forest cover ~30,085 sq km; scrub is not forest cover.
xs: The **38,436.58 sq km (23.59%)** figure **adds about 8,351.62 sq km of scrub**, which ISFR **does not count as forest cover** — option **(2)**.
xa: AP's area: **1,62,970 sq km**.
Forest cover = land > **1 ha**, canopy **≥ 10%**, any ownership.
SDG India Index **2023-24** puts AP at **18.28%**.

41.s:
With reference to protected areas under the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972, consider the following statements:
1. A National Park provides the highest degree of protection among the categories listed.
2. Grazing and private rights are not permitted in a National Park.
3. Some activities and rights may be regulated but allowed in a Wildlife Sanctuary.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
41.x: National Parks provide the highest protection, with no grazing or private rights. Wildlife Sanctuaries permit some regulated activities and rights; hence all three statements are correct.
41.tq: Combine closely related provisions and identify the option containing all correct statements.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4)** **1, 2 and 3**.
A **National Park** gives the **highest protection**, with **no grazing or private rights**.
In a **Wildlife Sanctuary** some activities and rights are **regulated but allowed**.
xa: **Conservation Reserve**: State, on **govt-owned** land next to or linking PAs (**Sec 36A**).
**Community Reserve**: State, on **private/community** land volunteered by the community.

41.s: A Conservation Reserve under Section 36A of the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972, is generally established on:

42.s:

42.s:

**Montreux Record** lists threatened sites — India's: **Keoladeo** and **Loktak**.

42.s: The Montreux Record is maintained for Ramsar sites that are which of the following?

o: Olive ridley turtle and saltwater crocodile
42.x: Rollapadu protects the Great Indian Bustard and blackbuck. Gharial and dolphin belong to National Chambal, the Asiatic lion to Gir, and olive ridleys and saltwater crocodiles to the Odisha coast (Gahirmatha, Bhitarkanika).
42.tq: Rollapadu = GIB + blackbuck grassland.
xs: **Rollapadu WLS** (AP) protects the **Great Indian Bustard and blackbuck** — option **(1)**.
Gharial/dolphin = **National Chambal**; Asiatic lion = **Gir**; olive ridley/saltwater crocodile = **Gahirmatha/Bhitarkanika**.
xa: AP has **13** WLS and **3** NPs.
AP's elephant reserve: **Rayala** (incl. Koundinya WLS).

42.s: Project Elephant was launched in which year and month?
42.x: Project Elephant was launched in February 1992.
42.tq: Test the precise commencement date of a conservation programme.
xs: **Project Elephant** began in **February 1992** — option **(1)**.
**1973** was Project Tiger (first TR **Corbett**); **1981** was India's first Ramsar site (**Chilika**).
xa: It covers **33 ERs in 14 states**.

42.s: As stated in the conservation framework of Project Elephant, India has how many elephant reserves distributed across how many States?
42.x: Project Elephant covers 33 elephant reserves in 14 States.
42.tq: Keep the reserve count and State count together to avoid swapping numerical pairs.
xs: Project Elephant has **33 elephant reserves in 14 states** — option **(4)**.
**29** is part of the 2017 count (**29,964**), not the number of reserves.
xa: ERs overlap **TRs, WLS and reserved forests**.
Odisha's **3** ERs: **Mayurbhanj, Mahanadi, Sambalpur**.

42.s:
Elephant reserves may overlap with which of the following categories of protected or reserved areas?
1. Tiger Reserves
2. Wildlife Sanctuaries
3. Reserved forests
Which of the statements given above are correct?
42.x: Elephant reserves can overlap with Tiger Reserves, Wildlife Sanctuaries and reserved forests. Hence, all three statements are correct.
42.tq: Test the overlapping-area relationship through a complete list of categories.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4)** **1, 2 and 3**.
Elephant reserves **overlap tiger reserves, wildlife sanctuaries and reserved forests**.
xa: Project Elephant: **Feb 1992**; **33 ERs in 14 states**.
Stored carbon in ERs rose **38%**, mostly from expanded protected forest.

42.s: According to the 2017 elephant population count, the estimated number of elephants was:
42.x: The 2017 count estimated India's elephant population at 29,964.
42.tq: Recall the exact population figure rather than the number of reserves or States.
xs: The **2017** count gave **29,964** elephants — option **(2)**.
**33** is the number of elephant reserves.
xa: Project Elephant: **Feb 1992**.
AP's ER: **Rayala** (incl. **Koundinya** WLS).

42.s:
Consider the following statements about elephant reserves (ERs):
1. Odisha's elephant reserves are Mayurbhanj, Mahanadi and Sambalpur.
2. Stored carbon in elephant reserves has risen by about 38%, mostly from expanded protected forest.
3. Elephant reserves are notified only in areas outside tiger reserves.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
42.x: Statement 1 is correct: Odisha's three ERs are Mayurbhanj, Mahanadi and Sambalpur. Statement 2 is correct: stored carbon in ERs rose about 38%. Statement 3 is wrong: ERs overlap tiger reserves, sanctuaries and reserved forests. So '1 only' misses 2, and options with 3 are wrong.
42.tq: ERs overlap TRs; Odisha ERs = Mayurbhanj, Mahanadi, Sambalpur.
xs: Statement 1 **correct**: Odisha's ERs are **Mayurbhanj, Mahanadi, Sambalpur**.
Statement 2 **correct**: stored carbon in ERs rose **38%**, mostly from expanded protected forest.
Statement 3 **wrong**: ERs **overlap TRs, WLS and reserved forests**.
So **1 and 2 only** — option **(2)**.
xa: **33 ERs in 14 states**; 2017 count **29,964**.
Odisha also has **6** Ramsar sites.

42.s: Which one of the following correctly identifies India's first Ramsar site and the year of its designation?
42.x: Chilika Lake in Odisha was India's first Ramsar site, designated in 1981.
42.tq: Discriminate between similar wetland names by linking the first site with its year.
xs: India's first Ramsar site was **Chilika Lake** (**1981**) — option **(2)**.
**Kolleru (2002)** is AP's only site; **Keoladeo** became a Ramsar site in **1981** too but is not the first listed.
xa: Newest: **Glaw Lake** (**2026**).
First TR: **Corbett (1973)**.

42.s: Which one of the following statements correctly describes the current relevance of tiger conservation in India?
o: Tiger-related conflict has ended because reserve boundaries are expanding.
Tigers outside reserves have no connection with conservation landscapes.
A growing share of tigers live outside reserves, increasing the possibility of human–wildlife conflict.
All tigers now live within notified Tiger Reserves.
42.x: A growing share of India's tigers is living outside notified reserves, which raises the possibility of conflict with human communities.
42.tq: Apply the conservation trend to its likely management consequence.
xs: A **growing share of tigers live outside reserves**, raising **human-wildlife conflict** — option **(3)**.
So conflict has not ended, and not all tigers are inside reserves.
xa: AP's **NSTR** had **63-67** tigers in AITE **2022**.
First TR: **Corbett (1973)**.

42.s: The tiger population recorded in the All India Tiger Estimation of 2022 for Andhra Pradesh's Tiger Reserve was approximately:
42.x: The All India Tiger Estimation 2022 recorded approximately 63–67 tigers in the State's Tiger Reserve.
42.tq: Recognise the correct numerical range without confusing it with reserve counts.
xs: **NSTR** had about **63-67 tigers** in AITE **2022** — option **(2)**.
NSTR is AP's **only** tiger reserve.
xa: ⚠ Trap: a note calling **SV and Papikondalu** "tiger reserves" conflicts with the count of **1** TR.
AP also has **1** ER (**Rayala**) and **1** BR (**Seshachalam, 2010**).

42.s: Which one of the following correctly presents the first and latest entries in the stated conservation chronology?
o: First Tiger Reserve—Corbett, 1973; first Ramsar site—Chilika, 1981; newest Ramsar site—Glaw Lake, 2026
First Tiger Reserve—Chilika, 1981; first Ramsar site—Corbett, 1973; newest Ramsar site—Glaw Lake, 2024
First Tiger Reserve—Gir, 2020; first Ramsar site—Chilika, 1973; newest Ramsar site—Glaw Lake, 2026
First Tiger Reserve—Corbett, 1981; first Ramsar site—Chilika, 1973; newest Ramsar site—Glaw Lake, 2025
42.x: Corbett was the first Tiger Reserve in 1973, Chilika was the first Ramsar site in 1981, and Glaw Lake became the newest Ramsar site in 2026.
42.tq: Use the first and latest markers to verify the entire sequence.
xs: First TR **Corbett (1973)**; first Ramsar site **Chilika (1981)**; newest Ramsar site **Glaw Lake (2026)** — option **(1)**.
Options (2) and (4) swap the years; Gir is linked to **Project Lion (2020)**, not the first TR.
xa: India joined Ramsar in **1982**; Convention adopted **1971**.
Glaw Lake = **101st** site, **3 Aug 2026**.

42.s: With reference to protected areas of Andhra Pradesh, which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: Tiger reserves — Sri Venkateswara and Papikondalu
42.x: AP has one elephant reserve, Rayala, which includes Koundinya WLS. Its one biosphere reserve is Seshachalam (2010), not Nallamala. Its only tiger reserve is NSTR (the SV/Papikondalu 'tiger reserves' line is a trap). AP has 3 national parks and 13 wildlife sanctuaries, not 13 national parks.
42.tq: AP = 1 TR (NSTR), 1 ER (Rayala), 1 BR (Seshachalam 2010), 3 NP, 13 WLS.
xs: **Elephant reserve — Rayala (incl. Koundinya WLS)** is correct — option **(1)**.
AP's BR is **Seshachalam (2010)**, not Nallamala; its only TR is **NSTR**; it has **3** NPs and **13** WLS.
xa: ⚠ Trap: "**SV and Papikondalu** tiger reserves" conflicts with the count of **1** TR.
NSTR: **63-67** tigers (AITE **2022**).

43.s: Arrange the soil horizons from the surface downward in the correct order.
43.x: The normal sequence is O, A, B, C and R: organic litter, topsoil, subsoil, weathered parent material and bedrock.
43.tq: Use the surface-to-bedrock order to arrange the horizons.
xs: From the surface down: **O → A → B → C → R** — option **(2)**.
**O** = organic litter; **A** = humus-rich topsoil; **B** = subsoil (accumulation); **C** = weathered parent material; **R** = bedrock.
Option (1) is the reverse order (bottom-up).
xa: The **E** horizon is the **leached** layer between A and B.
Good soil by volume: **mineral ~45%**, **organic ~5%**, **water ~25%**, **air ~25%**.
Topsoil holds the most **soil organic carbon**.

43.s: Which horizon of a soil profile is primarily characterised by the accumulation of minerals washed down from upper layers?
43.x: The B horizon is the subsoil zone where minerals washed down from upper horizons accumulate.
43.tq: Distinguish the leaching zone from the accumulation zone.
xs: The **B horizon** (subsoil) is the zone of **accumulation** — option **(2)**.
**A** = humus-rich topsoil; **R** = bedrock; **O** = organic litter.
xa: ⚠ **E** = leached; **B** = accumulation — the pair is often confused.
**C** horizon = weathered parent material.

43.s: Which one of the following represents the approximate volume composition of a good soil?
o: Mineral matter 45%, organic matter 5%, water 25%, air 25%
Mineral matter 50%, organic matter 25%, water 15%, air 10%
Mineral matter 25%, organic matter 45%, water 25%, air 5%
Mineral matter 5%, organic matter 45%, water 25%, air 25%
43.x: A good soil is approximately composed of 45% mineral matter, 5% organic matter, 25% water and 25% air by volume.
43.tq: Check that all four components and their percentages are correctly paired.
xs: Good soil by volume: **mineral matter 45%, organic matter 5%, water 25%, air 25%** — option **(1)**.
Option (4) swaps mineral and organic matter.
xa: **Soil organic carbon** binds particles into aggregates, raises infiltration and feeds microbes.
India's average SOC reportedly **fell from 1% to 0.3% over 70 years**.

43.s: Which one of the following statements about soil organic carbon is correct?
o: It binds soil particles into aggregates, raises infiltration and feeds microbes.
It reduces the water-holding capacity of clay soils in all conditions.
It disperses soil particles and reduces microbial activity.
It occurs mainly in sandy subsoil and is absent from topsoil.
