58.x: House Listing and Housing Census is planned for April–September 2026, followed by Population Enumeration in February 2027, with 1 March 2027 as the reference date.
58.tq: Combine phase, timing and reference-date facts in one coded question.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Phase I **House Listing and Housing Census**: **April-September 2026** (1 April - 30 September).
Phase II **Population Enumeration**: **February 2027**, reference date **00:00 hrs, 1 March 2027**.
xa: Snow-bound areas (**Ladakh, J&K, HP, Uttarakhand**): **17 Aug - 30 Sep 2026**, reference **1 Oct 2026**.
PE was advanced in poll-bound **UP, Punjab, Uttarakhand, Goa** and deferred in **Manipur** (**5 Sep 2026**).
Census 2011's reference date was also **1 March**.

58.s: How many questions were notified for Census 2027, and how many of them were new compared with Census 2011?
58.x: Forty questions were notified for Census 2027, including 13 new questions; Census 2011 had 29 questions.
58.tq: Pair two related figures and reject options that swap or alter one number.
xs: **40 and 13 respectively**: **40 questions** were notified (**14 Aug 2026**), **13** of them new — option **(2)**.
**Census 2011** had **29** questions.
xa: New questions include **digital literacy** and **bank accounts**.
The caste column is **open-ended**.
Census 2027 is the **first digital census**.

58.s:
Census 2027 is intended to provide the population base for which of the following?
1. Delimitation
2. Women's reservation
3. Replacement of the Census Act, 1948
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
58.x: Census 2027 will provide the population base for delimitation and women's reservation. It does not replace the Census Act, 1948.
58.tq: Find the unrelated legal proposition among two connected policy uses.
xs: Census 2027 gives the base for **delimitation** and **women's reservation** — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
It does not replace the **Census Act, 1948**, which remains the census's **legal basis**.
xa: **84th Amendment**: delimitation freeze till the first census after **2026**.
**106th Amendment, 2023** (Art. **334A**): **women's reservation**.
Southern states fear a **lower seat share** after delimitation.

58.s:
With reference to the constitutional provisions connected with Census 2027, consider the following statements:
1. The 84th Amendment is associated with the freeze on delimitation until the first census after 2026.
2. The 106th Amendment is associated with women's reservation.
3. Article 334A is connected with the women's reservation framework.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
58.x: The 84th Amendment is linked to the delimitation freeze, while the 106th Amendment and Article 334A are linked to the framework for women's reservation.
58.tq: Match each constitutional reference with its correct policy consequence.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
**84th Amendment**: seat freeze (on the **1971** census) till the **first census after 2026**.
**106th Amendment, 2023** and **Art. 334A**: **women's reservation**.
xa: The **42nd Amendment** began the delimitation freeze on the 1971 census.
Census legal basis: **Census Act, 1948**; **Union List Entry 69** (Art. **246**).
Census 2027's population base matters for delimitation.

58.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched regarding the Census Town criteria and status?
o: Male workers outside agriculture — At least 50 percent
Density threshold — At least 400 persons per square kilometre
58.x: The required proportion of male workers engaged outside agriculture is at least 75 percent, not 50 percent. The other three descriptions are correct.
58.tq: Find the altered threshold in a list of closely related criteria.
xs: **Male workers outside agriculture — at least 50 percent** is wrong — option **(2)**; the criterion is **>= 75%**.
The others are right: **population >= 5,000**, density **>= 400/sq km**, and a **village-status settlement**.
xa: Unchanged since **1981**.
The **RGI** will retain it for **Census 2027**.
**MoHUA** calls it outdated (**male bias, uniform thresholds**).

58.s: Which statement best reflects the position of Census Towns for Census 2027?
o: The Registrar General of India will discontinue the Census Town category completely.
The category will be converted into a statutory municipality in every case.
The category has been unchanged since 1951 and is accepted without criticism.
The Registrar General of India will retain the category, although the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs regards it as outdated.
58.x: The Registrar General of India is expected to retain the Census Town category for Census 2027, although the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs considers it outdated because of male bias and uniform thresholds.
58.tq: Separate the administrative decision to retain a category from the criticism of its criteria.
xs: The **RGI** will **retain** the Census Town category for **Census 2027**, though **MoHUA** calls it **outdated** — option **(4)**.
It has been **unchanged since 1981**, not 1951, and it is criticised for **male bias** and **uniform thresholds**.
xa: Criteria: **5,000** people, **75%** male non-farm workers, **400/sq km**.
The RGI decision was reported on **17 Sep 2026**.
The census is run by the **RG&CCI** under the **MHA**.

58.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the historical census sequence is correct?
o: The only decline in population occurred during 2001–11, and 2027 was the first synchronous census.
The only decline in population occurred during 1951–61, and 2011 was the first synchronous census.
The only decline in population occurred during 1911–21, and 1881 was the first synchronous census.
The only decline in population occurred during 1881–91, and 1872 was the first synchronous census.
58.x: The only population decline occurred during 1911–21. The first synchronous census was conducted in 1881.
58.tq: Combine two chronology facts and reject options that swap the event and date.
xs: The only decline came in **1911-21**, and **1881** was the **first synchronous census** — option **(3)**.
**1872** was the first census, but **non-synchronous**.
xa: ⚠ **1872** = first (**Mayo**); **1881** = first synchronous (**Ripon**).
1921 = **"Year of the Great Divide"**.
Last census held: **2011**.

58.s: Andhra Pradesh’s population growth rate fell from which figure to which figure, leading to the reported policy discussion on encouraging a third child?
58.x: Andhra Pradesh’s growth rate declined from 21.13 percent to 9.21 percent. The State subsequently offered incentives connected with having a third child.
58.tq: Read the direction of change correctly and distinguish State figures from the national figure.
xs: AP's growth fell from **21.13 percent** (**1981-91** peak) to **9.21 percent** (**2001-11**) — option **(2)**.
**17.70%** is **India's** 2001-11 growth, and **7.00%** is undivided AP's population share.
xa: AP's 2001-11 growth is about **half** India's.
AP now offers incentives for a **third child** (**May 2026**).
AP density **304 < 382** (India).

58.s: Which one of the following is identified as a major concern of southern States regarding delimitation after Census 2027?
o: Their geographical area may be reduced by constitutional amendment.
Their share of seats may decline because they controlled population growth more effectively.
Their density figures may be excluded from the Census.
They may lose all representation in the Lok Sabha.
58.x: Southern States, including Andhra Pradesh, fear a reduction in their seat share because delimitation based on population may disadvantage States that controlled population growth.
58.tq: Apply the demographic trend to its constitutional and political consequence.
xs: Southern states incl. **AP** fear their **seat share may fall** because they **controlled population growth** — option **(2)**.
The concern is seat share, not area, density data or total loss of representation.
xa: **UP, Bihar, MP, Rajasthan** grew faster than **Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, AP**.
**84th Amendment**: freeze till the first census after **2026**.

58.s: Which one of the following concerns has been raised by former officials regarding the population-enumeration process?
o: Possible links between NPR and NRC through the collection of parents’ details
Exclusion of all urban households from the enumeration
Abolition of the Registrar General’s office
Replacement of the Census by a purely agricultural survey
58.x: Former officials have expressed concern that details of parents may create possible links between the National Population Register and the National Register of Citizens.
58.tq: Identify the specific institutional relationship in a criticism-based question.
xs: Ex-officials fear **NPR-NRC links** through the collection of **parents' details** — option **(1)**.
No exclusion of urban households or abolition of the **RGI**'s office is mentioned.
xa: This concern was raised in **Sep 2026**.
Census 2027 also faces a **caste-method debate**.
The census is run by the **Registrar General and Census Commissioner** under the **MHA**.

59.s: Which one of the following is a positive check in Malthusian theory?
59.x: Famine, disease and war are positive checks because they raise the death rate. Moral restraint and late marriage are preventive checks that lower the birth rate.
59.tq: Separate checks that raise mortality from checks that reduce fertility.
xs: **Famine** is a **positive check** in Malthusian theory — so option **(3)** is correct.
Positive checks (**famine, disease, war**) work by **raising the death rate**.
**Late marriage** and **moral restraint** are **preventive checks**: they lower the **birth rate**, not raise deaths.
xa: **Malthus (1798)**: population grows **geometrically**, food **arithmetically**.
The APPSC-GS key ties the **overpopulation theory** to **Malthus**.
⚠ **Marxian view**: "overpopulation" is a product of **capitalism** (relative surplus population), not of nature.

59.s: Who propounded the theory presented in An Essay on the Principle of Population published in 1798?
59.x: T. R. Malthus propounded the population theory in An Essay on the Principle of Population, published in 1798.
59.tq: Match a classic work with its propounder.
xs: **T. R. Malthus** wrote **An Essay on the Principle of Population (1798)** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Paul Ehrlich** wrote **The Population Bomb (1968)**; **Warren Thompson** gave **demographic transition (1929)**; **Edwin Cannan** gave **optimum population**.
xa: Malthus: population in **geometric**, food in **arithmetic** progression (UPPSC 2024 asked these blanks).
**Positive checks**: famine, disease, war; **preventive checks**: moral restraint, late marriage.
**Frank Notestein** gave the formal **3-stage transition theory** (1940s-50s).

59.s: The Population Bomb, published in 1968, was written by:
59.x: Paul Ehrlich wrote The Population Bomb in 1968 and warned of famine resulting from overpopulation.
59.tq: Match a named work and date with its author.
xs: **The Population Bomb (1968)** was written by **Paul Ehrlich** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It warned of **mass famine** from **overpopulation**.
**Warren Thompson** = demographic transition (**1929**); **Frank Notestein** = formal 3-stage transition; **Edwin Cannan** = **optimum population**.
xa: **Malthus**'s **Essay on the Principle of Population** came out in **1798**.
⚠ Transition theory: **Thompson (1929)** first, **Notestein** formalised it in the **1940s-50s**.

59.s: The optimum population of a country is defined as the population size at which:
o: the birth rate equals the death rate
population density is uniform throughout the country
per-capita income is maximum for given resources and technology
59.x: Optimum population is the size at which per-capita income is maximum for the available resources and technology.
59.tq: Apply the definition to the economic outcome rather than confusing it with demographic balance or density.
xs: Optimum population is the size at which **per-capita income is maximum** — so option **(4)** is correct.
The concept is credited to **Edwin Cannan**.
Birth rate equal to death rate describes a **stationary** stage of demographic transition, not the optimum.
xa: **Malthus (1798)**: population **geometric**, food **arithmetic**.
**Paul Ehrlich**'s **The Population Bomb (1968)** warned of famine from overpopulation.
**Marxian view**: overpopulation stems from **capitalism**, via relative surplus population and unemployment.

59.s:
Assertion (A): In the Marxian view, overpopulation is not a product of nature alone.
Reason (R): It is regarded as a product of capitalism, expressed through relative surplus population and unemployment.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
59.x: Both statements are true, and the Marxian explanation of overpopulation as a product of capitalism, relative surplus population and unemployment directly explains the assertion.
59.tq: Test whether the reason directly explains the Marxian interpretation of overpopulation.
xs: **Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)**.
In the **Marxian view**, "overpopulation" is a product of **capitalism**, not of nature.
It shows up as **relative surplus population** and **unemployment** — exactly why it is not a natural fact (A).
xa: Contrast **Malthus (1798)**: overpopulation arises because population grows **geometrically** and food **arithmetically**.
Malthus's **positive checks** (famine, disease, war) raise the death rate.
**Edwin Cannan**: **optimum population** = size giving maximum per capita income.

59.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Theory or work)
a. Demographic transition theory
b. Formal three-stage transition theory
c. Optimum population
 d. The Population Bomb
List-II (Author)
i. Paul Ehrlich
ii. Edwin Cannan
iii. Warren Thompson
iv. Frank Notestein
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
59.x: Warren Thompson is associated with demographic transition theory, Frank Notestein with its formal three-stage formulation, Edwin Cannan with optimum population, and Paul Ehrlich with The Population Bomb.
59.tq: Begin with the distinctive Population Bomb–Ehrlich pair and verify the remaining matches.
xs: Correct code: **a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i** — option **(1)**.
**Demographic transition** — **Warren Thompson (1929)**; **formal three-stage** version — **Frank Notestein** (1940s-50s).
**Optimum population** — **Edwin Cannan**; **The Population Bomb (1968)** — **Paul Ehrlich**.
xa: **Malthus** wrote the **Essay on the Principle of Population (1798)**.
Notestein's idea: birth and death rates change with **economic development**.
The demographic transition has **5 stages**, from **high stationary** to **declining**.

59.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Frank Notestein — Formal three-stage transition theory
59.x: Optimum population theory is associated with Edwin Cannan. Thomas Malthus is associated with the Principle of Population and the overpopulation theory.
59.tq: Use the author-work mismatch trap to identify the incorrect pair.
xs: **Thomas Malthus — Optimum population theory** is wrongly matched — option **(4)**.
**Optimum population** belongs to **Edwin Cannan**; Malthus gave the **Principle of Population (1798)**.
The other pairs are right: **Ehrlich — Population Bomb (1968)**, **Thompson — transition (1929)**, **Notestein — formal 3-stage theory**.
xa: Malthus: population **geometric**, food **arithmetic**; positive and preventive **checks**.
APPSC-GS key: **overpopulation theory = Malthus**.
**Marxian view**: overpopulation is a product of **capitalism**.

59.s: According to Malthus's Essay on the Principle of Population (1798), population and food supply tend to grow respectively in:
59.x: Malthus held that population grows in geometric progression (1, 2, 4, 8...) while food supply grows only in arithmetic progression (1, 2, 3, 4...), so population outruns food. Option A reverses the two; C and D wrongly give both the same progression.
59.tq: Malthus: People Geometric, Food Arithmetic (UPPSC 2024).
xs: Population grows in **geometric** and food in **arithmetic progression** — option **(2)** is correct.
This is **Malthus's** argument in the **Essay on the Principle of Population (1798)**: population outruns food.
Option **(1)** reverses the two; options **(3)** and **(4)** give both the same progression.
xa: UPPSC 2024 asked these Malthusian blanks (**geometric, arithmetic**).
**Positive checks** (famine, disease, war) raise the death rate; **preventive checks** (moral restraint, late marriage) lower the birth rate.
⚠ **Optimum population** is **Edwin Cannan**'s idea, not Malthus's.

59.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched with Stage 2 of the demographic transition model?
o: High birth rate, falling death rate and population explosion — India, 1951–81
Low birth rate, low death rate and stable population — India, 1951–81
Very low birth rate, low death rate and declining population — India overall now
Falling birth rate, low death rate and slowing growth — pre-industrial society
59.x: Stage 2 is characterised by high but declining death rates, high birth rates and population explosion; India during 1951–81 is an example.
59.tq: Match the stage by checking all three elements: rates, growth pattern and example.
xs: Stage 2 (**Early expanding**) = **high birth rate, falling death rate, population explosion — India 1951–81** — option **(1)**.
**Low/low and stable** is **Stage 4** (example **AP**); **very low birth rate and declining** is **Stage 5**.
**Falling BR, low DR, slowing growth** is **Stage 3** (India overall now), not a **pre-industrial** society (Stage 1).
xa: **Stage 1**: **High stationary** — high BR, high DR, low growth.
**Stage 5** examples: **Japan, Germany** (birth rate below death rate).
Transition theory: **Thompson (1929)**, formalised by **Notestein**.

59.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched with the demographic transition stage indicated in the material?
59.x: India overall is placed in Stage 3, characterised by falling birth rates, low death rates and slowing growth. Andhra Pradesh is cited as a Stage 4 example, while Japan and Germany are in Stage 5.
59.tq: Use the country or region example to reject stage substitutions.
xs: **India overall now — Stage 3** (late expanding) is correctly matched — option **(3)**.
Stage 3 = **falling birth rate, low death rate, slowing growth**.
**AP** is the **Stage 4** example, and **Japan, Germany** are **Stage 5** (declining) — so options **(1)**, **(2)**, **(4)** are wrong.
xa: **Stage 2** (early expanding) example: **India 1951-81**, a population explosion.
**Stage 1** (high stationary) = **pre-industrial** societies.
**AP TFR 1.5** vs India **2.0** (SRS 2020) explains AP's advanced stage.

59.s:
Arrange the stages of demographic transition in the correct sequence:
A. Late expanding
B. Declining
C. High stationary
D. Low stationary
E. Early expanding
59.x: The sequence is high stationary, early expanding, late expanding, low stationary and declining.
59.tq: Use the progression of birth and death rates to order the stages.
xs: Correct order: **High stationary → Early expanding → Late expanding → Low stationary → Declining** = **C, E, A, D, B** — option **(1)**.
Stage **1** high/high; **2** high/falling; **3** falling/low; **4** low/low; **5** BR below DR.
xa: Examples: Stage 2 **India 1951-81**; Stage 3 **India overall now**; Stage 4 **AP**; Stage 5 **Japan, Germany**.
Growth is **low** in Stage 1, an **explosion** in Stage 2, **stable** in Stage 4, **declining** in Stage 5.
**Demographic winter**: fertility below **2.1** with an **inverted pyramid**.

59.s: Which of the following characterises the declining stage of demographic transition?
o: Falling birth rate and low death rate
High birth rate and falling death rate
High birth rate and high death rate
59.x: In the declining stage, the birth rate falls below the death rate, resulting in structural population decline.
59.tq: Focus on the defining relationship between birth and death rates.
xs: In the **declining stage** (Stage 5), the **birth rate falls below the death rate** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Falling BR and low DR** = Stage 3; **high BR and falling DR** = Stage 2; **high BR and high DR** = Stage 1.
xa: Stage 5 examples: **Japan, Germany**.
**Demographic winter**: persistent structural decline, fertility below **2.1**, **inverted pyramid**.
**Replacement level 2.1** keeps a population stable across generations.

59.s: “Demographic winter” refers to:
o: Persistent structural population decline associated with fertility below 2.1 and an inverted age pyramid
A phase of high birth and death rates caused by epidemics
Seasonal migration of elderly persons to warmer regions
A temporary fall in population during a severe winter season
59.x: Demographic winter denotes persistent structural decline, generally associated with fertility below 2.1 and an inverted population pyramid.
59.tq: Distinguish the demographic metaphor from a literal seasonal phenomenon.
xs: **Demographic winter** = **persistent structural decline**, fertility **below 2.1**, **inverted age pyramid** — option **(1)**.
It is not seasonal or temporary; it is a **structural** feature of very low fertility.
xa: **Replacement level 2.1**: population stays stable across generations.
**Demographic nightmare**: ES 2018-19 warning that the dividend is lost without **health, education, skills and jobs**.
**Shrinconomics**: AP Health Minister's warning (**1 Apr 2026**) on the "alarming" fall in fertility.

59.s: Which demographic feature characterised the British period in India?
o: Low birth rate, low death rate and rapid natural increase
High literacy and low mortality throughout the period
Low birth rate and absence of epidemics
High birth rate, high death rate, famines and epidemics
59.x: The British period was marked by high birth and death rates, frequent famines and epidemics, and generally poor demographic conditions.
59.tq: Identify the complete characteristic combination rather than one isolated feature.
xs: The British period had **high birth and death rates**, with **famines and epidemics** — option **(4)** is correct.
Annual growth was only about **0.19% (1891-1921)**.
A **decline** came in **1911-21**; **1921** is the "**great divide**".
xa: At independence, literacy was **18.33% (1951)** — male 27.2%, female 8.9%.
**Life expectancy** about **32 years (1951)**.
The **Sixth to Eighth Plans** kept up population-control efforts.

59.s: Which of the following correctly represents literacy in India in 1951?
59.x: In 1951, overall literacy was 18.33%, with male literacy at 27.2% and female literacy at 8.9%.
59.tq: Keep the overall, male and female figures in their correct order.
xs: **1951 literacy: overall 18.33%, male 27.2%, female 8.9%** — option **(1)** is correct.
The other options merely shuffle the same three figures.
xa: **Life expectancy** at independence was about **32 years (1951)**.
British period: **high birth and death rates**, famines and epidemics; growth about **0.19%** a year (1891-1921).
**1921** = the "**great divide**" of India's demographic history.

59.s: India's life expectancy at independence, around 1951, was approximately:
59.x: Life expectancy in India around 1951 was approximately 32 years.
59.tq: Select the historical estimate rather than a modern-life-expectancy distractor.
xs: India's **life expectancy** around **1951** was about **32 years** — option **(2)** is correct.
It reflects the legacy of the **British period**: high death rates, **famines and epidemics**.
xa: **1921** = "**great divide**"; decline in **1911-21**.
Today's **median age** is about **28**; it will reach **36 by 2036** and **40 by 2051**.

59.s: Which Plans continued population-control efforts in India?
59.x: Population-control efforts were continued during the Sixth, Seventh and Eighth Plans.
59.tq: Use the contiguous Plan range stated in the policy history.
xs: The **Sixth to Eighth Plans** kept up population-control efforts — option **(4)** is correct.
The backdrop was India's **Stage 2** population explosion (**1951-81**): high birth rate, falling death rate.
xa: The **Emergency (1975-77)** saw coercive **mass sterilisation**; the programme was renamed **Family Welfare** in **1977**.
A **1976** population policy followed the Emergency drive.
**Female sterilisation** is the dominant method: **37.9%** of married women (NFHS-5).

59.s: Which Census year is known as the 'great divide' in India's demographic history?
59.x: Population declined during 1911-21; after 1921 it grew continuously, so 1921 is called the 'great divide'. 1901 and 1911 lie in the earlier phase of slow growth (about 0.19% a year, 1891-1921), and 1951 is the first Census after independence.
59.tq: 1921 = great divide: decline before, steady rise after.
xs: **1921** is the "**great divide**" — option **(3)** is correct.
Population **declined in 1911-21**; after 1921 it grew continuously.
**1901** and **1911** fall in the slow-growth phase (about **0.19%** a year, **1891-1921**); **1951** is the first post-independence point (literacy **18.33%**).
xa: British period: **high birth and death rates**, **famines and epidemics**.
Life expectancy at independence: about **32 years (1951)**.

59.s: The term 'demographic dividend' refers to the growth potential arising when:
o: the proportion of dependants exceeds the working-age population
the elderly population becomes larger than the child population
the death rate exceeds the birth rate
the share of the working-age population rises relative to dependants
59.x: Demographic dividend refers to the growth potential created when the working-age share rises relative to the dependent population.
59.tq: Choose the precise definition rather than a reversed comparison.
xs: Demographic dividend = growth potential when **the share of the working-age population rises relative to dependants** — option **(4)**.
**UNFPA**: the **working-age share (15-64)** exceeds the non-working share (**0-14 and 65+**).
More dependants, older-than-child populations, or deaths exceeding births do not create a dividend.
xa: APPSC-G2 2017 key: "a rise in economic growth due to a rise in the **share of working people**".
Channels: more **labour supply**, **higher savings and investment**, lower **dependency ratio**, freed human capital.
**Demographic nightmare** (ES 2018-19): dividend lost without **health, education, skills and jobs**.

59.s: Which age group is generally used to define the working-age population for measuring the demographic dividend?
59.x: The UNFPA definition uses the 15–64 age group. Indian projections often use 15–59 years for specific estimates.
59.tq: Discriminate between closely related age-group conventions.
xs: The dividend's working-age group is **15–64 years** — option **(4)** is correct.
This is the **UNFPA/ILO** definition, keyed by **APPSC-G1 2022** and **APPSC-GS 2019**.
**15–59** is used in **Indian projections**; **0–14** is the dependent child group.
xa: ES 2018-19 used **20-59** for its peak estimate (**59%** about **2041**).
Non-working share = **0-14 and 65+**.

59.s: In Indian demographic projections, the working-age group is often taken as:
59.x: Although the UNFPA definition uses 15–64 years, Indian projections often use 15–59 years.
59.tq: Test a familiar pair by identifying the convention used in Indian projections.
xs: **Indian projections** often take the working-age group as **15–59 years** — option **(2)** is correct.
The **UNFPA/ILO** definition (asked by APPSC) is **15-64**, not used exclusively in India.
xa: ES 2025-26: about **65%** aged 15-59 at a peak about **2030**.

59.s: Which one of the following is NOT a usual channel through which demographic dividend can promote economic growth?
o: Increase in the proportion of dependants
59.x: Demographic dividend can operate through greater labour supply, higher savings and investment, a lower dependency ratio and the release of human capital. An increase in dependants works in the opposite direction.
59.tq: Find the option that reverses the direction of the demographic effect.
xs: An **increase in the proportion of dependants** is NOT a dividend channel — option **(2)**.
The channels are **more labour supply**, **higher savings and investment**, a **lower dependency ratio** and **freed human capital**.
More dependants raise the dependency ratio, working against the dividend.
xa: Dividend arises when working-age (**15-64**) exceeds non-working (**0-14 and 65+**).
**Demographic nightmare**: without **health, education, skills and jobs**, the dividend is lost (ES 2018-19).

59.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the demographic dividend window is correct?
o: It opens simultaneously in all States.
It is determined only by the old-age dependency ratio.
It opens at different times in different States.
It ends as soon as the birth rate begins to decline.
59.x: The demographic dividend window opens at different times in different States because their demographic transitions occur at different rates.
59.tq: Reject the absolute statement and identify the correct regional comparison.
xs: The dividend window **opens at different times in different States** — option **(3)** is correct.
**UNFPA**: India has the **longest window** in the world, five decades, **2005-06 to 2055-56**.
The **RBI** study shows the spread: **Kerala and Tamil Nadu** have crossed the turning point, while **Bihar, UP** have a wider window.
xa: MoHFW: the window closes **after 2041**.
⚠ Peak year differs: **2041** (ES 2018-19, MoHFW) vs **2030** (ES 2025-26).

59.s:
Consider the following statements about the estimated peak of India's demographic dividend:
1. The Economic Survey 2018-19 placed the peak around 2041, with about 59% of the population aged 20-59.
2. The Economic Survey 2025-26, using UN projections, placed the peak around 2030, with about 65% aged 15-59.
3. Both Economic Surveys placed the peak of the demographic dividend around 2041.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
59.x: Statement 1 is correct: ES 2018-19 put the peak about 2041 with 59% aged 20-59. Statement 2 is correct: ES 2025-26 (UN projections) put the peak about 2030 with about 65% aged 15-59. Statement 3 is wrong: the two Surveys differ (2041 vs about 2030). So A is right; B omits statement 1; C and D wrongly include statement 3.
xs: Statements **1 and 2 only** are correct — option **(1)**.

60.s: Which of the following represents the broad trend in India's child sex ratio during the period covered by the Census figures?

60.tq: Match the institution with the issue on which its intervention is specifically identified.
xs: The SC intervention concerns **PCPNDT implementation** and **male-child bias** — option **(2)** (**13 Jun 2026**).
Justices **Sanjay Karol and P.K. Mishra**: CSR shows "**clear signs of improvement**" but bias is "**deep-seated**".
xa: PCPNDT: tests only for **genetic/chromosomal abnormalities**; machines registered.
Also current: **CRS 2024** SRB **917**, registration above **99%**.

60.s: Which of the following correctly compares the cited Andhra Pradesh and India figures?
o: India has a higher sex ratio and a higher child sex ratio than Andhra Pradesh.
Andhra Pradesh has a higher sex ratio but a lower child sex ratio than India.
Andhra Pradesh has both a higher sex ratio and a higher child sex ratio than India.
Both Andhra Pradesh figures are below the corresponding Indian figures.
60.x: Andhra Pradesh is cited at 997 for sex ratio and 944 for child sex ratio, compared with India’s 943 and 918 respectively; both State values are higher.
60.tq: Test whether both columns in a comparison move in the same direction.
xs: **AP has both a higher sex ratio and a higher child sex ratio** than India — option **(3)**.
AP **997** vs India **943** (sex ratio); AP **944** vs India **918** (CSR).
xa: **AP ST** sex ratio **1,009**.
28-district recast: **Polavaram (1,051)** highest, **Markapuram (962)** lowest.

60.s: Which one of the following statements best explains why the CRS, SRS and Census figures should be compared cautiously?
o: They use identical definitions but different State boundaries.
They measure only the urban population.
They are all household surveys conducted in the same year.
They use different bases of measurement.
60.x: CRS, SRS and Census figures use different bases, so comparisons should be made like with like.
60.tq: Identify the methodological qualification rather than comparing figures mechanically.
xs: **CRS, SRS and Census use different bases** — option **(4)**; compare like with like.
E.g. SRB: **CRS 2024 917** vs **SRS 2022-24 918**; CRS and SRS rank **Nagaland** very differently.
xa: **NFHS-5 (1,020)** is a **household survey**, not comparable with **Census 943**.

60.s:
With reference to NFHS-5 and Census 2011, consider the following statements:
1. NFHS-5 reported a sex ratio of 1,020.
2. NFHS-5 is a household survey rather than a census.
3. The NFHS-5 figure is directly comparable with the Census figure of 943 without qualification.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
60.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because the household-survey estimate of 1,020 is not directly comparable with the Census figure of 943.
60.tq: Use the source-type distinction to reject an apparently straightforward numerical comparison.
xs: Statements **1 and 2 only** — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: NFHS-5 sex ratio **1,020**.
Statement 2 correct: NFHS-5 is a **household survey**, not a census.
Statement 3 wrong: it is **not directly comparable** with **Census 943**.
xa: NFHS-5 = first NFHS with **more women than men**; NFHS-4 was **991**.
NFHS-5: rural **1,037**, urban **985**.

61.s: According to the Census definition, a literate person is one who:
o: is aged seven years or above and can both read and write with understanding in any language
is aged five years or above and can read and write without understanding
is aged ten years or above and has completed primary education
is aged seven years or above and can only read in any language
61.x: A literate person is aged seven years or above and must be able to both read and write with understanding in any language. A person who can only read is not treated as literate.
61.tq: Use the exact official definition and distinguish ‘read and write with understanding’ from merely reading.
xs: Census literate = aged **7 and above** who can **both read and write with understanding** in any language — option **(1)**.
One who can **only read** is **not literate** — so option **(4)** fails.
Age **5+** was used only in **1951-1971**; completing primary school is not part of the test.
xa: Age **7+** has been used since **1981**.
**ULLAS** full literacy = **95%+** among those aged **15+**.
**PLFS** uses the same **7+** definition, but on a sample survey.

61.s: The age threshold of seven years for measuring literacy in the Indian Census was introduced from:
61.x: Censuses from 1951 to 1971 counted literacy for persons aged five years and above. The seven-years-and-above threshold was adopted from 1981.
61.tq: For close historical figures, identify the year marking the change rather than the years preceding it.
xs: The **7+** threshold was adopted from **1981** — option **(4)** is correct.
Censuses **1951-1971** counted literacy for ages **5+**.
xa: Literate = can **both read and write with understanding**; reading alone does not count.
⚠ Census and PLFS (both **7+**) are still **not comparable** — different samples.

61.s: In 1951, the proportion of women who were literate in India was:
61.x: Female literacy in 1951 was 8.9%, meaning that fewer than one in ten women were literate.
61.tq: Convert the percentage into the comparative expression used in the question.
xs: In **1951**, **less than one in ten** women were literate — option **(1)** is correct.
xa: Overall literacy **1951**: **18.33%**.
Male literacy: about **27% → 82%** in **60 years**.

61.s:
Arrange the following Census years in ascending order of India’s literacy rate:
A. 1951
B. 1981
C. 1961
D. 2001
61.x: The literacy rates rose from 18.33% in 1951 to 28.30% in 1961, 43.57% in 1981 and 64.83% in 2001. Therefore, the order is A, C, B, D.
61.tq: Arrange the years by the steadily increasing literacy percentages, not merely by visual year spacing.
xs: Literacy has risen at **every Census** since 1951.
xa: Largest decadal gain: the **1990s**.

61.s:
Consider the following statements about India’s literacy trend:
1. Literacy increased from 18.33% in 1951 to 74.04% in 2011.
2. Male literacy rose from about 27% to about 82% over the sixty-year period.
3. The largest decadal gain occurred during 2001–2011.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
61.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because the largest decadal gain occurred in the 1990s, while growth slowed in 2001–2011.
61.tq: Identify the false trend statement by testing the claimed decade against the stated growth pattern.
xs: Statements **1 and 2 only** — option **(1)**.
Statement 2 correct: male literacy about **27% → 82%** in **60 years**.
Statement 3 wrong: the largest gain was in the **1990s**; growth **slowed** in 2001-11.
xa: Women: less than **1 in 10** literate (1951) → **2 in 3** (2011).
Growth slowed in 2001-11 in **AP** as well.

61.s: In which inter-Census decade did India record its largest increase in literacy rate?
61.x: Literacy rose from 52.21% (1991) to 64.83% (2001), a gain of about 12.6 points, the largest of any decade. 1971-81 added about 9.1 points (34.45 to 43.57), 1981-91 about 8.6 points (43.57 to 52.21), and 2001-11 about 9.2 points (64.83 to 74.04), when growth slowed.
61.tq: Biggest literacy jump = the 1990s (1991-2001).
xa: The **National Literacy Mission** (**5 May 1988**) and **TLC** preceded this decade.

61.s:
With reference to the provisional Census 2011 literacy figures, consider the following statements:
1. Male literacy was 82.14%.
2. Female literacy was 65.46%.
3. The total literacy rate was 73.0%.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
61.x: The provisional figures were 82.14% for males and 65.46% for females. The total provisional figure was 74.04%, whereas 73.0% refers to the final figure.
61.tq: Separate provisional and final values before selecting the coded combination.
xs: Statements **1 and 2 only** — option **(1)**.
Provisional 2011: male **82.14%**, female **65.46%**.
Statement 3 wrong: the **provisional** total was **74.04%**; **73.0%** is the **final** figure.
xa: APPSC-GS 2023 key used **74.04%**.

61.s: The final Census 2011 literacy rate of India, as cited in the India Year Book, was approximately:
61.x: The final Census 2011 literacy rate was 73.0%, or 72.98% when expressed more precisely.
61.tq: Choose the rounded final value rather than the provisional or survey-based figures.
xs: Final Census 2011 literacy (IYB): **73.0%** (**72.98%**) — option **(3)**.
xa: Provisional figure: **74.04%** (most quoted).
Final male **80.9%**, female **64.6%**.

61.s: The literacy rate of India in 2001 was approximately:
61.x: India’s literacy rate in 2001 was 64.8% according to the cited India Year Book figure.
61.tq: Match the decade with its corresponding national literacy percentage.
xa: 1990s = **largest** decadal gain.

61.s:
Consider the following statements about the gender gap in literacy in India:
1. The national gender gap in literacy in Census 2011 was about 16 percentage points.
2. Rajasthan had the largest gender gap in 2011, about 28 percentage points.
3. By PLFS 2023-24 the national gender gap had widened to more than 20 percentage points.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
61.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: the 2011 national gap was 16 points and Rajasthan's was the largest at 28 points. Statement 3 is wrong: PLFS 2023-24 shows the gap narrowed to about 12.6 points (87.2 vs 74.6). So '1 only' misses statement 2, while '2 and 3 only' and '1, 2 and 3' wrongly include statement 3.
61.tq: Gap 16 nationally (2011), 28 in Rajasthan; it narrowed, not widened, by 2023-24.
xs: Statements **1 and 2 only** — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: national gap **16 percentage points** (2011).
Statement 2 correct: **Rajasthan** largest, **28 points**.
Statement 3 wrong: PLFS 2023-24 gap **narrowed** to about **12.6 points** (**87.2 vs 74.6**).
xa: Causes: **distance to schools + safety**, **early marriage**, **dowry**, **son preference**, **poverty**.
NSS 2017-18: lowest female literacy = **Rajasthan**.

61.s: Which of the following is NOT cited as a cause of the gender gap in literacy?
o: High concentration of specialised universities in cities
Distance to schools and safety concerns
61.x: The cited causes include distance to schools and safety, early marriage, dowry, son preference and poverty. Concentration of specialised universities in cities is not listed as a cause.
61.tq: Find the unrelated addition among a cluster of recognised social causes.
xs: **Concentration of specialised universities in cities** is not a cited cause — option **(2)**.
Causes cited: **distance to schools + safety**, **early marriage**, **dowry**, **son preference**, **poverty**.
xa: Gender gap: **16 points** (2011) → about **12.6** (PLFS 2023-24).
Largest deficit: **rural women**.
Higher-education female GER (**30.2**) is now **above male**.

61.s: According to Census 2011 provisional figures, the rural and urban literacy rates of India were respectively:
61.x: The Census 2011 provisional rural literacy rate was 68.9%, while the urban rate was 85.0%.
61.tq: Match the pair to the correct data source and distinguish Census figures from PLFS figures.
xs: Census 2011 (provisional): rural **68.9%**, urban **85.0%** — option **(4)**.
**77.5% / 88.9%** are the **PLFS 2023-24** rural/urban figures.
xa: Gap still about **11 points** in PLFS 2023-24.
Largest deficit: **rural women**.

61.s: Under PLFS 2023-24, the urban-rural literacy figures for India were approximately:
61.x: PLFS 2023-24 reported urban literacy of 88.9% and rural literacy of 77.5%, leaving a gap of about 11 percentage points.
61.tq: Keep the urban-rural order fixed and distinguish it from the male-female pair.
xs: **87.2 / 74.6** are the **male/female** figures; **85.0 / 68.9** are Census 2011 urban/rural.
xa: Gap still about **11 points**.

61.s: Which section of the population faces the largest literacy deficit in the rural-urban context?
61.x: Rural women face the largest literacy deficit. Rural areas also have lower literacy overall than urban areas.
61.tq: Apply the combined rural disadvantage and gender disadvantage to identify the most vulnerable group.
xs: **Rural women** face the largest literacy deficit — option **(3)** is correct.
Rural literacy lags urban (**68.9% vs 85.0%**, Census 2011), and women lag men.
xa: Gender gap 2011: **16 points**; largest in **Rajasthan (28)**.

61.s: Under PLFS 2023-24, India’s literacy rate for persons aged seven years and above was:
61.x: PLFS 2023-24 reported an overall literacy rate of 80.9% for persons aged seven years and above. The urban rate was 88.9%.
61.tq: Distinguish the overall survey rate from its urban component and from Census figures.
xa: **AP** in PLFS 2023-24: **72.6%** — among the **bottom** three.

61.s: Which one of the following correctly states the PLFS 2023-24 male-female literacy figures for India?
61.x: PLFS 2023-24 recorded male literacy of 87.2% and female literacy of 74.6%. Their difference was about 12.6 percentage points.
61.tq: Separate the male-female pair from the overall and urban-rural pairs in the same survey.
xs: **82.14 / 65.46** are Census 2011 **provisional**; **88.9 / 77.5** are PLFS **urban/rural**.
xa: Gap about **12.6 points** — down from **16** in 2011.
Overall **80.9%**.

61.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Bihar — 94.0% total literacy and 92.1% female literacy
Kerala — 94.0% total literacy and 92.1% female literacy
61.x: Kerala recorded 94.0% total literacy and 92.1% female literacy. Bihar had the lowest total literacy at 61.8% and female literacy at 51.5%.
61.tq: Check both components of each pair; APPSC commonly swaps values between high- and low-ranking units.
xs: **Kerala — 94.0% total, 92.1% female** — option **(4)** is correct.
**Bihar** is the **lowest** (**61.8%**, female **51.5%**); **Lakshadweep** is **91.8%**.
xa: Kerala male **96.1%**; **Mizoram** **91.3%** (third).
Provisional data had **Rajasthan** lowest in female literacy (**52.7%**).

61.s: Which one of the following had the lowest total literacy rate among the States in Census 2011?
61.x: Bihar had the lowest total literacy rate among the States, at 61.8%.
61.tq: Distinguish the lowest State in the Census ranking from later survey-based rankings.
xs: **Bihar** had the lowest literacy in Census 2011: **61.8%** — option **(4)**.
Bihar male **71.2%**, female **51.5%**.
xa: ⚠ Lowest: **Bihar** (Census 2011 final) vs **AP** (NSS 2017-18, PLFS bottom list).
Highest: **Kerala 94.0%**.

61.s: Lakshadweep occupied which position in the Census 2011 literacy ranking mentioned in the material?
61.x: Lakshadweep was second, with a literacy rate of 91.8%, after Kerala’s 94.0%.
61.tq: Use the ranking and the exact percentage together to discriminate between close alternatives.
xs: **Lakshadweep** was **second**, with **91.8%** — option **(3)**.
**Kerala 94.0%** first; **Mizoram 91.3%** third; **Bihar 61.8%** last.
xa: PLFS 2023-24 top: **Mizoram, Lakshadweep, Nagaland**.
Kerala female literacy **92.1%** — highest.

61.s: According to the NSS 75th round for July 2017–June 2018, which State was placed lowest among the States in literacy?
61.x: The NSS 75th round placed Andhra Pradesh lowest among the States. Its female literacy was approximately 59.5%; Rajasthan, not Uttar Pradesh, had the lowest female literacy in the cited comparison.
61.tq: Distinguish the State with the lowest overall literacy from the State with the lowest female literacy.
xs: **NSS 75th round (2017-18)** placed **Andhra Pradesh** lowest among states — option **(4)** (APPSC-GS 2022 key).
India **77.7%**; **AP female literacy about 59.5%**.
Lowest **female** literacy was **Rajasthan**, not UP.
xa: PLFS 2023-24 bottom: **Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh**.
⚠ Census 2011 lowest = **Bihar**.

61.s: Which of the following was the PLFS-based literacy ranking pattern cited for 2023-24?
o: Top: Kerala, Goa, Mizoram; bottom: Bihar, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh
Top: Mizoram, Lakshadweep, Nagaland; bottom: Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh
Top: Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh; bottom: Mizoram, Lakshadweep, Nagaland
Top: Kerala, Lakshadweep, Bihar; bottom: Andhra Pradesh, Rajasthan, Goa
61.x: The PLFS-based top units were Mizoram, Lakshadweep and Nagaland, while Andhra Pradesh, Bihar and Madhya Pradesh were at the bottom of the cited grouping.
61.tq: Match the complete top-bottom grouping rather than relying on one familiar high-literacy State.
xs: PLFS 2023-24: top **Mizoram, Lakshadweep, Nagaland**; bottom **Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh** — option **(2)**.
Option **(3)** simply reverses the two lists.

61.s:
Consider the following statements about the NSS 75th round (July 2017-June 2018) on literacy:
1. India's literacy rate was 77.7%.
2. Uttar Pradesh had the lowest female literacy among the States.
3. Andhra Pradesh's female literacy was about 59.5%.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
61.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct: the round put India at 77.7% and AP's female literacy at about 59.5% (AP was lowest overall). Statement 2 is the APPSC-GS 2022 trap: the lowest female literacy was in Rajasthan, not UP. So options C and D (which include 2) are wrong, and A misses statement 3.
61.tq: NSS 75th: AP lowest overall; Rajasthan (not UP) lowest female.
xs: Statements **1 and 3 only** — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: India **77.7%**.
Statement 2 wrong: lowest female literacy = **Rajasthan**, not UP (APPSC-GS 2022 trap).
Statement 3 correct: **AP female literacy about 59.5%**.
xa: AP was **lowest** among states in this round.
Census 2011 AP female literacy: **59.96%**.

61.s: Which one of the following correctly states the literacy rates of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in 2011?
61.x: The cited 2011 literacy rate was 66.1% for Scheduled Castes and 59.0% for Scheduled Tribes. Both were below the national literacy level of about 73–74%.
61.tq: Keep the social-category labels attached to the correct percentages and avoid confusing national and State figures.
xs: Both are below the national **73-74%**.
xa: Some notes give SC **66.4%**.

61.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Andhra Pradesh ST literacy — 48.8%; Telangana ST literacy — 49.5%
Andhra Pradesh ST literacy — 59.0%; Telangana ST literacy — 66.1%
Andhra Pradesh SC literacy — 48.8%; Telangana SC literacy — 49.5%
Andhra Pradesh ST literacy — 73.0%; Telangana ST literacy — 74.6%
61.x: The cited figures were 48.8% for Scheduled Tribe literacy in Andhra Pradesh and 49.5% in Telangana.
61.tq: Start with the sure State-category pair and reject options that substitute national or SC values.
xs: **AP ST literacy 48.8%**; **Telangana ST 49.5%** — option **(1)**.
**59.0%** is India's ST and **66.1%** India's SC literacy.
xa: Low literacy is one of the four **PVTG** criteria.
Literacy gap is widest in tribal **ASR** district (**Alluri Sitarama Raju**, **44.67%**).

61.s: Low literacy is recognised as one of the four criteria for identifying:
61.x: Low literacy is one of the four criteria used in relation to Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs).
61.tq: Link the social indicator to the exact administrative category rather than a broader population group.
xs: Low literacy is one of the **four criteria** for **Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs)** — option **(2)**.
ST literacy (**59%**, 2011) lags India's **73%**.
xa: **AP ST** literacy only **48.8%**.
AP's lowest-literacy district: tribal **Alluri Sitarama Raju (44.67%)**.

61.s: Which of the following correctly gives the literacy trend of Andhra Pradesh from 1981 to 2011?
61.x: The Andhra Pradesh sequence was 29.94% in 1981, 45.86% in 1991, 62.07% in 2001 and 67.35% in 2011.
61.tq: Use a complete State-specific sequence and reject options that substitute national or gender figures.
xs: Options **(2)** and **(3)** give **India's** figures.
xa: Rise of over **37 points**; best decade **1990s** (APSES 2024-25).

61.s: The total literacy rate of Andhra Pradesh in Census 2011 was:
o: higher than the national average by more than five points
higher than the national average by more than ten points
61.x: Andhra Pradesh recorded 67.35% literacy in Census 2011, below India’s national figure of about 72.98%.
61.tq: Use the direction of the comparison before considering the numerical values.
xs: AP's **67.35%** (2011) is **below the national average** (**72.98%**) — option **(1)**.
NSS 2017-18 even placed AP **lowest** among states (APPSC-GS 2022 key).
xa: ⚠ Minister's claim of **82.10%** for 2026 is disputed — no official estimate.

61.s: Among the 28 districts of Andhra Pradesh, as per the 2011 data recast in the CDI AP Survey 2025–26, which district recorded the highest literacy rate?
61.x: Visakhapatnam recorded the highest literacy rate among the 28 districts, at 79.05%.
61.tq: Use the district-ranking trap by distinguishing the 28-district figures from the earlier 13-district Census grouping.
xs: **Visakhapatnam** (**79.05%**) is highest among the **28 districts** — option **(4)**.
**West Godavari** topped the **13-district** era; **Alluri Sitarama Raju (44.67%)** is lowest in the 28-district map.
xa: 13-district lowest: **Vizianagaram (58.9%)**.
District data: **APSES Annexure 8.4**.

61.s: In the 13-district structure of Andhra Pradesh, which district had the highest literacy rate according to Census 2011?
61.x: In the 13-district era, West Godavari had the highest literacy rate, at 74.6%.
61.tq: Apply the confusable-pair method to distinguish the 13-district and 28-district rankings.
xs: 13-district era: **West Godavari** highest (**74.6%**) — option **(3)**.
**Visakhapatnam** tops only the **28-district** recast (**79.05%**).
xa: Lowest 13-district: **Vizianagaram (58.9%)**.
Female literacy above India's **64.63%**: **West Godavari, Krishna, East Godavari**.

61.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the lowest literacy rate in the 13-district era of Andhra Pradesh as per Census 2011?
61.x: Vizianagaram recorded the lowest literacy rate in the 13-district era, at 58.9%.
61.tq: Match the correct district with the correct historical district grouping and percentage.
xs: 13-district era lowest: **Vizianagaram — 58.9%** — option **(2)**.
**74.6%** belongs to **West Godavari** (highest); **Alluri Sitarama Raju 44.67%** is the 28-district lowest.
xa: 28-district highest: **Visakhapatnam 79.05%**.

61.s: Which of the following correctly gives the literacy rates of Andhra Pradesh according to Census 2011?
61.x: Andhra Pradesh recorded total literacy of 67.35%, male literacy of 74.77% and female literacy of 59.96% in 2011.
61.tq: Match the three state values in the correct total-male-female order.
xs: **72.98 / 80.88 / 64.63** are **India's** final figures.
xa: NSS 2017-18 AP female: about **59.5%**.

61.s: Which of the following correctly represents the lowest literacy rate in the 28-district map of Andhra Pradesh?
61.x: Alluri Sitarama Raju recorded the lowest literacy rate, at 44.67%, in the 28-district map.
61.tq: Check both the district name and the numerical value in the matched pair.
xs: 28-district lowest: **Alluri Sitarama Raju — 44.67%** — option **(3)**.
**Vizianagaram** was lowest in the **13-district** era (**58.9%**); **59.96%** is AP's female literacy.
xa: Highest: **Visakhapatnam 79.05%**.
AP **ST** literacy: **48.8%**.

61.s: Kottayam is associated with which of the following distinctions in the field of literacy campaigns?
o: India's first totally literate district in 1990
The first Union Territory to achieve full literacy in 2024
India's first fully literate town in 1989
The first state to achieve full literacy in 2025
61.x: Kottayam was the first fully literate town in 1989. Ernakulam was declared India's first totally literate district in 1990.
61.tq: Use the town–district distinction to separate closely related firsts.
xs: **Kottayam** = India's **first fully literate town (1989)** — option **(3)**.
**Ernakulam** = first totally literate **district (1990)**; **Ladakh** first UT (**2024**); **Mizoram** first state (**2025**).
xa: Ernakulam was the first successful **Total Literacy Campaign**.
TLC was the main strategy of the **NLM** (**5 May 1988**).

61.s: The National Literacy Mission was launched on:
61.x: The National Literacy Mission was launched on 5 May 1988, and the Total Literacy Campaign was its principal mass-campaign strategy.
61.tq: Distinguish the launch dates of successive adult-literacy programmes.
xs: **National Literacy Mission**: **5 May 1988** — option **(1)**.
**2 Oct 1978** = **NAEP**; **8 Sep 2009** = **Saakshar Bharat**; **5 Nov 2024** = AP ULLAS classes began.
xa: NLM aimed at **functional literacy**; its mass strategy was the **TLC**.
⚠ NAEP = age **15-35**; Saakshar Bharat and ULLAS = **15+**.

61.s: The principal mass-campaign strategy of the National Literacy Mission was:
61.x: The Total Literacy Campaign was the main mass-campaign strategy adopted under the National Literacy Mission.
61.tq: Identify the strategy associated with the correct mission rather than its successor schemes.
xs: The **Total Literacy Campaign** was NLM's main mass-campaign strategy — option **(2)**.
**ULLAS** began in **2022**; **Operation Blackboard (1987)** was a school-facilities scheme.
xa: First TLC district: **Ernakulam (Kerala)**, **1990**.
**Kottayam**: first fully literate town (**1989**).

61.s: Saakshar Bharat was launched on which occasion and primarily targeted which group?
o: International Literacy Day; adults aged 15 years and above, with focus on women
Republic Day; school children below 14 years
Gandhi Jayanti; farmers aged 18 years and above
61.x: Saakshar Bharat was launched on 8 September 2009, International Literacy Day, for adults aged 15 years and above, with special focus on women.
61.tq: Combine the date, occasion and target group to avoid scheme-name confusion.
xs: **Saakshar Bharat**: launched on **International Literacy Day** (**8 Sep 2009**) for adults **15+**, focus on **women** — option **(1)**.
Unlike **NAEP** (age **15-35**), it covered all adults aged **15+**.
xa: International Literacy Day: **UNESCO** day since **1966**, first observed **1967**.
**ULLAS** (**2022**) also targets non-literates aged **15+**.
ILD **8 Sep 2026** theme: "**Literacy for people, the planet and prosperity**".

61.s:
Arrange the following literacy programmes in chronological order of their commencement:
A. Saakshar Bharat
B. National Adult Education Programme
C. National Literacy Mission
D. Farmers' Functional Literacy Programme
61.x: The correct sequence is Farmers' Functional Literacy Programme (1967-68), National Adult Education Programme (1978), National Literacy Mission (1988), and Saakshar Bharat (2009).
61.tq: Place the earliest and latest programmes first, then arrange the two middle dates.
xs: Order: **Farmers' Functional Literacy (1967-68)** → **NAEP (1978)** → **NLM (1988)** → **Saakshar Bharat (2009)** = **D, B, C, A** — option **(1)**.
**TLC** (**1989-90**) came under the NLM, between NLM and Saakshar Bharat.
xa: **Operation Blackboard**: **1987**, under **NPE 1986**.

61.s: Which district became India's first totally literate district in 1990 through the Total Literacy Campaign?
61.x: Ernakulam (Kerala) was the first district where the Total Literacy Campaign succeeded, declared totally literate in 1990. Kottayam was the first fully literate town (1989), not district; Thiruvananthapuram and Alappuzha hold neither 'first'.
61.tq: First literate town Kottayam (1989); first district Ernakulam (1990).
xs: **Ernakulam (Kerala)** — first totally literate district, **1990**, via the **TLC** — option **(2)**.
**Kottayam** was the first fully literate **town** (**1989**), not district.
xa: ULLAS firsts: UT **Ladakh (2024)**; state **Mizoram (2025)**.
**Kerala** tops state literacy: **94.0%** (2011).

61.s: ULLAS is the abbreviated name of which programme?
o: Universal Literacy and Learning Assessment Scheme
Unified Learning and Language Advancement System
Understanding of Lifelong Learning for All in Society
Union Literacy Linkage and Adult Schooling
61.x: ULLAS stands for Understanding of Lifelong Learning for All in Society. It is also known as the Nav Bharat Saaksharta Karyakram or New India Literacy Programme.
61.tq: Test the exact official expansion against plausible look-alike expansions.
xs: **ULLAS** = **Understanding of Lifelong Learning for All in Society** — option **(3)**.
Also called **Nav Bharat Saaksharta Karyakram** / **New India Literacy Programme**.
xa: Motto: "**Jan Jan Saakshar**".
Outlay **₹1,037.90 crore** (Centre **₹700 crore**; States **₹337.90 crore**).
About **2.43 crore** adults enrolled.

61.s:
With reference to ULLAS or the New India Literacy Programme, consider the following statements:
1. It was introduced in 2022 under the Budget 2021-22.
2. Its implementation period is from 2022-23 to 2026-27.
3. It is a Centrally Sponsored Scheme under the Ministry of Education.
4. It is meant exclusively for learners below 15 years of age.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
61.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is false because ULLAS targets non-literates aged 15 years and above.
61.tq: Reject the extreme age restriction and verify the scheme’s year, tenure and ministry.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3 only** — option **(1)**.
ULLAS: launched **2022** (**Budget 2021-22**); runs **2022-23 to 2026-27**; **Centrally Sponsored Scheme** under the **Ministry of Education**.
Statement 4 wrong: it targets non-literates aged **15 and above**.
xa: It is **volunteer-based**; full literacy = **95%+**.
Five components: **FLN**, **critical life skills**, **basic education**, **vocational skills**, **continuing education**.

61.s: Which of the following is NOT a component of ULLAS?
o: Compulsory residential schooling for children below six years
61.x: ULLAS includes Foundational Literacy and Numeracy, Critical Life Skills, Basic Education, Vocational Skills and Continuing Education. Compulsory residential schooling for young children is not one of its components.
61.tq: Find the option outside the scheme’s adult-education framework.
xs: **Compulsory residential schooling for children below six** is NOT a ULLAS component — option **(2)**.
The five components: **FLN**, **critical life skills**, **basic education (equivalency)**, **vocational skills**, **continuing education**.
ULLAS serves adults **15+**, not young children.
xa: About **90%** pass rate in **FLNAT**.
Motto: "**Jan Jan Saakshar**".

61.s: The motto of ULLAS is:
61.x: The motto of ULLAS is “Jan Jan Saakshar”.
61.tq: Recall the exact official slogan rather than a generic literacy slogan.
xs: ULLAS motto: "**Jan Jan Saakshar**" — option **(3)**.
ULLAS = **Understanding of Lifelong Learning for All in Society**.
xa: **Uttarakhand**: **6th** fully literate state (**Jul 2026**, **98%+**).
**AP** ULLAS: **41,500** SHG volunteer teachers for **4,15,000** learners.

61.s: Which Union Territory was the first to attain the status of being fully literate under the stated 95% criterion?
61.x: Ladakh was the first Union Territory to attain full literacy, in 2024.
61.tq: Separate the first Union Territory from the first state in the sequence.
xs: **Ladakh** was the first fully literate UT (**2024**) — option **(4)**.
Full literacy (ULLAS) = **95%+** among those aged **15+**.
xa: First fully literate **state**: **Mizoram (2025)**.
Sequence: **Ladakh** → **Mizoram** → Goa, Tripura, Himachal → **Sikkim** → **Uttarakhand**.

61.s:
Which of the following is the correct sequence of the listed States in attaining full literacy, beginning with the first State?
A. Uttarakhand
B. Mizoram
C. Sikkim
D. Goa
61.x: Mizoram was the first State in 2025, followed by Goa, then Sikkim, and Uttarakhand as the sixth State in July 2026.
61.tq: Anchor the first and sixth positions, then arrange the intervening states.
xs: Order: **Mizoram** → **Goa** → **Sikkim** → **Uttarakhand** = **B, D, C, A** — option **(1)**.
**Mizoram** first state (**2025**); **Sikkim** **5th** state; **Uttarakhand** **6th** (**Jul 2026**).
xa: **Ladakh** (UT, **2024**) came before all.
**Tripura** and **Himachal Pradesh** also preceded Sikkim.

61.s:
The Andhra Pradesh implementation of ULLAS particularly focuses on which of the following groups?
1. Self-Help Group members
2. School cooks and helpers
3. Night watchmen
4. Anganwadi ayahs
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
61.x: The identified focus groups include SHG members, school cooks, helpers, night watchmen and anganwadi ayahs. Therefore, all four listed groups are included.
61.tq: Treat each occupational group as a separate inclusion point and check the all-inclusive option.
xs: **All four** groups — option **(4)**.
AP ULLAS focuses on **SHG members**, **school cooks**, **helpers**, **night watchmen**, **anganwadi ayahs** (APSES 2024-25).
xa: All **26** districts; **41,500** SHG volunteer teachers (**SERP**) for **4,15,000** learners.
Classes from **5 Nov 2024**; video lessons via **TCS**.
Target-oriented drive for districts **below the state average**.

61.s: A target-oriented adult literacy drive in Andhra Pradesh is specifically directed towards:
o: Only districts with no Self-Help Groups
Districts with literacy above the State average
61.x: The target-oriented adult literacy drive covers districts whose literacy is below the State average.
61.tq: Apply the direction of the targeting criterion rather than assuming universal uniformity.
xs: AP's target-oriented adult literacy drive covers **districts below the State average** — option **(1)**.
It runs alongside **ULLAS** in all **26** districts.
xa: AP ULLAS: **41,500** SHG volunteer teachers (**SERP**) for **4,15,000** learners.
Focus groups: **SHG members**, **school cooks**, **helpers**, **night watchmen**, **anganwadi ayahs**.
Lowest district: tribal **Alluri Sitarama Raju (44.67%)**.

61.s: The national benchmark for declaring a population ‘fully literate’ under ULLAS is literacy among at least:
o: 75% of persons aged 7 years and above
95% of persons aged 15 years and above
85% of persons aged 10 years and above
90% of persons aged 15 years and above
61.x: Under ULLAS, the national benchmark for being fully literate is 95% literacy among persons aged 15 years and above.
61.tq: Discriminate using both the percentage and the specified age group.
xs: Under **ULLAS**, "fully literate" = **95%+** among persons aged **15 and above** — option **(2)**.
The **7+** age is the Census/PLFS literacy definition, not the ULLAS benchmark.
xa: First fully literate UT: **Ladakh (2024)**; first state: **Mizoram (2025)**.
**Uttarakhand**: **6th** state, **Jul 2026**, **98%+**.
ULLAS motto: "**Jan Jan Saakshar**".

61.s: The target of NEP 2020 regarding youth and adult literacy is:
61.x: NEP 2020 sets the target of achieving 100% youth and adult literacy by 2030.
61.tq: Distinguish the literacy target and deadline from the foundational-learning deadline.
xs: NEP 2020 targets **100% youth and adult literacy by 2030** — option **(2)**.
**2035** is the target for **50% GER** in **higher education**, not school enrolment.
xa: Other targets: **100% GER in school by 2030**; **2 crore** out-of-school children back.
Assessment centre: **PARAKH**.
Structure: **5+3+3+4**.

61.s: NIPUN Bharat is primarily associated with foundational literacy and numeracy by which grade, and its extended deadline is:
61.x: NIPUN Bharat focuses on foundational literacy at the Grade-3 level, and its deadline was extended from 2025 to 2026-27.
61.tq: Separate NIPUN Bharat’s Grade-3 goal from NEP 2020’s broader adult-literacy target.
xs: **NIPUN Bharat**: foundational literacy by **Grade 3**, deadline now **2026-27** — option **(3)**.
NEP's original **2025** FLN target was moved.
xa: **NEP 2020** foundational stage covers ages **3-8**.
**FLN Index** (Institute for Competitiveness for **EAC-PM**): **Punjab** highest in the second edition.
ULLAS also has an **FLN** component for adults.

61.s:
Which of the following statements regarding the National Education Policy, 2020 is correct?
1. It is regarded as the first education policy of the 21st century.
2. It replaced the National Policy on Education, 1986.
3. It replaced a policy that had been in force for 34 years.
4. It introduced the 5+3+3+4 curricular structure.
61.x: All four statements are correct. NEP 2020 is the first education policy of the 21st century, replaced NPE 1986 after 34 years, and adopted the 5+3+3+4 structure.
61.tq: Check whether all statements belong to the same policy framework before selecting the complete combination.
xs: **All four** statements are correct — option **(4)**.
NEP 2020: **first education policy of the 21st century**; replaced the **34-year-old NPE 1986**.
Structure **5+3+3+4** (APPSC-GS 2025 key) = **12 years** of school + **3** of pre-school.
xa: Targets: **100% GER in school by 2030**; **50% GER** in higher education by **2035**.
**Operation Blackboard (1987)** came under **NPE 1986**.

61.s:
Match List-I with List-II regarding the stages of NEP 2020.

List-I (Stage)
a. Foundational
b. Preparatory
c. Middle
 d. Secondary

List-II (Age group)
i. 14–18 years
ii. 8–11 years
iii. 3–8 years
iv. 11–14 years

Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
61.x: The stages correspond respectively to Foundational—3–8, Preparatory—8–11, Middle—11–14 and Secondary—14–18 years.
61.tq: Start from the sure age pair and eliminate codes that shift the adjacent stages.
xs: Correct code: **a–iii, b–ii, c–iv, d–i** — option **(1)**.
**Foundational 3-8**, **Preparatory 8-11**, **Middle 11-14**, **Secondary 14-18**.
xa: Stage lengths: **5** (Foundational), **3** (Preparatory), **3** (Middle), **4** (Secondary).
It means **12 years of school + 3 of pre-school**.

61.s: Which of the following is NOT a target of NEP 2020 mentioned in relation to enrolment and literacy?
o: Bringing 2 crore out-of-school children back into education
61.x: The target for 100% youth and adult literacy is 2030, not 2025. The other three are stated NEP 2020 targets.
61.tq: Find the changed year in an otherwise familiar target statement.
xs: **100% youth and adult literacy by 2025** is wrong — option **(1)**; the target year is **2030**.
The real targets: **2 crore** out-of-school children back, **100% GER in school by 2030**, **50% GER in higher education by 2035**.
xa: ⚠ The **2025** date belongs to NEP's FLN-by-Grade-3 goal, now moved to **2026-27** under **NIPUN Bharat**.
Assessment centre: **PARAKH**.

61.s: PARAKH, mentioned in the context of NEP 2020, is associated with:
61.x: PARAKH is the assessment centre associated with NEP 2020.
61.tq: Identify the institutional function by asking what task the body is designed to perform.
xs: **PARAKH** is NEP 2020's **assessment centre** — option **(4)**, school assessment.
It is not a census, finance or adult-literacy body; adult literacy is handled by **ULLAS**.
xa: NEP 2020 replaced **NPE 1986**; structure **5+3+3+4**.
**FLN by Grade 3** → **NIPUN Bharat** (**2026-27**).
**Samagra Shiksha** supports **NEP 2020** and the **RTE Act 2009**.

61.s: Operation Blackboard was introduced in which year and under which policy?
61.x: Operation Blackboard was introduced in 1987 under the National Policy on Education, 1986.
61.tq: Separate the launch year from the year of the policy under which the programme operated.
xs: **Operation Blackboard**: **1987**, under **NPE 1986** — option **(1)**.
**Samagra Shiksha** came in **2018**; **NEP 2020** replaced NPE 1986.
xa: Aim: basic facilities for **primary schools in educationally backward areas** (APPSC-GS 2025 key).
Minimum: **two rooms**, **two teachers**, **teaching aids**.

61.s: Which of the following was NOT among the basic provisions associated with Operation Blackboard?
o: English laboratories in every government school
At least two rooms for a primary school
61.x: Operation Blackboard provided basic facilities such as two rooms, two teachers and teaching aids. English laboratories were part of the Nadu-Nedu facilities, not Operation Blackboard.
61.tq: Distinguish facilities of neighbouring education schemes by identifying the misplaced provision.
xs: **English laboratories** were not under Operation Blackboard — option **(1)**.
Operation Blackboard gave at least **two rooms**, **two teachers** and **teaching aids**.
**English labs** are among the **nine** facilities of AP's **Nadu-Nedu**.
xa: Operation Blackboard: **1987**, under **NPE 1986**.
Nadu-Nedu launched **14 Nov 2019**.

61.s:
Consider the following statements about Samagra Shiksha:
1. It was launched in 2018.
2. It is an umbrella scheme covering pre-school to Class 12.
3. It subsumed Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan, Rashtriya Madhyamik Shiksha Abhiyan and Teacher Education.
4. It covers children with disabilities under the Right to Education Act, 2009.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
61.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct: Samagra Shiksha (2018) covers pre-school to Class 12 and subsumed SSA, RMSA and Teacher Education. Statement 4 is wrong: it supports the RTE Act 2009, but children with disabilities are covered under the RPwD Act 2016. Hence '1 and 2 only' is incomplete, and options including 4 are wrong.
61.tq: Samagra = 2018, pre-school to 12, SSA + RMSA + TE; disability cover comes from RPwD Act 2016, not RTE.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3 only** — option **(2)**.
**Samagra Shiksha (2018)**: umbrella scheme **pre-school to Class 12**; subsumes **SSA, RMSA and Teacher Education**.
Statement 4 wrong: it supports the **RTE Act 2009**, but disabled children are covered under the **RPwD Act 2016**.
xa: It also supports **NEP 2020**.
**PM SHRI** upgrades **14,500+** schools as **green model schools**.

61.s: PM SHRI seeks to upgrade more than how many schools as green model schools?
61.x: PM SHRI seeks to upgrade more than 14,500 schools as green model schools.
61.tq: Use the approximate threshold carefully; do not replace “14,500+” with a rounded unrelated figure.
xs: **PM SHRI** upgrades **14,500+** schools as **green model schools** — option **(3)**.
The other figures are not cited; **14,500+** is the PM SHRI number to remember.
xa: **RUSA** continued till **2026**.
**Samagra Shiksha (2018)**: pre-school to **Class 12**.
AP's own school scheme: **Mana Badi Nadu-Nedu** (**14 Nov 2019**).

61.s: Mana Badi Nadu-Nedu was launched in Andhra Pradesh on:
61.x: Mana Badi Nadu-Nedu was launched on 14 November 2019.
61.tq: Use the date-specific scheme identification method and distinguish it from the 2018 launch of Samagra Shiksha.
xs: **Mana Badi Nadu-Nedu** was launched on **14 November 2019** — option **(3)**.
It transforms **government schools** in phases with **nine basic facilities**.
xa: Facilities: **toilets**, **drinking water**, **furniture**, **paint**, **repairs**, **lights and fans**, **green chalkboards**, **English labs**, **compound walls**.
⚠ **14 November** is the date; the year is **2019**, not 2018.

61.s: Which one of the following is NOT included among the basic facilities provided under Mana Badi Nadu-Nedu?
61.x: Nadu-Nedu includes facilities such as drinking water, green chalkboards and English laboratories. University hostels are not among its listed school facilities.
61.tq: Identify the out-of-scope facility in a scheme-specific list.
xs: **University hostels** are not a Nadu-Nedu facility — option **(1)**.
Nadu-Nedu's **nine** school facilities include **drinking water**, **green chalkboards** and **English labs**.
xa: Others: **toilets**, **furniture**, **paint**, **major/minor repairs**, **lights and fans**, **compound walls**.
Launched **14 Nov 2019**.

61.s: Which State recorded the highest FLN score in the second edition of the FLN Index referred to in the APPSC-GS 2022 key?
61.x: Punjab recorded the highest FLN score in the second edition of the FLN Index.
61.tq: Use the ranking fact directly and avoid substituting a generally high-literacy State for the indexed State.
xs: **Punjab** had the highest FLN score in the second edition — option **(2)** (APPSC-GS 2022 key).
The **FLN Index** is by the **Institute for Competitiveness** for the **EAC-PM**.
xa: **NIPUN Bharat** targets Grade-3 FLN by **2026-27**.
NEP 2020 foundational stage: ages **3-8**.

61.s:
Which of the following statements regarding educational gender indicators is correct?
1. Female GER in higher education rose to 30.2.
2. Female GER became higher than male GER.
3. Gender parity was reported at all school levels.

Select the correct answer.
61.x: All three statements are correct: female higher-education GER reached 30.2, exceeded male GER, and gender parity was reported at all school levels.
61.tq: Check whether the trend, comparison and school-level conclusion are jointly supported.
xs: **All three** are correct — option **(4)**.
Female higher-education GER rose **28.5 → 30.2** (2021-23), now **above male** GER.
**Gender parity** at all **school levels**.
xa: Source: MoSPI **Women and Men in India 2025** (**1 May 2026**).
NFHS-5: women with **10+ years** of schooling **41%**.

61.s: According to NFHS-5, the percentage of women with 10 or more years of schooling was:
61.x: NFHS-5 reported that 41% of women had 10 or more years of schooling; the corresponding NFHS-4 figure was 35.7%.
61.tq: Separate the schooling-attainment percentage from the overall women’s literacy percentage.
xs: **NFHS-5**: **41%** of women had **10+ years** of schooling — option **(2)**.
**35.7%** was the **NFHS-4** figure; **71.5%** is NFHS-5 **women's literacy**; **72.6%** is AP PLFS literacy.
xa: Female GER in higher education: **30.2** — above male.
PLFS 2023-24 female literacy: **74.6%**.

61.s: Census 2027 is expected to add a question relating to:
61.x: Census 2027 adds a digital literacy question.
61.tq: Identify the exact census indicator rather than a broader technology-related distractor.
xs: **Census 2027** adds a **digital literacy** question — option **(2)** (**15 Aug 2026**).
It extends literacy measurement beyond the basic **read and write with understanding** test.
xa: Census literate = **7+**, can **read and write with understanding**.
ULLAS full literacy = **95%+** among **15+**.
**Uttarakhand**: 6th fully literate state (**Jul 2026**).

61.s: According to PLFS 2023–24, the literacy rate of Andhra Pradesh among persons aged 7 years and above was:
61.x: PLFS 2023–24 recorded Andhra Pradesh’s literacy rate at 72.6% for persons aged 7 years and above.
61.tq: Separate the PLFS 2023–24 figure from the 2018–19, 2011 and 2025 figures.
xa: ⚠ Minister's **82.10%** claim for 2026 has no official source (**5 Sep 2026**).
PLFS 2023-24 bottom: **Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh**.

61.s: Which statement best explains why Census and PLFS literacy rates should not be directly compared?
o: They use different samples, although PLFS uses the same 7+ definition for its reported rate.
PLFS excludes all women from its sample.
Census uses a 15+ definition, whereas PLFS uses a 3+ definition.
Census measures only urban literacy, whereas PLFS measures only rural literacy.
61.x: PLFS is a sample survey: it uses the same 7+ definition of literacy as the Census, but different samples, so its rates are not directly comparable with Census figures. The other options are false - neither uses a 15+ or 3+ definition, and neither excludes women or covers only urban or rural areas.
61.tq: Apply the methodology distinction instead of comparing percentages mechanically.
xs: Census and PLFS use **different samples**, though PLFS uses the same **7+** definition — option **(1)**.
PLFS is a **sample survey**; the Census is a full count.
Neither uses a **15+** or **3+** literacy definition.
xa: ⚠ Political claims of 2026 literacy lack an **official source**.
PLFS 2023-24 India: **80.9%**; Census 2011: **74.04%** (provisional).

61.s:
Which of the following statements about Andhra Pradesh literacy is correct?
1. Its literacy rate was 67.35% in Census 2011.
2. Its PLFS 2025 literacy rate was 71.40%.
3. Its literacy rate remained below the all-India rate.
4. The widest literacy gap was reported in the tribal ASR district.
61.x: All four statements are correct: the figures were 67.35% in 2011 and 71.40% in PLFS 2025, Andhra Pradesh remained below India, and the widest gap was in the tribal ASR district.
61.tq: Combine numerical, comparative and regional statements into a single verification set.
xs: **All four** are correct — option **(4)**.
AP stays **below India** (**72.98%** in 2011); widest gap in tribal **ASR** district.
xa: ASR = **Alluri Sitarama Raju**, lowest at **44.67%**.

61.s: International Literacy Day is observed on:
61.x: International Literacy Day is observed on 8 September.
61.tq: Use the exact observance date and avoid confusing it with other education-related days.
xs: **International Literacy Day**: **8 September** — option **(3)**.
A **UNESCO** day since **1966**, first observed in **1967**.
xa: **Saakshar Bharat** was launched on ILD **2009**.
ILD **8 Sep 2026** theme: "**Literacy for people, the planet and prosperity**".
⚠ **14 November** = Nadu-Nedu launch date (2019).
