Statement 2 correct: India moved from **PL-480** wheat imports to **self-sufficiency**.
Statement 3 wrong: **regional imbalance** remained — **rainfed and hilly areas left out** — so option **(1)**, **1 and 2 only**.
xa: **Punjab, Haryana, western UP** turned from **food-deficit to surplus**.
The **eastern belt** (MP, Bihar, Odisha, WB, Assam) **lagged** in phase 1.
**BGREI** (**2010-11**) aimed to bring the Green Revolution to Eastern India.
Gains were captured by big landowners (**>10 ha**).

81.s: The New Agricultural Strategy associated with the Green Revolution in India began in:
81.x: The New Agricultural Strategy began in 1965 and combined HYV seeds, fertilisers, irrigation and minimum support price with the objective of foodgrain self-sufficiency.
81.tq: Use the strategy's starting year rather than the later year associated with the wider production surge.
xs: The **New Agricultural Strategy** began in **1965** — option **(2)**.
It brought a **mid-1960s surge** in foodgrain output.
xa: ⚠ Current notes date it **1968**.
Inputs: **HYV seeds**, chemical fertilisers, pesticides, **assured irrigation**, mechanisation, **MSP**.
Aim: **self-sufficiency in food grains**, ending dependence on **PL-480** imports.
**Borlaug** won the **Nobel Peace Prize 1970**.

81.s: Which of the following sets of inputs was central to the New Agricultural Strategy?
o: Land reclamation, fishing technology and livestock insurance
Organic manure, shifting cultivation and export subsidies
HYV seeds, fertilisers, irrigation and minimum support price
Rainwater harvesting, plantation crops and free trade
81.x: The strategy relied on HYV seeds, fertilisers, assured irrigation and MSP, with foodgrain self-sufficiency as its objective.
81.tq: Identify the complete input package rather than an isolated agricultural measure.
xs: The strategy rested on **HYV seeds**, **fertilisers**, **irrigation** and **minimum support price** — option **(3)**.
Fertilisers were esp. **nitrogenous**; irrigation was **assured canal/tube-well**; plus **pesticides** and **mechanisation**.
xa: Aim: **self-sufficiency in food grains**.
Fertiliser imbalance: N:P:K **10.9:4.1:1** vs ideal **4:2:1**.
⚠ **Shifting cultivation** (slash and burn) is a tribal practice, not a Green Revolution input.
Swaminathan's remedy: **Evergreen Revolution**.

81.s: M.S. Swaminathan is widely associated with being the:
81.x: M.S. Swaminathan is identified as the father of India’s Green Revolution.
81.tq: Match the prominent personality with the specific agricultural transformation.
xs: **M.S. Swaminathan** is the **Father of the Green Revolution in India** — option **(1)**.
He **brought HYV wheat to India**.
xa: ⚠ Father in the **world** = **Norman Borlaug** (Mexican dwarf wheat, Nobel **1970**).
Swaminathan's remedy for Green Revolution ills: the **Evergreen Revolution**.
**C. Subramaniam** was the Agriculture Minister who backed the strategy.
The strategy began in **1965**.

81.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the regional spread of the Green Revolution in India:
1. Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh recorded the biggest gains.
2. Rice registered important gains in the deltas of Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu.
3. Eastern states such as Madhya Pradesh, Bihar, Odisha, West Bengal and Assam led the first phase.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
81.x: Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh recorded the biggest gains, while rice gains were notable in the deltas of Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu. The listed eastern states lagged during the first phase, making statement 3 false.
81.tq: Find the wrong regional statement by distinguishing the leading north-western belt from the lagging eastern states.
xs: Statement 1 correct: **Punjab, Haryana, western UP** were the **core states**, food-deficit to surplus.
Statement 2 correct: the **south** gained via irrigation in the **AP and TN rice deltas**.
Statement 3 wrong: **MP, Bihar, Odisha, WB, Assam** — the **eastern belt** — **lagged** in phase 1; answer option **(1)**, **1 and 2 only**.
xa: The core belt lies in the **Trans- and Upper Gangetic Plains**.
**BGREI** (**2010-11**, under **RKVY**) targets Assam, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Odisha, eastern UP, West Bengal.
**Rainfed and hilly** areas were left out — regional imbalance.
Trans-Gangetic Plains (Punjab, Haryana, Delhi) have the **highest productivity**.

81.s: The Green Revolution in India mainly increased the production of:
81.x: Wheat (first phase) and rice (later, wider phase) gained most, as in the APPSC 2025 key. Pulses, oilseeds and coarse cereals lagged; cotton and sugarcane were not the focus of the strategy.
81.tq: Green Revolution = wheat first, then rice; pulses/oilseeds left behind.
xs: The Green Revolution mainly increased **wheat and rice** (APPSC 2025 key) — option **(2)**.
**Pulses, oilseeds, coarse cereals lagged**, so options 1 and 3 are wrong.
xa: First phase largely **wheat**; rice gained in the **later, wider phase**.
It locked the north-west into **rice-wheat monoculture** and groundwater over-use.
**Cotton, jute, sugarcane** were added to **NFSM** only in **2014-15**.
⚠ Father in world = **Borlaug**; in India = **Swaminathan**.

81.s: Which one of the following was NOT a major limitation of the Green Revolution mentioned in relation to Indian agriculture?
o: Neglect of pulses, oilseeds and millets
Complete equality in the distribution of gains among all landholders
Regional imbalance affecting rainfed and hill areas
81.x: The gains were not equally distributed; big landowners benefited most. Groundwater depletion, salinity, crop imbalance and regional imbalance were recognised limitations.
81.tq: Find the statement that reverses a known limitation instead of identifying one.
xs: The odd one out is **complete equality in the distribution of gains** — option **(3)**; gains were captured by **big landowners (>10 ha)**.
Real limitations: **groundwater depletion, salinity**; **pulses, oilseeds, millets neglected**; **rainfed and hilly areas left out**.
xa: Fertiliser imbalance: N:P:K **10.9:4.1:1** vs ideal **4:2:1**.
North-west locked in **rice-wheat monoculture** and groundwater over-use.
Remedy: Swaminathan's **Evergreen Revolution**.
Only about **12%** of irrigated area uses **drip or sprinkler**.

81.s: The fertiliser-use ratio of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium cited for Indian agriculture, compared with the ideal ratio, is:
81.x: The prevailing N:P:K ratio is cited as 10.9:4.1:1, whereas the ideal ratio is 4:2:1.
81.tq: Keep the observed ratio and ideal ratio in their correct order before comparing the figures.
xs: The N:P:K ratio is **10.9:4.1:1** compared with an ideal **4:2:1** — option **(3)**.
This **fertiliser imbalance** is a listed Green Revolution limitation — excess **nitrogen**.
xa: Inputs stressed chemical fertilisers, **esp. nitrogenous**.
Rice, wheat and sugarcane use **over two-thirds of India's urea**.
Other limitations: **groundwater depletion, salinity**, crop and regional imbalance.
Remedy: **Evergreen Revolution** (Swaminathan).

81.s: Swaminathan's proposed remedy for the adverse effects and ecological limitations of the Green Revolution is known as:
81.x: The Evergreen Revolution was proposed as a sustainable corrective approach associated with M.S. Swaminathan.
81.tq: Distinguish the sustainability-oriented term from revolutions associated with fisheries, milk or broad diversification.
xs: Swaminathan's remedy is the **Evergreen Revolution** — option **(2)**.
It answers Green Revolution ills: **groundwater depletion, salinity**, **rice-wheat monoculture**, fertiliser imbalance.
xa: Swaminathan = **Father of the Green Revolution in India**.
Borlaug = Father in the **world**, **Nobel Peace Prize 1970**.
Fertiliser imbalance: **10.9:4.1:1** vs ideal **4:2:1**.
Gains went to farmers with **>10 ha**.

81.s: The rice-wheat monoculture and excessive groundwater use associated with the Green Revolution became especially pronounced in:
81.x: The Green Revolution reinforced rice-wheat monoculture and groundwater over-use particularly in north-western India.
81.tq: Locate the environmental consequence in the region where the rice-wheat system became concentrated.
xs: **Rice-wheat monoculture** and **groundwater over-use** got locked in **north-western India** — option **(2)**.
The core belt was **Punjab, Haryana, western UP**.
xa: MSP + **free power** favour rice-wheat, e.g. **paddy in Punjab**.
Punjab-Haryana rotate **wheat, paddy, mustard, pulses**.
Rice-wheat (**paddy then wheat**) = **double cropping** of the Indo-Gangetic plains.
Climate-proofing needs procurement to diversify **beyond rice-wheat**.

81.s: The BGREI programme was launched in 2010-11 primarily for which of the following purposes?
o: Promoting oil-palm cultivation in coastal India
Increasing cotton exports from western India
Replacing rice cultivation with millets in dryland regions
Bringing the Green Revolution to the rice-based cropping system of Eastern India
81.x: BGREI, or Bringing Green Revolution to Eastern India, was launched in 2010-11 for the rice-based rice-wheat cropping system of Eastern India.
81.tq: Identify the programme from its purpose rather than from a similar scheme name.
xs: **BGREI** (**Bringing Green Revolution to Eastern India**) targets the **rice-based (rice-wheat) cropping system** of Eastern India — option **(4)**.
It was launched in **2010-11** under **RKVY**.
Oil palm falls under **NMEO-Oil Palm**, not BGREI.
xa: States: **Assam, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Odisha, eastern UP, West Bengal**.
The **eastern belt** had **lagged** in the first Green Revolution phase.
**NFSM** launched **2007-08** for rice, wheat, pulses.
**Lower Gangetic Plains** (West Bengal): **rice, jute**.

81.s: Which one of the following groups of States and region was covered under BGREI?
o: Assam, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Odisha, eastern Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal
Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, Gujarat, Maharashtra and Goa
Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Telangana and Andhra Pradesh
Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand and Ladakh
81.x: BGREI covers Assam, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Odisha, eastern Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal.
81.tq: Use the regional cluster to distinguish Eastern India from the established north-western Green Revolution belt.
xs: BGREI covers **Assam, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Odisha, eastern Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal** — option **(1)**.
Punjab and Haryana (option 2) are already the **core Green Revolution** states.
xa: BGREI: launched **2010-11** under **RKVY**.
Focus: **rice-based (rice-wheat) cropping system**.
⚠ Eastern belt **MP, Bihar, Odisha, WB, Assam** lagged in phase 1.
**West Bengal** = "**Rice Bowl of India**".

81.s:
With reference to the National Food Security Mission (NFSM), consider the following statements:
1. It was launched in 2007-08 for rice, wheat and pulses.
2. Its initial objectives included area expansion, productivity enhancement and improvement of soil fertility.
3. Nutri-cereals were added to it in 2014-15.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
81.x: NFSM began in 2007-08 for rice, wheat and pulses, with the stated production and soil-fertility objectives. Nutri-cereals were added later, in 2018-19.
81.tq: Track the original launch year separately from later additions.
xs: Statement 1 correct: NFSM launched **2007-08** for **rice, wheat, pulses**.
Statement 2 correct: aims were **area expansion, productivity, soil fertility**.
Statement 3 wrong: **nutri-cereals** were added in **2018-19**, not 2014-15 — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: **2014-15**: coarse cereals and **cotton, jute, sugarcane** added.
**2023-24**: **SMSP** (seeds) merged in.
**2024-25**: renamed **NFSNM**.
Funds: Rs **15,166.33 crore** released 2014-15 to 2024-25.

81.s: Coarse cereals and commercial crops such as cotton, jute and sugarcane were added to NFSM in:
81.x: Coarse cereals and commercial crops, including cotton, jute and sugarcane, were added to NFSM in 2014-15.
81.tq: Use the milestone sequence to separate the first expansion from the later nutri-cereal addition.
xs: Coarse cereals and **cotton, jute, sugarcane** joined NFSM in **2014-15** — option **(2)**.
**2018-19** added **nutri-cereals**; **2007-08** was the launch; **2010-11** was **BGREI**.
xa: NFSM began for **rice, wheat, pulses**.
**SMSP** merged in **2023-24**.
Renamed **National Food Security and Nutrition Mission** in **2024-25**.
Oilseeds/oil palm moved to **NMEO-Edible Oils**.

81.s: NFSM was renamed as the National Food Security and Nutrition Mission (NFSNM) in:
81.x: NFSM was renamed the National Food Security and Nutrition Mission in 2024-25.
81.tq: Match the renamed scheme with its precise milestone year.
xs: NFSM was renamed **NFSNM** in **2024-25** — option **(3)**.
**2023-24** was the **SMSP** merger; **2018-19** added nutri-cereals.
xa: NFSNM crops: rice, wheat, pulses, maize, barley, **Shree Anna**, cotton, jute, sugarcane.
**Oilseeds/oil palm** moved to **NMEO-Edible Oils**.
AP allocation: NFSNM ₹**2,194.07 lakh** (**60:40**).
NFSM launched **2007-08**.

81.s: Which of the following is NOT included among the crops covered by NFSNM?
81.x: NFSNM covers rice, wheat, pulses, maize, barley, Shree Anna, cotton, jute and sugarcane. Oilseeds and oil palm were moved to the NMEO initiatives.
81.tq: Find the crop group transferred to a separate oil mission.
xs: **Oilseeds** are not in NFSNM — they **moved to NMEO-Edible Oils** — option **(3)**.
NFSNM covers **rice, wheat, pulses, maize, barley, Shree Anna, cotton, jute, sugarcane**.
xa: **Shree Anna** = jowar, bajra, ragi, small millets.
NMEO target: about **70 million tonnes** by **2030-31**.
Edible-oil import dependence: **63.2% (FY16) → 56.25% (FY24)**.
Renamed NFSNM in **2024-25**.

81.s: The NMEO-Oilseeds and NMEO-Oil Palm initiatives aim at approximately what level of production by 2030-31?
81.x: The two missions target about 70 million tonnes by 2030-31.
81.tq: Link the target figure with the correct mission and terminal year.
xs: **NMEO-Oilseeds and NMEO-Oil Palm** target about **70 million tonnes** by **2030-31** — option **(3)**.
Their aim is to cut **edible-oil import dependence**.
xa: Import dependence fell from **63.2% (FY16)** to **56.25% (FY24)**.
Oilseeds and oil palm were **moved out of NFSNM** into NMEO-Edible Oils.
Oilseeds were **neglected** during the Green Revolution.
Black soil is listed with **cotton, jowar, oilseeds**.

81.s: Which one of the following statements regarding recent foodgrain production in India is correct?
o: Foodgrain production reached a record 357.73 million tonnes in 2024–25.
Foodgrain production in 2024–25 remained below 250 million tonnes.
Foodgrain production was exactly equal to horticulture production in 2024–25.
Horticulture production was lower than foodgrain production in 2024–25.
81.x: India recorded 357.73 million tonnes of foodgrain production in 2024–25. Horticulture production was higher at 367.72 million tonnes.
81.tq: Select the precise current figure while rejecting changed or reversed comparisons.
xs: Foodgrains hit a record **357.73 million tonnes in 2024-25** — option **(1)**.
**Horticulture** exceeded it at **367.72 MT**, so options 3 and 4 are wrong; option 2 (below 250) is far off.
xa: Rice **150.18 MT**; wheat **117.94 MMT**; millets **18.59 MMT**.
AP foodgrains (2024-25): **161.86 lakh MT** on **37.51 lakh ha**.
Gross cropped area **219.16 MH**; net sown **141 MH** (2021-22).
India is **largest producer and consumer of pulses**.

81.s: India's rice production and world position, as stated for the recent period, are correctly represented by which of the following?
o: About 150.18 MT; first in the world, surpassing China
About 117.94 MT; first in the world
About 18.59 MT; second in the world after China
About 145.28 MT; second in the world after China
81.x: India's rice production is stated as about 150.18 MT, placing it first in the world and ahead of China's 145.28 MT.
81.tq: Combine the output figure with the ranking rather than treating either clue alone.
xs: India produced **150.18 MT** of rice vs China's **145.28 MT**, making it **first in the world, surpassing China** — option **(1)**.
**117.94** is **wheat** output; **18.59** is **millets**; India was **earlier 2nd** after China.
xa: India is the **largest rice exporter**, **~40%** of world trade.
Some notes give rice output as **~154 MMT**.
**West Bengal** is the "**Rice Bowl of India**".
Rice is staple of **over half of India**.

81.s: India accounts for approximately what share of world rice trade and is described as which type of rice trader?
o: About 60 per cent; the largest rice importer
About 10 per cent; the second-largest importer
About 25 per cent; a marginal exporter
About 40 per cent; the largest rice exporter
81.x: India is described as the largest rice exporter and accounts for approximately 40 per cent of world rice trade.
81.tq: Use the percentage and the trade rank together to avoid a producer-exporter reversal.
xs: India is the **largest rice exporter**, with **~40%** of world rice trade — option **(4)**.
It is an exporter, not an importer.
xa: India is also the **largest producer**, **150.18 MT** vs China **145.28 MT**.
Leading rice state: **West Bengal**.
Wheat: India **2nd** in the world.
Millets: India **42.75%** of world output.

81.s: Which one of the following correctly describes India's recent position in global wheat production?
o: Production of 150.18 MMT and first position in the world
Production of 117.94 MMT and second position in the world
Production of 18.59 MMT and second position in the world
Production of 145.28 MMT and third position in the world
81.x: India's wheat production is stated as 117.94 MMT, placing it second in the world.
81.tq: Discriminate among crop-specific output figures and rankings.
xs: India produces **117.94 MMT** of wheat and is **2nd** in the world — option **(2)**.
**150.18** is rice (1st); **18.59** is millets; **145.28** is China's rice.
xa: Wheat is a **rabi** crop, **2nd** cereal in India.
Wheat states: **UP, MP, Punjab, Haryana**.
Rainfall **50-75 cm**; cool season, warm sun at ripening.
Foodgrains total **357.73 MT** (2024-25).

81.s: Which one of the following statements about India's agricultural area in 2021-22 is correct?
o: Geographical area was 141 million hectares and agricultural land was 77.9 per cent.
Geographical area was 328.7 million hectares and agricultural land was about 54.8 per cent of it.
Geographical area was 77.9 million hectares and agricultural land was 54.9 per cent.
Geographical area was 219.16 million hectares and agricultural land was 42.8 per cent.
81.x: India's geographical area was 328.7 million hectares, and about 54.8 per cent was agricultural land in 2021-22.
81.tq: Separate the geographical-area figure from net sown, net irrigated and gross cropped area figures.
xs: Geographical area **328.7 MH**, with **~54.8%** agricultural land — option **(2)**.
**141 MH** is **net sown area**; **77.9 MH** is **net irrigated**; **219.16 MH** is **gross cropped area**.
xa: Net sown area = **42.8%** of the geographical area.
Gross irrigated **120.3 MH** (**54.9%** of GCA).
Cropping intensity **155.4%** (2021-22).
About **51%** of net sown area is **rainfed**.

81.s: Which of the following correctly represents India's net sown area and gross cropped area in 2021-22?
o: Net sown area 328.7 MH; gross cropped area 77.9 MH
Net sown area 219.16 MH; gross cropped area 141 MH
Net sown area 141 MH; gross cropped area 219.16 MH
Net sown area 77.9 MH; gross cropped area 120.3 MH
81.x: India's net sown area was 141 million hectares and gross cropped area was 219.16 million hectares in 2021-22.
81.tq: Distinguish net area from gross area by identifying the larger figure as the repeatedly cropped area.
xs: Net sown area **141 MH**; gross cropped area **219.16 MH** — option **(3)**.
**328.7 MH** is the geographical area; **77.9** net irrigated; **120.3** gross irrigated.
xa: Cropping intensity **155.4%** (2021-22).
Net sown = **42.8%** of geographical area.
Gross irrigated is **54.9%** of GCA.
AP cropping intensity **1.88 in 2024-25**.

81.s: Approximately what percentage of India's net sown area is irrigated?
81.x: Only 56.4 per cent of India's net sown area is irrigated.
81.tq: Distinguish the percentage of net sown area irrigated from the percentage of gross cropped area irrigated.
xs: Only **56.4 per cent** of net sown area is irrigated (2026) — option **(3)**.
**Wells + tube wells** give **over 63%** of irrigation.
xa: About **51%** of net sown area is **rainfed**.
Net irrigated **77.9 MH**; gross irrigated **120.3 MH**.
Only about **12%** of irrigated area uses **drip or sprinkler**.
**Dryland farming**: **less than 750 mm** rainfall and no assured irrigation.

81.s: Which of the following is correctly stated about India's position in world agriculture?
o: India is the largest producer of all food grains.
India is the largest producer of pulses and millets.
India is the largest producer of oil palm and barley.
India is the largest producer of wheat and sugarcane in the world.
81.x: India is identified as the largest producer of pulses and millets. The other options make broader claims not supported by the stated facts.
81.tq: Reject an overbroad superlative and select the precisely stated crop groups.
xs: India is the **largest producer of pulses and millets** — option **(2)**.
Pulses: **largest producer and consumer**; millets: **42.75%** of world output.
In **wheat** India is only **2nd**, so option (4) is wrong.
xa: Millets: **18.59 MMT** on **12.86 million ha**.
India is now the **largest rice producer**, surpassing China.
India is the **largest rice exporter** (~**40%**).
**Bajra** gives ~**60%** of India's millet output.

81.s: In 2021–22, India's gross irrigated area and its share of gross cropped area were approximately:
81.x: In 2021-22 India's gross irrigated area was 120.3 million hectares, which is 54.9% of the gross cropped area of 219.16 MH. 77.9 MH is the net irrigated area, not the gross irrigated area, so options A and C are wrong, and option B has the wrong percentage.
81.tq: Match the area figure with the correct year-specific percentage.
xs: Gross irrigated area **120.3 MH**, **54.9%** of gross cropped area — option **(4)**.
**77.9 MH** is **net irrigated** area, so option (1) is wrong; option (2) has the wrong percentage.
xa: Gross cropped area **219.16 MH**.
Only **56.4%** of net sown area is irrigated (2026).
**Wells + tube wells** give **over 63%**.
Net sown area **141 MH** (**42.8%**).

81.s: The dominant cropping system of the Indo-Gangetic Plains is:
81.x: Rice-wheat is the dominant cropping system of the Indo-Gangetic Plains, with paddy followed by wheat as double cropping.
81.tq: Identify the standard regional crop sequence rather than an individual crop.
xs: **Rice-wheat** is the dominant system of the **Indo-Gangetic plains** — option **(1)**.
**Paddy followed by wheat** in one year is **double cropping**.
xa: **Punjab-Haryana** rotate **wheat, paddy, mustard, pulses**.
The system locked the **north-west** into **rice-wheat monoculture** and groundwater over-use.
**Lower Gangetic Plains** (West Bengal) = **rice, jute**; **Eastern Himalayan** = plantations, jhum.
**BGREI** focuses on the **rice-based (rice-wheat) cropping system** of Eastern India.

81.s: Intercropping is best described as:
o: Growing a crop only on fallow land
Sowing the next crop after complete removal of the previous crop
Growing one crop continuously for several years
Growing two or more crops together in definite rows
81.x: Intercropping involves growing two or more crops together in definite rows, such as tur with jowar or maize.
81.tq: Separate intercropping from mixed cropping by focusing on the definite row arrangement.
xs: **Intercropping** = **two or more crops together in definite rows** — option **(4)**.
Example: **tur with jowar or maize**.
xa: ⚠ **Mixed cropping** = seeds mixed, **no row pattern**; insures against failure.
**Parallel cropping**: crops of different growth habit, **no competition** (maize + green gram).
**Relay cropping**: next crop sown into the **standing crop** before harvest.
**Multiple/double**: crops in **succession** in one year (paddy then wheat).

81.s: Which one of the following examples represents parallel cropping?
o: Tur and jowar sown together in definite rows
Maize and green gram grown together without competition
The next crop sown into a standing crop before its harvest
Paddy followed by wheat in the same year
81.x: Parallel cropping involves two crops of different growth habit and duration growing without competition; maize plus green gram is the stated example.
81.tq: Discriminate parallel cropping from intercropping and relay cropping by its no-competition condition.
xs: **Parallel cropping** = two crops of **different growth habit and duration**, **no competition** — e.g. **maize and green gram**, option **(2)**.
Tur with jowar in rows is **intercropping**; sowing into a standing crop is **relay cropping**; paddy then wheat is **double cropping**.
xa: ⚠ **Intercropping** = in rows; **mixed cropping** = seeds mixed, no rows.
**Ratoon**: crop regrows from **stubble**; yield falls each cycle.
**Crop rotation**: fixed, planned sequence to keep soil fertile and cut pests.
Maize is a **kharif** crop led by **Karnataka, MP**.

81.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Mixed cropping involves sowing crops together without a definite row pattern.
2. Relay cropping involves sowing the next crop into the standing crop before harvest.
3. Ratoon cropping involves regrowth from stubble, and yield generally falls with each cycle.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
81.x: All three statements correctly describe mixed cropping, relay cropping and ratoon cropping respectively.
81.tq: Match each technical definition to its system before selecting the coded combination.
xs: Statement 1 correct: **mixed cropping** sows crops together, seeds mixed, **without row pattern**.
Statement 2 correct: **relay cropping** sows the next crop into the **standing crop before harvest**.
Statement 3 correct: a **ratoon** regrows from **stubble** and **yield falls each cycle** — so **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)**.
xa: Mixed cropping **insures against failure**.
**Intercropping** keeps crops in **definite rows** (tur with jowar or maize).
**Parallel cropping**: maize + green gram, no competition.
**Double cropping**: paddy followed by wheat.

81.s: A pulse-cereal rotation is useful primarily because it:
o: Prevents any crop from being harvested in the year
Removes all nutrients from the soil
Requires continuous flooding of the field
Leaves fixed nitrogen for the succeeding crop
81.x: Leguminous pulses fix atmospheric nitrogen and leave fixed nitrogen in the soil for the succeeding cereal crop.
81.tq: Apply the biological function of legumes to the purpose of crop rotation.
xs: A **pulse-cereal rotation** **leaves fixed nitrogen for the next crop** — option **(4)**.
Pulses **fix atmospheric nitrogen**, so the succeeding cereal benefits.
xa: **Crop rotation** = fixed, planned sequence to **keep soil fertile** and **cut pests**.
Punjab-Haryana rotate **wheat, paddy, mustard, pulses**.
Pulses grow in **both seasons**: **tur/arhar** (kharif), **gram** (rabi).
Fertiliser imbalance N:P:K **10.9:4.1:1** vs ideal **4:2:1** shows excess nitrogen use.

81.s: Which one of the following best describes the recent diversification of agriculture in Andhra Pradesh?
o: A complete shift from crops to mining
A movement from horticulture towards only wheat cultivation
A movement from food grains towards fruits, vegetables, spices and oil palm
A shift from agriculture towards exclusively plantation forestry
81.x: Andhra Pradesh is diversifying from food grains towards fruits, vegetables, spices and oil palm.
81.tq: Identify the direction of structural change rather than just naming a crop.
xs: AP is moving **from food grains to fruits, vegetables, spices, oil palm** (APSES 2024-25) — option **(3)**.
AP is not leaving crops for mining or forestry; it is shifting toward **higher-value horticulture** and **oil palm**.
xa: AP cropping intensity: **1.88 in 2024-25**, up from **1.21** in 2023-24.
AP foodgrains (2024-25): **161.86 lakh MT** on **37.51 lakh ha**; paddy **127.15 lakh MT**.
**Maize** is surging in **Godavari and Krishna** for **poultry feed**.
Millets are spreading after the **Iran war** and **El Nino** deficits (May 2026).

81.s: India's cropping intensity in 2021-22 was approximately:
81.x: India's cropping intensity was 155.4% in 2021-22, reflecting a gross cropped area well above the net sown area. 121% and 188% resemble Andhra Pradesh's figures (1.21 in 2023-24, 1.88 in 2024-25), and 100% would mean no multiple cropping.
81.tq: India cropping intensity ≈ 155%.
xs: India's **cropping intensity** was **155.4%** in **2021-22** — option **(3)**.
It reflects gross cropped area (**219.16 MH**) well above net sown area (**141 MH**).
**121** and **188** echo AP's figures (**1.21** in 2023-24, **1.88** in 2024-25); **100%** would mean no multiple cropping.
xa: Multiple/double cropping = two or more crops **in succession in one year**.
Gross irrigated **120.3 MH** (**54.9%** of GCA).
Net sown area is **42.8%** of the geographical area (**328.7 MH**).

81.s: Which of the following statements regarding millets in India is correct?
o: India produces 42.75% of world millet output, but bajra contributes less than 10% of domestic output.
Millets occupy 18.59 million hectares and account for 60% of world cereal output.
India accounts for less than 10% of world millet output, and ragi contributes about 60% of India's millet output.
India accounts for 42.75% of world millet output, and bajra contributes about 60% of India's millet output.
81.x: India is the largest millet producer, accounting for 42.75% of world output; bajra contributes about 60% of India's millet output.
81.tq: Check each percentage against the correct reference base—world output or India's millet output.
xs: India gives **42.75%** of world millet output, and **bajra** gives about **60%** of India's millet output — option **(4)**.
**18.59** is millet output in **MMT** (on **12.86 million ha**), not area; ragi is not the 60% millet.
xa: India is the **largest millet producer** (21 May 2026).
Major millets: **Bajra** (pearl), **Jowar** (sorghum), **Ragi** (finger).
**Rajasthan** is largest in bajra; **Karnataka** in ragi.
**2023** = UN **International Year of Millets**; brand **Shree Anna**.

81.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
81.x: Bajra, jowar and ragi are major millets. Foxtail, little, kodo and proso are minor millets.
81.tq: Start with the sure classification pair and eliminate the reversed groupings.
xs: **Ragi** (finger millet) is a **major millet** — option **(2)**.
Major: **Bajra, Jowar, Ragi**; minor: **foxtail, little, kodo, proso** — so foxtail is minor and bajra/jowar are major.
xa: Bajra = ~**60%** of India's millet output.
Local names: **foxtail (kangni)**, **little (kutki)**, **kodo (kodon)**, **proso (chena)**.
**Ragi** suits **red soils**; **Karnataka** leads.
Millets are branded **Shree Anna**.

81.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
81.x: Kodo millet is also called kodon; ragi is finger millet and belongs to the major millet group.
81.tq: Use the exact local names to detect the incorrect millet pairing.
xs: **Kodo millet — Ragi** is wrongly matched — option **(1)**; kodo is **kodon**, and **ragi** is **finger millet**, a major millet.
The other pairs are right: **proso = chena**, **little = kutki**, **foxtail = kangni**.
xa: Major millets: **Bajra (pearl), Jowar (sorghum), Ragi (finger)**.
⚠ **Chena** is also the name for shifting cultivation in **Sri Lanka**.
**Karnataka** is the largest **ragi** producer.
Shree Anna under NFSNM = **jowar, bajra, ragi, small millets**.

81.s: The term 'Shree Anna' is associated with:
81.x: Millets have been branded as Shree Anna. The term gained prominence in connection with the International Year of Millets.
81.tq: Discriminate between a campaign label and the crop category it represents.
xs: **Shree Anna** is the brand for **millets** — option **(1)**.
It gained prominence with the **2023** UN **International Year of Millets**.
xa: Under **NFSNM**, Shree Anna = **jowar, bajra, ragi, small millets**.
India is the **largest millet producer**, **42.75%** of world output.
Millets are **mostly kharif**, **climate-resilient, low-input** crops.
Oilseeds moved to **NMEO-Edible Oils**, not NFSNM.

81.s: The United Nations declared which year as the International Year of Millets?
81.x: 2023 was observed as the UN International Year of Millets, with India actively promoting the initiative.
81.tq: Recall the specific year associated with an international agricultural observance.
xs: **2023** was the UN **International Year of Millets** — option **(3)**, pushed by India.
Millets were branded **Shree Anna**.
xa: India is the **largest millet producer**: **18.59 MMT**, **42.75%** of world output.
**Nutri-cereals** were added to NFSM in **2018-19**.
**Bajra** gives ~**60%** of India's millet output.
Millet leaders: **Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Karnataka**.

81.s: Dryland farming in India generally refers to cultivation in areas having:
o: Less than 750 mm rainfall and no assured irrigation
More than 1,500 mm rainfall with assured irrigation
Exactly 1,000 mm rainfall and canal irrigation
Less than 250 mm rainfall with compulsory greenhouse cultivation
81.x: Dryland farming is practised in areas receiving less than 750 mm rainfall and lacking assured irrigation.
81.tq: Apply both conditions—rainfall limit and absence of assured irrigation—rather than using rainfall alone.
xs: **Dryland farming** = areas with **less than 750 mm** (under **75 cm**) rainfall and **no assured irrigation** — option **(1)**.
Such areas grow **millets + pulses**.
xa: About **51%** of net sown area is **rainfed**.
Only **56.4%** of net sown area is irrigated.
Millets are **climate-resilient, low-input** crops of **dryland/rainfed tracts**.
⚠ Rice needs **above 100 cm**; wheat **50-75 cm**.

81.s: Which group of crops is predominantly produced in India's rainfed areas?
81.x: Rainfed areas, which constitute about 51 per cent of net sown area, produce most of India's millets, pulses and oilseeds.
81.tq: Connect the rainfed-area characteristic with its principal crop group.
xs: Rainfed areas yield **most millets, pulses, oilseeds** — option **(1)**.
About **51%** of net sown area is **rainfed**.
xa: **Dryland farming**: under **750 mm** rainfall, no assured irrigation → millets + pulses.
Pulses are **rain-fed, low-moisture** crops.
Only about **12%** of irrigated area uses **drip or sprinkler**.
Rainfed and hilly areas were **left out** of the Green Revolution.

81.s: The shifting cultivation system known as ‘Dipa’ is associated with which of the following regions?
o: The agency areas of Andhra Pradesh and Odisha
81.x: Dipa is the local name for shifting cultivation in Bastar, Chhattisgarh. Podu is associated with the agency areas of Andhra Pradesh and Odisha.
81.tq: Use the exact local-name and location association rather than confusing neighbouring tribal regions.
xs: **Dipa** is shifting cultivation in **Bastar, Chhattisgarh** (APPSC 2025) — option **(1)**.
**Kumari** belongs to the **Western Ghats**; **Masole** to **Central Africa**; **Podu** to the **AP and Odisha agency**.
xa: Dipa is also reported from the **Andaman**.
APPSC-GS 2025 key: **Dipa**.
**Bewar / Dahiya** = Madhya Pradesh; **Jhum** = north-east.
Method: **slash and burn**, then move on.

81.s:
Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
1. Tamrai — Thailand
2. Chena — Sri Lanka
3. Bewar — Madhya Pradesh
4. Kumari — Western Ghats
81.x: Tamrai is associated with Thailand, Chena with Sri Lanka, Bewar with Madhya Pradesh and Kumari with the Western Ghats.
81.tq: Check each local-name pair independently before selecting the coded combination.
xs: All four pairs are right: **Tamrai — Thailand**, **Chena — Sri Lanka**, **Bewar — Madhya Pradesh**, **Kumari — Western Ghats** — option **(4)**.
**Tamrai** and **Chena** are foreign names; **Bewar (Dahiya)** and **Kumari** are Indian names.
xa: **Bewar** is also called **Dahiya** (MP).
**Kumari** spans **Kerala, Karnataka**.
**Conuco / Ray / Taungya** = Venezuela / Vietnam / Myanmar.
**Ponam (Poonam)** = Kerala; **Pama Dabi / Koman / Bringa** = Odisha.

81.s: Which of the following communities are associated with the practice of shifting cultivation in Andhra Pradesh?
81.x: In Andhra Pradesh, shifting cultivation is practised by the Konda Reddi, Koya and Savara communities. The practice involves slash-and-burn cultivation followed by movement to another site.
81.tq: Identify the communities linked to the regional practice instead of relying on general tribal associations.
xs: In AP, shifting cultivation is practised by the **Konda Reddi, Koya, Savara** — option **(3)**.
The method is **slash and burn**, then move on.
xa: AP's form is **Podu / Penda** in the **Eastern Ghats** agency; **Pondu** is a variant spelling.
APPSC 2025: the South Indian state practising **jhumming** = **Andhra Pradesh**.

82.tq: Compare the climatic and site requirements of plantation crops.
xs: Tea: **20-30°C**, **150-300 cm** rainfall, **deep, well-drained, acidic hill slopes** — option **(2)**.
Option 1 is **rubber**, option 3 **cotton**, option 4 **coffee**.
xa: Tea tolerates **no waterlogging**.
Tea began in the **first half of the 19th century** in the **Brahmaputra valley (Assam)**.
**Darjeeling Tea** = India's **first GI-tagged product**.
**Tea Board** HQ = **Kolkata**.

82.s: Coffee cultivation is best associated with which of the following conditions?
o: 20–30°C, waterlogged alluvial plains and heavy rainfall
15–28°C, shade, 150–250 cm rainfall and deep well-drained humus-rich soil
25–35°C, flood plains and high humidity without shade
82.x: Coffee requires about 15–28°C, shade, 150–250 cm rainfall and deep, well-drained, humus-rich soil, especially in the Western Ghats.
82.tq: Select the precise crop-condition combination.
xs: Coffee needs **15-28°C**, **shade**, **150-250 cm** rainfall and **deep, well-drained, humus-rich** soil — option **(2)**.
**21-37°C** with black soil is **cotton**; **25-35°C** is **rubber**.
xa: Coffee grows in the **Western Ghats**; types **Arabica** and **Robusta**.
Arabica was introduced in the **Baba Budan hills**, Chikkamagaluru.
**Karnataka** gives about **70%** of India's coffee.
**Coffee Board** HQ = **Bengaluru**; AP grows **Araku** coffee.

82.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Rubber requires a humid climate and about 25–35°C.
2. Rubber generally requires 200–300 cm rainfall.
3. Laterite soils of the Western Ghats are associated with rubber cultivation.
4. Rubber is best suited to frost-prone dry interiors.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
82.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Rubber requires a warm, humid and high-rainfall environment, whereas frost-prone dry interiors are unsuitable.
82.tq: Reject the climate-incompatible statement.
xs: Statements 1-3 correct: rubber needs **25-35°C**, humid; **200-300 cm** rain; **laterite** soils of the **Western Ghats**.
Statement 4 wrong: frost-prone dry interiors do not suit a humid, high-rainfall crop — so **1, 2 and 3 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: Rubber leaders: **Kerala**, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka.
India is **5th** in natural rubber.
**Rubber Board** HQ = **Kottayam**.
Rubber is a **plantation crop** — labour- and capital-intensive.

82.s: Jute cultivation is most closely associated with which combination?
o: Cool dry climate and black soils
Cold climate, acidic hill slopes and low rainfall
Semi-arid climate and deep sandy loam
Hot humid climate, heavy rainfall and alluvial flood plains
82.x: Jute requires a hot, humid climate, high rainfall and alluvial soils of flood plains, particularly in the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta.
82.tq: Link a fibre crop with its characteristic physical setting.
xs: Jute needs a **hot, high-humidity** climate, **heavy** rainfall and **alluvial flood plains** of the **Ganga-Brahmaputra delta** — option **(4)**.
Black soils, acidic hill slopes and sandy loam suit **cotton** or **tea**, not jute.
xa: Jute leaders: **West Bengal**, Bihar, Assam.
India is **1st** — the **largest raw jute producer**.
Jute = **Golden Fibre**.
**Jute Packaging Materials Act, 1987**: **100% food grains and 20% sugar** in jute.

82.s:
Which of the following are regarded as relatively water-efficient alternatives in the context of Indian agriculture?
1. Millets
2. Pulses
3. Oilseeds
4. Paddy in Punjab and sugarcane in Maharashtra
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
82.x: Millets, pulses and oilseeds are water-efficient alternatives. Paddy in Punjab and sugarcane in Maharashtra reflect subsidy distortions rather than climate suitability.
82.tq: Separate sustainable alternatives from subsidy-induced crop patterns.
xs: **Millets, pulses, oilseeds** are the **water-efficient alternatives** — **1, 2 and 3 only**, option **(1)**.
**Paddy in Punjab + sugarcane in Maharashtra** reflect **subsidy distortions, not climate suitability** (Jun 2025).
xa: Sugarcane is a **long-duration** crop of **10-15 months**.
Oilseed area, production and productivity **rose** (ES 2025-26).
ICAR released **13** climate-resilient oilseed varieties.
**Yellow Revolution** = oilseeds.

82.s:
Consider the following pairs of soil and suitable crops:
1. Black soil - cotton, chillies and tobacco
2. Red soil - groundnut, tobacco and ragi
3. Laterite soil - jute
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
82.x: Pair 1 is correct: black soils (clayey, moisture-retentive) suit cotton, chillies and tobacco. Pair 2 is correct: red soils suit groundnut, tobacco and ragi. Pair 3 is wrong: laterite soil of the Western Ghats is linked to rubber, while jute grows on alluvial flood plains of the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta. Hence '1 and 2 only'.
82.tq: Black = cotton; red = groundnut/ragi; laterite = rubber; alluvial delta = jute.
xs: Pair 1 correct: **black soil — cotton, chillies, tobacco**.
Pair 2 correct: **red soil — groundnut, tobacco, ragi**.
Pair 3 wrong: **laterite** suits **rubber**; jute grows on **alluvial flood plains** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: Black soils have **clay over 62%** and retain moisture.
Black soils of **western AP** grow cotton, chillies, tobacco.
Cotton soil is **regur**, pH **5.8-8.0**.
Sugarcane grows on **alluvial/black** soil.

82.s: Tea plantations in India began in the first half of the nineteenth century in the:
82.x: The first tea plantations were begun in the first half of the nineteenth century in the Brahmaputra Valley of Assam.
82.tq: Link the historical origin of plantation tea with its geographical valley rather than with a hill region.
xs: Tea plantations began in the **first half of the 19th century** in the **Brahmaputra Valley (Assam)** (APPSC-G2 2025) — option **(4)**.
The **Nilgiri Hills** grow tea and coffee but were not the first.
xa: **Assam** is the leading tea state.
**Darjeeling Tea** = India's **first GI-tagged product**.
West Bengal tea areas: **Darjeeling, Dooars**.
Colonial plantations were **European-dominated, export-oriented**.

82.s:
With reference to plantation crops, consider the following statements:
1. Tea, coffee, rubber and coconut are plantation crops.
2. Plantation crops are generally labour-intensive and capital-intensive.
3. Colonial plantations of tea, coffee, rubber and indigo were largely European-dominated and export-oriented.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
82.x: All three statements are correct. These crops are high-value plantation crops requiring substantial labour and capital, and the colonial plantation sector was dominated by Europeans and oriented towards exports.
82.tq: Combine classification, production characteristics and historical ownership in one statement question.
xs: Statement 1 correct: **tea, coffee, rubber, coconut** are plantation crops.
Statement 2 correct: they are **high-value, labour- and capital-intensive**.
Statement 3 correct: colonial plantations (**tea, coffee, rubber, indigo**) were **European-dominated, export-oriented** — option **(4)**.
xa: Tea began in the **Brahmaputra valley** in the first half of the **19th** century.
**CPCRI** (plantation crops) = **Kasaragod**.
Coffee: **Arabica** + **Robusta** in the Western Ghats.
**Nilgiri Hills** (TN) grow tea and coffee.

82.s: Arabica coffee in India is particularly associated with the:
82.x: Arabica coffee is associated with the Baba Budan Hills in Chikkamagaluru, Karnataka. The two principal coffee varieties mentioned are Arabica and Robusta.
82.tq: Use the specific hill–variety association to distinguish coffee geography from tea geography.
xs: **Arabica** coffee is linked to the **Baba Budan hills**, **Chikkamagaluru** (Karnataka) — option **(3)**.
**Darjeeling** is a **tea** area, not coffee.
xa: India's two coffees: **Arabica** and **Robusta**.
**Kodagu** (Karnataka) also grows coffee.
**Karnataka** gives about **70%** of India's coffee.
AP coffee: **Araku**, **ASR district** (clusters proposed).

82.s:
Which of the following pairs of coffee-growing areas and states is correctly matched?
1. Kodagu — Karnataka
2. Araku and ASR district — Andhra Pradesh
3. Nilgiri Hills — Tamil Nadu
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
82.x: Kodagu is in Karnataka, Araku and the ASR district are associated with coffee clusters in Andhra Pradesh, and the Nilgiris are in Tamil Nadu. All three pairs are correct.
82.tq: Verify each place–state pair before accepting the complete combination.
xs: All three are correct: **Kodagu — Karnataka**, **Araku/ASR — AP**, **Nilgiri Hills — Tamil Nadu** — option **(4)**.
The **Nilgiris** grow both **tea and coffee**.
xa: AP coffee clusters were proposed in APSES **2024-25**.
Karnataka's **Baba Budan hills** saw Arabica introduced.
Coffee needs **15-28°C**, **shade**, **150-250 cm**.
**Coffee Board** = **Bengaluru**.

82.s: Darjeeling Tea has the distinction of being India’s:
82.x: Darjeeling Tea was India’s first product to receive a Geographical Indication tag.
82.tq: Identify the exact official distinction rather than confusing GI status with MSP or export status.
xs: **Darjeeling Tea** was India's **first GI-tagged product** — option **(3)**.
It is neither an MSP crop nor a GM crop.
xa: Darjeeling and **Dooars** are West Bengal's tea areas.
Tea began in the **Brahmaputra valley (Assam)**.
India is **2nd in tea** after **China**.
**Lakadong turmeric** (Meghalaya) is known for **high curcumin**.

82.s:
Which of the following conditions explains the higher productivity of sugarcane in the tropical belt compared with the sub-tropical belt?
1. Cool nights with clear skies
2. Latitudinal position
3. Long hours of sunshine
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
82.x: The tropical advantage is attributed to cool nights with clear skies, favourable latitudinal position and long hours of sunshine. These conditions contribute to higher yield and sucrose content.
82.tq: Treat each listed climatic factor separately before selecting the combined code.
xs: The tropical advantage comes from **cool nights with clear skies**, **latitudinal position** and **long hours of sunshine** — all three, option **(4)** (APPSC-G1 2023 key: I, II, III).
These give the tropical belt **higher yield and sucrose**.
xa: Tropical belt: **Maharashtra, Karnataka, TN, AP**.
Tropical crushing: **Oct to May/June**; sub-tropical: **Nov to Feb**.
**UP** still leads in area and production.
Sugarcane gets **FRP**, not MSP.

82.s: Which one of the following correctly compares tropical and sub-tropical sugarcane regions?
o: Tropical regions have lower yield and a shorter crushing season.
Tropical regions have higher yield and sucrose content and a longer crushing season.
Sub-tropical regions have higher sucrose content and crushing from October to June.
Both regions have identical yield and crushing seasons.
82.x: Tropical sugarcane has higher yield and sucrose content, with a longer crushing season from October to May or June. The sub-tropical season is generally November to February.
82.tq: Compare both yield and season together; a reversed comparison is the main trap.
xs: **Tropical** sugarcane has **higher yield and sucrose** and a **longer crushing season** — option **(2)**.
Tropical crushing runs **Oct to May/June**; sub-tropical only **Nov to Feb**.
xa: Reasons: **cool nights, latitudinal position, long sunshine**.
North (**UP-Bihar**) concentration: alluvium rich in **lime + potash**, level land, dense market.
**Western UP** = main sugar-mill belt.
Sugarcane is a **10-15 month** crop.

82.s:
Consider the following statements about sugarcane cultivation in India:
1. It is a long-duration crop of about 10-15 months.
2. It requires cold and dry conditions.
3. It grows well in alluvial or black soil.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
82.x: Statement 1 is correct: sugarcane is a long-duration crop of about 10-15 months. Statement 2 is wrong: it needs hot and humid conditions, not cold and dry. Statement 3 is correct: it grows on alluvial or black soil. So '1 and 3 only'; '1 only' misses statement 3, and the options with 2 include a false statement.
82.tq: Sugarcane = long (10-15 months), hot-humid, alluvial/black soil.
xs: Statement 1 correct: sugarcane is a **long-duration** crop of **10-15 months**.
Statement 2 wrong: it needs **hot and humid**, not cold and dry, conditions.
Statement 3 correct: it grows on **alluvial/black soil** — so **1 and 3 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: **UP** leads in area and production.
Tropical belt has **higher yield and sucrose**.
Sugarcane in **Maharashtra** is cited as a **subsidy distortion**.
ICAR released **6** sugarcane varieties (5 Jan 2026).

82.s: Which one of the following best explains the concentration of sugarcane cultivation in the Uttar Pradesh–Bihar region?
o: Predominance of shifting cultivation and steep slopes
Scarcity of alluvial soil and absence of markets
Cool nights, black soil and very short crushing season
Fertile alluvium rich in lime and potash, level land, dense markets and compact cane blocks
82.x: The northern concentration is supported by fertile alluvium rich in lime and potash, level land, dense markets and sugarcane grown in compact blocks. Western Uttar Pradesh is the principal sugar-mill belt.
82.tq: Apply several linked geographical conditions to a regional production scenario.
xs: UP-Bihar concentration rests on **fertile alluvium rich in lime + potash**, **level land**, **dense market** and **cane in compact blocks** — option **(4)**.
**Western UP** is the main **sugar-mill belt**.
xa: Sub-tropical north has **lower** yield and sucrose and crushes **Nov to Feb**.
⚠ **Cool nights with clear skies** explain the **tropical** advantage, not the north.
Sugarcane gets **FRP** instead of MSP.
**Golden Revolution** = horticulture, honey (not sugarcane).

82.s: Which one of the following statements about sugarcane support pricing is correct?
o: Sugarcane receives both MSP and FRP simultaneously.
Sugarcane receives FRP instead of MSP.
Sugarcane is not covered by any administered price mechanism.
Sugarcane receives MSP but not FRP.
82.x: Sugarcane is covered by the Fair and Remunerative Price (FRP), not the Minimum Support Price (MSP).
82.tq: Discriminate between the two administered price terms rather than treating them as interchangeable.
xs: Sugarcane gets **FRP instead of MSP** — option **(2)**.
**MSP** covers **22 crops**; sugarcane is outside that list.
xa: **7 MSP oilseeds**: groundnut, rapeseed-mustard, soybean, sesamum, sunflower, safflower, nigerseed.
**Jute Corporation of India** buys raw jute at **MSP** when prices fall.
Sugarcane is a **10-15 month** crop.
**UP** leads sugarcane.

82.s: Which one of the following is a Rabi oilseed only, as identified for Indian cropping seasons?
82.x: Mustard is identified as a Rabi-only oilseed in the given classification. Groundnut and sesamum are Kharif oilseeds, while sunflower can be grown in both seasons.
82.tq: Separate the Rabi-only crop from Kharif crops and the crop grown in both seasons.
xs: **Mustard** is the oilseed grown as **rabi only** (APPSC-G2 2025 trap) — option **(4)**.
**Groundnut, sesamum** are **kharif**; **sunflower** grows in **both seasons**.
xa: Rabi oilseeds: **rapeseed-mustard, linseed, safflower**.
Kharif oilseeds: **groundnut, soybean, sesamum, castor, nigerseed**.
**7 MSP oilseeds** include rapeseed-mustard.
**Yellow Revolution** = oilseeds.

82.s: Which one of the following sets consists entirely of Kharif oilseeds?
o: Mustard, linseed, safflower, soybean and sunflower
Groundnut, soybean, sesamum, castor and nigerseed
Rapeseed-mustard, groundnut, linseed, castor and safflower
Mustard, sesamum, linseed, nigerseed and safflower
82.x: Groundnut, soybean, sesamum, castor and nigerseed are listed as Kharif oilseeds. Mustard, linseed and safflower are Rabi oilseeds, while sunflower is grown in both seasons.
82.tq: Check every item in the group because one misplaced season changes the answer.
xs: All-kharif set: **groundnut, soybean, sesamum, castor, nigerseed** — option **(2)**.
**Mustard, linseed, safflower** are **rabi**; **sunflower** is both seasons.
xa: **Gujarat** grows **86.6%** of castor and **44.3%** of groundnut.
⚠ Rabi-only oilseed = **mustard**.
**NMEO-Oilseeds** covers groundnut, sesamum, castor, sunflower etc.
Groundnut grows on **red soils**.

82.s: The number of oilseeds covered under the Minimum Support Price system, as listed, is:
82.x: Seven oilseeds are listed under MSP: groundnut, rapeseed-mustard, soybean, sesamum, sunflower, safflower and nigerseed.
82.tq: Count the named members of the category instead of confusing them with the total MSP crop count.
xs: **7** oilseeds are under **MSP**: **groundnut, rapeseed-mustard, soybean, sesamum, sunflower, safflower, nigerseed** — option **(3)**.
MSP covers **22 crops** in all; sugarcane gets **FRP**.
xa: Kharif oilseeds: groundnut, soybean, sesamum, castor, nigerseed.
Rabi oilseeds: **rapeseed-mustard, linseed, safflower**.
⚠ **Castor** and **linseed** are not in the MSP list.
NMEO missions target nearly **70 million tonnes by 2030-31**.

82.s: The National Mission on Edible Oils–Oilseeds and the National Mission on Edible Oils–Oil Palm aim at nearly what production level by 2030–31?
82.x: The two missions aim at nearly 70 million tonnes by 2030–31.
82.tq: Test the target year and production figure as a combined current-affairs quantity.
xs: **NMEO-Oilseeds + NMEO-Oil Palm** target nearly **70 million tonnes by 2030-31** — option **(3)**.
The other figures (**50**, **30**, **100**) do not match the stated target.
xa: NMEO-Oilseeds: **groundnut, sesamum, castor, sunflower** etc.
NMEO-Oil Palm: **AP leads** oil-palm area, production, productivity.
Oilseed area, production and productivity **rose** (ES 2025-26).
**Yellow Revolution** = oilseeds.

82.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Jute-ICARE — Jute
2. NMEO-Oil Palm — Oil palm
3. Technology Mission on Cotton — Cotton
4. NMEO-Oilseeds — Groundnut, sesamum, castor and sunflower
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
82.x: All four pairs are correctly matched. Jute-ICARE concerns jute, NMEO-Oil Palm concerns oil palm, the Technology Mission on Cotton concerns cotton, and NMEO-Oilseeds covers several oilseeds.
82.tq: Match each scheme with its specific crop sector.
xs: All four pairs match: **Jute-ICARE — jute**, **NMEO-Oil Palm — oil palm**, **Technology Mission on Cotton — cotton**, **NMEO-Oilseeds — groundnut, sesamum, castor, sunflower** — option **(4)**.
Each scheme is named for its crop: **ICARE** for jute retting, **Oil Palm** and **Oilseeds** under **NMEO**, and the cotton mission for **cotton**.
xa: JUTE-ICARE = **Improved Cultivation and Advanced Retting Exercise**, with retting consortium **SONA**.
Technology Mission on Cotton = **Silver Fibre Revolution**.
**AP** leads oil-palm area, production and productivity.
**Paat-Mitro app** (**2023**) is for jute farmers.

82.s: The Paat-Mitro mobile application is associated with which crop?
82.x: Paat-Mitro was launched in 2023 for jute farmers.
82.tq: Direct recall of a crop-specific application.
xs: **Paat-Mitro** (**2023**) is an app for **jute** farmers (APPSC 2024) — option **(4)**.
Cotton, oil palm and sugarcane have their own missions — not Paat-Mitro.
xa: **Jute Crop Information System** (since 2023) is run by the **National Jute Board**.
**JUTE-ICARE**: certified seed + microbial retting consortium **SONA**.
Jute = **Golden Fibre**; India is the **largest raw jute producer**.
**Jute Corporation of India** buys raw jute at **MSP**.

82.s: JUTE-ICARE is an initiative involving:
o: Certified seed and the microbial retting consortium SONA
Drip irrigation for oil palm and coconut
82.x: JUTE-ICARE, or Improved Cultivation and Advanced Retting Exercise, involves certified seed and the microbial retting consortium SONA.
82.tq: Expand the acronym and identify its operational components.
xs: **JUTE-ICARE** gives **certified seed** and the **microbial retting consortium SONA** — option **(1)**.
ICARE = **Improved Cultivation and Advanced Retting Exercise**.
xa: **Paat-Mitro** app (**2023**) for jute farmers.
Jute grows on **alluvial flood plains** of the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta.
**National Jute Board** (Kolkata) runs the National Jute Development Programme.
Jute goods face **Bangladesh's** export competition.

82.s: Under the Jute Packaging Materials Act, 1987, the prescribed packing requirement is:
o: 50% of food grains and 50% of sugar in jute
100% of food grains and 20% of sugar in jute
100% of food grains and 100% of sugar in jute
20% of food grains and 100% of sugar in jute
82.x: The Act requires 100% of food grains and 20% of sugar to be packed in jute, subject to the stated provisions.
82.tq: Recall paired statutory percentages accurately.
xs: The **Jute Packaging Materials Act, 1987** requires **100% food grains and 20% sugar** in jute — option **(2)**.
Options 1, 3 and 4 misstate the two shares.
xa: **Jute Corporation of India** buys raw jute at **MSP** when prices fall.
**National Jute Board**: jute-viscose apparel with **NIFT** for **2026** Commonwealth Games.
India is the **largest raw jute producer**.
Jute leaders: **West Bengal**, Bihar, Assam.

82.s: Which of the following functions is associated with the National Jute Board?
o: Managing the National Bamboo Mission exclusively
Running the National Jute Development Programme and Jute Crop Information System
Fixing the minimum support price for all agricultural commodities
82.x: The National Jute Board runs the National Jute Development Programme and the Jute Crop Information System, which has operated since 2023.
82.tq: Identify the correct institutional function.
xs: The **National Jute Board** runs the **Jute Crop Information System** with the **National Jute Development Programme** — option **(3)**.
The Jute Crop Information System has run **since 2023**.
xa: National Jute Board HQ = **Kolkata**.
It made **jute-viscose apparel** with **NIFT** for the 2026 Commonwealth Games.
⚠ **National Bamboo Mission** is a **MIDH** sub-scheme, not the Jute Board's.
**Paat-Mitro** app (**2023**) for jute farmers.

82.s: When market prices fall, the Jute Corporation of India purchases raw jute at:
o: A price fixed by the National Horticulture Board
82.x: The Jute Corporation of India buys raw jute at the minimum support price when market prices fall.
82.tq: Apply the institutional role to a market-price scenario.
xs: The **Jute Corporation of India** buys raw jute at the **minimum support price** (MSP) when market prices fall — option **(1)**.
Export parity or spot prices are not the jute support mechanism.
xa: **Jute Packaging Materials Act, 1987**: **100% food grains, 20% sugar** in jute.
**JUTE-ICARE** with the retting consortium **SONA**.
**National Jute Board** = Kolkata.
Jute = **Golden Fibre**; Golden Fibre Revolution = jute.

82.s:
Which of the following statements regarding cash crops in Andhra Pradesh is correct?
1. Chilli and tobacco are grown in the black-soil belt.
2. Guntur is a major chilli-trade hub.
3. The Tobacco Board is headquartered at Guntur.
4. Andhra Pradesh ranks first among States in chilli production and second in turmeric.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
82.x: All four statements are correct in the stated assessment. Andhra Pradesh's black-soil belt supports chilli and tobacco, Guntur is the chilli-trade hub and Tobacco Board seat, and the State ranks first in chillies and second in turmeric.
82.tq: Combine crop region, market centre, institution and rank.
xs: Statement 1 correct: **chillies + tobacco** grow in AP's **black-soil belt**.
Statements 2 and 3 correct: **Guntur** is the **chilli-trade hub** and seat of the **Tobacco Board**.
Statement 4 correct: AP is **1st in chillies**, **2nd in turmeric** (APSES 2024-25) — option **(4)**.
xa: Black soils of **western AP** grow **cotton, chillies, tobacco**.
⚠ **Lakadong turmeric** is from **Meghalaya** (high curcumin).
AP also leads **oil palm** and grows **Araku** coffee.
Black soils have **clay over 62%**.

82.s: Lakadong, known for its high curcumin content, is a turmeric variety associated with:
82.x: Lakadong turmeric of Meghalaya is known for its high curcumin content.
82.tq: Match a distinctive crop variety with its State.
xs: **Lakadong turmeric** is from **Meghalaya**, known for **high curcumin** — option **(1)**.
**AP** is **2nd in turmeric** among states, but Lakadong is not AP's.
xa: AP is **1st in chillies**.
**Meghalaya** also leads in **pineapple**.
**Mission Golden Spice** was highlighted in Jul 2026.
**Spices Board** = **Kochi**; **IISR** = **Kozhikode**.

82.s: India occupies which position in the world in fruit and vegetable production?
82.x: India is stated to be the second-largest producer in the world of fruits and vegetables.
82.tq: Direct recall of a world production rank.
xs: India is **second** in the world in **fruits and vegetables** — option **(1)**.
India is the **largest milk producer** (APPSC G2 2025 key) — a separate first.
xa: Horticulture (**362-367 MT**) now exceeds food grains.
It gives about **30.4%** of agricultural GDP from **under 14%** of cropped area.
**AP** is India's **largest fruit producer (15.6%)**.
India is also **2nd** in **sugar**.

82.s:
Which of the following statements regarding horticulture in India is correct?
1. Horticulture output is about 362–367 million tonnes.
2. Horticulture contributes about 30.4% of agricultural GDP.
3. It comes from under 14% of the cropped area.
4. Horticulture output has exceeded food-grain output.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
82.x: All four statements are correct in the stated assessment. Horticulture output is about 362–367 MT, exceeds food-grain output and contributes around 30.4% of agricultural GDP from under 14% of cropped area.
82.tq: Check several quantitative dimensions of one sector together.
xs: All four are correct: output **362-367 MT**, **30.4%** of agricultural GDP, from **under 14%** of cropped area, and it **exceeds food grains** — option **(4)**.
So horticulture is high-value: a large output share from a small share of cropped area.
xa: **MIDH** lifted productivity to **12.56 MT/ha**.
India is **2nd** in world fruits and vegetables.
**AP** = largest fruit producer, **406.38 lakh MT** on **18.57 lakh ha**.
**Golden Revolution** = horticulture, honey.

82.s: Which State is stated to be India's largest fruit producer, with a share of about 15.6%?
82.x: Andhra Pradesh is stated to be India's largest fruit producer, accounting for about 15.6% of production.
82.tq: Direct recall of a state-level production lead.
xs: **Andhra Pradesh** is India's **largest fruit producer (15.6%)** — option **(2)**.
xa: Earlier: **18.23 lakh ha**, **365.92 lakh MT** (APSES 2024-25).
⚠ **Bihar** = **litchi**; **Meghalaya** = **pineapple**.
AP also leads **oil palm**.

85.s: Which statement correctly describes the location of cotton textile industries?
o: They are necessarily located at cotton-producing farms because cotton is weight-losing.
They can be located only near coalfields.
They are non-weight-losing and therefore are not bound to raw-material sites.

85.x: Cotton textiles are non-weight-losing industries and therefore are not necessarily tied to the location of raw cotton.
85.tq: Separate non-weight-losing cotton textiles from weight-losing industries.
xs: Cotton textiles are **non-weight-losing**, so they are **not bound to raw-material sites** — option **(3)**.
In Weber's terms **cotton** is a **pure localised** material — it loses no weight in processing.
Weight-losing (**gross**) materials are **iron ore, coal, sugarcane**, which pull plants to the raw material.
xa: **Material Index** = weight of localised raw materials / weight of finished product.
**MI > 1** → locate at raw material; **MI < 1** → at market.
**Lancashire** (Manchester) and **Osaka** are cotton-textile centres.
**Osaka** = "**Manchester of the East**".

85.s: According to Weber’s least-cost theory, an industrial firm seeks a location where the combined cost of which factors is least?
o: Raw materials, climate and exports only
85.x: Alfred Weber’s 1909 least-cost theory considers the combined transport, labour and agglomeration costs.
85.tq: Recall the three cost components of the theory.
xs: **Alfred Weber (1909)**: a firm locates where total **transport + labour + agglomeration** costs are least — option **(1)**.
This is the **least-cost theory**.
xa: ⚠ **Weber** = least cost; **Losch** = maximum profit / market area; **Isard** = substitution; **Florence** = Location Quotient.
**Locational triangle**: two raw-material sources + one market.
**Isodapanes**: lines of equal extra transport cost.
**Agglomeration economies**: savings when firms cluster.

85.s: In Weber’s locational triangle, the three vertices represent:
o: one raw-material source and two ports only
two markets and one labour centre
two raw-material sources and one market

85.tq: Identify the vertices before judging the location point.
xs: Weber's **locational triangle** = **two raw-material sources and one market** — option **(4)**.
The **least-transport-cost point** lies **inside** it.
xa: **Isodapanes**: labour or agglomeration savings can pull a firm off that point.
**Material Index** decides raw-material vs market pull.
Weber's theory dates to **1909**.
**Ubiquities** (water, air) are available everywhere and do not pull location.

85.s: The Material Index (MI) is calculated as:
o: weight of finished product divided by weight of localised raw materials
transport cost divided by labour cost
market distance divided by raw-material distance
weight of localised raw materials divided by weight of finished product
85.x: Material Index equals the weight of localised raw materials divided by the weight of the finished product.
85.tq: Distinguish the numerator and denominator in the formula.
xs: **MI = weight of localised raw materials / weight of finished product** — option **(4)**.
Option 1 inverts the ratio.
xa: **MI > 1** → locate **at raw material**; **MI < 1** → **at market**.
Steel: about **4 tonnes** of raw material → **1 tonne** of steel, so MI is high.
**Gross (weight-losing)**: iron ore, coal, sugarcane.
**Pure localised**: lose no weight (cotton).

85.s: If the Material Index of an industry is greater than one, the industry tends to locate:
o: at a neutral point unrelated to materials

85.tq: Apply the MI threshold to infer the location tendency.
xs: **MI > 1** → the industry locates **near the raw-material source** — option **(2)**.
**MI < 1** → it locates **at the market**.
xa: MI = weight of **localised raw materials** / weight of **finished product**.
Steel plants sit on **coalfields/ore fields** — a weight-losing case.
**Cotton textiles** are non-weight-losing and not bound to raw material.
**Footloose** industries are tied to neither.
