85.s:
Consider the following pairs of iron and steel region and its location:
1. Atlantic Coast — USA
2. Ural — Russia
3. Ruhr — Eastern Europe
Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched?
85.x: Pair 1 is correct: the Atlantic Coast region (Baltimore, Bethlehem) is in the USA. Pair 2 is correct: the Ural region (Magnitogorsk, Chelyabinsk) is in Russia. Pair 3 is wrong: the Ruhr (Essen, Duisburg, Dortmund) is in Germany, in Western Europe. So '1 and 2 only', as in the APPSC-G1 2023/2024 key.
85.tq: Ruhr = Germany (Western Europe), never Eastern Europe.
xs: Pair 1 correct: **Atlantic coast — USA** (Baltimore, Bethlehem).
Pair 2 correct: **Ural — Russia** (Magnitogorsk, Chelyabinsk).
Pair 3 wrong: **Ruhr** is in **Germany** (Western Europe) — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(2)** (APPSC-G1 2023/2024 key).
xa: Ruhr centres: **Essen, Duisburg, Dortmund**.
**Donbas** = **Ukraine** (Donetsk).
**Lorraine** = France (Metz, Nancy).
**Chotanagpur** = "Ruhr of India".

85.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
85.x: Lancashire, including Manchester, is a major cotton-textile region of the United Kingdom.
85.tq: Begin with the familiar region–industry association.
xs: **Lancashire** (Manchester, UK) = **cotton textiles** — option **(1)**.
**Flanders** = woollen/linen textiles; **Po Valley** = engineering, automobiles, textiles; **Great Kanawha Valley** = **chemicals**.
xa: **Osaka** = cotton textiles; "**Manchester of the East**".
**St. Petersburg** = shipbuilding.
**Detroit** = automobiles.
**Cuba** = cigars.

85.s: The Po Valley industrial region is particularly associated with:
85.x: The Po Valley, with centres such as Milan and Turin, is associated with engineering, automobiles and textiles.
85.tq: Match the region with its industrial combination.
xs: The **Po Valley** (Milan, Turin), Italy = **engineering, automobiles, textiles** — option **(4)**.
**Woollen/linen textiles** = **Flanders**; **chemicals** = **Great Kanawha Valley**; **shipbuilding** = **St. Petersburg**; **cigars** = **Cuba**.
xa: **Lancashire** = cotton textiles.
**Kinki** = textiles, heavy industry.
**Detroit** = automobiles (UPPSC 2022).
**Chennai** = "Detroit of India".

85.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
85.x: Cuba is associated with cigars, not iron and steel. Osaka, Detroit and St. Petersburg are associated respectively with cotton textiles, automobiles and shipbuilding.
85.tq: Locate the industry deliberately swapped with a familiar centre.
xs: **Cuba — iron and steel** is wrong — option **(3)**; Cuba is known for **cigars** (UPPSC 2022).
Correct: **Detroit — automobiles**, **St. Petersburg — shipbuilding**, **Osaka — cotton textiles**.
xa: **Pittsburgh** = iron and steel.
**Great Kanawha Valley** = chemicals.
**Aberdeen** = "Oil capital of Europe".
**Osaka** = "Manchester of the East".

85.s: Kinki, comprising Osaka, Kobe and Kyoto, is best described as a:
o: dense industrial belt with textiles and heavy industry
85.x: Kinki is a dense industrial belt of Japan associated with textiles and heavy industry.
85.tq: Use the regional description rather than a single-industry label.
xs: **Kinki** (Osaka-Kobe-Kyoto) is a **dense industrial belt** with **textiles, heavy industry** — option **(2)**.
Cigars belong to **Cuba**; shipbuilding to **St. Petersburg**.
xa: **Osaka** = **cotton textiles**; "Manchester of the East".
**Kitakyushu** (Kyushu) = steel, **Yawata**.
**Asian Tigers**: South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore, Hong Kong.
**Lancashire** = UK cotton textiles.

85.s:
Which of the following is not a United States industrial region or centre in the classification given?
1. Cincinnati–Indianapolis
2. Great Kanawha Valley
3. Michigan lake region
4. Midlands
Select the correct answer.
85.x: Midlands is an industrial region of England, not of the United States. Cincinnati–Indianapolis, Great Kanawha Valley and the Michigan lake region are associated with the USA.
85.tq: Use geographical exclusion to detect the non-US region.
xs: **Midlands** is **not** a US industrial region — it is in **England** (RPSC 2023) — so **4 only**, option **(4)**.
**Cincinnati-Indianapolis**, **Great Kanawha Valley**, **Michigan lake region** are US regions.
xa: Great Kanawha Valley (**West Virginia**) = **chemicals**.
**Detroit** = automobiles.
**Pittsburgh** = iron and steel.
**Rust Belt** = old north-eastern US and Great Lakes belt.

85.s: The nickname ‘Manchester of the East’ refers to:
85.x: Osaka in Japan is known as the ‘Manchester of the East’.
85.tq: Distinguish city nicknames with similar industrial associations.
xs: "**Manchester of the East**" = **Osaka**, Japan — option **(3)**.
**Aberdeen** = "Oil capital of Europe"; **Chennai** = "Detroit of India"; **Chotanagpur** = "Ruhr of India".
xa: Osaka = **cotton textiles** (UPPSC 2022).
The original **Manchester** lies in **Lancashire** (UK cotton textiles).
Osaka is part of **Kinki** (Osaka-Kobe-Kyoto).
**Rust Belt** = north-eastern US and Great Lakes.

85.s: The term ‘Ruhr of India’ is associated with:
85.x: Chotanagpur is known as the ‘Ruhr of India’.
85.tq: Separate the regional nickname from city-based nicknames.
xs: "**Ruhr of India**" = **Chotanagpur** — option **(1)**.
**Chennai** is "**Detroit of India**"; **Mumbai-Pune** is an agglomeration cluster.
xa: The real **Ruhr** is in **Germany** — **Essen, Duisburg, Dortmund**.
Steel plants sit on **coalfields/ore fields**.
**TISCO Jamshedpur (1907)**.
Ruhr is an **old Western region in decline**.

85.s: The ‘Rust Belt’ or ‘Rust Bowl’ refers to the:
o: new software corridor of southern India
old manufacturing belt of the north-eastern USA and Great Lakes
85.x: Rust Belt or Rust Bowl denotes the old manufacturing belt of the north-eastern United States and the Great Lakes region.
85.tq: Identify the spatial extent behind the nickname.
xs: The **Rust Belt / Rust Bowl** = the **old manufacturing belt of the north-eastern US and Great Lakes** — option **(2)**.
**Aberdeen** (Scotland) is the "Oil capital of Europe" — not the Rust Belt.
xa: Great Lakes steel centres: **Pittsburgh, Gary, Cleveland, Buffalo, Duluth**.
The **US Rust Belt**, **Ruhr** and **Lorraine** have all declined.
Steel leadership moved to **China and India**.
**Detroit** = automobiles.

85.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: Samara — Industrial region affected by the Ukraine conflict in August 2026
85.x: Lorraine is an old Western industrial region that declined; it is not identified as India's Detroit. Chotanagpur is India's Ruhr, Chennai is India's Detroit, and Samara was affected by the Ukraine conflict in August 2026.
85.tq: Find the wrongly assigned regional comparison or event rather than the correctly matched entries.
xs: **Lorraine — India's Detroit** is wrong — option **(3)**; **Lorraine** is a **French** steel region (Metz, Nancy).
Correct: **Chennai = India's Detroit**, **Chotanagpur = India's Ruhr**, **Samara** hit by Ukraine in **Aug 2026**.
xa: Lorraine is an **old Western region in decline**.
The real **Detroit** = US automobiles.
**Samara** is a Russian industrial region.
**Osaka** = "Manchester of the East".

85.s: The revised Index of Core Industries referred to in the current industrial context has which one of the following base years?
85.x: The revised Index of Core Industries has 2022-23 as its base year.
85.tq: Discriminate among close base-year figures by focusing on the exact revision year.
xs: The revised **Index of Core Industries** has base **2022-23** (July 2026) — option **(3)**.
**Iron ore** was added, making **nine** industries.
xa: Combined IIP weight **32.88%**.
**Electricity** has the highest weight.
India's crude steel: **168.4 MT**.
India steel target: **300 MT by 2030**.

85.s: In the revised Index of Core Industries with base 2022-23, which one of the following was added and how many industries does the index comprise after the addition?
85.x: Iron ore was added to the revised Index of Core Industries, bringing the number of industries to nine.
85.tq: Pair the newly added item with the correct count instead of matching either detail in isolation.
xs: **Iron ore** was added, making **nine** industries — option **(1)**.
The revised index has base **2022-23** (July 2026).
xa: Combined IIP weight **32.88%**.
**Electricity** carries the highest weight.
Iron ore is a **gross (weight-losing)** material.
Steel: about **4 tonnes** of raw material → **1 tonne** of steel.

86.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
86.x: Sugar is raw-material-based because cane is weight-losing and perishable. Bakery is market-based (B wrong), iron and steel is raw-material-based, about 4 t of input per tonne (C wrong), and cement is raw-material-based on limestone, not footloose (D wrong).
86.tq: Classify industries by weight change and location tendency.
xs: **Sugar** is a **raw-material-based** industry — so option **(1)** is correct: sugarcane is **perishable** and the input is **weight-losing**.
**Bakery** is **market-based** (weight-gaining or fragile products, located near consumers).
**Iron and steel** is raw-material-based (about **4 t** of input per tonne), and **cement** is raw-material-based on **limestone** — neither is market-based or footloose.
xa: **Power-oriented**: **aluminium**, needing **14,000-15,000 kWh** per tonne.
**Footloose** examples: **software**, **electronics**, and **cotton textiles** (cotton is a "pure" material).
⚠ Both **sugar** and **iron & steel** are weight-losing, so Weber puts them near raw material (**MI > 1**).

86.s: Market-based industries are generally located near consumers because their products are:
86.x: Market-based industries such as bakeries and soft-drink production locate near consumers because their products are weight-gaining or fragile.
86.tq: Apply the product-characteristic test to market location.
xs: Market-based industries locate near consumers because their products are **weight-gaining or fragile** — option **(3)**.
Examples given: **bakery** and **soft drinks**.
**Weight-losing and perishable** inputs describe **raw-material-oriented** industries (sugar, iron & steel, cement), not market-based ones.
Dependence on cheap electricity is **power orientation** (aluminium).
xa: In Weber's theory, **MI < 1** or **ubiquitous inputs** (such as **water**) pull an industry **near the market**.
**Footloose** industries locate anywhere with **skills and links** — software, electronics, diamond polishing.
Location factors include **raw material**, **power**, **market**, **labour**, **transport**, water and **government policy**.

86.s: Which group of ports is specifically identified as serving mineral and petroleum hinterlands?
o: Kolkata, Haldia, Nhava Sheva and Porbandar
86.x: The east-coast ports of Chennai, Visakhapatnam, Paradip and Tuticorin serve mineral and petroleum hinterlands.
86.tq: Recall the complete port group associated with mineral and petroleum hinterlands.
xs: The east-coast ports **Chennai, Visakhapatnam (Vizag), Paradip and Tuticorin** serve **mineral and petroleum hinterlands** — option **(3)**.
**Ports** are listed among the Indian examples of **transport** as a location factor.
xa: Transport as a factor covers **roads, railheads and ports**.
Other Indian examples: minerals (**Chotanagpur** steel, coal), **cheap labour** (West Bengal), market, government policy, clustering.
**Visakhapatnam** itself is a centre of **shipbuilding** and **steel**.

86.s: Why is the steel belt concentrated on the Chota Nagpur Plateau?
o: Because raw materials required by steel plants are weight-losing
Because all major ports of India are located there
Because the region has the largest consumer market in India
Because the region has no dependence on power
86.x: The steel belt lies on the Chota Nagpur Plateau because the principal raw materials are weight-losing and are therefore advantageously processed near their source.
86.tq: Apply the raw-material weight-loss principle to explain industrial location.
xs: The steel belt sits on the **Chota Nagpur Plateau** because steel's raw materials are **weight-losing** — option **(1)**.
Weight-losing inputs (**MI > 1**) pull the plant **near raw material**; iron & steel uses about **4 t** of input per tonne of output.
The plateau is not cited for ports or for the largest consumer market.
xa: The steel belt covers **Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh and West Bengal**.
The **Chotanagpur** region is called the "**Ruhr of India**" — centres **Jamshedpur, Ranchi, Dhanbad, Bokaro**.
Its growth is linked to the discovery of **coal** (UPPSC 2004).

86.s:
Consider the following statements regarding industrial location:
1. Proximity to raw material can reduce transport cost.
2. Availability of skilled and inexpensive labour may influence location.
3. Tax concessions and subsidies can affect industrial location.
4. Access to water is irrelevant to industrial location.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
86.x: Raw material, labour and government incentives are location factors. Water is also an important factor for several industries, so statement 4 is false.
86.tq: Identify the single reversed statement among otherwise standard location factors.
xs: **Statements 1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: **raw material** proximity **cuts transport cost** — correct.
Statement 2: **labour** (skilled and cheap) is a location factor — correct.
Statement 3: **government policy** (**tax breaks, subsidies, SEZs**) affects location — correct.
Statement 4 is wrong: **water** is itself listed among the location factors.
xa: Full factor list: raw material, **power**, **market**, labour, **transport**, water, government policy, **clustering**, environment.
Cheap labour example: **West Bengal**.
Weber treats **water** as a **ubiquitous input** that pulls industry towards the market.

86.s:
Which of the following combinations is correctly matched?
1. Iron and steel — raw-material orientation
2. Aluminium — power orientation
3. Software — market or footloose orientation
4. Sugar — raw-material orientation
86.x: Iron and steel, sugar and cement are generally raw-material-oriented; aluminium is power-oriented; and software is market-oriented or footloose. All four matches are correct.
86.tq: Test the orientation of industries by matching each with its dominant location factor.
xs: All four matches are correct — **1, 2, 3 and 4**, option **(4)**.
**Iron and steel** and **sugar** are **raw-material**-oriented (weight-losing; cane is perishable).
**Aluminium** is **power**-oriented, needing **14,000-15,000 kWh** per tonne.
**Software** is **market/footloose**-oriented, locating anywhere with skills and links.
xa: **Cement** is also raw-material-oriented (**limestone**).
Market-based examples: **bakery** and **soft drinks** (weight-gaining, fragile).
Footloose PYQ: footloose = **software / diamond** (APPSC 2019).

86.s: The term ‘footloose industries’ refers to industries which generally
o: use light inputs and have negligible transport costs
depend mainly on coalfields and iron-ore deposits
require very large quantities of bulky raw material at the production site
86.x: Footloose industries use light inputs, incur negligible transport costs and are not tightly tied to a particular raw-material source.
86.tq: Discriminate footloose industries from raw-material-bound industries by their input and transport characteristics.
xs: Footloose industries **use light inputs and have negligible transport costs** — option **(2)**.
They depend on **internet, logistics and skilled people**, not on a fixed raw-material site.
Dependence on **coalfields and iron ore**, or on bulky raw material, describes **raw-material-oriented** industries such as iron & steel.
xa: Examples: **diamond polishing, electronics assembly, software**.
Clusters: **Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune, Noida**.
PYQ: raw material is not the main factor for **electronics** (UPPSC 2015).

86.s: Which of the following sets consists entirely of examples of footloose industries?
o: Diamond polishing, electronics assembly and software
Iron and steel, software and sugar
Iron and steel, sugar and cement
86.x: Diamond polishing, electronics assembly and software are identified as footloose industries. Iron and steel, sugar and cement are associated with raw-material orientation, while aluminium is power-oriented.
86.tq: Use the all-correct set method to separate footloose examples from raw-material-bound industries.
xs: **Diamond polishing, electronics assembly and software** are all footloose — option **(1)**.
**Iron and steel**, **sugar** and **cement** are **raw-material**-oriented, so options (2), (3) and (4) fail.
**Aluminium** is **power**-oriented.
xa: Footloose industries have **light inputs** and **negligible transport cost**.
Footloose clusters: **Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune, Noida**.
⚠ **Cotton textiles** are also listed as footloose because cotton is a "**pure**" material.

86.s: Which one of the following pairs of cities is associated with clustering of footloose industries?
86.x: Bengaluru and Hyderabad are among the identified clusters of footloose industries; Pune and Noida are also included in this group.
86.tq: Recognise industrial clustering by linking footloose industries with their major urban clusters.
xs: **Bengaluru and Hyderabad** are clusters of footloose industries — option **(4)**.
**Renukoot** and **Muri** are **aluminium** centres; **Aonla** makes **fertilisers**; **Sivakasi** makes fireworks and matches; **Pithampur** makes automobiles.
xa: The other footloose clusters are **Pune** and **Noida**.
Footloose examples: **diamond polishing, electronics assembly, software**.
Bengaluru-Tamil Nadu region: IT — the "**Silicon Valley of India**".

86.s: Alfred Weber’s least-cost theory of industrial location was formulated in
86.x: Alfred Weber formulated the least-cost theory in 1909.
86.tq: Recall the distinctive year associated with the least-cost theory.
xs: **Alfred Weber** formulated the least-cost theory in **1909** — option **(2)**.
His plant locates where **total transport cost is lowest**, then adjusts for **labour** and **agglomeration**.
xa: **MI > 1** (weight-losing, e.g. iron & steel, sugar) → near **raw material**.
**MI < 1** or ubiquitous inputs (water) → near **market**.
**Pure raw material** (e.g. cotton) → anywhere between source and market.

86.s: According to Alfred Weber’s least-cost theory, a plant initially seeks a location where
86.x: Weber’s theory gives initial importance to minimising total transport cost; labour and agglomeration are considered subsequently as adjustments.
86.tq: Identify the primary decision rule in Weber’s least-cost approach.
xs: Under **Weber's** least-cost theory, a plant first locates where **total transport cost is lowest** — option **(1)**.
Only then is the site **adjusted for labour and agglomeration**.
Neither high labour cost nor compulsory government ownership is part of the theory.
xa: Weber formulated it in **1909**.
Weight-losing inputs (**MI > 1**) pull the plant towards raw material; **MI < 1** pulls it towards the market.
A **pure** raw material such as **cotton** leaves the plant free between source and market.

86.s: Which one of the following statements regarding a Material Index below one is correct?
o: It may favour location near the market, particularly when inputs are ubiquitous.
It necessarily indicates a weight-gaining industry located near raw material.
It means that water cannot be used as an input.
It proves that the industry is footloose in every case.
86.x: A Material Index below one, or the use of ubiquitous inputs such as water, may favour location near the market. It does not automatically make every such industry footloose.
86.tq: Avoid the extreme-word trap and distinguish a tendency from an absolute rule.
xs: A **Material Index below one** may favour location **near the market**, particularly with **ubiquitous inputs** — option **(1)**.
Weber's example of a ubiquitous input is **water**, so water can certainly be an input.
**MI < 1** is not a weight-losing case near raw material; that is **MI > 1**.
xa: **MI > 1**: weight-losing, e.g. **iron & steel, sugar** → near raw material.
**Pure raw material** (no weight loss, e.g. **cotton**) → free to locate between source and market.
⚠ Market-based industries (bakery, soft drinks) are **weight-gaining or fragile** — not the same as footloose.

86.s: In Weber's least-cost theory, a 'pure' raw material such as cotton, which loses no weight in processing, allows the industry to be located:
o: Anywhere between the source and the market
86.x: A pure raw material has no weight loss, so transport cost is the same whether raw material or product is moved; the plant is free to locate anywhere between source and market. Weight-losing inputs (MI > 1) pull it to the source (A); weight-gaining or ubiquitous inputs (MI < 1) pull it to the market (B); a port location (D) is not implied by the theory.
86.tq: Pure material (cotton) = free location; weight-losing = source; ubiquitous = market.
xs: A **pure raw material** such as **cotton** loses no weight, so the plant can locate **anywhere between the source and the market** — option **(3)**.
**Weight-losing** inputs (**MI > 1**) pull the plant to the raw-material source.
**MI < 1** or ubiquitous inputs (water) pull it to the market.
xa: This is why **cotton textiles** are listed as **footloose** in the orientation table.
**Alfred Weber (1909)**: least total transport cost first, then labour and agglomeration adjustments.
Iron & steel needs about **4 t** of input per tonne — a classic weight-losing case.

86.s: Which one of the following industrial regions is associated with Jamshedpur, Ranchi, Dhanbad and Bokaro?
86.x: Jamshedpur, Ranchi, Dhanbad and Bokaro are major centres of the Chotanagpur industrial region, known as the ‘Ruhr of India’.
86.tq: Use the centre-region association to identify the correct industrial belt.
xs: **Jamshedpur, Ranchi, Dhanbad and Bokaro** are centres of the **Chotanagpur industrial region** — option **(1)**.
**Hugli** centres are **Kolkata, Howrah, Haldia**; **Gurugram-Delhi-Meerut** centres include Faridabad and Noida; **Kollam-Thiruvananthapuram** includes Kochi.
xa: Chotanagpur is called the "**Ruhr of India**" — steel, coal, heavy engineering, power.
Its growth is linked to the discovery of **coal** (UPPSC 2004).
The steel belt spans **Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, West Bengal**.

86.s:
Consider the following pairs:

1. Mumbai-Pune — Engineering, petrochemicals, IT, automobiles and pharmaceuticals
2. Hugli — Jute, engineering, paper and chemicals
3. Gujarat — Petrochemicals, refining, textiles and diamonds
4. Chotanagpur — Steel, coal, heavy engineering and power

Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
86.x: All four pairs are correct: Mumbai-Pune has engineering, petrochemicals, IT, automobiles and pharma; Hugli has jute, engineering, paper and chemicals; Gujarat has petrochemicals, refining, textiles and diamonds; Chotanagpur ('Ruhr of India') has steel, coal, heavy engineering and power.
86.tq: Check each region against its characteristic industrial specialisation.
xs: All four pairs are correct — **1, 2, 3 and 4**, option **(4)**.
**Mumbai-Pune**: engineering, petrochemicals, IT, automobiles, pharma; **Hugli**: **jute**, engineering, paper, chemicals.
**Gujarat**: petrochemicals, refining, textiles, **diamonds**; **Chotanagpur**: steel, coal, heavy engineering, power.
xa: Mumbai's satellite towns: **Thane, Navi Mumbai, Pimpri-Chinchwad**.
Gujarat centres: **Ahmedabad, Vadodara, Surat, Jamnagar**.
Coastal Gujarat is called an "**industrial workshop**" (UPPSC 2001).

86.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Industrial region)

a. Bengaluru-Tamil Nadu
b. Visakhapatnam-Guntur
c. Gurugram-Delhi-Meerut
 d. Kollam-Thiruvananthapuram

List-II (Principal industries)

i. Cashew, coir and rubber
 ii. Steel, shipbuilding, petroleum, fertilisers, pharmaceuticals and food processing
 iii. IT, aerospace, biotechnology, electronics and automobiles
 iv. Automobiles, electronics and light industry

Which of the following is correct?
86.x: Bengaluru-Tamil Nadu is associated with IT and advanced industries; Visakhapatnam-Guntur with steel and petroleum-related industries; Gurugram-Delhi-Meerut with automobiles and electronics; and Kollam-Thiruvananthapuram with cashew, coir and rubber.
86.tq: Start with the sure pair and eliminate codes using the industry-region association.
xs: Correct code **a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i** — option **(1)**.
**Bengaluru-Tamil Nadu**: IT, aerospace, biotech, electronics, automobiles; **Visakhapatnam-Guntur**: steel, shipbuilding, petroleum, fertilisers, pharma, food processing.
**Gurugram-Delhi-Meerut**: automobiles, electronics, light industry; **Kollam-Thiruvananthapuram**: **cashew, coir, rubber**.
xa: Bengaluru is the "**Silicon Valley of India**".

Automobiles of the Gurugram belt are at **Gurugram-Manesar** (Maruti Suzuki).

86.s: Which of the following automobile hubs is located in Andhra Pradesh and is associated with Isuzu and Kobelco?
86.x: Sri City in Andhra Pradesh is identified as an automobile hub associated with Isuzu and Kobelco.
86.tq: Match the automobile hub with its state-specific industrial association.
xs: **Sri City** in **Andhra Pradesh** is the automobile hub linked with **Isuzu and Kobelco** — option **(4)**.
**Gurugram-Manesar** (Haryana), **Sanand** (Gujarat) and **Pimpri-Chinchwad** (Pune's satellite) are other hubs, not in AP.
xa: Automobile hubs listed: **Chennai ("Detroit of India")**, **Pune**, **Gurugram-Manesar**, **Sanand**, **Sri City**.
**Pithampur** (MP) is also an automobile centre (UPPSC 2015).
AP's corridors: **VCIC**, **CBIC** and **HBIC**.

86.s: The growth of the Chotanagpur industrial region is particularly linked to the discovery of which resource?
86.x: The growth of Chotanagpur is closely linked to the discovery and availability of coal, along with other mineral resources.
86.tq: Identify the principal resource responsible for the growth of an industrial region.
xs: Chotanagpur's growth is linked to the discovery of **coal** — option **(4)** (UPPSC 2004).
The region's industries are **steel, coal, heavy engineering and power**.
xa: Centres: **Jamshedpur, Ranchi, Dhanbad, Bokaro**.
Nicknamed the "**Ruhr of India**".
The **steel belt** there exists because steel's raw materials are **weight-losing**.

86.s:
Assertion (A): Coastal Gujarat is described as an industrial workshop.
Reason (R): The region has important textile, pharmaceutical and petrochemical activities.

Choose the correct answer.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
86.x: Both statements are true, and the concentration of textile, pharmaceutical and petrochemical industries explains the description of coastal Gujarat as an industrial workshop.
86.tq: Test whether the stated industrial specialisation explains the regional description.
xs: **Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)** (UPPSC 2001).
Coastal Gujarat is called an "**industrial workshop**" because of its **textiles, pharma and petrochemicals**.
xa: Gujarat region centres: **Ahmedabad, Vadodara, Surat, Jamnagar**.
Its key industries: petrochemicals, **refining**, textiles, **diamonds**.
**Koyali** (Gujarat) has an **oil refinery**; **Sanand** is an automobile hub.

86.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: Kolkata, Howrah and Haldia — Hugli industrial region
Indore, Dewas and Pithampur — Kollam-Thiruvananthapuram industrial region
Gurugram, Delhi and Meerut — Gurugram-Delhi-Meerut industrial region
Ahmedabad, Vadodara, Surat and Jamnagar — Gujarat industrial region
86.x: Indore-Dewas-Pithampur is a minor industrial belt of Madhya Pradesh, not a centre group of the Kollam-Thiruvananthapuram industrial region.
86.tq: Find the wrong centre-region association among otherwise familiar pairs.
xs: **Indore, Dewas and Pithampur — Kollam-Thiruvananthapuram** is wrongly matched — option **(2)**.

86.s: Which one of the following is a minor industrial belt of Madhya Pradesh?
86.x: Indore-Dewas-Pithampur is a minor industrial belt of Madhya Pradesh. Mandideep near Bhopal is another such belt in the state.
86.tq: Distinguish Madhya Pradesh industrial belts from minor regions of other states.
xs: **Indore-Dewas-Pithampur** is a minor industrial belt of **Madhya Pradesh** — option **(1)**.
**Bhojpur-Munger**, **Kolhapur-South Kannada** and **Northern Malabar** are minor regions elsewhere, not MP belts.
xa: MP's second belt: **Mandideep** near **Bhopal**.
MP has **5 SEZs**: 3 IT/ITeS at **Indore and Gwalior**; mineral- and agro-based at **Jabalpur**.
**Pithampur** = automobiles (UPPSC 2015).

86.s: Mandideep, an industrial area associated with Madhya Pradesh, is located near which city?
86.x: Mandideep is an industrial belt located near Bhopal in Madhya Pradesh.
86.tq: Use the centre-location association to identify the correct district or city.
xs: **Mandideep** lies near **Bhopal** — option **(4)**.
It is one of the two **MP belts**, with **Indore-Dewas-Pithampur**.
xa: **Indore** and **Gwalior** host MP's IT/ITeS SEZs; **Jabalpur** hosts its mineral- and agro-based SEZ.
**Pithampur** is an automobile centre (UPPSC 2015).

86.s: Which one of the following is NOT included among the minor industrial regions and districts listed for India?
86.x: Mumbai-Pune is a major industrial region, whereas Adilabad-Nizamabad, Allahabad-Varanasi-Mirzapur and the Brahmaputra valley are listed among minor industrial regions.

xs: **Mumbai-Pune** is a **major** industrial region, not a minor one — option **(3)**.
**Adilabad-Nizamabad**, **Brahmaputra valley** and **Allahabad-Varanasi-Mirzapur** are on the minor regions list.
xa: Other minor regions: **Ambala-Amritsar, Saharanpur-Muzaffarnagar-Bijnor, Jaipur-Ajmer, Bhojpur-Munger, Durg-Raipur, Bilaspur-Korba**.
Mumbai-Pune industries: engineering, petrochemicals, IT, automobiles, pharma.
Mumbai's satellite towns: **Thane, Navi Mumbai, Pimpri-Chinchwad**.

86.s: Which Indian city, hosting Hyundai, Renault-Nissan, Ashok Leyland and Daimler, is called the 'Detroit of India'?

86.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

A. Muri

C. Koyali

86.x: Gurugram is an automobile centre associated with Maruti Suzuki. Panki is associated with fertilisers, Visakhapatnam with shipbuilding and steel, and Modinagar with rubber.

Aluminium and steel belong to **Chota Nagpur** (Muri, Jamshedpur); coal and thermal power to **Singrauli**.

**Gurugram** and **Pithampur** = automobiles.

xs: All four pairs are correct — **1, 2, 3 and 4**, option **(4)**.
**Pithampur** = **automobiles** (UPPSC 2015); **Sivakasi** = fireworks and **safety matches**.
**Renukoot** = **aluminium** (HINDALCO); **Aonla** = **fertilisers**.

xs: **DLW Varanasi** now makes **electric locomotives** — option **(3)** (UPPSC 2017).
Aluminium is **Muri/Renukoot**, fertiliser is **Aonla/Panki**, and powerlooms are **Bhiwandi**.

**Modinagar** = **rubber**; **Barabanki** = **polyfibre**; **Panki** (Kanpur) = **fertilisers**; **Kanpur** = **explosives**.

86.s: The policy of placing steel plants at Salem, Visakhapatnam and Hospet away from raw-material bases illustrates:
o: the exclusive importance of market proximity
the complete rejection of industrial planning
a policy override aimed at balanced regional growth
86.x: The 1956 Industrial Resolution and the Fourth Plan (1969–74) sought balanced regional growth, leading to the placement of these steel plants away from raw-material bases.
86.tq: Apply policy objectives to an apparent location exception.
xs: Placing steel plants at **Salem, Visakhapatnam and Vijayanagar (Hospet)** away from raw materials was a **policy override** for **balanced regional growth** — option **(3)**.
The **IPR 1956** sought balanced regional growth and put the public sector in backward regions.
The **Fourth Plan (1969-74)** called for measures to attract industry to backward areas.
xa: The Centre gave **subsidies** to units in backward areas.
Criticism: such PSUs struggled — **skilled-labour gaps**, **costly subsidies**, **political concentration**.
Correctives: **SEZs** (Vallarpadam, Nanguneri), **NIMZs** and **corridors**.

86.s:
Consider the following statements about policy measures for balanced regional industrial growth in India:
1. The Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956 recognised balanced regional growth and placed public-sector units in backward regions.
2. The Fourth Five-Year Plan (1969-74) called for measures to attract industry to backward areas.
3. Public-sector plants at Salem, Visakhapatnam and Vijayanagar (Hospet) were placed right next to their raw-material sources.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
86.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct as stated. Statement 3 is wrong: Salem, Visakhapatnam and Vijayanagar were deliberately placed away from raw materials for regional balance. So B (1 and 2 only) is right; A omits statement 2, C and D wrongly include statement 3.
86.tq: Salem-Vizag-Vijayanagar = sited AWAY from raw materials (policy override).
xs: **Statements 1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: **IPR 1956** recognised balanced regional growth and placed the public sector in backward regions — correct.
Statement 2: the **Fourth Plan (1969-74)** called for attracting industry to backward areas — correct.
Statement 3 is wrong: **Salem, Vizag and Vijayanagar** plants were placed **away from** raw-material bases.
xa: This siting is called a **policy override** in India.
The Centre gave **subsidies** to units in backward areas.
**ES 2025-26**: most clusters too small, with **regulatory rigidities**.

86.s:
Which of the following has been cited as a criticism of placing public-sector units in backward regions?

1. Lack of adequate location factors
2. Shortage of skilled labour
3. Costly subsidies
4. Political concentration

Select the correct answer.
86.x: The main criticisms include inadequate location factors, shortages of skilled labour, expensive subsidies and political concentration.
86.tq: Select the complete set of stated criticisms rather than treating regional dispersal as uniformly successful.
xs: All four are cited criticisms — **1, 2, 3 and 4**, option **(4)**.
PSUs in regions **lacking location factors** struggled, with **skilled-labour gaps**, **costly subsidies** and **political concentration**.
xa: Policy base: **IPR 1956** and the **Fourth Plan (1969-74)**.
Examples: steel plants at **Salem, Vizag, Vijayanagar (Hospet)**.
Regional pattern: **South and West** lead; **East and North-East** lag.

86.s: Which broad regional pattern of industrial development is identified in India?
o: East and North-East are the principal powerhouses, while the South lags
Only the North has significant industrial concentration
South and West are powerhouses, while the East, North-East and parts of the North lag
All regions have attained an identical level of industrial development
86.x: Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra, Gujarat and Karnataka are described as industrial powerhouses, whereas the East, North-East and parts of the North lag behind.
86.tq: Use the reversed-comparison trap to distinguish leading and lagging regions.
xs: **South and West are powerhouses**, while the **East, North-East and parts of the North lag** — option **(3)**.
The powerhouses named are **Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra, Gujarat and Karnataka**.
xa: Correctives: **SEZs**, **NIMZs** and **corridors**.
**ES 2025-26**: most clusters are **too small**, limiting integration into **global value chains**.
Manufacturing is **16-17% of GDP**, with a target of **25%** by **2047**.

86.s:
Which of the following are identified as corrective measures for regional industrial imbalance?

1. Special Economic Zones
2. Industrial corridors
3. Concentration of all investment in existing metropolitan centres

Select the correct answer.
86.x: SEZs and industrial corridors are identified as corrective measures. Concentrating all investment in existing metropolitan centres would aggravate, not correct, regional imbalance.
86.tq: Reject the extreme policy statement and retain the two recognised corrective measures.
xs: **SEZs and industrial corridors** are the correctives — **1 and 2 only**, option **(3)**.
Concentrating all investment in metropolitan centres is not listed; it would deepen the imbalance.
The notes' corrective list: **SEZs** (e.g. **Vallarpadam, Nanguneri**), **NIMZs** and **corridors**.
xa: **SEZ Act 2005**, in force **10 Feb 2006**, with single-window clearance.
**NIMZ** comes from the **National Manufacturing Policy 2011**.
**11** national industrial corridors are under **NICDP**.

86.s: What problem affecting Indian industrial clusters was highlighted in the Economic Survey 2025–26?
o: Clusters are concentrated only in mineral-producing districts
Most clusters are too small and face regulatory rigidities that limit integration into global value chains
Industrial clusters have completely replaced SEZs
Most clusters are too large and face no regulatory barriers
86.x: The Economic Survey 2025–26 noted that many Indian clusters are too small and face regulatory rigidities, limiting their integration into global value chains.
86.tq: Identify the precise current-affairs diagnosis rather than reversing its size and regulatory conditions.
xs: **ES 2025-26**: most clusters are **too small** and face **regulatory rigidities**, limiting integration into **global value chains** — option **(2)**.
The notes do not say clusters are mineral-only, too large, or a replacement for SEZs.
xa: Regional pattern: **TN, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Karnataka** lead; the **East and North-East** lag.
India has **4,500+** mapped industrial parks.
**India Industrial Land Bank** (**27 Aug 2020**) maps **4,100+** parks/estates/SEZs.

86.tq: Distinguish the newly proposed budget node from existing Andhra Pradesh corridor nodes.
xs: Budget 2026-27's integrated **East Coast Industrial Corridor** has a node at **Durgapur** (**Purvodaya**) — option **(2)**.
**Krishnapatnam North** is the **CBIC** AP node; **Orvakal** is the **HBIC** node; **Kopparthy** is a **VCIC** node.
xa: The **East Coast Economic Corridor** runs **Kolkata-Kanyakumari** (also given as Kolkata-Chennai-Tuticorin).
**VCIC** is its first phase, ~**800 km**, backed by **ADB**.
Budget 2026-27 also lets SEZ units sell to the **Domestic Tariff Area** at concessional duty.

86.s:
Consider the following statements about the National Industrial Corridor Development Corporation (NICDC):
1. It was formerly known as the Delhi-Mumbai Industrial Corridor Development Corporation (DMICDC).
2. It was set up in August 2024, when the Cabinet approved 12 new industrial smart cities.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
86.x: Statement 1 is correct: NICDC is the former DMICDC. Statement 2 is wrong: NICDC (ex-DMICDC) was set up in January 2008; August 2024 is when 12 new industrial smart cities were approved. Hence 1 only (A); B, C and D are wrong because statement 2 is false and statement 1 is true.
86.tq: Aug 2024 = 12 new smart cities, not NICDC's birth (Jan 2008).
xs: Only **statement 1** is correct — **1 only**, option **(1)**.
Statement 1: **NICDC** is the former **DMICDC** — correct.
Statement 2 is wrong: NICDC was set up in **Jan 2008**; **Aug 2024** is when **12 new industrial smart cities** were approved.
xa: The second implementing body is **NICDIT** (**₹3,000 crore** in BE 2026-27).
After the Aug 2024 approval, NICDP has **20 projects** across **11** corridors.
**BHAVYA** parks are run by **NICDC**.

86.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the industrial corridors of Andhra Pradesh:
1. The Visakhapatnam-Chennai Industrial Corridor has an approximate length of 800 km.
2. The Chennai-Bengaluru Industrial Corridor extends across Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka.
3. The Hyderabad-Bengaluru Industrial Corridor has Orvakal as its Andhra Pradesh node.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
86.x: All three statements are correct. VCIC is approximately 800 km long, CBIC covers Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka, and Orvakal is the AP node of HBIC.
86.tq: Check each corridor against its length, states and node before selecting the coded combination.
xs: All three statements are correct — **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)**.
Statement 1: **VCIC** is about **800 km** — correct.
Statement 2: **CBIC** covers **Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and AP** — correct.
Statement 3: **HBIC**'s AP node is **Orvakal** (Kurnool) — correct.
xa: Orvakal node: **2,621 acres**, **₹1,781 crore**.
CBIC AP node: **Krishnapatnam North** — **10,834 acres**, **₹2,139 crore**.
ADB support of **US$ 840 million** for AP corridors (AP Survey 2025-26).

86.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Industrial corridor)
a. VCIC
b. CBIC
c. HBIC

List-II (Associated feature)
i. Orvakal node
ii. Krishnapatnam node
iii. Part of ECEC and ADB-funded

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
86.x: VCIC is part of the ECEC and is ADB-funded; CBIC has the Krishnapatnam node; HBIC has the Orvakal node.
86.tq: Start from the sure corridor-node pairs and eliminate inconsistent combinations.
xs: Correct code **a-iii, b-ii, c-i** — option **(1)**.
**VCIC** is the first phase of the **ECEC** and is **ADB**-funded.
**CBIC** has the **Krishnapatnam** node; **HBIC** has the **Orvakal** node.
xa: VCIC AP nodes: **Vizag, Chittoor, Kopparthy**.
CBIC partner: **Japan (JICA)**; length **560 km**.
**APIIC** manages **571 industrial parks** and is the nodal agency in AP.

86.s: The Andhra Pradesh nodes of the Visakhapatnam-Chennai Industrial Corridor (VCIC) are:
86.x: VCIC's AP nodes are Visakhapatnam, Chittoor and Kopparthy (about 33,000 acres). Krishnapatnam is the CBIC node and Orvakal the HBIC node (B, D wrong); Durgapur is the Budget 2026-27 East Coast Industrial Corridor node (C wrong).
86.tq: VCIC = Vizag-Chittoor-Kopparthy; CBIC = Krishnapatnam; HBIC = Orvakal.
xs: VCIC's AP nodes are **Vizag, Chittoor and Kopparthy** — option **(1)**.
**Krishnapatnam** is the **CBIC** node and **Orvakal** the **HBIC** node.
**Durgapur** is the Budget 2026-27 **East Coast Industrial Corridor** node; **Sri City** is an automobile hub.
xa: VCIC AP nodes cover **33,000 acres** at **₹5,000 crore**.
ADB loan for VCIC: **₹3,300 crore** (2024-25).
⚠ Some notes (Jan 2026) list **7** nodes with **JICA** as partner; others give **ADB** and three nodes.

86.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched in relation to Defence Industrial Corridors?
o: Tamil Nadu — Chennai, Coimbatore and Hosur
Tamil Nadu — Madurai, Salem and Tiruchirappalli
Uttar Pradesh — Chitrakoot, Kanpur and Lucknow
Uttar Pradesh — Aligarh, Agra and Jhansi
86.x: The Tamil Nadu Defence Industrial Corridor has Chennai, Coimbatore, Hosur, Salem and Tiruchirappalli; Madurai is not listed among its five nodes.
86.tq: Find the swapped or substituted node in the corridor list.
xs: **Tamil Nadu — Madurai, Salem and Tiruchirappalli** is wrongly matched — option **(2)**: **Madurai** is not a TN DIC node.
TN's **5** nodes: **Chennai, Coimbatore, Hosur, Salem, Tiruchirappalli**.
UP's **6** nodes: **Aligarh, Agra, Jhansi, Chitrakoot, Kanpur, Lucknow** — so options (3) and (4) are correct pairs.
xa: There are **two** Defence Industrial Corridors.
Together they have **₹74,756 crore** of commitments.
The first DIC was announced **between Chennai and Bengaluru** (APPSC-GS 2019).

86.s:
Consider the following statements about India’s Defence Industrial Corridors:
1. The Uttar Pradesh corridor has six nodes.
2. The Tamil Nadu corridor has five nodes.
3. Together, the two corridors have investment commitments of ₹74,756 crore.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
86.x: The Uttar Pradesh corridor has six nodes, the Tamil Nadu corridor has five nodes, and the two together have investment commitments of ₹74,756 crore.
86.tq: Combine node-count and investment figures, checking whether the aggregate statement is also supported.
xs: All three statements are correct — **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)**.
Statement 1: the **Uttar Pradesh** DIC has **6** nodes — correct.
Statement 2: the **Tamil Nadu** DIC has **5** nodes — correct.
Statement 3: the two DICs together have **₹74,756 crore** of commitments — correct.
xa: UP nodes: **Aligarh, Agra, Jhansi, Chitrakoot, Kanpur, Lucknow**.
TN nodes: **Chennai, Coimbatore, Hosur, Salem, Tiruchirappalli**.
First DIC: **Chennai-Bengaluru** stretch (APPSC-GS 2019).

86.s: India’s first Defence Industrial Corridor was announced along which stretch?
86.x: India’s first Defence Industrial Corridor was announced along the Chennai-Bengaluru stretch.
86.tq: Avoid confusing the first Defence Industrial Corridor with the names of major economic corridors.
xs: The first Defence Industrial Corridor was announced along the **Chennai-Bengaluru** stretch — option **(1)** (APPSC-GS 2019 answer key).
**Amritsar-Kolkata**, **Visakhapatnam-Chennai** and **Delhi-Mumbai** are **industrial** corridors (AKIC, VCIC, DMIC), not DICs.
xa: India has **two** DICs — **Uttar Pradesh** (**6** nodes) and **Tamil Nadu** (**5** nodes).
Investment commitments: **₹74,756 crore**.
⚠ Don't confuse with **CBIC**, the Chennai-Bengaluru **industrial** corridor (**560 km**, Japan/JICA).

86.s: Which of the following pairs of SEZ examples and states is correctly matched?
86.x: Vallarpadam is an example from Kerala and Nanguneri is an example from Tamil Nadu. SEZs are intended to attract investment and exports, including in lagging regions.
86.tq: Start with the state-location pair to test the distribution of SEZ examples.
xs: **Vallarpadam — Kerala**; **Nanguneri — Tamil Nadu** — option **(1)**.
Both are SEZ examples aimed at attracting **investment and exports in lagging regions**.
xa: **SEZ Act 2005**, in force **10 Feb 2006**, with **single-window clearance**.
Status (**31 Mar 2025**): **368 notified, 276 operational** SEZs.
**MP** has **5 SEZs**: 3 IT/ITeS at **Indore and Gwalior**; mineral- and agro-based at **Jabalpur**.

86.s: Which one of the following statements about SEZs is correct?
o: They are identical to NIMZs in structure and purpose
They are established exclusively in already developed metropolitan regions
They aim to attract investment and exports, including in lagging regions
They are intended to reduce industrial exports from India
86.x: SEZs are intended to attract investment and exports and can serve as instruments for promoting development in lagging regions.
86.tq: Apply the stated purpose of SEZs to a regional-development situation.
xs: SEZs aim to **attract investment and exports**, including in **lagging regions** — option **(3)**.
**NIMZs** are distinct from SEZs — bigger integrated townships with different governance, exit and fiscal rules.
Examples in lagging regions: **Vallarpadam (Kerala)**, **Nanguneri (TN)**.
xa: SEZs are listed among the **correctives** for regional imbalance, with NIMZs and corridors.
**SEZ Act 2005** came into force on **10 Feb 2006**.

86.s:
Consider the following statements about Special Economic Zones (SEZs) in India:
1. The SEZ Act, 2005 came into force on 10 February 2006.
2. The SEZ framework provides single-window clearance.
3. Budget 2026-27 allows SEZ manufacturing units to sell their entire output in the Domestic Tariff Area without any duty.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
86.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: Budget 2026-27 gave a one-time permission to sell to the Domestic Tariff Area at concessional duty, capped as a share of exports, not duty-free unlimited sales. So B is right; A omits statement 2, C and D include the false statement 3.
86.tq: DTA sales: one-time, concessional duty, capped - not duty-free.
xs: **Statements 1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: the **SEZ Act 2005** came into force on **10 Feb 2006** — correct.
Statement 2: it provides **single-window clearance** — correct.
Statement 3 is wrong: Budget 2026-27 gave a **one-time** permission to sell to the **Domestic Tariff Area** at **concessional duty**, **capped** as a share of exports.
xa: Status (**31 Mar 2025**): **368 notified, 276 operational** SEZs; **6,695** units.
SEZ examples: **Vallarpadam (Kerala)**, **Nanguneri (TN)**.
NIMZs are **bigger than SEZs** and distinct from them.

86.s: As on 31 March 2025, the number of notified and operational SEZs in India was respectively
86.x: As on 31 March 2025, India had 368 notified SEZs, of which 276 were operational.
86.tq: Keep the order of the two categories intact while using paired numerical data.
xs: As on **31 Mar 2025**: **368 notified** and **276 operational** SEZs — option **(3)**.
**6,695** is the number of **units** in SEZs, not of SEZs.
xa: SEZs employed **31.8 lakh** people.
**SEZ Act 2005**, in force **10 Feb 2006**.
**India Industrial Land Bank** maps **4,100+** parks/estates/SEZs on **6.56 lakh ha**.

86.s: National Investment and Manufacturing Zones are associated with which policy and targets?
o: Budget 2026–27; manufacturing at 50% of GDP and 100 million jobs
National Manufacturing Policy 2011; manufacturing at 25% of GDP and 100 million jobs
SEZ Act 2005; manufacturing at 16–17% of GDP and 10 million jobs
National Manufacturing Policy 2005; manufacturing at 10% of GDP and 25 million jobs
86.x: NIMZs are under the National Manufacturing Policy 2011, which targeted manufacturing at 25% of GDP and 100 million jobs.
86.tq: Match the policy, year and two numerical targets as one linked fact set.
xs: **NIMZs** come from the **National Manufacturing Policy 2011**, targeting manufacturing at **25% of GDP** and **100 million jobs** — option **(2)**.
The **SEZ Act** is of **2005**; **16-17%** is manufacturing's **current** share of GDP, not a target.
xa: NIMZs are **large integrated townships**, **bigger than SEZs**.
They differ from SEZs in **governance, exit and fiscal rules**.
The **25%** target is set for **2047**.

86.s: Which statement best distinguishes NIMZs from SEZs?
o: NIMZs are exclusively agricultural zones without manufacturing activity.
NIMZs are large integrated townships and are bigger than SEZs, with differences in governance, exit and fiscal rules.
NIMZs are small export enclaves with exactly the same governance and fiscal rules as SEZs.
86.x: NIMZs are conceived as large integrated townships, bigger than SEZs, and differ from them in governance, exit and fiscal rules.
86.tq: Compare the scale and regulatory features rather than relying on the common industrial purpose.
xs: NIMZs are **large integrated townships**, **bigger than SEZs**, differing in **governance, exit and fiscal rules** — option **(2)**.
So they are neither small export enclaves nor identical in rules to SEZs, and they are built around township development.
xa: NIMZs come from the **National Manufacturing Policy 2011**.
Targets: manufacturing **25% of GDP**, **100 million jobs**.
SEZs: **SEZ Act 2005**, in force **10 Feb 2006**, single-window clearance.

86.s: BHAVYA is expanded as
o: Basic Heavy Assets and Value-added Yojana
Bharat High-value Agriculture and Village Yojana
86.x: BHAVYA stands for Bharat Audyogik Vikas Yojana.
86.tq: Test the exact expansion of the industrial development programme.
xs: **BHAVYA** = **Bharat Audyogik Vikas Yojana** (2026) — option **(2)**.
It provides **100 plug-and-play industrial parks** at **₹33,660 crore**.
xa: Parks are chosen by **challenge mode** and run by **NICDC**.
**India Industrial Land Bank** (**27 Aug 2020**) maps **4,100+** parks.

86.s:
Consider the following statements about BHAVYA:
1. It provides for 100 plug-and-play industrial parks.
2. Its allocation is ₹33,660 crore.
3. It covers FY 2026–27 to 2031–32.
4. The parks are selected through challenge mode and run by NICDC.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
86.x: All four statements correctly describe BHAVYA: 100 parks, ₹33,660 crore, the period FY 2026–27 to 2031–32, challenge-mode selection and operation by NICDC.
86.tq: Use a complete coded combination when all listed programme attributes are correct.
xs: All four statements are correct — **1, 2, 3 and 4**, option **(4)**.
**BHAVYA**: **100 plug-and-play industrial parks**, **₹33,660 crore**.
Period **FY 2026-27 to 2031-32**; parks chosen by **challenge mode**, run by **NICDC**.
xa: BHAVYA = **Bharat Audyogik Vikas Yojana**.
**NICDC** is the ex-**DMICDC**, set up **Jan 2008**.
India has **4,500+** mapped industrial parks.

86.s: The India Industrial Land Bank, launched on 27 August 2020, mapped approximately:
o: 4,100+ industrial parks, estates and SEZs on 6.56 lakh ha
86.x: The Land Bank mapped over 4,100 parks, estates and SEZs covering 6.56 lakh ha. 368 is the number of notified SEZs (B); 100 parks and Rs 33,660 crore belong to BHAVYA (C); 571 is the number of APIIC parks in AP (D).
86.tq: Land Bank 2020: 4,100+ parks, 6.56 lakh ha.
xs: The **India Industrial Land Bank** (**27 Aug 2020**) mapped **4,100+** parks, estates and SEZs on **6.56 lakh ha** — option **(1)**.
**368** is the number of **notified SEZs**; **100** parks and **₹33,660 crore** belong to **BHAVYA**; **571** is the **APIIC** park count in AP.
xa: India now has **4,500+** mapped industrial parks.
SEZ status (31 Mar 2025): **276** operational.
BHAVYA period: **FY 2026-27 to 2031-32**.

86.s: Which one of the following correctly lists the industrial corridors associated with Andhra Pradesh?
o: East Coast, Delhi–Mumbai and Golden Quadrilateral only
VCIC, CBIC and Hyderabad–Bengaluru Industrial Corridor
86.x: The Andhra Pradesh corridors listed are VCIC, CBIC and the Hyderabad–Bengaluru Industrial Corridor.
86.tq: Identify the exact corridor set and reject options mixing corridors with projects or industrial centres.
xs: AP's corridors are **VCIC, CBIC and the Hyderabad-Bengaluru Industrial Corridor (HBIC)** — option **(4)**.
**Durgapur** is an East Coast Industrial Corridor node; **Sivakasi** and **Pithampur** are industrial centres, not corridors.
xa: AP nodes: **Vizag, Chittoor, Kopparthy** (VCIC); **Krishnapatnam North** (CBIC); **Orvakal** (HBIC).
ADB support of **US$ 840 million** for AP corridors (AP Survey 2025-26).
**APIIC** manages **571 industrial parks**.

86.s: The ADB support associated with Andhra Pradesh’s industrial corridors is
86.x: ADB support associated with the Andhra Pradesh industrial corridors is US$ 840 million.
86.tq: Check both the currency and the place value in the stated support figure.
xs: ADB support for AP's industrial corridors is **US$ 840 million** — option **(2)** (AP Survey 2025-26).
It is in US dollars, not rupees; ₹ figures belong elsewhere (ADB loan **₹3,300 crore** for VCIC).
xa: AP corridors: **VCIC, CBIC, HBIC**.
VCIC partner: **ADB**; first phase of the **East Coast Economic Corridor**.
**APIIC** is AP's nodal agency, managing **571 industrial parks**.

86.s: India has more than 4,500 mapped industrial parks, while manufacturing currently accounts for approximately what share of GDP, with a target for 2047?
86.x: India has more than 4,500 mapped industrial parks; manufacturing contributes about 16–17% of GDP, with a target of 25% by 2047.
86.tq: Match the present share with the future target while retaining the direction of change.
xs: Manufacturing is **16-17% of GDP**, with a target of **25%** by **2047** — option **(2)**.
India has **4,500+** mapped industrial parks.
xa: The **National Manufacturing Policy 2011** also set the **25% of GDP** target, with **100 million jobs**.
**India Industrial Land Bank** (**27 Aug 2020**): **4,100+** parks on **6.56 lakh ha**.
Industrial growth is concentrated in **southern and western** states.

86.s: The nodal agency managing about 571 industrial parks in Andhra Pradesh is:
86.x: The Andhra Pradesh Industrial Infrastructure Corporation (APIIC) is the nodal agency and manages 571 industrial parks. NICDC (A) and NICDIT (D) are national corridor bodies; APFDC (C) is the AP Forest Development Corporation.
86.tq: AP parks = APIIC (571).
xs: **APIIC** is AP's nodal agency and manages **571 industrial parks** — option **(2)**.
**NICDC** and **NICDIT** are the **national** corridor implementing bodies, not AP agencies.
xa: AP corridors: **VCIC, CBIC, HBIC**; ADB support **US$ 840 million**.
**NICDC** (ex-DMICDC, **Jan 2008**) runs **BHAVYA** parks.

87.s:
Consider the following statements about the steel sector:
1. India is the world's largest crude steel producer.
2. China accounts for over 50% of world steel production.
3. The National Steel Policy 2017 targets 300 MT of steel capacity by 2030-31.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
87.x: Statement 1 is wrong: India is the 2nd largest crude steel producer, after China. Statement 2 is correct: China produces over 50% of world steel. Statement 3 is correct: NSP 2017 targets 300 MT capacity (and 255 MT production) by 2030-31. So C is right; A and D include the false statement 1, B omits statement 3.
87.tq: India = 2nd after China; NSP 2017 = 300 MT capacity, 255 MT output.
xs: **Statements 2 and 3** are correct — option **(3)**.
Statement 1 is wrong: India is the **2nd largest** crude steel producer, **after China**.
Statement 2: **China** produces **over 50%** of world steel — correct.
Statement 3: **National Steel Policy 2017** targets **300 MT capacity** by **2030-31** — correct.
xa: ⚠ **300 MT** = capacity target; **255 MT** = production target.
NSP 2017 inputs needed: **437 MT iron ore** and **161 MT coking coal**.

87.s: India’s crude steel production in 2025–26 was recorded as
87.x: Crude steel production in 2025–26 was 168.4 MT, representing a 10.7 percent increase and approximately 9 percent CAGR since 2021–22.
87.tq: Distinguish annual production from installed capacity.
xs: India's crude steel output in **2025-26** was **168.4 MT** — option **(4)**.
It grew **10.7%**, with a CAGR of about **9%** since **2021-22**.
xa: India is the **2nd largest** crude steel producer after **China**.
NSP 2017 target: **255 MT** production by **2030-31**.

87.s:
Which one of the following correctly represents the process mix in India’s steel industry?

Blast furnace–basic oxygen furnace : Electric arc furnace : Induction furnace
87.x: The process mix is 43% BF–BOF, 22% EAF and 35% induction furnace.
87.tq: Preserve the order of the three processes while comparing their shares.
xs: The process mix is **43% BF-BOF : 22% EAF : 35% induction furnace** — option **(3)** (India Steel Association, **8 Sep 2026**).
**56%** is the BF-BOF share **projected for 2030**, not the current share.
xa: Mini/secondary units use the **electric arc** and **induction furnaces** — the **22%** and **35%** shares.
Induction furnaces work in **small batches** and are **energy-efficient**.
India is the **leading producer** of **sponge iron (DRI)**.

87.s: India is the leading producer of which of the following?
o: Sponge iron or direct reduced iron
87.x: India is the leading producer of sponge iron, also known as direct reduced iron (DRI).
87.tq: Use the exact product synonym to avoid confusing sponge iron with crude steel.
xs: India is the **leading producer** of **sponge iron (DRI)** — option **(2)**.
In aluminium India is **2nd largest** primary producer, not the leader; in copper India is a **net importer** of concentrate.
xa: Mini/secondary units melt **scrap or sponge iron** in electric arc and induction furnaces.
India is the **2nd largest** crude steel producer after China.
Copper world leader: **Chile**.

87.s: Mini and secondary steel units generally melt scrap or sponge iron in:
87.x: Mini and secondary steel units use electric arc furnaces and induction furnaces to melt scrap or sponge iron.
87.tq: Match the production process with the appropriate furnace technology.
xs: Mini and secondary units melt scrap or sponge iron in **electric arc and induction furnaces** — option **(4)**.
These account for **22%** (EAF) and **35%** (induction) of India's process mix.
**Blast furnaces** belong to the integrated **BF-BOF** route (**43%**).
xa: Induction furnaces: **small batches**, **energy-efficient**.
BF-BOF share projected at **56% by 2030**.
India leads in **sponge iron (DRI)** production.

87.s: Which statement correctly distinguishes induction furnaces from electric arc furnaces in mini-steel production?
o: Induction furnaces require iron ore mines to be located at the plant site.
Induction furnaces cannot melt sponge iron.
Induction furnaces are used only for primary aluminium production.
Induction furnaces handle small batches and are energy-efficient.
87.x: Induction furnaces are suitable for small batches and are energy-efficient; they can melt scrap or sponge iron in secondary steel production.
87.tq: Select the precise functional distinction rather than a statement that reverses the furnace role.
xs: Induction furnaces handle **small batches** and are **energy-efficient** — option **(4)**.
They melt **scrap or sponge iron** in mini/secondary units, so they can melt sponge iron and need no iron-ore mine at the site.
xa: Induction furnaces hold **35%** of the process mix; EAF **22%**; BF-BOF **43%**.
India is the **leading producer** of sponge iron.
**Rourkela** was the first public integrated plant; **Vizag** the first shore-based plant.

87.s: Why does India continue to import substantial quantities of coking coal despite domestic production?
o: Domestic coking coal is high in ash
Domestic iron ore is unsuitable for steelmaking
Coking coal is not used in blast furnaces
87.x: Domestic coking coal is high in ash, which makes imports necessary despite domestic production.
87.tq: Identify the quality-based cause rather than a false absolute statement.
xs: India imports coking coal because **domestic coal is high-ash** — option **(1)**.
In **2024-25** coking coal output was **66.49 MT** but imports were **57.07 MT**.
Iron ore is adequate: output **289.398 MT**, imports only **6.4 MT**.
xa: NSP 2017 needs **161 MT coking coal** and **437 MT iron ore** by 2030-31.
NSP targets: **300 MT capacity**, **255 MT** production.
Indian steel emits **2.54 tCO2/t** vs **1.9** world average.

87.s: The Production Linked Incentive scheme for Specialty Steel was approved in
87.x: The PLI scheme for Specialty Steel was approved in 2021.
87.tq: Match the scheme with its approval year and avoid confusing it with the National Steel Policy year.
xs: The **PLI for Specialty Steel** was approved in **2021** — option **(3)**.
**2017** is the year of the **National Steel Policy**, not the PLI.
xa: **Green hydrogen**: Ministry of Steel has **₹455 crore** for pilots till **2029-30** (National Green Hydrogen Mission).
NSP 2017 targets **300 MT** capacity by **2030-31**.
Iron and steel is coming under the **Carbon Credit Trading Scheme** — **255 plants** from FY 2026-27.

87.s:
The National Steel Policy, 2017 envisages by 2030–31:

1. Steel capacity of 300 MT.
2. Crude steel production of 255 MT.
3. Iron ore requirement of 437 MT.
4. Coking coal requirement of 161 MT.

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
87.x: The policy targets 300 MT capacity and 255 MT crude steel production by 2030–31, requiring 437 MT iron ore and 161 MT coking coal.
87.tq: Check all four policy targets and input requirements together.
xs: All four are correct — **1, 2, 3 and 4**, option **(4)**.
**NSP 2017** targets by **2030-31**: **300 MT capacity** and **255 MT** crude steel production.
Inputs needed: **437 MT iron ore** and **161 MT coking coal**.
xa: ⚠ **300 MT** is capacity; **255 MT** is production.
Iron ore output (2024-25): **289.398 MT** — adequate.
Coking coal imports (2024-25): **57.07 MT**, as domestic coal is **high-ash**.

87.s: Under the National Green Hydrogen Mission, the Ministry of Steel has an allocation for green-hydrogen pilot projects in steel of:
87.x: The Ministry of Steel has Rs 455 crore for green-hydrogen pilots in steel till 2029-30. Rs 25,938 crore is the PLI-Auto outlay (B); Rs 33,660 crore is BHAVYA (C); Rs 3,000 crore is NICDIT in BE 2026-27 (D).
87.tq: Green H2 in steel: Rs 455 crore to 2029-30.
xs: The Ministry of Steel has **₹455 crore** for green-hydrogen pilots in steel **till 2029-30** — option **(1)**.
This falls under the **National Green Hydrogen Mission**.
xa: The **PLI for Specialty Steel** was approved in **2021**.
Indian steel emits **2.54 tCO2/t** vs **1.9** world average — **10-12%** of national CO2.
**EU CBAM** exposure is a key criticism of Indian steel.

87.s: The power-oriented location of aluminium smelters is primarily explained by the fact that they are generally established near:
o: hydroelectric or captive thermal power sources
87.x: Because aluminium smelting consumes 14,000–15,000 kWh per tonne, smelters are located near hydel or captive thermal power sources rather than being governed solely by proximity to mines.
87.tq: Apply the raw-material-versus-power distinction to an industrial-location scenario.
xs: Aluminium smelters are placed near **hydel or captive thermal power** — option **(4)**.

89.s: In the Visakhapatnam–Chennai Industrial Corridor (VCIC), the southern and northern portions are associated respectively with:

89.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes footloose industries from resource- or location-bound industries?
o: IT alone is port-bound, while shipbuilding is completely footloose.

89.x: IT and electronics are relatively footloose industries. Steel is raw-material-bound and shipbuilding is generally port-bound.
89.tq: Separate industries with flexible location requirements from those tied to raw materials or ports.
xs: **IT and electronics** are **footloose**, whereas **steel and shipbuilding** are **raw-material- or port-bound** — option **(2)**.
IT is located by **engineering talent** and a tech ecosystem, not raw materials.
xa: IT clusters: **Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune, Chennai, Noida/NCR**.
Electronics PLI: **4-6%** on incremental sales.

90.s: Which one of the following is an agro-based industry?

xa: Other agro-based: **sugar, jute, food processing, dairy** (Amul, Anand).

90.s: Why do agro-based industrial units generally locate near the source of raw materials?
o: Agricultural raw materials are usually heavier after processing

Agricultural raw materials are always imported
Agro-based industries require no transport facilities

xs: Agro-based units locate near raw material because the materials **lose weight or perish** — option **(2)**.

xa: Agro-based examples: **cotton textiles, sugar, jute, food processing, dairy**.

90.s:

xs: Ascending order **B, D, A, C** — option **(1)**.

90.s: The Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises was formed in 2007 by merging which two ministries?

90.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes heavy industries from light industries?

Heavy industries are confined to services, whereas light industries are confined to mining

xa: Heavy: **iron and steel**, heavy engineering (**HEC Ranchi**), **shipbuilding**.

91.s:
Match the proposed BHAVYA initiative with its location.

List-I
 a. Drone City
 b. Tekulodu Aerospace and Defence Park
 c. Makavaripalem Organic Food Park
 d. Veldurthi Mega Textile Park

List-II
 i. Anakapalli
 ii. Sri Sathya Sai district
 iii. Palnadu

Petrochemicals belong to the **Kakinada-Vizag PCPIR**; cement to the **Kadapa-Kurnool belt**.
xa: ⚠ **AMTZ** = Visakhapatnam; **Drone City** = Kurnool; **Space City** = Tirupati.
Vizag node: **bulk drugs, steel**; **Parawada Pharma City**.
Vizag hosted the **CII Partnership Summit** (**14-15 Nov 2025**).

91.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched with the VCIC node concerned?
o: Kopparthy — leather and automobile manufacturing only
Naidupeta — information technology and steel only

91.s: KRIS City, associated with the Krishnapatnam Industrial Area, is located in which district of Andhra Pradesh?

**₹125-500 cr** is **Sub-Large**; **₹501-1,000 cr** is **Large**; **above ₹5,000 cr** is **Ultra Mega**.
xa: Capital subsidy: **12%** of FCI (Sub-Large/Large); up to **15%** Mega/Ultra Mega.
**+5%** for women/SC/ST/BC.

91.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the capital subsidy under the stated industrial policy is correct?
o: It is uniformly 5% of FCI for all categories without any additional provision.
It is 25% of FCI for all large industries and 45% for all mega industries.

xa: Net SGST reimbursement: **100% for 5 years**.
Employment Creation Subsidy: up to **10% of FCI**; decarbonisation subsidy up to **6% of FCI**.
Categories: Sub-Large **₹125-500 cr**; Ultra Mega **>₹5,000 cr**.

xs: **Employment Creation Subsidy — up to 10% of FCI** is correct — option **(1)**.
Power cost is **₹1/unit for 2 years**, not ₹10 for five.
Decarbonisation subsidy is up to **6%** of FCI; stamp duty is **100%**, not 50%.
xa: Capital subsidy: **12%** (Sub-Large/Large), up to **15%** (Mega/Ultra Mega).

91.s: Which of the following is NOT a stated target of the AP Industrial Development Policy 4.0?

xs: MSME Policy 4.0 capital subsidy is **25%** general and **45%** special categories — option **(3)** is correct.
**12%** and **15%** are the large/mega rates under the **Industrial Development Policy 4.0**.
xa: Caps: **₹25 lakh / ₹1.5 cr / ₹7 cr**.
Goal: **"One Family, One Entrepreneur" by 2030**.
AP Cluster Development Programme: **G.O. 17**, **45 MSME clusters/CFCs**, up to **80%** aid.

91.s: Which of the following is identified as a criticism or constraint affecting Andhra Pradesh's industrial development?

Complete absence of industrial investment along the coast

92.s: In the present system of National Highway numbering, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: Odd-numbered highways generally run east-west and increase from north to south.
Even-numbered highways generally run north-south and increase from west to east.
National Highways are numbered exclusively according to their length.
Odd-numbered highways generally run north-south and increase from west to east.
92.x: Odd-numbered National Highways generally run north-south and their numbers increase from west to east. Even-numbered highways generally run east-west and increase from north to south.
92.tq: Use the directional numbering rule and reject the reversed comparison.
xs: **Odd-numbered NHs run north-south and rise from west to east** — option **(4)** is correct.
**Even-numbered** NHs run **east-west** and rise from **north to south**, so options 1 and 2 swap the rules.
Numbering follows **direction**, not length.
xa: Longest NH: **NH-44** (Srinagar-Kanyakumari, **4,112 km**); shortest: **NH-966B** (**8 km**).
**NH-27** (Porbandar-Silchar) is an east-west road; **NH-16** runs Kolkata-Chennai along the east coast.
NHs = **1.46 lakh km**, ~**2%** of road length but ~**40%** of traffic.

xs: **NH-19** links **Delhi - Kolkata** (old **NH-2**) — option **(1)** is correct.
**NH-27** is Porbandar-Silchar; **NH-16** is Kolkata-Chennai; **NH-48** is Delhi-Mumbai-Chennai.
xa: NH-19 and NH-48 are **GQ arms**.
NHAI HAM corridors around **Varanasi** link **NH-19** and **NH-31** (16 Jul 2026).
GQ joins **Delhi-Mumbai-Chennai-Kolkata** (~**5,846 km**).

92.s: Which National Highway runs from Kolkata to Chennai along the eastern coast and crosses coastal Andhra Pradesh?
